parts.title: How memory and learning work
parts.summary: Working memory, cognitive load, desirable difficulties, forgetting, adult learning, deliberate practice.

topics.title: Design for a very small working memory
topics.theory: Memory architecture: three stores, about four chunks

situation.text: You have a lot to cover and a room of people who are new to it. The easy move is to put everything on the slides and keep going.

items: Choose the few ideas people must leave with. Three or four, not ten.
Introduce them one at a time. Let people use each one before you add the next.
Group related details under one idea, so they travel together.
Move anything people can look up later off the slide and into a handout.

why.text: Working memory is where people hold new information while they think about it. It is small: about three to five things at once.

Past that limit people start dropping items, and what is dropped is unlikely to be learned. Once ideas are grouped and practised they move into long-term memory, which frees the space again. Experts seem to hold more because their chunks are bigger.

The limit of about four chunks is on what a person can hold in mind at one moment. "About four new ideas at a time" is a design rule of thumb drawn from that limit. No study sets the number of ideas a session can carry.

why.caption: New information has to pass through a small working memory before it can settle in long-term memory.

why.title: The magical number 4 in short-term memory
why.found: Reviewed a wide range of studies and concluded that the real limit is three to five chunks. The famous "seven" was a rough estimate.
why.means: Plan for about four new ideas at a time, not seven.

items.title: About four
items.text: The number of new ideas a person can hold at once.

items.title: Chunks, not items
items.text: A group of related details counts as one thing.

items.title: Practice frees space
items.text: An idea that has settled in long-term memory stops taking up room.

try.text: Take a dense block of your own content. Regroup it so a newcomer meets no more than four new ideas at a time. Write down what you grouped and why.

try.title: A one-hour induction
try.text: Before: nine policies on nine slides. After: three groups (how you get paid, how you stay safe, who to ask), one short activity for each, and the detail in a handout.

items: Adding slides does not help if each slide still carries six ideas.
"Seven, plus or minus two" is the older figure. Later work puts the limit nearer four.
What counts as "new" depends on the person. A room of experts can take far more.

quiz.q: Roughly how many new ideas can a person hold at once?
quiz.a: About four.

quiz.q: Why do experts seem to hold more?
quiz.a: Their chunks are bigger. A group of related details counts as one thing.

quiz.q: What should move off the slide?
quiz.a: Anything people can look up later. Put it in a handout.

topics.title: Cut the load that teaches nothing
topics.theory: Cognitive load, worked examples, expertise reversal

situation.text: Your material is accurate and complete, and people still look lost. Often the content is not the problem. The way it is presented is using up the thinking space people need.

items: Cut anything that makes people work without teaching them: decoration, repetition, hunting for the right place on the page.
For newcomers, show a fully worked example before you ask them to solve one.
Put words next to the picture they describe, not on a separate slide or page.
Do not narrate full sentences that are also written on the screen, above all beside a diagram. A few key words on screen while you talk are fine.
As people improve, take the support away. Help that suits a beginner slows an expert down.

why.text: Mental effort during learning comes from two places. Some is the real difficulty of the subject. Some is wasted on poor design. Only the second kind is worth cutting.

Three effects come up constantly. Beginners learn more from studying worked solutions than from solving problems unaided. Splitting related information across places forces people to hold one part while they find the other. Reading out full sentences that are also on the screen, beside a picture, is thought to overload people. And all of this reverses with expertise: support that helps a novice gets in the way of someone who already knows.

The read-aloud rule has limits. A meta-analysis of 57 studies found that narration with matching on-screen text did better than narration alone. The gain showed up for people with little prior knowledge, when the material set the pace, when there were no pictures, and when the screen showed key terms and not the full script. So the thing to avoid is a narrator reading whole sentences off a slide that also carries a diagram.

Whether to show an example first or set a problem first is an open question, and this site recommends each in different places (1.2, 2.13 and 2.19). Example first has the stronger case for people who are new to a subject and learning a procedure, where an unaided attempt would swamp working memory. Problem first is supported by a pooled analysis of 53 studies (Sinha and Kapur, 2021). It did better when learners could bring what they already knew to the problem and a full explanation followed. Those studies were of school and university students learning concepts in maths and science. Younger primary pupils did better when taught first, and so did learners of general skills not tied to a subject. A rule of thumb, and no more than that: go example first when people are new and the goal is to carry out a procedure correctly. Go problem first when they have some background, the goal is understanding, and you have time to teach it properly straight after.

items.title: Cut the waste first
items.text: Remove effort that comes from the design, not the subject.

items.title: Examples before problems
items.text: Newcomers learn more from a worked solution.

items.title: Fade the help
items.text: What helps a beginner holds an expert back.

try.text: Find one resource you know is hard to follow. List what makes people work without teaching them. Redesign it, and label each fix with the effect it addresses.

try.title: A software guide
try.text: Before: a screenshot on one page, six steps on the next, and the trainer reading the steps aloud. After: each step is labelled on the screenshot, one worked run-through comes first, and the trainer talks while the slide stays quiet.

items: Do not strip out the difficulty that belongs to the subject. That effort is the learning.
The different kinds of load are hard to measure separately. Use the idea as a design guide, not as a measuring tool.
In a mixed room, one level of support will be wrong for someone. Give the experienced people the harder version.

quiz.q: Which kind of mental effort is worth cutting?
quiz.a: The effort caused by the design: decoration, repetition, hunting for the right place. Not the difficulty that belongs to the subject.

quiz.q: What helps a beginner more than solving problems unaided?
quiz.a: Studying a fully worked example first.

quiz.q: What happens to that support as people become expert?
quiz.a: It starts to get in the way. Take it away as they improve.

checkFindings: All three references were already checked and are kept. Tier A confirmed without a new search.

Kirschner, Sweller and Clark (2006), opened for topic 1.8, also says the advantage of guidance fades only once learners have enough prior knowledge. That agrees with the last step and the third watch item.
Left as it is: the paragraph that starts 'Three effects' lists three effects and then the reversal with expertise, which reads correctly.

topics.title: Make practice harder in the ways that help
topics.theory: Desirable difficulties: spacing, retrieval, interleaving, generation

situation.text: The session went smoothly and everyone said it was clear. Two weeks later very little is left. Smooth is often the problem.

items: Spread practice over time. Come back to the key ideas after a gap, not only on the day.
Ask people to recall before you remind them. A short quiz with no notes beats a recap.
Once the basics are in, mix related problem types so people must work out which approach fits.
Ask for an answer before you give one, even if the answer is wrong.
Tell people why the harder practice is there. Otherwise they will resist it.

why.text: Conditions that feel harder in the moment often make learning last longer. Pulling something out of memory with effort strengthens it more than seeing it again.

Four techniques follow from this: spacing, retrieval practice, interleaving and generation. There is no single correct gap for spacing. In one large study the best gap was about 20 to 40 per cent of the time until the test when the test was a week away, and about 5 to 10 per cent when it was a year away. The best gap still grew in days as the test moved further off. Longer goals need longer gaps.

why.title: Test-enhanced learning
why.found: Students either re-read a passage or tested themselves on it. After five minutes the re-readers remembered more. After two days and after a week the self-testers did, even though the re-readers had been more confident.
why.means: Swap the recap for a recall exercise, and expect it to feel worse on the day.

items.title: Space it
items.text: Practice spread over days beats one long session.

items.title: Recall it
items.text: Retrieving an idea strengthens it more than re-reading it.

items.title: Mix it
items.text: Mixed practice teaches people to tell situations apart.

try.text: Take a lesson you already teach. Mark where each of the four techniques could go, then rewrite its practice schedule.

try.title: A weekly team session
try.text: Before: a recap slide closes each session. After: each session opens with three questions on last week, answered from memory in pairs, and the practice cases mix this week's type with earlier ones.

items: Difficulty only helps people who know enough to get through it. Newcomers may need some straightforward, blocked practice first.
Interleaving helps most when the things being mixed are related and easy to confuse. The pooled studies advise caution with word lists and explanatory texts.
Learners usually rate the easier method as more effective. Their sense of it is unreliable.
The four are not equally well supported. A major review of study techniques gave its top rating to practice testing and spaced practice, and a middle rating to interleaving.

quiz.q: Name the four difficulties that help.
quiz.a: Spacing, retrieval practice, interleaving and generation.

quiz.q: In the passage study, who remembered more after a week?
quiz.a: The students who tested themselves, although the re-readers had felt more confident.

quiz.q: When might harder practice not help?
quiz.a: When people do not yet know enough to get through it. Newcomers may need straightforward practice first.

The Dunlosky rating for generation is not in its abstract, so nothing is said about it.
checkFindings: Confirmed the suspected error. The Cepeda (2008) abstract on PubMed says the best gap was about 20 to 40 per cent of a one-week test delay and about 5 to 10 per cent of a one-year delay, in a study of more than 1,350 people. The page said 'about a fifth' for a test 'a few weeks away'. Corrected.

Generation now has a checked source: Bertsch and colleagues (2007) pooled 86 studies and found that people remembered material they produced themselves better than material they only read (d = .40 in the abstract). The number is not on the page.

Added Dunlosky and colleagues (2013). Its abstract rates practice testing and distributed practice as high utility and interleaved practice as moderate. Added one watch item so the page does not present the four as equal.
Both new links point to the page that was actually opened: the Bertsch abstract on a co-author's own publications site, and the Dunlosky abstract on a co-author's university publications record.
Tier A kept.
topics.tierReason: Spacing and retrieval practice are supported by several meta-analyses and got the top rating in a major review of study techniques. Interleaving and generation are supported by one meta-analysis each, with conditions.

topics.title: Do not trust how fluent the room looks

situation.text: You need to judge whether a session worked. The room was engaged, answers came quickly and the feedback forms are warm.

items: Do not judge a method by how fluent people look during the session.
Check again after a delay, when the easy familiarity has worn off.
Compare methods on what people can do later, not on how the session felt.
Teach learners to distrust the feeling of "I know this" that comes from re-reading.

why.text: How well people perform during a session is a poor guide to what they have learned. Methods that raise performance on the day often produce the weakest retention, and the reverse.

Memory fades without reinforcement, which is the original reason for coming back to material later. And people misjudge their own learning: easy study feels productive, effortful practice feels worse, and the truth is usually the other way round.

items.title: Performance is not learning
items.text: Fluency on the day says little about next month.

items.title: Test after a delay
items.text: The delayed check is the honest one.

items.title: Feelings mislead
items.text: Easy study feels better and works worse.

try.text: Pick a course you know. Find one place where looking fluent has been taken as having learned. Design a delayed check that would show the truth.

try.title: A customer call course
try.text: Before: the course is judged on the end-of-day form and a role-play straight after the demonstration. After: the same role-play is run cold three weeks later, and that result decides what gets redesigned.

items: The forgetting curve is an illustration, not a precise law. Do not quote exact percentages from it.
A delayed check that shows a drop is useful information, not a failure of the session.
Do not swing to making everything hard. See the topic on difficulties that help.

quiz.q: Why is a fluent session a poor sign of learning?
quiz.a: Performance on the day says little about what people can do later. The two often move in opposite directions.

quiz.q: What is the honest check?
quiz.a: One made after a delay.

quiz.q: Which kind of study feels better and works worse?
quiz.a: Easy study, such as re-reading.

openPoints: Ebbinghaus (1885) itself was not opened.
checkFindings: Kept the two checked references. Tier A confirmed without a new search.

Replaced the unopened Ebbinghaus (1885) entry with a modern source that was opened: Murre and Dros (2015), PLOS ONE. One person relearned lists over about 70 hours at gaps from 20 minutes to 31 days, and the results closely matched the original curve. The curve was not perfectly smooth. This supports the watch item that the curve is an illustration and that exact percentages should not be quoted.
topics.tierReason: The gap between performance during training and lasting learning is documented across many experiments in the checked integrative review.

topics.title: Tell adults why, and start from their problems
topics.theory: Adult learning, used as a rule of thumb

situation.text: You are planning for experienced adults who did not choose to be there and want to know what is in it for them.

items: Say why the session matters to their work, in the first few minutes.
Start from a problem they recognise, not from the subject.
Ask what they already do, and build on it.
Give real choices where you can: which case, which order, which example.

why.text: The classic account of adult learning says adults are more self-directed, bring experience, care about problems more than subjects and need to know why. These are useful starting points for design.

They are rules of thumb, not laws. They describe adult learners more than they explain how learning works. Knowles himself came to treat the adult and child approaches as two ends of one line, each suited to some situations.

items.title: Why first
items.text: Adults want the reason before the content.

items.title: Problems, not subjects
items.text: Organise around what people need to solve.

items.title: A rule of thumb
items.text: Useful for design. Not settled science.

try.text: Rewrite the opening of one module for a specific audience. State the why, and tie it to a problem that audience really has.

try.title: A mandatory records session
try.text: Before: "Today we cover the records policy, sections one to six." After: "Last month two of you lost an afternoon looking for a signed form. In the next hour we fix that. Pick the case you want to start with."

items: Experience cuts both ways. People bring knowledge to build on, and misconceptions to manage.
Do not present these principles as proven. Say they are a working guide.
Choice needs structure. Too much freedom leaves newcomers lost.

quiz.q: What do adults want before the content?
quiz.a: The reason it matters to their work.

quiz.q: How should you organise the material?
quiz.a: Around problems people recognise, not around the subject.

quiz.q: How firmly should you state these principles?
quiz.a: As a rule of thumb. They describe adult learners. They are not laws of learning.

openPoints: Merriam (2001), Andragogy and self-directed learning, New Directions for Adult and Continuing Education: found by the search but the page would not open.
No source was found that reports direct tests of the andragogy assumptions, so the page no longer says 'the evidence is mixed'.
Confirm on the Routledge page whether Robinson is a named author of the 9th edition.
checkFindings: Tier D confirmed.

Knowles: the current edition confirmed as the 9th, 2020, Routledge, 392 pages. The publisher's description covers andragogy and self-directed, experiential and problem-centred learning, which is what the page uses it for. The Routledge page did not come up in the search, so the description was read on a bookseller's listing and that is the page linked. Swap in the Routledge page when someone can open it.

The bookseller page was unclear about whether Petra Robinson is a named author of the 9th or the 10th edition, so the label says 'Knowles and colleagues'. The outline's 'Knowles (1984)' date is replaced by the current edition.

Merriam (2001) would not open. Used a later open article by the same author, Merriam (2017), PAACE Journal of Lifelong Learning 26, 21 to 37. It supports the caution on this page: no single theory explains adult learning, the six assumptions say more about adult learners than about learning, Knowles came to see pedagogy and andragogy as a continuum, and critics object to its focus on the individual.
Rewrote the 'evidence is mixed' sentence and the matching quiz answer to say only what that source supports.
topics.tierReason: Andragogy is a set of assumptions about adult learners that is widely used in practice. The sources opened describe it and its critics and do not report direct tests of it.

topics.title: Build practice at the edge of ability

situation.text: People have done the job for years and have stopped improving. You are asked to make them better at something they already do.

items: Name one specific weakness to work on, not the whole skill.
Set the task just beyond what the person can do comfortably.
Give feedback straight away, on that weakness.
Repeat, adjust, and repeat again.
Never promise mastery from hours alone.

why.text: Experience by itself does not build expertise. Improvement comes from practice that is effortful, aimed at a weakness, pitched at the edge of ability and followed by feedback.

The "10,000 hours" figure is a popularisation. The research behind it was about a particular kind of effortful practice kept up for years, not a count of hours. A later pooling of studies found that deliberate practice explained about a quarter of the difference in performance in games, about a fifth in music and sport, and under one per cent in professions.

How much deliberate practice explains is disputed. Ericsson and Harwell (2019) argued that the pooled analysis counted many kinds of structured practice that do not meet the original definition. When they kept only the studies that did, practice time explained 29 to 61 per cent of the difference in performance after correcting for measurement error. So do not read the figure for professions as proof that practice hardly counts at work. It may say more about how loosely practice was measured in those studies.
Feedback straight away suits a skill that is still being learned. For when a delay can help, see 2.27.

items.title: Aim at a weakness
items.text: General repetition keeps people where they are.

items.title: Edge of ability
items.text: Hard enough that errors happen and teach.

items.title: Hours are not enough
items.text: Twenty years can be one year repeated.

try.text: Choose a skill you are developing. Design one drill for it. Write down the weakness it targets, the level of challenge and where the feedback comes from.

try.title: An experienced presenter
try.text: Before: she runs the whole talk again and is told it was fine. After: she practises only the first ninety seconds, five times, with one note on pace after each run.

items: Comfortable repetition feels like practice and is not.
Practice at the edge is tiring. Keep it short and plan recovery.
Without feedback, people practise their mistakes.

quiz.q: What separates deliberate practice from repetition?
quiz.a: It targets one weakness, sits at the edge of ability and comes with feedback.

quiz.q: What is wrong with "10,000 hours"?
quiz.a: Hours alone do not produce expertise, and practice explains only part of the difference between performers.

quiz.q: What happens without feedback?
quiz.a: People practise their mistakes.

openPoints: Ericsson's objection to '10,000 hours': candidates not opened are Ericsson and Harwell (2019), Frontiers in Psychology, and Ericsson and Pool (2016), Peak. Gladwell (2008) was not searched.
The Macnamara (2014) percentages on the page were not re-opened in this pass. PubMed returned empty pages today.
checkFindings: Kept the two checked references. Tier B confirmed without a new search.

One search was spent on Ericsson's objection to the 10,000 hours rule. It returned news articles and a 2019 Frontiers review by Ericsson and Harwell that would not open. The sentence saying he objected is removed and replaced with a statement the 1993 summary supports.
topics.tierReason: Deliberate practice is well described, but the pooled studies show it explains a modest and very uneven share of performance, and almost none in the professions.

topics.title: Start from what people already know

situation.text: You teach a correct idea clearly. People nod, and go on using the wrong one they arrived with.

items: Find out what people already believe before you teach.
Build on what is right.
Name a common wrong idea and show where it fails.
Give the correct idea, then have people use it.
Check again later. Old ideas come back.

why.text: New learning is built on what people already know. What they know helps when it is accurate and gets in the way when it is not.

A wrong idea that is not addressed tends to survive the lesson. Telling people the right answer is often not enough. It works better to name the wrong idea, say plainly that it is wrong and explain why.

How much existing knowledge helps varies a great deal. One pooling of many studies found that people who knew more beforehand still knew more afterwards, but on average they did not gain more from the teaching. Do not assume the experienced people in the room will learn fastest.

why.title: Refutation text facilitates learning
why.found: Pooled 44 comparisons with 3,869 learners. Texts that named a common wrong idea and refuted it led to more learning than other texts on the same subject, a moderate effect (g = 0.41) that held across many settings.
why.means: Name the wrong idea, say it is wrong and explain why, instead of only presenting the right one.

try.text: Before your next session, write three wrong ideas people are likely to bring. Plan how you will surface and test each.

try.title: A feedback skills session
try.text: Before: the trainer explains the model and people nod. After: people first write how they would give a hard message, try it on a partner, see where it lands badly, then meet the model and redo it.

items: Do not humiliate people for a wrong idea. Most were taught it.
Do not be afraid to name the wrong idea. The worry that repeating it makes it stronger has not held up well in later studies. Label it clearly as wrong and put the correct idea next to it.
Experienced groups bring wrong ideas too. Check theirs as well.

quiz.q: What is new learning built on?
quiz.a: What people already know.

quiz.q: What happens to a wrong idea that is not addressed?
quiz.a: It tends to survive the lesson.

quiz.q: What works better than telling people the right answer?
quiz.a: Showing the old idea fail, then offering the better one.

openPoints: The quiz answer 'Showing the old idea fail, then offering the better one' and the remember card 'Show it failing' still use the old wording. They are close to the source but not exact. Consider 'Name it, refute it'.
Ambrose and colleagues, How Learning Works, and Ausubel (1968): not searched.
Lewandowsky and colleagues, The Debunking Handbook 2020: the handbook's own page or DOI was not opened.
The link for Simonsmeier is the authors' own copy on the University of Trier site, which shows the abstract. The journal page was not opened.
checkFindings: Confirmed the suspected error. Swire-Thompson, DeGutis and Lazer (2020) conclude that backfire effects are not a reliable finding and that recent studies often fail to find them. The watch item 'Repeating a myth can strengthen it' is rewritten.

The Debunking Handbook 2020 itself did not open. Its authors' own web page did, and it says recent research has not found a familiarity backfire effect under conditions where it was expected. That page is a blog post, so it is not in the reference list. The advice to state the fact first therefore has no checked source and is no longer on the page.

Simonsmeier and colleagues (2022): 8,776 effect sizes. Prior knowledge strongly predicted knowledge after teaching (r = .534) but on average hardly predicted how much people gained (r = -.059), with a very wide spread. Added a short paragraph. The first why paragraph is left as it is.

Schroeder and Kucera (2022) supports the third and fourth steps. Added as the study block. Reworded 'They need to see the old idea fail' to match what was tested, which was text that names and refutes a wrong idea.
'Experienced groups hold stronger wrong ideas' had no source. Softened.
Removed the two unopened outline references (Ambrose and colleagues, Ausubel). Updated the note above the reference list.

topics.title: Know the main theories of learning and what each is good for
topics.theory: A map of learning theories: behaviourist, cognitive, constructivist, social, experiential

situation.text: A client asks which learning theory your course is "based on". You are not sure what the choices are.

items: Learn the five families in one line each.
For a skill that needs fluency, borrow from behaviourism: practice, feedback, reinforcement.
For understanding, borrow from cognitive theory: memory, load, recall.
For judgement, borrow from constructivism: problems and discussion.
For norms and craft, borrow from social and experiential theory: watching, doing, reflecting.

why.text: Behaviourism looks at what people do and what follows. Cognitive theory looks at memory and thinking. Constructivism says people build understanding from experience. Social theory says people learn by watching and working with others. Experiential theory says people learn by doing and reflecting.
Each explains some kinds of learning well and others badly. A working trainer uses them as tools for different jobs.

One well-known comparison written for course designers matches the theory to the learner as well as the task. It suggests behaviourist methods for facts and set procedures, cognitive methods for applying rules to new problems, and constructivist methods for experienced people facing messy problems.

items.title: Tools for jobs
items.text: Match the theory to the kind of learning.

try.text: Take one course you know. Find one activity that fits each family. Note which family is missing.

try.title: A client question
try.text: A client asks what the course is based on. You answer by activity: drills with feedback for the till routine, recall quizzes for product facts, case discussion for complaints, and shadowing for the tone of the shop floor.

items: Theory names are used to sell products. Ask what the method is.
Constructivist does not mean unguided. Newcomers need guidance.
This is a map. Each family has a large literature.
Kolb's learning cycle is widely used and loosely defined. A review of the research found it unclear what counts as a concrete experience.

parts.title: Spot the myths
parts.summary: Why brain myths spread, the big ones debunked, and how to test a claim.

topics.title: Know why smart people believe brain myths

situation.text: A supplier, a colleague or your own old slides make a confident claim about "how the brain learns". It sounds scientific and you are tempted to repeat it.

items: Treat any "brain-based" claim as unproven until you have seen the source.
Trace the claim back to the finding it came from. Check what that finding really showed.
Ask who gains if you believe it.
Apply the same test to your own materials and branding.

why.text: A neuromyth is a real finding about the brain or learning that has been stretched or distorted. They spread because they are plausible and often flattering.

Two findings explain why careful people fall for them. In one experiment, adding irrelevant brain language made weak explanations more satisfying to people without neuroscience training. Experts were not taken in. In a survey of 242 teachers in the UK and the Netherlands, all of them interested in the neuroscience of learning, teachers believed about half of the myths they were shown. Those who knew more about the brain believed more of them. Interest is not protection.

items.title: A distortion, not a lie
items.text: Most myths start from something true.

items.title: Brain words persuade
items.text: Neuroscience language makes weak claims sound strong.

items.title: Interest is not immunity
items.text: Knowing more about the brain did not protect teachers.

try.text: Take one real marketing claim for "brain-based" training. Trace it back to the finding it distorts, and write one sentence on what the finding actually supports.

try.title: A slide in a sales deck
try.text: A slide says the method "rewires neural pathways for faster learning". You ask for the study. It is a small memory experiment with students that never tested the product. You leave the slide out.

items: A trainer is a trusted source. When you repeat a myth, it spreads with your authority behind it.
Do not overcorrect into dismissing all neuroscience. The findings are real. The stretching is the problem.

topics.title: Drop learning styles and the other big myths

situation.text: A client asks for training that suits "visual, auditory and kinaesthetic learners", or a questionnaire to sort people by style.

items: Stop sorting people by learning style. Remove the questionnaires.
Choose the medium that suits the content: show a process, describe a principle, practise a skill.
Use more than one medium when it helps understanding, for everyone.
When someone raises a myth, name what is true in it before you correct it.

why.text: People do have preferences. What the evidence does not support is sorting people by style and teaching each group differently.

The same goes for other popular ideas. People are not left-brained or right-brained learners. Brain scans of more than a thousand people showed that each side has its own specialised networks, and gave no sign that a person favours one side overall. Learning styles persist because the idea is intuitive, flattering and gives people a tidy label.

The picture is not a clean zero. A 2024 pooling of 21 studies found a small average benefit when teaching matched a person's style. Only about a quarter of the measures showed the pattern the idea needs, and the studies were weak. The authors judged the benefit too small and too rare to be worth the time and cost.

why.title: A meta-analysis of the learning styles matching hypothesis
why.found: Pooled 21 studies with 1,712 learners. Matched teaching gave a small average benefit (g = 0.31), but only 26 per cent of the outcome measures showed matching helping more than one style, and study quality was low.
why.means: Do not spend time sorting people by style. Choose the medium that fits the content.

items.title: Preference is not benefit
items.text: Liking a style does not mean learning better from it.

items.title: Match the content
items.text: Pick the medium for the subject, not for the person.

items.title: Several media, for all
items.text: Mixing media is sound. Matching to styles is not.

try.text: Audit one course or brochure for myths. Rewrite the parts that rest on them.

try.title: A course brief
try.text: Before: a questionnaire sorts the group into visual, auditory and kinaesthetic, with a handout for each. After: no questionnaire. Everyone watches the process demonstrated, reads the principle, then practises the skill.

items: Do not shame people for believing it. Most were taught it by a trainer.
Related claims need the same care: "digital natives", fixed attention spans, and big effects from hydration or sugar.
Using several media is good practice. Say so, or people hear "pictures do not matter".

topics.title: Test any learning claim before you repeat it
topics.theory: Evaluating a claim: evidence levels, effect sizes, red flags

situation.text: A report, a vendor or a conference talk claims a method "improves learning by 40%". You have to decide whether to act on it.

items: Find out what kind of evidence it is: a story, one study, several studies, or a pooled analysis of many.
Ask "compared to what?". An effect means little without the comparison.
Look at the size of the effect, not only whether it was "significant".
Check who paid for the research and who gains from the claim.
Write down what would have to be true for the claim to hold.
Ask whether people were put into the groups at random. If they were not, something else about the groups may explain the difference.
For a pooled analysis, ask how good the pooled studies were. Many weak studies added together are still weak.

why.text: Evidence comes in strengths. A single story is the weakest. One study is better. Findings repeated by others are better still, and a careful pooling of many studies is the strongest common form, as long as the studies in it are sound. Design counts as well as number. An experiment that assigns people to groups at random can show cause, and a correlation cannot. Topic 1.10 shows the catch with pooling: the pooled effect for learning styles is positive, and it rests on weak studies.

A result can be statistically significant and still too small to matter in practice. The usual warning signs are brain language with no reference, the phrase "brain-based", a claim that flatters the buyer, no comparison group, and a commercial interest that is not declared.

The funding point has been measured in medicine. A Cochrane review found that drug and device studies paid for by the maker reported favourable results and conclusions more often than studies with other funding.

items.title: Compared to what?
items.text: The most useful question about any claim.

items.title: Size matters
items.text: Significant is not the same as important.

items.title: Follow the interest
items.text: Ask who gains if you believe it.

try.text: Take three competing claims about learning. Rank them by strength of evidence. For each, write one sentence on what would make it trustworthy.

try.title: A vendor brochure
try.text: A brochure says a platform "improves learning by 40%". You ask three things: compared to what, measured how, and who ran the study. The answer is a vendor survey of user confidence with no comparison group. You treat it as a story.

items: This is a way of judging, not a guarantee. Strong evidence in schools may not carry over to your workplace.
Apply it to your own favourite methods as well.
Lack of evidence is not evidence against. Some useful practices are simply unstudied.

Do not judge size by the old small, medium and large labels alone. Most real-world education programmes produce effects that count as small on that scale. Ask about cost and how widely the method can be used as well.

parts.title: The body matters
parts.summary: Sleep, stress and energy across a training day.

topics.title: Protect sleep on multi-day programmes

situation.text: You are planning a residential, a bootcamp or a run of full days. The temptation is to fill every hour, including the evenings.

items: Protect the nights. End early enough for a full night of sleep.
Do not run fourteen-hour days. Tired people take in less, and short nights put the day's learning at risk.
Start each morning by recalling yesterday before adding anything new.
Build in real breaks, and a quiet period after demanding sessions.

why.text: Sleep helps new memories settle. A major review describes them being strengthened and reorganised overnight. That may be one reason practice spread over days works better than one long sitting: sleep falls between the sessions.

Too little sleep hurts at both ends. Pooled studies found that a lost night before learning weakened taking in new material, and a lost night after learning weakened keeping it. The second effect was the smaller one. The authors warn that both are probably overstated, because studies that found nothing were less likely to be published.

why.title: Sleep deprivation and memory
why.found: Two pooled analyses of about fifty years of experiments. Losing a night of sleep before learning harmed memory, and losing a night after learning harmed it less. Both effects shrank once missing unpublished studies were allowed for.
why.means: Protect the nights on a multi-day course, and keep your claims about sleep modest.

items.title: Sleep is part of the course
Long days cost learning
items.text: The extra hours can cost retention.

try.text: Take the timetable of a real multi-day programme. Ignore the content. Mark where sleep is cut short and where there is no gap to settle, then redesign the rhythm.

try.title: A three-day residential
try.text: Before: sessions run until 9pm and a team task is due at breakfast. After: teaching ends at 5.30pm, the evening is social and optional, and day two opens with twenty minutes recalling day one.

items: Keep claims modest. The mechanism is real, and it is easy to inflate.
Popular books on sleep often claim more than the research shows. Lead with the research reviews instead.
Social evenings matter on a residential. Protect sleep without banning them.
The experiments mostly compare a whole lost night with normal sleep. Nobody has tested course timetables directly. Treat the early finish as sensible caution, not a proven gain.

topics.title: Take needless stress out of the room

situation.text: People arrive tense: a restructure is under way, the session is assessed, or senior people are in the room.

items: Remove public failure. Let people try things in pairs before the whole room.
Take out time pressure that serves no purpose.
Reduce status threat: mix groups, and have senior people go second.
Say plainly that mistakes are expected here.
Know your limits. You are not a therapist, and you should know where to refer someone.

why.text: Stress gets in the way of recalling what you know. A pooled analysis of 113 laboratory studies found that stress just before or during recall made memory worse. Stress before or during learning usually did the same. A learner who feels threatened is not only uncomfortable. They are less able to take things in and to show what they know.

Timing matters. In the same analysis, stress that came just after learning tended to help memory for what had been learned. So stress is not always harmful. It does the damage when it arrives while people are taking material in or being asked to recall it.

A review written for teachers adds two points. Stress can make it harder to update what you already know when new information arrives. It may also push people away from flexible thinking and towards rigid habits. Both matter when the aim of the session is to change how people work.

why.title: Acute stress and memory: a meta-analysis
why.found: Across 113 laboratory studies with 6,216 people, stress before or during learning usually made memory worse, and so did stress just before or during recall. Stress just after learning usually helped. The effects at recall were larger for emotional material.
why.means: Keep pressure out of the moments when people take in new material or are asked to recall it.

items.title: Threat blocks learning
items.text: A frightened learner takes in less.

items.title: Timing matters
items.text: Stress during learning or recall tends to hurt. Stress just after learning can help.

try.text: List the stress triggers in one real programme: public failure, time pressure, status threat. Design each one out.

try.title: An assessed workshop
try.text: Before: each person presents alone to the room while the director scores them. After: people rehearse in pairs first, the director joins a group as a participant, and scoring happens on a later day.

items: Describe this in plain terms. Detailed claims about stress hormones are easy to overstate.
Removing threat does not mean removing challenge.
Some people arrive carrying things you cannot see. Give everyone a way to step out.
The research here is laboratory work on short bursts of stress, mostly with students. The steps on this page are sensible practice built on it. They have not been tested in training rooms.

quiz.q: Is all pressure harmful?
quiz.a: No. In laboratory studies, stress just after learning tended to help memory. Stress before or during learning, or at recall, tended to hurt.

topics.title: Plan the day around energy, not the clock

situation.text: You have a full-day agenda. The hardest content sits straight after lunch because that is where it fitted.

items: Draw the energy of the day: where it is high, where it dips.
Put the most demanding work where energy is highest.
Break early. Do not wait until people are flagging.
Use movement and a change of activity to reset attention.
Fill the low points with lighter work: recall, discussion, practice.

why.text: Alertness affects performance. Too little and people drift. Too much and they tighten up. The usual picture is a curve that rises and then falls. It began in 1908 as a narrow finding about the strength of a stimulus and the forming of habits. Later writers restated it in terms of stress, arousal and motivation. Treat it as a rough guide and not a precise law.
Rest, water and movement are real conditions for attention. Their effects are modest. Claims that hydration or sugar transform concentration are overstated.

Short breaks do help energy. A pooling of 22 study samples found that breaks of ten minutes or less left people with more energy and less fatigue. The effects were small. They did not reliably improve performance, and the gain showed only on less demanding tasks. Longer breaks helped performance more, so after heavy thinking plan more than ten minutes.

why.title: Micro-breaks: a meta-analysis
why.found: Across 22 study samples with 2,335 people, breaks of ten minutes or less raised energy and reduced fatigue by a small amount (d about 0.36 and 0.35, compared with no break). The overall effect on performance was not significant. Longer breaks gave a larger performance gain.
why.means: Use short breaks to restore energy, and give a longer break after the most demanding segment.

items.title: Plan energy, not minutes
items.text: For many people the same hour is worth more at 10am than at 2pm.

items.title: Break early
items.text: Do not wait until people are flagging.

items.title: Modest effects
items.text: Rest and movement help. They are not magic.

try.text: Take a full-day agenda and redraw it by energy. Decide where the breaks, the movement and the lighter segments go, and say why.

try.title: A full-day agenda
try.text: Before: the new pricing model sits at 1.30pm, straight after lunch. After: pricing moves to 10am. After lunch people walk to a wall chart and work through practice cases in threes.

items: The curve dates from 1908 and has been stretched well beyond the original work.
Natural attention cycles are a promising idea, not an established rule for session length.
Do not push harder when energy drops. Change the activity.

topics.title: Use movement where it helps the learning
topics.theory: Exercise, movement and acting things out

situation.text: People have sat for three hours. Someone suggests "brain gym" exercises to "activate both hemispheres".

items: Use a short walk or stretch to reset energy between segments.
When the content is an action, have people do it, not only read about it.
Let people stand, move or work at a wall.
Make movement optional and accessible.
Do not claim more for it than a modest lift.

why.text: A pooled analysis of studies on a single bout of exercise found that its effect on thinking is real and generally small. Movement helps a little. It is not a method of teaching.

Acting something out is a different matter. People remember an action phrase better when they perform it than when they only read it, and a large review found this effect is strong. It is less clear that doing beats watching someone else do it.

try.text: Take a three-hour agenda. Add two movement breaks and one point where people physically do the thing being taught.

try.title: A manual handling session
try.text: Before: slides on lifting technique, then a quiz. After: a short stretch break, then everyone performs the lift with an empty box. Anyone who prefers can stay seated and coach a partner.

items: Not everyone can or wants to move. Offer a seated version.
The acting-out studies used simple action phrases. Complex ideas may not benefit the same way.
Long-term claims about exercise and brain growth are promising and easy to overstate.

parts.title: Motivation and safety
parts.summary: Motivation, psychological safety, early wins, peer teaching, and skill versus will.

topics.title: Give people choice, progress and connection

situation.text: The training is mandatory and nobody wants to be there. Someone suggests prizes or a leaderboard.

items: Give meaningful choice: which case, which order, how to show what they have learned.
Set challenges people can meet, and show them their progress.
Build connection: pairs, small groups, shared problems.
Explain the value of the task before you reach for rewards.
Keep rewards for tasks that are dull but necessary.

why.text: One of the better-supported accounts of motivation says people need three things: a sense of choice, a sense of getting better, and a sense of connection to others. Design for those and people engage more willingly.

External rewards can backfire. A pooling of 128 experiments found that tangible rewards reduced people's interest in tasks they already enjoyed, while positive feedback increased it. Motivation also depends on two judgements: whether I expect to succeed, and whether I value the result. You can design for both.

The rewards finding has a boundary. The analysis covered tasks people already found interesting. The harm came from tangible rewards that people expected, whether given for taking part, for finishing or for reaching a standard. Tangible rewards that came as a surprise showed no effect, and positive feedback raised interest. None of this says a reward harms motivation for a task people find dull, which is why the step above keeps rewards for those.

Other researchers read the evidence differently. Cameron and Pierce pooled about 100 experiments and argued that the harm is small and confined to tangible rewards promised in advance and given regardless of how well people do. Deci and colleagues reply that this analysis mixed dull and interesting tasks. Both sides agree that praise and feedback on performance do no harm.

items.title: Choice
items.text: People commit to what they have had a say in.

try.text: Take one mandatory, unpopular topic. Reframe it so people expect to succeed and can see why it matters, without adding rewards.

try.title: Mandatory data protection
try.text: Before: a leaderboard and a voucher for the top score. After: people pick the case closest to their own job, see their progress through it, and work it out in pairs.

items: Your job is rarely to make content fun. It is to help people see its value.
Points and badges are not neutral. On a task people already like, a prize they expect can lower their interest in it. For when game elements help, see 2.22.
What a task costs people, in time and effort, lowers motivation as surely as low value does.

topics.title: Make it safe to be wrong out loud
topics.theory: Psychological safety and the error climate

situation.text: You ask a question and nobody answers. People are not short of ideas. They are working out whether it is safe to be wrong in front of this group.

items: Show your own mistakes early.
Frame activities as learning, not as judgement.
Invite people in by name and by turn, not only the confident few.
Treat a wrong answer as useful, and say why.
Build this before you ask people to take risks, not after.

why.text: Psychological safety is a shared belief that it is safe to take a risk in this group: to ask, to admit a mistake, to offer a half-formed idea. Learning depends on exactly those behaviours.

The idea grew out of a study of eight hospital units. The units with more open leaders recorded more drug errors, not fewer, and the likely reason is that people there felt able to report them. A later study of 51 teams in a manufacturing company found that psychological safety went with more learning behaviour. Safety is not the same as being nice. It is candour with respect.
Training that encourages individuals to make errors and learn from them is covered in 1.22. It is evidence about a practice method for one person at a time, not about how safe a group feels.

items.title: Safe to be wrong
items.text: Without it, people stop trying things aloud.

try.text: Script the first ten minutes of a session to build safety. Name each move and the behaviour it is meant to open up.

try.title: Opening a session
try.text: Before: "Any questions?" and silence. After: the trainer describes a mistake of her own from last month, asks pairs to compare first guesses, then takes one answer from each pair in turn.

items: It does not appear by itself, least of all when senior and junior people share a room.
What feels safe differs between cultures. Directness and hierarchy change the picture.
One sharp remark from the trainer can undo an hour of work.
Calling on someone by name with no warning can feel like a trap. Say at the start that you will invite people in, give thinking time or a pair conversation first, and let anyone pass without comment.

topics.title: Engineer an early win
topics.theory: Belonging, self-efficacy and staying the course

situation.text: On a long programme people drift away by week three. Those who leave often decided early that they could not do it, or did not belong.

items: Design a task in the first session that everyone can complete and that matters.
Show people like them who have succeeded.
Build belonging on purpose: names, pairs, a shared first task.
Help people read nerves as readiness, not as a warning.

why.text: Belief in your own ability to succeed is built from four things: succeeding at something real, seeing people like you succeed, being told you can by someone credible, and how you read your own nerves. The theory says the more dependable the source, the more that belief changes. A real success is hard to argue with.

Belonging matters most to people with a reason to doubt it. In a study of US college students, a short exercise that eased doubts about fitting in raised the grades of Black students and made no difference to white students. That is a college study, not a workplace one, so use it as a pointer and not as proof.

items.title: Win early
items.text: A real success in the first session.

items.title: Belonging is uneven
items.text: It matters most to those with reason to doubt it.

try.text: Design the first achievable win for a course you run. Check that it is a real success, and that it happens in the opening session.

try.title: Week one of a long programme
try.text: Before: the first session is an overview and a reading list. After: by the end of session one each person has built one small working thing and shown it to a partner.

items: A win that is too easy teaches nothing and can feel patronising.
Belonging is cheap to build at the start and expensive to repair later.

topics.title: Have learners teach each other

situation.text: You have a cohort with mixed experience and not enough of your own time to coach everyone.

items: Have each person prepare to teach one part to a partner.
Give peer feedback a structure: what to look for, and how to say it.
Keep every individual accountable inside group work.
Make sure it is safe to be wrong in front of peers first.

why.text: Preparing to teach, and teaching, deepens learning for the person doing the teaching. Explaining forces you to organise what you know and find the gaps.

The best-known version is peer instruction, used for ten years in introductory physics at Harvard. Students answer a question alone, discuss it with a neighbour, then answer again. The authors report better grasp of the concepts and better problem solving than before they introduced it.

Peer feedback helps too. A pooling of 54 controlled studies in schools and universities found that students who assessed each other's work did somewhat better than students who had no assessment, and somewhat better than students assessed by the teacher. Give it a structure so people know what to look for.

A pooling of 28 studies backs this up. People who prepared to teach learned more than people who studied with no thought of teaching. People who prepared and then taught gained more again, most of all when the teaching was a real exchange with questions and answers.

why.title: Learning by preparing to teach and teaching: a meta-analysis
why.found: Across 28 studies, preparing to teach improved learning compared with studying without expecting to teach (g = 0.35). Preparing and then teaching improved it more (g = 0.56). Interactive teaching gave larger gains than teaching with no exchange.
why.means: Have people prepare and then teach a partner who can ask questions, not only prepare.

items.title: Teaching is learning
items.text: Explaining exposes what you do not know.

items.title: Structure the feedback
items.text: Tell people what to look for and how to say it.

try.text: Design a peer-teaching activity where each learner teaches a segment to a partner. Say how you will hold each individual accountable.

try.title: A mixed cohort
try.text: Before: the trainer explains all four procedures. After: each person prepares one procedure and teaches it to a partner from a checklist. The trainer closes with a short quiz that everyone answers alone.

items: Without accountability, some people coast in groups.
Peer teaching can spread errors. Check the key points afterwards.
It depends on psychological safety. Build that first.

topics.title: Check it is a skill problem before you train

situation.text: A manager says "we need training on X". Before you design anything, find out whether training can fix it.

items: Ask: could they do it if they really had to?
If yes, look at the environment: expectations, tools, feedback, incentives.
If no, training may help. Find out exactly what they cannot do.
Tell the sponsor what you found, and what you recommend in place of a course.
Be ready to decline work that will not help.

why.text: Poor performance has many causes, and lack of skill is only one. People may not know what is expected, may lack the tools, may get no feedback, or may be rewarded for doing something else.

Training aimed at those problems wastes money and costs you credibility. Motivation, safety and belonging are the conditions for learning. Diagnosis decides whether learning is the right answer at all.

items.title: Could they, if they had to?
items.text: If yes, it is not a skill problem.

items.title: Sometimes say no
items.text: Declining is part of the job.

try.text: Take a real request for training. Run it through the question. Decide whether to accept it, reshape it or decline it, and write what you would say to the sponsor.

try.title: A request for email training
try.text: A manager asks for a course on writing clearer emails. You ask whether the team could do it if they had to. They can. The cause is a template that forces long replies. You recommend changing the template.

items: Sponsors often arrive with the solution already chosen. Test it gently.
A mixed cause is common. Train the skill part and say plainly what training will not fix.
Declining well means offering what would work.

topics.title: Aim people at getting better, not at looking good

situation.text: People in the room avoid the hard exercise because they do not want to look bad.

items: Frame tasks as practice, not as a test of ability.
Praise effort that was well aimed, and the method used.
Show progress against a person's own past work.
Keep comparison between learners private.
Do not promise that attitude alone changes results.

why.text: People who aim to get better tend to learn more and perform better, in study and at work. A large pooling of studies found that link. The same analysis found that aiming to avoid looking bad went with worse results. Aiming to look good showed no clear link either way. These are associations. They do not prove that changing someone's goal changes their results.

The idea of a "growth mindset" is popular and its evidence is disputed. Two pooled analyses in 2018 found a weak link between mindset and achievement and weak effects of mindset programmes, with possible gains for students at academic risk or from poorer backgrounds. A large US school experiment in 2019 found better grades among lower-achieving pupils after a session of under an hour. A 2023 review of 63 studies concluded that the apparent benefits most likely come from weak study design and bias. All of this research is on school and college students. Do not build a workplace programme on it.

why.title: Goal orientation: a meta-analysis
why.found: A learning goal orientation was positively correlated with learning, academic performance, task performance and job performance. Aiming to prove ability was uncorrelated with them. Aiming to avoid looking incompetent was negatively correlated. Goals set by the situation showed stronger links than goals as a personal trait.
why.means: Set up the task so that the goal in the room is to improve, since the goal a situation creates matters more than the one people arrive with.

items.title: Avoiding looking bad
items.text: The goal most clearly linked with worse results.

try.text: Rewrite the introduction to one hard exercise so it is framed as practice. Remove anything that ranks people.

try.title: Introducing a hard exercise
try.text: Before: "Let's see who can get this right." After: "This is practice. Most people need a few goes. Compare your second attempt with your first, not with your neighbour's."

items: Telling people to "have a growth mindset" does little.
Leaderboards can push people towards looking good, or towards hiding to avoid looking bad.
Effort praised without direction is wasted.

topics.title: Treat mistakes in practice as information

situation.text: The software course walks everyone through each click so nobody goes wrong. A week later people freeze at the first unexpected screen.

items: Give a short orientation, then let people explore.
Tell them errors are expected and useful.
When an error happens, ask what it tells them.
Teach how to recover.
Review the common errors together.

why.text: Training that encourages people to make errors and learn from them has been pooled across 24 studies. It came out ahead of training that avoids errors, most of all when people later met a task they had not practised.
Two parts of the method did the work: letting people explore actively, and telling them plainly that errors are welcome. It suits skills where the real job will throw up surprises.

why.title: Error management training: a meta-analysis
why.found: Across 24 studies with 2,183 people, training that encouraged errors beat error-avoiding or purely exploratory training by a moderate margin (d = 0.44). The gain was larger after training than during it, and largest on tasks that differed in structure from those practised (d = 0.80).
why.means: Use it when people will face unfamiliar situations, and judge it by later performance, not by how smooth the session looked.

items.title: Best for new tasks
items.text: The gain shows when things are unfamiliar.

try.text: Take one step-by-step exercise. Rewrite it as exploration with three written prompts about errors.

try.title: A software exercise
try.text: Before: "Click here, then here, then here." After: "Create an invoice any way you can. You will hit error messages. When you do, note what the message says and what you tried next."

items: Where an error is dangerous or costly, use a simulator.
Complete beginners may need a worked example first.
It fails in a room where mistakes are punished.
Expect the session itself to look messier. The gain showed after training more than during it.

parts.title: Play, emotion and experience
parts.summary: Play, curiosity, and learning by doing and reflecting.

topics.title: Use play on purpose, not as a break
topics.theory: Play and playful learning in adults

situation.text: The agenda has "energiser" after lunch. It has nothing to do with the content.

items: Decide what the play is for: trying things safely, seeing a system, building trust.
Choose a form that fits: role-play, simulation, building, games with rules.
Make joining in a choice.
Debrief: what happened, what it shows, what to do with it.

why.text: Play lets people try things without real consequences. That lowers the cost of error. Supporters of playful learning also say it helps people take risks and think more freely. That has rarely been tested with adults. The debrief is where the learning is made explicit.

Evidence for play in adult learning is thin. A 2018 review of playful learning in higher education called adult play under-explored and found no settled line of research. The debrief has the stronger record. A pooling of 46 samples found that people and teams who held a structured debrief performed about a fifth to a quarter better than those who did not. Most of those studies were not full experiments.

why.title: Do debriefs improve performance? A meta-analysis
why.found: Across 46 samples with 2,136 people, a debrief improved performance by about 25 per cent compared with no debrief (d = 0.67), or about 21 per cent with three outlying studies removed. Teams and individuals gained alike. Facilitated debriefs looked better than unfacilitated ones, though very few studies had no facilitator.
why.means: Keep time for a facilitated debrief after every playful activity.

items.title: Debrief
items.text: Without it, it was a break.

try.text: Take one playful activity you use. Write the purpose in one line and three debrief questions.

try.title: After lunch
try.text: Before: a ball-throwing energiser. After: a ten-minute card game in which teams trade with incomplete information, then three questions on what happened and where the same thing shows up in handovers at work.

items: Some people find play exposing. Offer a role as observer.
Play that mocks the content undermines it.
Check the activity is accessible to everyone in the room.

topics.title: Make people curious before you tell them

situation.text: You open with the agenda and the learning objectives. Nobody is wondering about anything.

items: Start with a question, a puzzle or a result that does not fit.
Let people guess before you explain.
Give enough background that the gap feels closable.
Answer it. Do not leave people hanging.

why.text: One influential account says curiosity arises when people notice a gap in what they know or understand. A laboratory study of trivia questions found that people remembered answers better when they were curious. They also remembered unrelated faces shown while they waited for the answer. Both effects were still there a day later.
Emotion marks what is worth remembering. Strong emotion can also narrow attention and crowd out detail.

why.title: Curiosity and memory
why.found: People in a brain scanner saw trivia questions they had rated for curiosity, then waited for each answer while an unrelated face was shown. They later remembered more of the answers they had been curious about, and more of the faces shown while curiosity was high. This is one small laboratory study.
why.means: Open with a question people want answered, and treat the memory benefit as a likely bonus, not a promise.

try.text: Rewrite the first three minutes of a session to open with a question people will want answered.

try.title: Opening a session
try.text: Before: "Here are today's five objectives." After: the trainer describes two teams who had the same training, one still using it a month later, and asks pairs to guess what was different. Then she shows the answer.

items: A gap too wide feels hopeless. Give a foothold.
A teaser unrelated to the content distracts.
The trivia study was a laboratory task. Treat it as a pointer.

topics.title: Let people do it, then make them reflect

situation.text: The outdoor exercise was a great afternoon. Nobody can say what they learned from it.

items: Give people a real task to do.
Ask what happened.
Ask why, and what it is like at work.
Ask what they will do differently.
Have them try that soon.

why.text: Experience alone does not teach. People learn from an experience when they reflect on it and connect it to something they will do.

The best-known model is Kolb's cycle of doing, reflecting, forming an idea and trying again. It is widely used. A 2020 review found the model unclear about what counts as a concrete experience and proposed a revised version that still needs testing. Use the cycle as a prompt for the debrief and not as a law.

The reflecting half has better support than the cycle. Ten experiments with more than 4,000 people found that stopping to reflect on what you have done can teach more than extra practice, once you have some experience to reflect on. A pooling of 46 samples found that structured debriefs improved later performance by about a fifth to a quarter.

why.cite: Di Stefano, Gino, Pisano and Staats (working paper, revised 2023)
why.title: Learning by thinking
why.found: In ten experiments with 4,340 people, reflecting on past experience could produce more learning than extra practice. It helped most early on, once people had enough experience to reflect on, and the gain carried over to related tasks. How people reflected made a difference.
why.means: Stop the activity early enough to reflect, and do it while the skill is still new.

items.title: Do, then reflect
items.text: The second half is the lesson.

items.title: A prompt, not a law
items.text: The cycle is a guide with gaps.

try.text: Take one activity. Write the debrief as three questions: what happened, why it matters, what next.

try.title: An outdoor exercise
try.text: Before: the raft is built, everyone cheers and the coach leaves. After: twenty minutes are kept back. The group says what happened when the plan changed, where that happens at work, and what each person will try on Monday.

items: The activity eats the time meant for the debrief. Protect it.
Reflection needs safety.
Do not sort people into "learning styles" from this model.

parts.title: What the learner brings
parts.summary: How skill develops, what people bring with them, and how they manage their own learning.

topics.title: Know the stages of learning a skill
topics.theory: Stages of skill acquisition: from spoken steps to automatic

situation.text: A new starter can log a refund in the ticket system if she reads the steps under her breath and nobody talks to her. Her team lead says she has been trained. Put a customer on the phone at the same time and the whole thing falls apart.

items: Decide which stage people must reach before they leave you: can do it with the prompt card, without the card, or while holding a conversation.
At the start, give the steps in words and show them once at normal speed and once slowly. Let people say the steps aloud as they work.
Keep everything else quiet while the steps are still spoken. No customer, no clock, no second task. Working memory has no room for them yet (1.1).
Move to repetition with feedback. Aim for many short runs on varied cases, not one long run.
Watch for the sign that someone has moved on: the card stays on the desk and the muttering stops. Only then add the second demand, such as talking to a customer while doing it.
Say plainly what the course will not do. Fast, automatic performance comes from weeks of use. Agree with the manager where those repetitions will happen.
Check accuracy again once people are fluent. A step that has become automatic with a mistake in it is harder to change than one still being read from a card.

why.text: Paul Fitts described skill learning in three stages in the 1960s. First people work out what to do, slowly and with errors. Then they join the parts and the errors fall. Finally the skill runs with little attention.

John Anderson's theory explains the change. A new skill starts as facts about what to do. People hold those facts in working memory and often rehearse them in words. With practice, the facts are built into the procedure itself. They no longer have to be recalled and held, so the spoken rehearsal drops away and the load on working memory falls. After that, practice keeps tuning the procedure: it gets applied more widely, more precisely and faster.

The stages and the mechanism are research, drawn from laboratory studies of tasks such as geometry proofs. The step list above is a trainer's application of them. No opened study says how many repetitions a workplace skill needs, so treat the numbers as starting points.

why.title: Acquisition of cognitive skill
why.found: Sets out a theory in which a skill begins as stated facts that are interpreted step by step, is then compiled into procedures that no longer need those facts held in working memory, and is afterwards tuned by further practice.
why.means: Let beginners talk themselves through the steps, protect them from extra demands, and add the second task only when the talking has stopped.

try.text: Watch someone carry out a task they learned in the last fortnight. Do not help. Note where they read, where they mutter and where they pause. Then say aloud to a colleague, in one minute, which stage the person is in and what practice you would give them next.

try.title: A worked example: a support team learning a new ticket system

head: Stage
What you see
What the trainer does
When
rows: Reads each step from the card. Says the steps under her breath. Slow, with slips.
Demonstrates twice. Gives a six-step card. One refund at a time, no caller.
Glances at the card for steps four and five only. Fewer slips. Still stops if spoken to.
Twelve short practice tickets of mixed types. One piece of feedback after each.
Card unused. Can log the refund while a colleague plays the caller.
Adds the caller. Listens for accuracy, not speed.
Week 2, on live tickets with a buddy
Fluent, and skipping the reason code.
Corrects the one step, has her say it aloud for five tickets.

items: Adding the customer too early. If people still need to say the steps, a conversation uses the same space. Take the second demand away and try again later.
Calling it done at stage one. Name the stage people reached in your handover to the manager.
Experts who cannot explain. People at the automatic stage have often lost the words for what they do. Ask them to demonstrate slowly and write the steps yourself.

topics.title: Know what the learner brings
topics.theory: Trainee characteristics: motivation to learn, self-efficacy and prior ability

situation.text: Two people sit through the same new-manager workshop. One has asked for it for a year. The other was sent after a complaint and expects to be bad at it. You gave them the same session and you will not get the same result.

items: Find out three things before you design: what people can already do, whether they chose to come, and whether they expect to succeed. A short form or a call with their manager is enough.
Ask about the workplace as well. Will their manager make time for them to use this?
Open by showing that people like them have done it. A short story or demonstration from a peer does more than telling them they can.
Say what the training is worth to them in their own terms: fewer escalations, an easier Monday meeting, a step towards a role.
Take out avoidable anxiety. Tell people in the joining note what will happen, whether anything is assessed, and that practice is private. Topic 2.21 covers the note.
Give an early task everyone can complete (1.18), then raise the difficulty.
When you report results, name what the session could not change. Prior ability and a cold workplace are not fixed by a good afternoon.

why.text: A meta-analysis of twenty years of training research found that what trainees bring predicts what they take away. Motivation to learn was related to knowledge gained, to skill, and most strongly to using the training afterwards. Belief in your own ability to succeed, measured before training, was related to the same outcomes. General mental ability was the strongest predictor of knowledge gained.

The same study looked at what sits behind motivation to learn. People who believed outcomes were under their own control were more motivated. Anxious people were less so, and older trainees slightly less. A supportive climate at work went with higher motivation. Motivation still predicted outcomes after ability was taken into account.

These are correlations between measures, not experiments. They show what goes together. They do not prove that raising someone's confidence will raise their learning, because people who have done well before tend to be both more confident and quicker to learn. The steps follow the authors' advice to build self-belief early and make the benefits clear. They are not tested one by one. The figures are correlations (r), not d values.

why.title: Toward an integrative theory of training motivation
why.found: Pooling 20 years of studies, motivation to learn was related to knowledge (.27), skill (.16) and transfer (.58). Self-efficacy before training was related to knowledge (.30), skill (.32) and transfer (.47). Cognitive ability was related to knowledge (.69), skill (.38) and transfer (.43).
why.means: Find out who is in the room before you design, build belief and show the value early, and check the climate people go back to.

try.text: Ring one manager who is sending people to your next session. Ask the four questions below out loud and write the answers as they speak. Then change one thing in your opening ten minutes because of what you heard, and rehearse the new opening aloud once.

try.title: A worked example: four questions to a sending manager, before a new-manager programme
lines: "Who chose this for them: you, them, or HR?"
"What have they already done that is close to this? Have they run a one-to-one before?"
"If I asked them today whether they will be good at it, what would they say?"
"In the fortnight after, when will they get to try it, and will you ask them how it went?"
What the trainer heard: six of eight were sent, two have never run a one-to-one, most expect to find feedback conversations hard, and the manager had not planned anything afterwards.

What changed: the session opens with a team lead from last year's group describing her first awkward one-to-one. The first practice is a three-minute check-in everyone can do. The manager agrees to ask about it at the next team meeting.

try.title: Words you can use in the first five minutes
lines: "Some of you asked to be here and some of you were told to come. Both are fine."
"Nothing today is marked and nothing goes back to your manager from me."
"By lunch you will have run one short conversation that you could use this week. I will show you one first."
"Maya did this course last spring. I have asked her to tell you what her first try was like."

items: Blaming the learner. "They were not motivated" is a finding about the set-up as much as the person. Ask what they were told and what waits for them back at work.
Pep talks. Telling people they can do it is the weakest way to build belief. Show a peer, then give a real success.
Screening people out. Ability predicts learning, and that is a reason to adjust support and pace.
