topics.title: Teach people to manage their own learning

situation.text: You launch a four-week self-paced product course for a customer team. Week one looks busy. By week three most people have stalled halfway through module two and nobody has told you why.

items: At the start, have each person set a goal for the course that is specific and a stretch. "Pass the product check at 90 per cent by the 28th" beats "get through it".
Agree the effort in hours and put it in the diary. Three 30-minute blocks a week, named days. Effort that has no slot does not happen.
Build short prompts into the course itself, at the start, in the middle and near the end of each module.
Plan for the stall. Ask each person to write what they will do in the week when work gets in the way. Topic 5.2 gives the when-and-then form.
Show progress against the goal each week, to the learner first. A count of modules done is enough.
Check in once at the midpoint, by message or a ten-minute call. Ask about the goal and the hours.
Keep study-skills teaching short and tied to the goal. Teach the techniques in 5.16 when people need them, not as a separate module.

why.text: Self-regulated learning is what people do to steer their own learning: setting goals, putting in effort, keeping going, checking how it is going. In a classroom the trainer does much of this for them. In self-paced formats nobody does.

A meta-analysis of 430 studies of adults in work-related training asked which of these habits go with learning. Four stood out: the level of the goal people set, persistence, effort, and belief in their own ability. Together they explained 17 per cent of the differences in learning after ability and prior knowledge were taken into account. Planning, monitoring, asking for help and controlling emotion showed no reliable link with learning when measured separately.

Prompts are one tested way to act on this. In an online course, trainees who were asked reflective questions throughout learned more than a control group and fewer of them dropped out. The gain in learning came through spending more time on the material.

The four-habit finding is correlational. The prompt finding is an experiment in online training. The step list combines both with ordinary practice, and the wording of the prompts below is this site's, not the study's.

why.title: Self-regulated learning in work-related training
why.found: Across 430 studies and 90,380 trainees, goal level, persistence, effort and self-efficacy had the strongest links with learning and together explained 17 per cent of the variance after cognitive ability and pre-training knowledge. Planning, monitoring, help seeking and emotion control were not significantly related to learning.
why.means: Put your design effort into goals, time on task and keeping people going. A planning template alone is unlikely to help.

try.text: Take a self-paced course you run or have taken. Write the goal question and three prompts for its first module. Then read them aloud to a colleague and ask whether they sound like a person or a form. Rewrite the ones that sound like a form.

try.title: A worked example: prompts in a four-week product course for a customer team

head: When
Prompt on screen
What it is for
rows: What score do you want on the product check on the 28th? Which three half-hours this week are yours?
What do you want to be able to do by the end of this one?
Are you taking this in, or reading with half your mind on your inbox? If the second, stop and come back at your next slot.
Close the module. Write the two things a customer would most need you to know. Now check.
Recall, and a check on progress
You planned six half-hours. How many happened? What will you do in the week that goes wrong?
Ten-minute call: goal, hours, one thing in the way.

items: Easy goals. "Finish the course" asks for attendance. Push for a level and a date.
Prompts that nag. More than two or three a module and people click through them.
Leaving it all to the learner. Managing your own learning is itself a skill, and newcomers to a subject are worst placed to judge how they are doing (1.4). Give more structure to novices.
Treating a stall as a motivation problem. Ask about hours first. Often the diary slot was never protected.

parts.title: Plan the programme
parts.summary: Needs, competencies, the shape over time, managers, and what happens before and after.

topics.title: Find the real need behind the request

situation.text: A manager asks for "a course on X". That is a proposed solution, not a diagnosed need.

items: Write down the gap: what people do now, and what they should do.
Find the cause. Is it skill and knowledge, or tools, incentives and unclear expectations?
Gather evidence from more than the requester: performance data, observation, interviews.
Put the gap in terms the sponsor cares about.

why.text: A programme built on an untested request can miss the real problem however well it is made. A short analysis lowers that risk.
The request and the real need are often different things. Your job is to test the request against evidence from several people, then say what you found.

A review of the research on workplace training recommends a training needs analysis before anything is built. It should say what needs to be trained, for whom, and in what kind of organisation. A meta-analysis of leadership training found that programmes built on a needs analysis did better than those that were not.

items.title: Request is not need
items.text: "We need a course" is a guess at a solution.

items.title: Find the cause
items.text: Skill, or the environment around the skill?

items.title: More than one voice
items.text: Do not rely on the requester alone.

try.text: Take a real training request. Write a one-page needs analysis that separates what was asked for from the cause you found.

try.title: Illustration: the request and the need
try.text: Request: a course on time management for a support team. A week of looking shows the team waits two days for approvals from another department. The need is a faster approval step. Training would cover only the small part about prioritising calls.

items: Sponsors may resist diagnosis because it delays the course. Keep it short and show what it saves.
Performance data can be missing or poor. Say so, and use observation.
A mixed cause is common. Name the part training can fix.

topics.title: Define what good looks like in the role

situation.text: You have a pile of topics and no clear picture of what a capable person in the role can actually do.

items: List the knowledge, skills and behaviours that make someone capable in the role.
Sort them into levels: foundation, intermediate, advanced.
Order them into a path from newcomer to expert.
Show the path to the learner and the sponsor.

why.text: A competency model turns a list of topics into a path with a purpose. It lets you show a learner and a sponsor exactly what capability is being built.
Published frameworks can speed this up. They also have limits, and they describe a typical role, not this one.

The best-known guidance on competency models sets out twenty good practices for building, presenting and using them. Its authors say these come from experience and have not been tested in studies. Treat a competency model as a useful working tool, not as a proven method.

items.title: Capability first
items.text: Define what good looks like before choosing content.

items.title: A visible path
items.text: Learners should see where they are going.

try.text: Draft a competency model for a real role. Sequence it into a levelled path from newcomer to expert.

try.title: Illustration: topics turned into capability
try.text: Before: a topic list for new team leaders. Delegation, feedback, rotas, absence. After: a foundation level that reads "runs a weekly one-to-one" and "gives feedback on a specific piece of work", with intermediate and advanced levels above it.

items: Models go stale. Review them when the role changes.
Too much detail makes a model nobody uses.
A framework borrowed from elsewhere needs checking against the real job.
A model that only describes today's job dates quickly. Good models are tied to what the organisation is trying to do and can look ahead to what the role will need.

topics.title: Shape the programme over weeks, not days

situation.text: The plan is two packed days. Everything is covered once, in topic order, and never returned to.

items: Build the programme around whole, realistic tasks that get harder.
Add separate drills only for the sub-skills that need them.
Bring key ideas back over weeks and months.
Choose the order on purpose: simple to complex, concrete to abstract, known to unknown.

why.text: The shape of a programme over time is a design decision. One approach to complex skills argues that people learn them best by practising meaningful whole tasks of rising difficulty, with part-practice for the pieces.
Spacing applies at the scale of a programme as well as a session. Revisiting the same ideas at greater depth is one way to build it in.

A large review of spacing studies found that the best gap between sessions grows with the time people need to remember the material. Most of those studies tested recall of words and facts, so applying it to a whole programme is a reasonable extension, not a tested rule. A meta-analysis of leadership training also found better results when sessions were spread out.

why.title: A review of spaced practice
why.found: The review pooled 839 assessments from 317 experiments on verbal recall. Spreading study over time helped later memory, and the gap that worked best grew longer as the delay before the final test grew longer.
why.means: Set the gaps in a programme by how long people need to keep the skill, with longer gaps for learning that must last months.

items.title: Whole tasks
items.text: Practise the real job, made easier at first.

items.title: Order on purpose
items.text: Do not default to the order of the textbook.

try.text: Take a set of competencies. Arrange them into a spaced, whole-task programme across a realistic period.

try.title: Illustration: two days reshaped
try.text: Before: two full days covering twelve topics once. After: one day built around three realistic cases, then four ninety-minute sessions over eight weeks. Each session returns to an earlier case with a harder version.

items: Clients often want it done in one block. Offer a shorter event with follow-up sessions.
Whole tasks can overwhelm newcomers. Simplify the task, do not split it into unrelated pieces.
A long programme loses people. Plan how you keep them.

topics.title: Give managers a job before, during and after
topics.theory: Stakeholders, managers and the transfer environment

situation.text: The course is good and nothing changes at work. Nobody asked the learners' managers to do anything.

items: Treat the workplace as part of the design.
Give each manager three jobs: set expectations before, release time during, follow up after.
Write those jobs on one page.
Agree with the sponsor what support the programme needs before you start.
Design for three audiences: sponsor, manager, learner.

why.text: The classic model of transfer names three influences: the learner, the training design and the work environment. The work environment is the one a trainer controls least, and it is easy to neglect.
A learner's manager sets expectations and reinforces, or fails to. Hoping managers will support the learning is not a plan. Giving them specific actions is.

A meta-analysis of 89 studies found that a supportive work environment goes with more transfer. The link was stronger for open skills such as leadership than for closed skills such as using software. The studies show an association. They did not test a one-page manager guide, which is one practical way to act on the finding.

why.title: What predicts transfer of training
why.found: Across 89 studies, transfer was positively related to a supportive work environment, and to the learner's ability, conscientiousness and motivation. Links were stronger for open skills such as leadership. Results looked better than they were when the same person rated both the support and the transfer.
why.means: Plan manager support most carefully for people skills, and do not rely on learners' own ratings alone to judge transfer.

items.title: The workplace is a variable
items.text: Design it as carefully as the content.

items.title: One page
items.text: A manager will read one page.

try.text: Draft a one-page manager guide for a real programme. Say what managers do before, during and after.

try.title: Illustration: a one-page manager guide
try.text: Before: ten minutes to agree one thing the person will work on. During: cover their calls for the day. After: ask in the next one-to-one what they tried and what got in the way.

try.title: A worked example: one-page manager brief for a customer service programme, "Handling difficult calls"

head: When
What we ask you to do
Time
Words you could use
rows: Agree with each person one type of call they find hard. Tell them the workshop matters to you.
"Which calls do you dread? Take one of those with you on Tuesday. I want to hear how it goes."
Cover their calls so they are not pulled out. Do not message them about work.
"You are off the phones on Tuesday. I have it covered."
Ask what they tried, and listen to one recorded call together against the three-step checklist attached.
"Play me a call where you used it. What did you notice?"
Praise one use of the three steps you hear on the floor. Raise it once in a team meeting.
"I heard you name it and own it on that call. That is exactly it."
Tell us what has changed and what has not. Two lines by email is enough.
"Complaints passed up to me are down, and people still rush the next step."
A three-step reply to an angry caller: name it, own it, next step. One day, with practice in threes.
The trainer's name, email address and phone number.

items: Managers are busy. Ask for ten minutes, three times.
Some managers are the problem. Find another sponsor for those learners.
Do not promise transfer you cannot influence.
If you are external, you may never meet the managers. Ask the sponsor to send the brief under their own name, and ask for ten minutes on a managers' call to talk it through.

topics.title: Design the before and after, not only the event
topics.theory: The pre, during and post framework

situation.text: All the effort goes into the day itself. Nothing happens before it, and nothing after.

items: Before: set expectations, wake up what people already know, and have the manager conversation.
Ask a few questions before teaching, even if people get them wrong.
After: schedule recall, a task to apply, and a check-in.
Tell learners their part: prepare, use it soon, teach someone, come back to it.

why.text: The event is the middle third. A well-run session with no preparation and no follow-up fades in a predictable way.

Trying to answer questions before learning, even wrongly, can improve what is remembered later, as long as people then meet the right answers. The gain is mostly for the points you asked about. It is a form of generation.

why.title: The pretesting effect
why.found: In five experiments, people who tried to answer questions about a text before reading it did better on a later test than people given extra reading time. This held even for questions they had got wrong at the start.
why.means: Open with a few questions on the points that matter most, then make sure the session answers them.

items.title: The middle third
items.text: The event is one part of three.

items.title: Ask first
items.text: A question before teaching primes the answer.

try.text: Map before, during and after for a real programme. Write one action for each phase, for you and for the learner.

try.title: Illustration: one programme in three parts
try.text: Before: three questions by email and a short talk with the manager. During: the session answers those three questions. After: a recall quiz in week one, one task to try on the job, and a twenty-minute check-in in week four.

items: Pre-work that is not used in the room teaches people to skip it.
Follow-up needs an owner and a date, or it does not happen.
Keep pre-work short.
Pre-questions work best for clearly stated facts. They help less with questions that need complex reasoning, and most of the evidence comes from students in laboratory studies.

topics.title: Design for the kind of programme it is
topics.theory: Programme types: onboarding, leadership development, compliance

situation.text: You use the same design for induction, a leadership course and fire safety.

items: Name the type of programme.
Induction: what people need in week one, then spread the rest.
Compliance: aim at what people do, and test that.
Leadership: practice on real work, over months.
Technical skills: worked examples, then practice with feedback.

why.text: Programmes differ in what success means. Induction succeeds when someone can do the job and feels they belong. Compliance succeeds when behaviour is safe and lawful. Leadership development succeeds when people lead differently.
Copying one format across all of them ignores those differences.

Research supports two of these directly. A meta-analysis of newcomers found that being clear about the role, feeling able to do the job and feeling accepted by colleagues link induction to later performance and staying. A meta-analysis of leadership training found better results with practice, feedback and sessions spread over time.
Two of these types have a full topic of their own in this part: "Design onboarding that gets people productive" and "Do compliance training properly".

items.title: Name the type
items.text: Each has its own test of success.

try.text: Take two programmes of different types. For each, write what success would look like on the job.

try.title: Illustration: one topic, two tests of success
try.text: Fire safety. Before: a slide module and a pass mark. After: each person walks their own exit route and shows where the nearest extinguisher is. Leadership. Before: a two-day course. After: one skill practised with their own team each month.

items: Compliance training built only to prove attendance may change little.
Induction overloads week one.
Leadership courses are often events with no practice.

topics.title: Design for people early in their career
topics.theory: Early-career learners: onboarding, graduates and apprentices

situation.text: The audience is graduates and apprentices in their first job. Much of your material assumes they know how a workplace runs.

items: Check what they know. Assume little about the workplace and a lot about their ability.
Use worked examples and plenty of structure.
Teach the unwritten rules: who to ask, how to raise a problem.
Build belonging and an early win.
Involve their line manager or buddy.

why.text: Seniority and knowledge are different things. People early in a career are usually beginners in the job, so the guidance for beginners applies: more structure, more examples, support that fades.

There is no good evidence that generations learn in different ways. Research on generations at work finds small differences or none, and very few studies have tested training by generation. Age, career stage and experience explain more.

A meta-analysis of 70 samples of newcomers found three signs of settling in: being clear about the role, feeling able to do the job and feeling accepted. These linked what the organisation did, and how much newcomers sought information, to later performance, satisfaction and staying. That is the case for teaching the unwritten rules openly.

why.title: How newcomers settle in
why.found: Across 70 samples, role clarity, self-efficacy and social acceptance carried the effect of an organisation's induction practices and of newcomers' information seeking through to job performance, satisfaction, commitment and staying.
why.means: Design early-career programmes to build clarity, confidence and acceptance, as well as knowledge.

try.text: Take a session written for experienced staff. Mark every assumption about the workplace a newcomer would miss.

try.title: Illustration: an assumption made visible
try.text: Before: "Escalate anything unusual to the duty manager." After: who the duty manager is today, how to reach them, what counts as unusual, and a sample message. Then a practice case, with the sample message removed the second time.

items: Do not talk down. New is not the same as slow.
A beginner in a room of experts will not ask.
Their manager shapes whether any of it is used.

quiz.a: No.

quiz.q: Do generations learn differently?

openPoints: No study specific to UK graduates or apprentices was found. The Bauer meta-analysis covers newcomers in general and includes people moving from education into work.

topics.title: Design for managers and senior leaders

situation.text: The audience is managers. They are short of time, sceptical, and have been on leadership courses before.

items: Start from a problem they have this month.
Keep input short. Spend the time on practice with real cases.
Use their experience: have them advise each other.
Set a task to try with their own team.
Follow up, with their own manager involved.

why.text: Managers bring experience, so support aimed at beginners can get in their way. They also bring habits, and habits change through practice and feedback on real work.

A meta-analysis of 335 samples found that leadership training works on average. Programmes did better when they were built on a needs analysis, gave feedback, used several methods including practice, and spread sessions over time. Face-to-face and on-site delivery were also linked with better results.

why.title: A meta-analysis of leadership training
why.found: Across 335 samples, leadership training improved reactions, learning, behaviour at work and results. It was more effective when based on a needs analysis, when it included feedback and practice, and when sessions were spaced, on site and face to face.
why.means: Build a leadership programme from a diagnosed need, with practice and feedback in every session and gaps between sessions.

items.title: Over time
items.text: One event rarely changes how people lead.

try.text: Take a leadership topic. Design ninety minutes with no more than fifteen minutes of input.

try.title: Illustration: ninety minutes on difficult conversations
try.text: Ten minutes of input on one way to open the conversation. Sixty minutes in threes, each manager rehearsing a real conversation they are due to have while the others give feedback. Twenty minutes to plan when they will hold it and who will ask how it went.

items: Experienced people can be beginners in a new skill.
Status makes it hard to practise in front of peers. Build safety.
Models with neat names sell well. Check the evidence.
The meta-analysis pools many kinds of programme. It shows what tends to go with better results, not that any one design will work in your setting.

topics.title: Design for executives
topics.theory: Executive education: short time, status in the room and learning from peers

situation.text: You have ninety minutes with an executive team. Phones are on the table and nobody wants to be taught.

items: Agree with the sponsor what one decision or change the session is for.
Send a one-page brief in advance.
Open with their data or their problem.
Have them work with each other. You facilitate.
End with who will do what, by when.
Offer a private follow-up.

why.text: Executives have little time and much at stake in front of peers. Being seen not to know can feel costly, so safety is likely to matter more as rank rises. In practice they often give more weight to the views of peers than to those of a trainer.
These are observations from practice. The research on what works for executives in particular is thin.

One piece of research does bear on the safety point. A study of 51 teams in a manufacturing company found that teams whose members felt safe to take risks with each other showed more learning behaviour, and that this went with better team performance. It studied ordinary work teams, not executives.

items.title: Status
items.text: Not knowing is costly. Protect people.

try.text: Design a ninety-minute executive session with one purpose and no more than ten minutes of input.

try.title: Illustration: one purpose
try.text: Before: "An update on customer complaints for the executive team." After: "By the end, the team agrees which two complaint types to fix first and who owns each." The one-page brief carries the data, so the ninety minutes go on the decision.

items: The most senior person can close the room down by speaking first.
Do not simplify the content. Shorten it.
A session with no decision is forgotten.

topics.title: Know the learner's working day before you design
topics.theory: The modern learner and their context

situation.text: The design assumes people will do an hour of pre-work at a quiet desk. Your learners work shifts on a shop floor.

items: Find out when, where and on what device people can learn.
Ask what interrupts them.
Fit the design to that: shorter pieces, offline access, protected time.
Ask managers to release the time.
Test with two or three real learners.

why.text: A design that does not fit the working day is unlikely to be used. Time, place, device and interruptions decide whether people can take part at all.

The popular claim of a fixed, short attention span is not supported. A review of lecture studies found no good data for a limit of ten to fifteen minutes. People are busy and interrupted, which is a different problem with a different answer.

Designing by generation is not supported either. A meta-analysis of 20 studies and about 20,000 people found that generations differed little or not at all in job satisfaction, commitment and intention to leave. A 2020 report from the US National Academies concluded that generational labels are not a sound basis for managing people. It found that age, career stage, experience and working conditions explain more, and that people within a generation differ about as much as people across generations.
Very few studies have tested training by generation at all. Ask about each group's working day, experience and role, and design for those.

why.title: Generations at work, a meta-analysis
why.found: Pooling 20 studies and 19,961 people across four generations, the differences in job satisfaction, commitment to the organisation and intention to leave were small and in many cases close to zero. The authors concluded that meaningful generational differences probably do not exist for these attitudes.
why.means: Do not build separate designs for age cohorts. Find out about people's roles, experience and working conditions.

try.text: Shadow or interview two learners about a normal day. List three changes your design needs.

try.title: Illustration: a design refitted to a shift
try.text: Before: sixty minutes of online pre-work on a desktop. After: three five-minute pieces that work on the shared tablet in the break room, with ten minutes released at the start of a shift and a printed card for the shop floor.

items: Mobile-friendly does not mean a phone is the right place to learn it.
Learning in people's own time has a cost. Say who bears it.
Do not design around generations.

quiz.q: What four things about the working day shape a design?
quiz.a: Time, place, device and interruptions.

quiz.q: What happens to a design that does not fit the day?
quiz.a: It is unlikely to be used.

quiz.a: No good data support one. People are busy and interrupted.

The draft said time, place, device and interruptions decide more than the content does. No source makes that comparison, so it was removed.

parts.title: Design the course
parts.summary: Objectives, design models, sequencing and pace.

topics.title: Write objectives you could observe

situation.text: The course aims say people will "understand" and "be aware of". Nobody can tell whether it worked.

items: Start from what people must be able to do at the end.
Write each objective as something you could watch someone do.
Decide how you will assess it before you plan the teaching.
Check every activity and every assessment against an objective. Cut what matches none.
Use the form "who does what, under what conditions, to what standard". The worked example under Try it shows three aims rewritten this way.

why.text: Designing backwards means choosing the capability first, then the assessment, then the teaching. Objectives, activities and assessment must point at the same target. When they do not, the course is misaligned, and people are taught one thing and assessed on another.

Bloom's taxonomy is a useful ladder for pitching the level of thinking. The 2001 revision names six levels: remember, understand, apply, analyse, evaluate and create. Its authors say the levels overlap, so use it as a guide, not a strict hierarchy.

items.title: Observable
items.text: If you cannot see it, you cannot assess it.

try.text: Take a set of vague aims. Rewrite them as observable objectives. Check each activity and assessment against them.

try.title: Illustration: an aim rewritten
try.text: Before: "Understand the complaints process." After: "Given a written complaint, log it, choose the right category and send the holding reply within the standard time." The assessment is three sample complaints handled at a desk.

try.title: A worked example: three weak objectives rewritten as observable ones
lines: The form: WHO does WHAT, under WHAT CONDITIONS, to WHAT STANDARD.
Weak 1: "Understand the new pricing tiers."
Observable 1: "Given a customer's size and usage, the account manager chooses the right tier and explains the price in under two minutes, correctly for all three test customers."
Weak 2: "Be aware of the returns policy."
Observable 2: "At the till, with a customer waiting and no manager to ask, the store assistant decides whether to refund, exchange or refuse, and gets four out of five sample cases right."
Weak 3: "Appreciate the importance of regular one-to-ones."
Observable 3: "In the four weeks after the workshop, the new manager holds a 30-minute one-to-one with each team member and records one agreed action from each."
Check each one: could two people watch and agree whether it happened?
Verbs you can use: choose, explain, demonstrate, list, sort, calculate, write, log, diagnose, repair, decide, present, handle, compare.
Verbs to avoid: understand, know, appreciate, be aware of, be familiar with, learn about.
For judgement, describe the performance: "decides and gives a reason a senior colleague would accept".

items: Tightly specified objectives can narrow learning. Leave room for judgement.
Higher-order skills are harder to write as objectives. Describe the performance, not a checklist.
An objective nobody assesses is a wish.

quiz.q: What is wrong with "understand"?
quiz.a: You cannot observe it, so you cannot assess it.

quiz.q: What is the order in backward design?
quiz.a: Capability, then assessment, then teaching.

quiz.q: What is alignment?
quiz.a: Objectives, activities and assessment all point at the same target.

openPoints: Mager, Preparing Instructional Objectives: not searched for or opened.

The publisher page for Understanding by Design does not spell out the three stages of backward design. The order 'capability, then assessment, then teaching' fits the chapter order but was not read in the publisher's own words.
The watch item that tightly specified objectives can narrow learning has no checked source.
checkFindings: Biggs (1996) confirmed. It sets out constructive alignment: objectives stated as performances, teaching activities chosen to produce them, and assessment of the same performances. This supports the alignment paragraph.

Wiggins and McTighe confirmed on the Pearson page for the expanded second edition, which Pearson published with ASCD. The page lists backward design as the first chapter and has chapters on thinking like an assessor before planning the teaching. The ASCD page itself was not among the search results.

Anderson and Krathwohl (2001) was not opened as a book. Krathwohl (2002) is the short overview of that revision by one of its editors and is listed in its place. The Bloom sentence now gives the six revised levels and the reason it is not a strict hierarchy.

topics.title: Use design models as checklists, not rules
topics.theory: ADDIE, SAM, Gagné and Merrill, used critically

situation.text: Someone insists the project must follow ADDIE, or SAM, step by step.

items: Learn the main models well enough to borrow from each.
Use ADDIE as a list of phases not to forget.
Prototype early when the brief is uncertain.
Use Gagné or Merrill to check a single lesson has the parts it needs.
Pick and blend to fit the project. Say why.

why.text: ADDIE (analyse, design, develop, implement, evaluate) is a useful checklist. Its critics say it is dated and less efficient than iterative ways of working. SAM, the Successive Approximation Model, is an iterative alternative that its authors present as simpler. Gagné offers a sequence for one lesson. Merrill centres learning on real problems.
These are lenses, not laws. Kolb's learning cycle is influential and its evidence is contested.

items.title: Lenses, not laws
items.text: Choose the model that fits the project.

items.title: Prototype early
items.text: A rough version teaches you more than a plan.

items.title: Check the lesson
items.text: Does it have a real problem, activation, demonstration, application and integration?

why.title: The four models at a glance

head: Model
What it is
When it helps
Its weakness
rows: Five phases for a whole project: analyse, design, develop, implement, evaluate.
As a list of phases, so that analysis and evaluation are not forgotten.
Critics call it dated and slower than iterative ways of working. Followed step by step, it can become a ritual.
An iterative way to run a project: build a rough version early, test it, improve it, repeat.
When the brief is uncertain or keeps changing.
The case for it over ADDIE is made by its own authors. Treat that as an argument.

A sequence for one lesson: gain attention, state the objectives, recall what people know, present the content, guide the learning, have people perform, give feedback, assess, and help them keep and transfer it.
To check that a single lesson has not skipped practice, feedback or recall.
It covers one lesson, not the programme round it. The events are meant to be adapted to the content and to what learners already know.
Five principles: learning centres on a real problem, with activation of what people know, demonstration, application and integration into their work.
To check that a lesson is built round a real problem, with something shown and something practised.
It is a set of principles, so it says little about how to run the project.
The sources opened describe them. None reports a test of one model against another.

try.text: Take one real project. Say which model or blend you would use, given its constraints.

try.title: Illustration: blending for one project
try.text: A new product launches in six weeks and the brief keeps changing. Use the ADDIE phases as a list so evaluation is not forgotten. Build a rough first session in week one and test it with three people. Check each lesson has a real problem, a demonstration and practice.

items: A model can become a ritual. Ask what each step is for.
Clients may expect the model they know. Explain your choice in their terms.
Do not teach Kolb's cycle as proven.
The case for SAM over ADDIE is made by SAM's own authors. Treat it as an argument, not a tested result.

topics.title: Start with full support, then take it away

situation.text: Newcomers are thrown at a full problem on the first morning and sink.

items: Break content into pieces small enough to hold.
Begin with a fully worked example.
Move to part-worked problems, where people finish the solution.
End with problems solved alone.
Remove each support once people no longer need it.

why.text: Structure is not neutral. A sequence that starts with full support and withdraws it lets a newcomer climb without overload. This applies the expertise reversal effect: support that helps at first holds people back later.

There is a competing finding. Letting people struggle with a problem before teaching can work better under some conditions. One reading is that the two bodies of evidence meet on prior knowledge: struggle is more likely to help people who know enough to learn from it.

Whether to show an example first or set a problem first is an open question, and this site recommends each in different places (1.2, 2.13 and 2.19). Example first has the stronger case for people who are new to a subject and learning a procedure, where an unaided attempt would swamp working memory. Problem first is supported by a pooled analysis of 53 studies (Sinha and Kapur, 2021). It did better when learners could bring what they already knew to the problem and a full explanation followed. Those studies were of school and university students learning concepts in maths and science. Younger primary pupils did better when taught first, and so did learners of general skills not tied to a subject. A rule of thumb, and no more than that: go example first when people are new and the goal is to carry out a procedure correctly. Go problem first when they have some background, the goal is understanding, and you have time to teach it properly straight after.

why.title: The expertise reversal effect
why.found: This review brings together studies showing that the teaching methods that work best change with what the learner already knows. Guidance that helps beginners can stop helping, or get in the way, once people know more.
why.means: Check prior knowledge first, start beginners with full support and take each support away as they improve.

items.title: Fade the support
items.text: Take it away as skill grows.

items.title: Prerequisites first
items.text: Teach what the next thing depends on.

try.text: Take one topic. Design a progression from worked example to independent practice, with support that fades.

try.title: Illustration: fading on one task
try.text: Reading a customer invoice. First, a fully worked invoice with each check explained. Next, an invoice with the first three checks done and two left to finish. Last, a fresh invoice with no notes. People who pass a quick check at the start skip to the last one.

items: Support left in place too long bores experienced people.
Struggle first is not a licence to leave newcomers stuck.
Check prior knowledge before choosing the starting point.

quiz.q: What comes between a worked example and solving alone?
quiz.a: A part-worked problem that the learner finishes.

quiz.q: What do you do with support as skill grows?
quiz.a: Remove it.

quiz.q: Who benefits from struggling before being taught?
quiz.a: Most likely people who already know enough to learn from the struggle.

openPoints: Sweller, worked examples and completion problems. No original paper was opened on this topic. The web search allowance for this run ran out before this could be looked up. Only pages already returned by an earlier search could be opened.
Kapur, productive failure. Not opened. Sinha and Kapur (2021), a meta-analysis of problem solving before instruction, is the source to check the claim about who benefits.

topics.title: Put the hard content where the energy is
topics.theory: Pacing, attention and the energy curve

situation.text: The session runs at one flat intensity from nine to five, and the room fades after lunch.

items: Break content into segments and change the activity between them.
Plan the opening, the dips and the close on purpose.
Put demanding work where energy is high.
Where energy dips, re-order, add recall or take a break.
Treat breaks as part of the learning.

why.text: There is no fixed attention span. Attention depends on interest, difficulty and design, and on how well the session is taught. A review of lecture studies found no good data for a limit of ten to fifteen minutes.
Breaking material into segments is widely recommended to help people process it. A pause between segments also gives people time to take stock.

why.title: Attention span during lectures
why.found: This review traced the claim that attention falls after ten to fifteen minutes and found it rests mostly on repeated citation, with little sound primary data. The most consistent pattern was that attention varied with the teacher more than with the format.
why.means: Do not plan around a fixed attention limit. Plan for variety that serves the content, and work on delivery.

items.title: Do not push through a dip

try.text: Map the energy of a full-day agenda. Re-order it so demanding content sits where energy is highest.

try.title: Illustration: one day re-ordered
try.text: Before: policy update at nine, the hardest case study straight after lunch. After: the hard case study at ten, a recall quiz and paired discussion after lunch, the policy update in a short slot mid-afternoon, and a break before the close.

items: Variety for its own sake distracts. Each change should serve the content.
Do not quote a "ten-minute attention span". The source is weak.
Claims about natural attention cycles are promising, not settled.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Bradbury (2016), Attention span during lectures: 8 seconds, 10 minutes, or more? Advances in Physiology Education.

topics.bodyStatus: 1 source checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: Is there a fixed attention span?
quiz.a: No. Attention depends on interest, difficulty and design.

quiz.q: What do you do when energy dips?
quiz.a: Re-order, add recall or take a break. Do not push harder.

quiz.q: What are breaks for, besides rest?
quiz.a: They give people time to take stock before the next segment.

topics.tierReason: The attention span myth is well examined, but the advice on energy, breaks and placing hard content has only limited support that could be checked.
openPoints: Mayer, the segmenting principle. Not opened. Rey and colleagues (2019), a meta-analysis of the segmenting effect, is the source to check. The web search allowance for this run ran out before this could be looked up. Only pages already returned by an earlier search could be opened.
Wilson and Korn (2007), Attention during lectures: beyond ten minutes, would be a second source on the myth. Not opened.
No source was opened for an energy dip after lunch, for the effect of breaks on learning, or for natural attention cycles. The page already calls the last of these unsettled.
Bradbury (2016) is classed by PubMed as an editorial. It is a review of the literature, not a new study.
checkFindings: Replaced the attention-span placeholder with Bradbury (2016). It supports the draft's warning not to quote a ten-minute attention span. It does not address a shrinking span, so that wording was replaced with what the source examined.
Added the source's main positive finding, that attention varied more with the teacher than with the format.
The draft said memory begins to settle in the gap between segments, in the why section and in a quiz answer. No source could be opened for this, so both were softened.
Mayer's segmenting principle could not be opened. The sentence now says segmenting is widely recommended.

topics.title: Use problems, cases or enquiry when judgement is the goal

situation.text: You want people to exercise judgement. The course gives them rules and a quiz.

items: Choose a realistic problem or case with no single right answer.
Check people have the knowledge the case needs.
Have small groups work it, with a clear output.
Bring out the reasoning, not only the answer.
Close with the principles the case shows.

why.text: Problems and cases suit judgement, because people practise weighing evidence and deciding. They work when people already have enough knowledge to reason with.
For newcomers, working things out with little guidance is slow and overloading. Teach the basics directly first.

Pooled studies of problem-based courses in higher education found a clear gain in skills. Students gained slightly less knowledge, but remembered more of what they did learn. Guidance is what makes the difference. Discovery with no help did worse than direct teaching. Discovery with feedback, worked examples and prompts to explain did better than other methods.

why.title: Does discovery-based instruction enhance learning?
why.found: Two pooled analyses covered 164 studies. Discovery with no help did worse than explicit teaching (d = -0.38). Discovery with support such as feedback, worked examples and prompts to explain did better than other methods (d = 0.30).
why.means: Keep the problem or case, and build in guidance, feedback and a debrief.

items.title: Knowledge first
items.text: People reason with what they know.

items.title: Draw out the principle
items.text: Do not stop at the answer.

try.text: Write one case for your subject, with the decision to be made and the output you want from groups.

try.title: Illustrative: from rules to a case
try.text: Before: a slide of escalation rules and a five-question quiz. After: groups of three get a messy customer complaint with two defensible responses. They have 15 minutes to choose one and write their reasons. The debrief compares the reasoning, then names the principles.

items: A case with an obvious answer is a quiz.
Groups drift without a deadline and an output.
Several cases beat one. People generalise from variety.
Most of the research comes from universities and medical schools. Workplace courses are less studied, so check your own results.

quiz.q: What are problems and cases best for?
quiz.a: Judgement.

quiz.q: What must people have first?
quiz.a: Enough knowledge to reason with.

quiz.q: How should you close a case?
quiz.a: With the principles it shows.

topics.tierReason: Pooled studies show problem-based and guided enquiry methods help skills and application, but unguided discovery does worse than direct teaching, so the result depends on prior knowledge and on how much guidance you give.
openPoints: The watch item 'Several cases beat one. People generalise from variety.' rests on the analogical transfer literature. No source for it was opened. Left unchanged.
checkFindings: Kirschner, Sweller and Clark (2006) supports the draft: guided teaching beats minimal guidance for novices, and the advantage fades once people have enough prior knowledge. No text change needed.

Added Schmidt and colleagues (2007), the published reply, because a competent reader would expect it. It accepts the point about novices but argues problem-based learning is guided, not minimally guided. This fits the draft's 'knowledge first, then cases' position.

Hmelo-Silver (2004) supports the first step (a complex problem with no single right answer, small groups, reflection). It also says most studies are in medical and gifted education. Added a watch item on that limit.

Dochy and colleagues (2003): skills clearly better, knowledge slightly lower but better retained. The draft did not mention the knowledge cost, so a paragraph was added to why. The pooled skills figure (0.46) is in the results section, not the abstract, so it is left off the page.
Alfieri and colleagues (2011) added as the study block. Both effect sizes are in the abstract.

parts.title: Design the experience
parts.summary: Who is in the room, the journey they take, and where it drags.

topics.title: Design for the range of people, not the average
topics.theory: Personas and the myth of the average learner

situation.text: The course is designed for "the typical learner". In the room, nobody is typical.

items: List the ways your learners really differ: prior knowledge, motivation, context, constraints.
Build two or three personas from real data.
Design for the edges as well as the middle.
Offer more than one way to take in content and to show learning.

why.text: Almost nobody is average on every measure, so a design aimed at the average fits few people. One person can be strong on one dimension and weak on another.
This is about real differences such as prior knowledge and context. It is not learning styles, which the evidence does not support.

items.title: Nobody is average
items.text: A design for the average fits no one.

items.title: Not learning styles
items.text: Variability is real. Teaching to styles is not supported.

try.text: Build two contrasting personas for a real course. Name one design change each one demands.

try.title: Illustrative: two personas, two changes
try.text: A spreadsheet course. Persona one is new, has never written a formula and dreads tests. Persona two is an analyst, bored by basics and short of time. Design changes: an optional primer and practice file for one, a skip-ahead challenge for the other.

items: Invented personas are stereotypes. Ground them in data.
Too many personas paralyse the design. Two or three is enough.
Designing for the edges often helps the middle too.

quiz.q: Why not design for the average learner?
quiz.a: Almost nobody is average on every measure.

quiz.q: Name three real ways learners differ.
quiz.a: Any three of: prior knowledge, motivation, context, constraints.

quiz.q: How is this different from learning styles?
quiz.a: These differences are evidenced. Matching teaching to learning styles is not.

topics.tierReason: Personas and designing for a range of people are widely used design practice with little direct testing in training. The warning about learning styles is well supported.
openPoints: The sentence 'One person can be strong on one dimension and weak on another' is a main idea in Rose's book, but the publisher's description does not state it. Left unchanged.
'Two or three personas is enough' is practitioner advice. No source confirmed a number.
checkFindings: Build note followed: 'Stefaniak (2020), Learning Experience Design' is not in the list and could not be searched for. Pruitt and Grudin (2003) is added as a verified reference for personas built from data.

Rose: the publisher's description confirms the argument that no one is average and that systems built for a typical person fail most people. The page opened is the 2017 HarperCollins edition, with the subtitle 'Unlocking our potential by embracing what makes us different'. The 2016 first edition date came from a search listing, not from the publisher page.
CAST: the current version is Guidelines 3.0, released 30 July 2024. Its three headings are multiple means of engagement, of representation, and of action and expression. This supports step four.
Pashler and colleagues (2008) added to support the learning styles sentence. Two short strings were reworded so they say what the review says.
The Pruitt and Grudin abstract supports grounding personas in qualitative and quantitative data. It does not discuss stereotypes or the right number of personas.

topics.title: Map the journey from first email to follow-up

situation.text: You have designed the day in detail. The joining instructions and the week after were left to someone else.

items: Map the whole journey: first hearing about it, pre-work, the event, first use, follow-up.
Mark the moments that can build or break motivation and belonging.
Design the first contact and the first session with care.
Design the return to work.

why.text: Two fragile parts of a programme are the start and the return to work. If you design only the event, those are left to chance.
People judge an experience largely by its most intense moment and by how it ends. That is a reason to design a strong high point and a deliberate close.

A pooled analysis found that the peak and the end shape how people rate an experience afterwards about as strongly as the average of the whole, and that length hardly matters. This is about how the programme is remembered and rated. It does not show that people learn more.

why.title: A meta-analysis of the peak-end rule
why.found: Across 174 effect sizes, ratings given after an experience were strongly related to its peak and its end (r = 0.58). That was about as strong as the link with the average of all moments. The length of the experience had almost no effect.
why.means: Design the high point and the close on purpose, and do not treat good ratings as proof of learning.

items.title: Beyond the event
items.text: The journey starts with the first email.

items.title: Moments that matter
items.text: A few points decide how it feels.

items.title: Peak and end
items.text: People remember the high point and the finish.

try.text: Map the full journey for a real course. Mark the moments that matter and design the high point and the ending.

try.title: Illustrative: a two-day course, mapped
try.text: The map shows three weak moments: a joining email with no reason to come, a flat last hour and silence afterwards. The redesign adds a short note from the manager, a closing practice round and a check-in two weeks later.

items: Intensive formats need a designed "after" most of all.
A journey map is a guess until you test it with learners.
The administration is part of the experience.

Kahneman, Fredrickson, Schreiber and Redelmeier (1993), When more pain is preferred to less: adding a better end. Psychological Science, 4(6).
Alaybek and colleagues (2022), All's well that ends (and peaks) well? A meta-analysis of the peak-end rule and duration neglect. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 170.
Hoogerheide and Paas (2012), Remembered utility of unpleasant and pleasant learning experiences: is all well that ends well? Applied Cognitive Psychology, 26(6).

topics.bodyStatus: 4 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: Which two parts of a programme are easily left to chance?
quiz.a: The start and the return to work.

quiz.q: What do people judge an experience by?
quiz.a: Its most intense moment and its ending.

quiz.q: Where does the journey begin?
quiz.a: When someone first hears about the programme.

topics.tierReason: Journey mapping is a service design practice with little direct testing in training. The peak-end finding is well supported for how experiences are rated afterwards, not for how much is learned.
openPoints: No source was opened for the importance of the first contact or of the return to work (the training transfer literature). The steps are left as practitioner advice.
checkFindings: The placeholder 'The outline cites the service-design literature without naming a study' is replaced with Stickdorn and colleagues (2018). The publisher's description does not mention journey maps, but the table of contents on the same page lists them in several chapters. The authors' own method page was also read. It says maps built on assumptions can mislead and should be replaced with research-based ones, which supports the watch item on testing the map with learners.

'Kahneman, the peak-end rule' is replaced with the 1993 cold-water study. The page opened is the Association for Psychological Science page for the article. It shows the abstract and journal but not the author list or year, which are taken from the standard citation.

Alaybek and colleagues (2022) confirm the peak-end effect is large, and add that the average of the experience matters about as much. The draft's 'largely by its most intense moment and by how it ends' slightly overstates this. A paragraph was added to why to give the fuller picture and to separate ratings from learning.
Hoogerheide and Paas (2012) tested the rule in a learning task with primary school children. The page opened is the record in the authors' university repository, not the journal page.
The claim that the start and the return to work are 'the most fragile' parts had no source. Softened in the paragraph and the quiz.

topics.title: Plan a peak and a proper ending
topics.theory: The emotional arc and experience mechanics

situation.text: The content is sound and the session feels flat from start to finish.

items: Open a question people want answered before you answer it.
Set tasks where challenge matches skill.
Plan one high point and build towards it.
Close on purpose. Do not run out of time.
Use story and challenge only where they carry the content.

why.text: Emotion affects attention, motivation and memory, so the feel of a course is a design matter. Curiosity arises from a gap between what people know and what they want to know. Absorption is more likely when challenge and skill are balanced, though that link is moderate and correlational (8.2).
Engagement is a means. A session can be enjoyable and teach little.
A planned high point and a deliberate close change how people rate and remember the session. That is worth having, but it is a rating effect. Check learning separately.

why.title: Curiosity and memory for answers
why.found: People read trivia questions and rated their curiosity. They spent tokens or waiting time to see answers they were more curious about. One to two weeks later they recalled surprising answers better when they had been more curious.
why.means: Open with a question people want answered, let them guess, then give the answer.

items.title: Match challenge to skill
items.text: Too easy bores. Too hard frightens.

try.text: Design the emotional arc of one session. Say where you create curiosity, where you aim for absorption, and how you close.

try.title: Illustrative: an arc for one session
try.text: A data protection session opens with a realistic email and one question: what went wrong here. People guess before the answer comes. The hardest case sits two thirds of the way in. The last ten minutes are a short practice and one commitment.

items: Interesting but irrelevant material can lower learning.
Game elements can backfire. See the topic on gamification.
A big finish with no follow-up is theatre.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Kang and colleagues (2009), The wick in the candle of learning: epistemic curiosity activates reward circuitry and enhances memory. Psychological Science, 20(8).
Alaybek and colleagues (2022), All's well that ends (and peaks) well? A meta-analysis of the peak-end rule and duration neglect. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 170.
Park, Flowerday and Brünken (2015), Cognitive and affective effects of seductive details in multimedia learning. Computers in Human Behavior, 44.

topics.bodyStatus: 3 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: Where does curiosity come from?
quiz.a: A gap between what people know and what they want to know.

quiz.q: When does absorption arise?
quiz.a: It is more likely when challenge and skill are balanced. The link is moderate, not a guarantee.

quiz.q: Is engagement the goal?
quiz.a: No. It is a means to learning.

topics.tierReason: Single ideas here have support, such as curiosity helping memory and endings shaping ratings, but designing an emotional arc to improve learning in training has little direct testing.
openPoints: Csikszentmihalyi (1990), Flow: no publisher page could be opened, so the book is not in the list. The sentence 'Absorption arises when challenge and skill are balanced' is therefore unchecked and left unchanged.
Loewenstein (1994), The psychology of curiosity, Psychological Bulletin: the abstract page could not be opened. The theory is described in Kang and colleagues (2009), which is listed in its place.

Sundararajan and Adesope (2020), Keep it coherent: a meta-analysis of the seductive details effect, Educational Psychology Review. Found in search at link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10648-020-09522-4 but the page would not load. It would be a better source than Park (2015) for the watch item. A 2025 multi-level meta-analysis in the same journal (10.1007/s10648-025-10099-z) also appeared in search and was not opened.
The opening sentence 'Emotion affects attention, motivation and memory' has no opened source.
checkFindings: 'Thaler and Sunstein, Nudge' is removed. Nothing in the topic text draws on it and it was not opened.

The curiosity sentence is supported. Kang and colleagues (2009) describe the information-gap account as curiosity arising from a gap between what a person knows and wants to know, and found that higher curiosity went with better later recall. The copy read is the one hosted on a co-author's university page.
The watch item on irrelevant material was stated as a rule. The one study opened shows a mixed result, so it now says 'can'.
Alaybek and colleagues (2022) support planning a high point and a close, for ratings. A short paragraph was added so readers do not read this as a learning effect.
No effect size is given for this topic because none of the sources tests the whole practice.

topics.title: Remove the friction that frustrates, keep the friction that teaches

situation.text: Learners complain the course is hard. Some of that difficulty teaches. Some is the login page.

items: List every point where learners struggle.
Sort each one: does it teach, or does it only frustrate?
Remove the second kind: confusing navigation, unclear instructions, admin, technical barriers.
Keep the first kind: recall, effort, working it out.

why.text: Some friction is the effort that builds lasting learning. Some is waste. Confusing the two is a common and costly mistake, because smoothing everything removes the learning along with the annoyance.
Polish does not replace effectiveness. A good-looking course can still fail to teach.

The difficulties that help include spacing, recall from memory, mixing topics and making errors you then correct. A difficulty stops being useful when people lack the background to overcome it. Learners often feel they are learning less under these conditions, which is why they ask for them to be removed.
Trying a problem before being taught is one such difficulty. Pooled studies found it beat teaching first, by a moderate margin. Younger children did better when taught first.

Whether to show an example first or set a problem first is an open question, and this site recommends each in different places (1.2, 2.13 and 2.19). Example first has the stronger case for people who are new to a subject and learning a procedure, where an unaided attempt would swamp working memory. Problem first is supported by a pooled analysis of 53 studies (Sinha and Kapur, 2021). It did better when learners could bring what they already knew to the problem and a full explanation followed. Those studies were of school and university students learning concepts in maths and science. Younger primary pupils did better when taught first, and so did learners of general skills not tied to a subject. A rule of thumb, and no more than that: go example first when people are new and the goal is to carry out a procedure correctly. Go problem first when they have some background, the goal is understanding, and you have time to teach it properly straight after.

why.title: When problem solving followed by instruction works
why.found: A pooled analysis of 53 studies and 166 comparisons. Problem solving followed by instruction did better than instruction followed by problem solving (g = 0.36). The gain was larger when the design followed productive failure principles closely. Pupils in school years 2 to 5 did better with instruction first.
why.means: Consider letting people who have some background attempt a hard, solvable problem before you teach the method, then teach it properly. The studies were of school and university students, not adults at work.

items.title: Protect the effort
items.text: Do not smooth away recall and struggle.

try.text: Run a friction audit on a real course. Classify each point and decide what to remove and what to protect.

try.title: Illustrative: sorting a friction list
try.text: Learners report four struggles: a login that times out, instructions spread over three emails, recall questions at the start of each module, and a case with no model answer until they have tried it. Remove the first two. Keep the last two, and say why.

items: Learners will ask you to remove the useful difficulty too. Explain why it stays.
Walk through as a newcomer. You cannot see friction you are used to.
Confusion that never resolves is not productive.

items.label: Bjork and Bjork (2020), Desirable difficulties in theory and practice. Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition, 9(4).
Sinha and Kapur (2021), When problem solving followed by instruction works: evidence for productive failure. Review of Educational Research, 2021.

topics.bodyStatus: 2 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: What are the two kinds of friction?
quiz.a: Friction that teaches, and friction that only frustrates.

quiz.q: Name two examples of friction to remove.
quiz.a: Any two of: confusing navigation, unclear instructions, admin, technical barriers.

quiz.q: What happens if you smooth everything?
quiz.a: You remove the learning with the annoyance.

openPoints: The aesthetic-usability effect (Kurosu and Kashimura 1995, Tractinsky and colleagues 2000, Norman's Emotional Design) was not searched for. If the owner wants the point back, it needs one of those sources.
The Sinha and Kapur abstract also gives a larger estimate after adjusting for publication bias. It is left out because the method could not be judged from a summary.
The claim that confusing the two kinds of friction is a common and costly mistake has no source. It is the page's own argument.
checkFindings: Bjork and Bjork (2020) confirmed on the authors' own lab page. It is a short commentary with no abstract, so the text itself was summarised. It supports the idea that some difficulty builds lasting learning and adds the condition that the learner must be able to overcome it.
Kapur's productive failure confirmed through the Sinha and Kapur (2021) meta-analysis. The effect size comes from its abstract.

The Norman reference is removed. The first pass warned that the attribution is doubtful, and it could not be checked. The sentence that people judge attractive designs as easier to use is removed with it.
The label no longer says 'see topic 1.3'.
topics.tierReason: Effortful practice such as recall, spacing and trying a problem before being taught is supported by pooled studies, but it only helps when learners can meet the challenge, and the friction audit itself is an untested practitioner tool.

topics.title: Build anticipation before the event
topics.theory: Anticipation, priming and what happens before training

situation.text: The joining email is a calendar invite and a car park map.

items: Tell people why this matters to them and what they will be able to do.
Send one question to think about, or a short task.
Have the manager talk to them before they come.
Give a first sight of the people and the place.
Keep it short.

why.text: What happens before training affects what people get from it. A pooled analysis looked at five pre-training steps: advice on what to pay attention to, strategies for checking your own understanding, advance organisers, goal orientation and preparatory information. All helped learning. The first two helped most consistently.
Whether looking forward to a course changes what people take from it has not been tested directly. Treat anticipation as a reasonable aim, not a proven effect.

why.title: Pre-training interventions and learning
why.found: A doctoral meta-analysis of 359 studies with 37,038 participants. Pre-training interventions had consistently positive effects on learning. Advice on where to direct attention and strategies for monitoring your own learning gave the most consistent gains.
why.means: Before the course, tell people what to look out for and give them a question to check their own understanding against.

items.title: One question
items.text: Give people something to think about.

try.text: Rewrite a joining email so it says why, asks one question and names what people will be able to do.

try.title: Illustrative: a joining email, before and after
try.text: Before: date, room and parking. After: two lines on why the course matters to this team, one thing people will be able to do afterwards, one question to bring an answer to, and a photo of the room and the trainer.

items: Over-selling sets up disappointment.
Pre-work that is not used is resented.
Too much contact before the event is noise.
The research tested structured steps used with the training itself. A joining email is a looser version, so check your own results.

quiz.q: Does what happens before training matter?
quiz.a: Yes. It affects what people get from it.

quiz.q: Name two things to include in a joining message.
quiz.a: Any two of: why it matters, one question, what people will be able to do.

checkFindings: Build note followed in part. The 2010 journal article by Mesmer-Magnus and Viswesvaran could not be opened. topics.title: Tell learners what to expect, and what not to

situation.text: People arrive expecting a lecture and get role-play. Or expecting answers and get questions.

items: Say in advance what the session involves, and what it does not.
Say what effort is expected of them.
Say what they will and will not be able to do at the end.
Repeat it at the start, and check for surprises.

why.text: A realistic preview lets people prepare and choose. The research behind it comes from recruitment, not training. Pooled studies of realistic job previews found that candidates who got one started with lower expectations, and that previews went with fewer leavers and better job performance. Nobody has shown the same for a training course, so treat this as a reasonable borrowing.
Being honest about limits also protects your credibility.

why.title: Realistic job previews: a meta-analysis
why.found: A pooled analysis of 40 studies. Realistic job previews went with lower starting expectations, fewer people dropping out of recruitment, lower turnover and higher job performance. Timing, medium and setting changed the size of the effect.
why.means: Give an honest preview of the course, and remember the evidence is borrowed from hiring.

items.title: Preview
items.text: What it is, and what it is not.

items.title: Honest outcomes
items.text: Do not promise mastery in a day.

try.text: Write a five-line preview for one course: what happens, what you will ask of people, what they will leave with, what they will not.

try.title: Illustrative: a five-line preview
try.text: You will spend most of the day practising in threes. There is one short role-play, and you can observe first. Bring a real conversation you need to have. You will leave with a plan for it. You will not leave an expert after one day.

items: A preview that warns too much puts people off.
Managers set expectations too. Brief them.
If the format changes, tell people.
In the recruitment studies, when and how the preview was given changed its effect. Try yours on a few people first.

items.label: Phillips (1998), Effects of realistic job previews on multiple organizational outcomes: a meta-analysis. Academy of Management Journal, 41(6). Research on recruitment, not on training.

topics.bodyStatus: 1 source checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: What should a preview say?
quiz.a: What the session involves, what it does not, and what effort is expected.

quiz.q: Where does the research on realistic previews come from?
quiz.a: Recruitment. Job previews went with lower starting expectations and fewer leavers. The idea is borrowed for training, not tested there.

quiz.q: What does honesty about limits protect?
quiz.a: Your credibility.

openPoints: Studies of previews before training were not opened: Hicks and Klimoski (1987), Academy of Management Journal, and Tannenbaum, Mathieu, Salas and Cannon-Bowers (1991), Journal of Applied Psychology. Both are leads from memory. If confirmed, the rating could rise to C.
Premack and Wanous (1985) was not searched for. Phillips (1998) is the later meta-analysis.
The sentence that honesty about limits protects your credibility is practitioner advice with no source.
checkFindings: The placeholder is replaced with Phillips (1998), a meta-analysis of realistic job previews. The page now says plainly that this research is from recruitment.
The unsupported sentence about expectation gaps is removed from the why section and the quiz.
The abstract gives directions of effect and no effect sizes, so none is quoted.
topics.tierReason: The evidence for realistic previews comes from recruitment. No study of previews given before a training course was opened, so for training this is sensible practice, not a tested method.

topics.title: Use game elements only where they help

situation.text: Someone proposes points, badges and a leaderboard to "drive engagement".

items: Say what behaviour you want more of.
Use game elements that give clear goals, feedback and visible progress.
Be wary of competition and rewards for tasks people already value.
Tie every element to the objective.
Check whether learning improved, not only activity.
Test each element by taking it away. If the practice gets worse without it, keep it. If nothing changes, it is decoration.

why.text: A pooled analysis of gamification studies found small positive effects on three kinds of outcome: what people learned (g = 0.49), their motivation (g = 0.36) and their behaviour (g = 0.25). The effect on what people learned held up in the more rigorous studies. The other two were less steady.
Rewards can reduce interest in tasks people already enjoy. Leaderboards can motivate those near the top and discourage the rest.
In the same analysis, a story wrapped round the tasks helped behaviour, and so did competition when it was combined with collaboration. Which design choices help learning itself is not yet settled.

It helps to separate two kinds of fun. Fun that carries the practice is built into the task: a clear goal, feedback on each attempt, progress the learner can see, and a story that gives the task a reason. Remove it and the practice gets worse. Decoration sits on top: points for turning up, badges for opening a page, a theme that has nothing to do with the skill. Remove it and the practice is unchanged. The first kind matches the elements this page already recommends, and the pooled analysis found that a story round the tasks helped behaviour. The analysis does not show that a more enjoyable session teaches more, so "make it fun" is a sound brief only when the fun is in the practice.

why.title: The gamification of learning: a meta-analysis
why.found: Pooled effects of gamification were small and positive: g = 0.49 for cognitive outcomes (19 studies), g = 0.36 for motivation (16 studies) and g = 0.25 for behaviour (9 studies). Only the cognitive effect stayed stable in the high-rigour studies.
why.means: Expect a modest gain at best, and measure learning, not activity.

items.title: Small, variable effects
items.text: It can help. It is not a cure.

items.title: Goals, feedback, progress
items.text: The elements that earn their place.

try.text: Take one gamified element you use. Write what behaviour it drives and whether that behaviour is learning.

try.title: Illustrative: one element, checked
try.text: Before: points for every page opened, and a leaderboard. After: a progress bar that fills only when a practice task is passed, with feedback on each attempt. No ranking. The check is whether practice scores rise, not whether logins do.

try.title: A worked example: a brief for a creative team (launch training for store staff)
lines: What people practise: the first 30 seconds with a shopper who picks up the new handset.
Goal the learner sees: "Find out what this shopper needs in three questions."
Feedback: after each attempt the shopper character reacts, and one line says what the question revealed.
Progress: five shoppers, each harder than the last. A bar fills when a shopper is helped, not when a screen is opened.
Story: a Saturday on the shop floor, opening to close.
Please do not add: points for logging in, a leaderboard between stores, or mini-games unrelated to the conversation.
How we will judge it: scores on the fifth shopper, and what field trainers see in store.

items: Points for clicking reward clicking.
Novelty wears off.
Some people dislike competing. Offer another route.
A client or creative team asks you to "make it fun". Agree what people will practise first, then ask for the goal, the feedback, the progress and the story to be built round that.
