items.label: Sailer and Homner (2020), The gamification of learning: a meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 32(1).

topics.bodyStatus: 1 source checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: How large are the effects of gamification on learning?
quiz.a: Small on average. Steadiest for what people learn, less steady for motivation and behaviour.

quiz.q: A creative team proposes a space theme, points for every module opened and a leaderboard between regions. What do you ask for instead?
quiz.a: Ask what people will practise, then for a clear goal, feedback on each attempt, visible progress and a story tied to that task. Points for opening modules reward opening modules, and ranking discourages those near the bottom.

quiz.q: A client says, "Our brand is fun, so the training must be fun." What do you say?
quiz.a: Agree, and put the fun in the practice: a challenge with a goal, quick feedback and a story from their customers' world. Check each element by asking whether the practice would be worse without it.

openPoints: Deci, Koestner and Ryan (1999), Psychological Bulletin: not opened. The sentence that rewards can reduce interest in tasks people already enjoy has no checked source on this page.
The leaderboard sentence has no checked source.
Later meta-analyses (Bai, Hew and Huang 2020, Huang and colleagues 2020, and others) were not searched for.
The abstract summary read did not state the comparison condition. From general knowledge the studies compared gamified with non-gamified learning.
checkFindings: Sailer and Homner (2020) confirmed on the University of Augsburg repository record. Effect sizes are from the abstract: cognitive g = 0.49, motivational g = 0.36, behavioural g = 0.25. The authors call all three small, so the draft's word 'small' stands, although 0.49 is at the upper end of that label.
Build note followed. 'Steadiest for learning outcomes' matches the abstract and is now in the page and the quiz.
'Wide variation between studies' and 'Design choices mattered' are replaced with what the abstract reports.

A paragraph is added on competition with collaboration. The page tells readers to be wary of competition, and the meta-analysis found competition helped behaviour when paired with collaboration. A practitioner would expect to see both.
Deci, Koestner and Ryan (1999) is removed from the list because it was not opened in this run. The old label 'Checked on topic 1.16' is not carried forward.
topics.tierReason: One meta-analysis found small positive effects, steady for what people learn and less steady for motivation and behaviour, and what makes gamification work is still unsettled.

topics.title: Design for different minds from the start
topics.theory: Inclusion, neurodiversity and Universal Design for Learning

situation.text: A participant tells you on the day that they cannot follow fast speech, read small text or sit still for ninety minutes.

items: Ask about needs in advance, in plain words.
Offer more than one way to take in content: spoken, written, visual.
Offer more than one way to take part and to show learning.
Send materials ahead.
Build in breaks, movement and quiet.
Make adjustments normal for everyone.

why.text: Designing for a range of people from the start is fairer, and usually easier, than fixing it for one person on the day. A widely used framework suggests offering several means of engagement, of presenting content and of responding.
Many adjustments help everyone. Evidence that the framework as a whole raises learning is still developing.

items.title: More than one way
items.text: To take in, take part and respond.

try.text: Take one session. List three points where a different way of taking part would cost you nothing.

try.title: Illustrative: asking in advance
try.text: The joining form asks what would help you take part, with examples: slides in advance, captions, a seat near the door, regular breaks. Nobody is asked why. Slides go to everyone two days ahead and each hour includes a five-minute break.

items: Do not ask people to disclose a diagnosis.
This is not learning styles. It is access and choice.
In the UK, the Equality Act 2010 sets duties to make reasonable adjustments. This is general information, not legal advice.
Designing for everyone does not remove the need for individual adjustments. Some people will still need something specific, so keep asking.

quiz.a: From the start.

quiz.q: What three things should have more than one route?
quiz.a: Taking in content, taking part and showing learning.

quiz.a: No. Ask what people need.

parts.title: Assess and give feedback
parts.summary: Checking what people can do, fairly, and telling them what to do next.

topics.title: Test little and often

situation.text: The only assessment is a test at the end. By then it is too late to act on what it shows.

items: Check where people start before you teach.
Add short, low-stakes checks during the course.
Use each check to adjust what you do next.
Keep the stakes low so people will risk being wrong.

why.text: Assessment has three purposes: to find the starting point, to guide learning while it happens, and to judge it at the end. The middle one is widely seen as a strong lever on learning, though estimates of its size vary.
Every test is also a learning event, because recalling strengthens memory. A short quiz teaches as it measures.

The benefit of a test shows up later, not at once. In one well-known experiment, students who reread a passage recalled more five minutes afterwards. Students who were tested on it recalled more after two days and after a week. Rereading also made people more confident, without the lasting memory to match.

why.title: Test-enhanced learning
why.found: Students read prose passages, then either reread them or took recall tests with no feedback. After five minutes the rereaders recalled more. After two days and after one week the tested group recalled substantially more.
why.means: Swap some review time for short recall quizzes, and judge them by what people remember next week.

items.title: Checks guide teaching
items.text: Use the result to change the next step.

try.text: Take a course. Add three low-stakes checks. Say what each measures and how it changes what you do.

try.title: Illustrative: three checks in one day
try.text: Start: four questions on paper, unmarked, to see what people already know. Mid-morning: each pair explains one idea aloud while you listen. After lunch: a two-minute recall quiz. The trainer drops one planned section because the first check showed people already had it.

items: A check nobody acts on is wasted.
Graded quizzes raise the stakes and lower honesty.
Feedback timing matters. Sometimes a delay helps. The rule of thumb for choosing is in 2.27.

quiz.q: What are the three purposes of assessment?
quiz.a: To find the starting point, to guide learning, and to judge it at the end.

quiz.q: Why does a quiz teach?
quiz.a: Recalling strengthens memory.

quiz.q: Why keep the stakes low?
quiz.a: So people will risk being wrong.

The watch item 'Sometimes a delay helps memory' has no checked source.
The three purposes of assessment (diagnostic, formative, summative) are standard terms. No source for the three-part scheme was opened.
Black and Wiliam reviewed school and college classrooms. Workplace training was not their subject.
checkFindings: Black and Wiliam (1998) confirmed on a University of Glasgow copy of the article. Its summary says several studies give firm evidence that strengthening frequent feedback to learners produces substantial learning gains. This supports the paragraph on the middle purpose of assessment.

topics.title: Assess the real task, not a quiz about it

situation.text: Facilitators are certified with a multiple-choice quiz. Nobody has watched them run a room.

items: Ask what the person must do in real life.
Set a task as close to that as you safely can.
Watch the performance.
Write the criteria down as a rubric and share it in advance.

why.text: A written test cannot certify a skill that is performed. Authentic assessment measures someone doing something close to the real task, in place of answering questions about it.
A rubric makes the criteria explicit, so people know what good looks like. Check that assessors agree by comparing marks on a sample.
A review of rubric research concluded that the criteria are what matter most. Criteria that count trivial things pull attention away from the substance of the work.

items.title: Match the format to the skill
Share the rubric
items.text: People should know what good looks like.

try.text: Design a performance assessment with a rubric for a real skill. Check the task mirrors the workplace.

try.title: Illustrative: certifying a facilitator
try.text: Before: a 20-question multiple-choice quiz. After: each person runs a 15-minute segment with a real group. Two observers use a shared rubric with four criteria, such as how questions are handled. The rubric is sent a week ahead.

try.title: A worked example: rubric for a recorded sales conversation (first meeting, 20 minutes)

head: Criterion
Not yet
Meets the standard
Strong
rows: Starts on the product. The customer is not asked how long they have or what they want from the call.
States the purpose and checks the time available. Asks what the customer wants from the call.
Does both, and refers to something specific about the customer's business found before the call.
Asks fewer than three questions, or only yes or no questions. Talks for most of the first ten minutes.
Asks at least four open questions. Plays back the customer's main problem in the customer's words, and the customer agrees.
Also asks what the problem costs and who else it affects. The customer talks for more than half of this part.
Lists features in a fixed order. No feature is tied to anything the customer said.
Presents no more than three features. Ties each to a need the customer stated.
Leaves out features the customer does not need and says so. Checks after each one whether it answers the need.
The call ends with "I will send you some information". No date and no named person.
A specific next step is agreed, with a date and who will do what.
The customer proposes or confirms the step in their own words. A second contact is named.

items: Observation costs time. Budget for it.
A rubric that rewards the trivial will be gamed.
Simulations help where the real task is unsafe.
A realistic task is not valid by default. Ask the same questions of it as of any test: what the score means and what follows from using it.
Two assessors should mark the same recording separately before the rubric is used for real. Where they disagree, rewrite the level description until they do not.

topics.title: Check the test measures what you think it does

situation.text: Scores are high and everyone is pleased. Nobody has asked what the test actually measures.

items: Ask what the assessment really measures.
Look for things that affect the score and are not the skill: reading load, cultural references, test technique.
Check two assessors would give the same result.
Check it matches the objectives and what was taught.

why.text: Validity is whether an assessment measures what it claims to. Measuring the wrong thing accurately is still useless. Reliability is whether it gives consistent results across assessors and occasions.
The two can pull against each other. Realistic tasks are often harder to mark consistently.

Validity is not a fixed property of a test. In Messick's account it is a judgement about what the scores mean and how they are used, and it includes the consequences of using them. Content, links to other measures and consequences are all evidence for the same question.

items.title: Validity
items.text: Does it measure what it claims?

try.text: Critique an assessment for threats to validity. Propose fixes.

try.title: Illustrative: what a test really measures
try.text: A customer service test uses long written scenarios. People with strong reading skills score highest, whatever their service skills. The fix: shorter scenarios, some played as audio, and a second marker on a sample to check agreement.

items: High scores on a poor measure tell you nothing.
A pass mark should be reasoned, not picked.
Assessment shapes what people study. Check what yours rewards.

topics.title: Give feedback people can act on

situation.text: Feedback on the exercise reads "Great job" or "Needs work". Nobody knows what to do next.

items: Say where the person is heading.
Say how they are doing against that.
Say what to do next.
Comment on the task and the method, not the person.
Give time to act on it.

why.text: The most useful feedback answers three questions: where am I going, how am I doing, and what next. Feedback about the task and the process helps. Praise of the person is among the least effective kinds.
Fair assessment removes barriers that have nothing to do with the skill, so that it measures capability and not disadvantage.

Feedback is not always good. A pooled analysis found that it improved performance on average, yet more than a third of feedback interventions made performance worse. Feedback worked less well as it pulled attention away from the task and towards the self.

When to give feedback has no single answer. A review of the feedback research (Shute, 2008) found the timing studies in conflict, with many field studies favouring immediate feedback and many laboratory studies favouring a delay. Its working guidelines are to give feedback straight away when the task is hard for the person, or is a procedure they are still learning. Consider holding it back when the task is easy for them, or when the aim is for them to apply an idea somewhere new. The review presents these as provisional and says the point about applying ideas needs more research.

A reasonable reading for a training room: correct a new procedure while it is being practised, as 1.6 advises. Let people finish a recall quiz or a case before you go through the answers, as 2.24 allows. Both are consistent with the review. Neither is settled.

why.title: The effects of feedback interventions on performance
why.found: A meta-analysis of 607 effect sizes and 23,663 observations. Feedback improved performance on average (d = 0.41), but over one third of feedback interventions reduced it. Feedback became less effective as it moved attention from the task towards the self.
why.means: Keep feedback on the task and the next step, and leave out comments on the person.

items.title: Three questions
items.text: Where to, how am I doing, what next.

items.title: Time to act
items.text: Feedback nobody can use is wasted.

try.text: Rewrite a weak piece of feedback so it addresses the task and gives a clear next step.

try.title: Illustrative: feedback, before and after
try.text: Before: Needs work. After: The aim is a brief the group can act on without asking you questions. Yours gives the task clearly but no time limit or output. Add both, then try it on a colleague before Thursday.

items: Feedback only works where people feel safe enough to hear it.
Marking by judgement carries bias. Use rubrics and compare notes with another assessor.
Too much feedback at once is not used.

parts.title: Plan for the workplace
parts.summary: Diagnosis, compliance, onboarding, scale and the methods that suit work skills.

topics.title: Know what training can do, on average
topics.theory: Training effectiveness: what the pooled workplace studies show

situation.text: In a scoping call a finance director asks you whether training works at all, or whether people just enjoy a day out. You need an honest answer in two sentences, and you need to avoid promising the average.

items: Answer the question directly. On average, well-designed training in organisations works, and the pooled effects are medium to large.
Give the comparison with the number. The main meta-analysis pooled comparisons between groups and left out studies that only measured one group before and after.
Say what was measured. The average was about the same for what people felt, what they learned, what they did at work and what the organisation got. Far fewer studies measured the last of those.
Do not promise the average for this programme. Results varied with the training method and with the kind of skill.
Move the conversation from whether to how. The research review that sits beside the meta-analysis says what happens before and after the session matters as much as the session.
Offer three commitments that follow from it: a needs analysis first (2.1), methods built on sound principles of learning, and a plan for use and evaluation afterwards (2.4, 2.5).
Write the claim into the proposal in the same careful words.

why.text: Arthur and colleagues pooled 397 results from studies of training in organisations. The average effect was d = 0.60 for reactions, 0.63 for learning, 0.62 for behaviour at work and 0.62 for organisational results. The authors call this medium to large. The method used and the kind of skill trained were both related to how well training worked.

Read the figures with their limits. They compare groups, and the paper says little about what the comparison groups received. The results figure rests on 26 studies and the learning figure on 234. Team training was excluded, and so were trainee factors such as motivation and ability. Only 22 of the 397 results reported a needs analysis, too few to show whether one helps.

Salas and colleagues reviewed the wider research for a general audience. Their conclusion is that training works when it is designed well, and that the design reaches beyond the session: analyse the need and prepare the climate beforehand, use sound instructional methods and build the right mindset during, and check transfer and evaluate afterwards. It is a narrative review and gives no pooled number.

why.title: Effectiveness of training in organizations
why.found: A meta-analysis of training in organisations. Sample-weighted average effects were d = 0.60 for reaction measures (15 studies), 0.63 for learning (234), 0.62 for behaviour (122) and 0.62 for results (26). Single-group before-and-after studies were excluded.
why.means: You can say training works on average and by a worthwhile margin. Say what was compared, and do not carry the average over to one programme.

try.text: Ask a colleague to play a sceptical finance director. Give your answer to "does training work?" aloud in under 40 seconds, using the lines below as a base. Record it. Listen back for any sentence that sounds like a guarantee and say it again without one.

try.title: Words you can use with a sceptical sponsor
lines: "Fair question. The short answer is yes, on average, and by a decent margin."
"The best pooled study covers a few hundred results from workplaces. Trained groups came out ahead of comparison groups on learning, on what people did at work, and on business results."
"Two cautions. That is an average, and it hides a wide spread. And fewer studies measured business results than measured learning."
"What separates the good programmes is mostly outside the session: whether the need was checked first, and whether anyone made room for people to use it after."
"So I will not promise you the average. I will tell you what has to be in place for this one to work, and how we will know."

try.title: A worked example: what you can and cannot claim

head: You want to say
Supported
Say it like this
rows: Yes, on average, for organisational training against comparison groups.
"Pooled studies show a medium to large average effect."
It changes behaviour, not only knowledge.
Yes on average. 122 studies measured behaviour.
"The average effect on behaviour at work was about the same as on learning."
"Some studies show business results. We should measure yours."
Our programme will deliver a 0.6 effect.
No. Averages do not transfer to one case.
A needs analysis makes it work better.
Recommended by the research review. Too few studies in the meta-analysis to tell.
"The research review recommends it, and it lowers the risk of training the wrong thing."

items: Quoting d = 0.62 to a client with no comparison. A number without "compared with what" invites the wrong reading. Use words unless they ask.
Treating four similar averages as proof that happy learners perform better. The paper did not test that link, and topic 6.2 shows reactions and learning are only loosely related.
Forgetting what was left out. These studies are of individual training with a comparison group. Team training and before-and-after studies are not in the average.

topics.title: Run a performance diagnosis

situation.text: A sales director asks for a refresher course because the team is not using the new product pitch. They were all trained on it three months ago.

items: Pin down the gap in something you can count or watch. Ask: "What are people doing now, what should they be doing, and how do you know?" Topic 2.1 covers the gap.

Check six causes, in this order: expectations, feedback, tools and resources, incentives, skills and knowledge, capacity and motives. Check the first four first. They belong to the organisation and a course cannot fix them.
Ask one plain question for each cause. The worked example below gives them. Write down evidence, not impressions.

Talk to the sponsor, two or three line managers, and four to six of the people doing the job. Include one or two who already do it well. Add whoever owns the tools and the pay plan. Allow 30 minutes each.
Watch the work: three to five calls or meetings, live or recorded. Ask for data the client already holds, such as usage reports.
Write one page: the gap, what you found under each cause, a verdict in two sentences, and a fix with a named owner for each cause that matters. Say which part training can fix.
Talk the sponsor through the page first. Pass each non-training fix to its owner, such as sales operations or the HR partner.
Offer the diagnosis as its own small piece of work: two to three days of your time across two weeks, a fixed fee, one page and a one-hour readout, with no commitment to buy the course afterwards.

why.text: This is practitioner method. The six-cause list follows Thomas Gilbert's Behavior Engineering Model, set out in his book Human Competence. The model sorts causes into those in the work environment and those in the person. Chevalier (2003) presents it as a systematic way to find what is getting in the way of performance. Winiecki (2015) points out that it has been reworked so often that versions differ. So choose one list and keep to it.
None of these sources tests whether diagnosing this way leads to better results. The research case for analysing the need first is in topic 2.1. The framework gives you a fixed order of questions.

Topics 1.20, 9.3 and 9.14 touch the same idea and leave open who pays. If you are external, nobody has agreed to give you access until the course is sold. A small paid diagnosis gives you a reason to ask for interviews and data, and makes "this is mostly not a training problem" a finding the client paid for. If the client will not buy it, do the small version: three 30-minute calls and one data export. Mark every cause you could not check as "not checked".

try.text: Take a request you have had, or one from a past job. Fill in the six causes on one page from what you already know. Mark each line "known" or "guess". Then record yourself giving the two-sentence verdict aloud, as you would to the sponsor.

quiz.q: Which four of the six causes belong to the organisation and not the person?
quiz.a: Expectations, feedback, tools and resources, and incentives.

quiz.q: A support manager asks for a course on a new ticketing system. Agents were trained last month and still use the old one. You have two days. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask the six questions of a few agents, a manager and whoever owns the system, and look at usage data. You are checking whether the old system is still switched on, expected or simply faster before you assume a skill gap.

quiz.q: Your diagnosis finds the main cause is the commission plan. The sponsor says, "Fine, but can you still run the course?" What do you do?
quiz.a: Offer to train only the part that is a skill gap, and put the commission finding in writing with the owner named. That way nobody later judges the course on a result it could not have produced.

topics.title: Do compliance training properly
topics.theory: Compliance training: the record and the behaviour

situation.text: A client needs every member of staff through data protection training by the end of the quarter. Everyone clicks through the current hour-long module, and the same mistakes keep happening.

items: Ask the client's compliance or risk owner which rule this training serves, what an auditor or regulator would ask to see, and what has gone wrong recently. Do not guess the law yourself.
Write two aims side by side. One is the record: proof that named people were trained on a dated version. The other is the behaviour: the two or three things people must do so the risk falls.
Target by risk. Everyone gets a short core. Roles that handle the risk every day get more time, real cases and practice.
Build the test from job situations, with wrong answers that are real mistakes. Set the pass mark with the compliance owner.

Offer a test-out where the rule allows it. People take the scenario test first. Those who pass skip the teaching and still get a record. Ask the compliance owner first, because some rules may require the training itself.
Keep refreshers short: 10 to 15 minutes on changes and on recent errors. The client sets the interval.
Agree the record before launch: who, which version, the date, the result, and a copy of the material as delivered.
Report completion to whoever answers to the auditor, and a behaviour measure, such as incidents or spot checks, to whoever owns the risk.

why.text: The auditor needs evidence and the business needs fewer incidents. Topic 6.7 warns that completions alone say little. In regulated training the record is still something the client may be asked to produce.

The Health and Safety Executive says employers must give everyone who works for them clear instructions and information, and adequate training and supervision. That includes contractors and self-employed people. It asks for particular attention to new recruits, people changing jobs and young employees. Its guidance on work equipment says training should cover how the equipment is used, the risks and the precautions. Training may need refreshing at suitable intervals, with no fixed period given, and should normally happen in working hours at no cost to the employee.

The Information Commissioner's Office sets out what it expects when it audits data protection training. All staff are covered. Induction training comes before a person has access to personal information, and within a month of starting. Refreshers happen at appropriate intervals. Completion is monitored and followed up. The organisation keeps copies of the material and records of who received it. An end assessment can carry a minimum pass mark. The ICO calls these ways to meet its expectations, not mandatory steps, and says the guidance is under review. This is general information, not legal advice.

Risk-based targeting, testing out and short refreshers are design practice. Neither body prescribes them. The HSE leaflet on training does give five steps that fit: decide what training is needed, set priorities, choose methods, deliver it, and check that it worked.

try.text: Take one compliance module you have sat through. Write the two aims for it: the record, and the two or three behaviours. Then write one scenario question and read it aloud to a colleague. See whether they can answer without the module.

quiz.q: What are the two duties of compliance training?
quiz.a: Evidence that named people were trained, and behaviour that lowers the risk.

quiz.q: A client wants to let experienced staff skip the annual module if they pass a test first. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask the client's compliance owner whether the rule allows it, and get the answer in writing. If it does, build the test from job scenarios and keep a record for those who test out.

quiz.q: Completion is at 98 per cent and the same data protection mistake happened twice last month. The client says the training is working. What do you say?
quiz.a: The record is in good order and the behaviour has not changed. Suggest a short refresher built on that exact mistake, checked with a scenario, and a behaviour measure reported beside completion.

topics.title: Design onboarding that gets people productive
topics.theory: Onboarding: first day, first week, first 90 days

situation.text: A new account manager spends week one in back-to-back presentations from every department. In week five they still cannot run a customer call alone, and their manager asks what the induction was for.

items: Agree with the hiring manager what "productive" means, as things you could watch. For example: runs a renewal call alone, or forecasts their accounts within the agreed margin. Set a date for each.
Work back from those into three milestones at 30, 60 and 90 days. Each one is something the person can do, not something they have attended.
Before day one, send the first-week timetable, the name of their buddy and what to bring. Ask IT for accounts and equipment to be ready. A first day spent waiting for a password is remembered.
Day one has four jobs: meet the manager and the buddy, get systems working, see the real work being done, and complete one small real task before going home.
In week one, teach only what the person needs in order to start. Topic 2.6 makes this point. Put everything else on a dated list across the 90 days, close to when it will be used.
Give the manager a written part: a 30-minute one-to-one every week, and a review at each milestone against the agreed list. Topic 2.4 covers manager briefs.
Give the buddy a part too: one shadowing session in week one, and a standing 15 minutes twice a week for the first month for the questions nobody wants to ask the manager.
At 90 days, ask the new starter what they needed earlier and what could have waited. Change the plan for the next person.

why.text: Most of this is practitioner judgement about order and load. The test of an onboarding plan is how soon someone can do the job without help, so the plan is written as milestones the manager can check.

One piece of research shapes the aims. A meta-analysis of 70 samples of newcomers found that three things carried the effect of an organisation's induction through to later performance, satisfaction and staying: being clear about the role, feeling able to do the job, and feeling accepted by colleagues. Topic 2.7 describes it. That is why day one includes a real task and a buddy as well as information. The study is about what goes with good outcomes across many organisations. It did not test a 30-60-90 plan.

The manager matters more than the programme. You can design a good first week and have it undone by a manager who cancels the one-to-ones. If you are external, you rarely control that. Write the manager's part down, get the sponsor to send it, and build the milestone reviews into the manager's diary before the person starts.

try.text: Pick a role you know. Write three things a person in it should be able to do alone by day 90, each as something you could watch. Then explain the plan aloud, in two minutes, as if to the hiring manager. If you find yourself listing sessions, go back to the milestones.

quiz.q: Six department heads each want an hour with new starters in week one. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask each what the new starter must be able to do with their department, and when that first comes up. Give them a slot near that date, and keep week one for what the person needs in order to start.

topics.title: Design for scale

situation.text: Your one-day workshop went well with twelve people. The client now wants it delivered to 600 staff in four countries by eight facilitators you have never met.

items: Decide what is fixed and what is local before you write anything else. Fix the outcomes, the practice tasks, the assessment and the timings of the main blocks. Leave the examples, the stories and the opening to the facilitator.

Write the facilitator guide as the product. At scale the guide is the design, and your own delivery is one instance of it. The topic "Write a facilitator guide someone else can deliver from" in Stage 3 shows a page.

Pilot twice. Run the first pilot yourself to fix the design. Have someone else run the second from the guide alone while you watch and say nothing. Every question they ask you afterwards is a gap in the guide.

Train the facilitators in three passes. They take the workshop as participants. They teach back one segment each and get feedback. They co-deliver once with someone already signed off. Topic 5.10 covers sign-off by observation.
Plan the waves. Start with one site and two facilitators. Fix what breaks, then widen. Leave a week between the first two waves for changes.

Control versions. Keep one master set. Print the version number and date in the footer of every page and slide. Release changes in numbered batches with a short change note. Topic 3.18 covers the filing.
Hold a 30-minute facilitator call every week for the first month, then monthly. Ask two questions: what did you change, and what did people get stuck on.
Check for drift. Observe a sample of sessions against the fixed elements, and compare assessment results by facilitator.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. Topic 5.10 notes that the research on train-the-trainer is thin, and no study of how to scale a design was opened for this topic.

The reasoning runs like this. A design that lives in your head varies every time someone else delivers it. Some variation helps: a facilitator who uses their own examples is more believable than one reading yours. Some variation breaks the design, such as cutting the practice to make room for more talk. So you separate the two in writing. What you fix is whatever the outcome depends on. What you leave open is whatever makes the session belong to that room.

Scale also changes what the client is buying. A head of learning buying for 600 people is asking how you will keep session 40 as good as session 4, what it costs per person, and what happens when a facilitator leaves. Pilots, sign-off and version control are your answers. They also take time, and that time belongs in the quote.

try.text: Take a session you have run or designed. List every element and mark it "fixed" or "local", with a reason. Then hand your notes for one 20-minute segment to a colleague and ask them to deliver it to you with no briefing. Write down each point where they hesitate or ask.

quiz.q: Why run the second pilot with someone else delivering from the guide alone?
quiz.a: It shows where the guide is not enough. Each question they ask is a gap to fill.

quiz.q: A local facilitator wants to drop the afternoon practice and add a talk from the regional manager. What do you do?
quiz.a: Say no to cutting the practice, because it is a fixed element the outcome depends on. Offer the regional manager ten minutes at the opening, which is local.

quiz.q: Assessment results from one facilitator's sessions are well above everyone else's. What do you do?
quiz.a: Watch one of their sessions before drawing a conclusion. They may be doing something worth copying, or marking to a different standard, and the numbers alone cannot tell you which.

topics.title: Choose group size and staffing
topics.theory: Group size, feedback time and when to add a facilitator

situation.text: You quoted for twelve. A week before the workshop the client says, "We have had a lot of interest. Can we make it twenty?"

items: Start from the promise. If the session promises that each person will practise the skill and get feedback from a trainer, the limit is feedback time.
Do the sum. Count the minutes of practice time in the day. Divide by the length of one observed turn, including feedback. That is the number of turns one trainer can watch.

Use this example to check your own. A turn of six minutes with four minutes of feedback is ten minutes, so one trainer watches six turns an hour. A day with three hours of practice gives 18 watched turns. Twelve people get one each with some to spare. Nine people get two each.

Set your position before the client asks. For a skills workshop with trainer feedback, a common practitioner ceiling for one trainer is 12, or 16 with less feedback each. State it in the proposal with the reason.
Add a second facilitator when the sum does not work, when groups will be in separate rooms, or when the content may upset people and someone may need to step out with a participant.
Change the design as numbers change. The table below shows how.

Plan for the day the numbers are wrong. If six turn up where twelve were expected, run pairs and lengthen the debriefs. If twenty turn up, cut one activity, keep the practice, and say aloud what has changed.
When the client wants to add people, give three options: a second facilitator, a second date, or the same day with less individual feedback. Say what each one costs them.

why.text: All of this is practitioner judgement. No research on the best group size for workplace training was opened for this topic, and the numbers here are working figures that experienced trainers use. Check them against your own sum.

The reasoning is simple arithmetic. Input scales well: sixty people can hear a ten-minute explanation as easily as six. Practice with feedback does not scale, because a trainer can only watch one conversation at a time. So the more a session depends on watched practice, the smaller the group one trainer can serve. A session that is mostly discussion or planning can take more people.

Group size is also the first place a client tries to save money, because adding people looks free. Showing the sum changes the conversation. The client can see that eight more people means either less feedback for everyone or a second trainer, and can choose.

try.text: Take a session plan you have. Add up the practice minutes and do the sum for 8, 16 and 30 people. Then rehearse aloud, with a colleague playing the client, your answer to "Can we make it twenty?" Record it and listen for whether you gave a reason and a choice.

quiz.q: In a skills workshop with trainer feedback, what sets the limit on group size?
quiz.a: Feedback time: how many practice turns one trainer can watch in the practice minutes available.

quiz.q: Your day has two hours of practice and each watched turn takes ten minutes. Sixteen people are booked and each has been promised trainer feedback. What do you do?
quiz.a: One trainer can watch twelve turns, so four people would miss out. Bring a second facilitator, shorten the turns, or tell the client the promise has to change.

quiz.q: Six people arrive for a workshop planned for twelve in trios. What do you do?
quiz.a: Drop the trios and run the practice in pairs or in front of the group, with longer debriefs. Tell the group they will get more individual feedback than planned.

topics.title: Teach interpersonal skills by showing, practising and giving feedback

situation.text: You have 60 minutes to teach a sales team how to handle a price objection. The current session explains a model on slides.

items: Choose one skill small enough to perform in three minutes. Write its three to five key points as rules that say what to do and why, such as "Ask what they are comparing the price with, so you answer the real objection."
Show the key points first. Then show a model: a live demonstration with a colleague, or a two-minute video. Keep the key points off the screen while the model runs.
Show a poor version as well as a good one. Ask which key points were missing.
Give one quiet minute for each person to picture using the points in a conversation they have coming up.
Have people write their own practice scenarios from real customers.
Practise in threes: one person plays the seller, one plays the customer from the scenario, one observes with the key points on a card. Rotate.
Give feedback after each turn against the key points only. The observer speaks first, then you. Then the person retries the weakest point.
Close with a goal and a manager. Each person writes when they will next use the skill. Their manager, briefed beforehand, asks about it within a week.

why.text: This method is called behaviour modelling training: describe the key points, show a model, let people practise, and give feedback.

why.title: A meta-analysis of behaviour modelling training
why.found: The review pooled 117 studies. Effects were largest on learning outcomes, smaller on behaviour at work and smaller again on results. Knowledge gains faded with time. Skill and job behaviour held or grew. Skill grew most when key points were given as rules and when training time was longest. Transfer was greatest with models of both good and poor behaviour, practice scenarios written by trainees, instructions to set goals, managers who were also trained, and rewards and sanctions for the skill at work.
why.means: Write the key points as rules, show a poor example beside the good one, let people practise on their own cases, and plan the goal and the manager's part before the session.

why.text: Most steps above follow one of those findings. Two do not come from the abstract: keeping the key points off the screen during the model, and picturing the conversation before practising. Both are from a later summary of this research. Only the abstract of the meta-analysis was read, so no effect sizes are given here.

The findings are patterns across many studies. They show what went with better results and do not promise that one feature will work in your session. The smaller effect on results at work is a reminder that what managers do afterwards carries weight (topic 2.4).
If you are external and cannot reach the managers, send each participant home with their goal on a card and one question for their manager to ask.

try.text: Write the key points of a short interpersonal skill as rules. Then record yourself on your phone modelling it twice with a friend: once well, once with two points missing. Check that a stranger could name what was missing.

try.title: Key points written as rules, for the flipchart
lines: 1. Pause and thank them for raising it, so they know you are not going to argue.
2. Ask what they are comparing the price with, so you answer the real objection.
3. Link the price to the one result they told you matters most, so the number has something to stand against.
4. Ask what would need to be true for the price to make sense, so the next step is theirs.

items: The model is too polished and people decide they could never do it. Use a believable colleague.
Key points written as a script get recited. Keep them as rules with reasons.
The poor model is a joke. Make it the ordinary mistake.
The demonstration runs long and practice is cut. Hold each model to two minutes.
Feedback wanders to personality. Hold it to the key points.

parts.title: Enablement programmes
parts.summary: How enablement differs from training, and how to plan it, launch a product, train retail staff and partners, coach through managers and run a large event. Mostly professional practice, and labelled as such.

topics.title: Know what enablement is

situation.text: A client introduces herself as head of sales enablement and asks what you would do about ramp time in her new markets. You have designed courses for years and you are not sure what she is asking you for.

items: Learn the working definition. Enablement is a standing service that gives customer-facing people what they need to sell or serve: content, training, coaching and tools. It is judged on commercial results, not on courses delivered.
Set it beside training. Training is one of the four things enablement supplies. A course has an end date. Enablement runs all year and changes whenever the product, the price or the market changes.
Find out who owns it in this client. Ask three questions in the first meeting: who does the enablement lead report to, who writes the product messaging, and who owns the sales system and its data.

Draw the client's map on one page. Put the enablement team in the middle. Round it put product marketing (messaging and launch content), sales operations (systems, data, targets), sales managers (coaching) and the learning team (platform, leadership programmes).
Ask which commercial measure the work is tied to before you propose anything. Typical ones are ramp time, win rate and sales of a new product. Then ask who can give you the figures.
In every proposal, name which of the four supplies you are providing and who provides the other three. A workshop with no content, coaching or tool behind it is a training event.

why.text: This topic is professional practice. There is no agreed academic definition of enablement and very little research on it. The one academic study opened for this page says as much in its abstract.

The description above is the common working one in technology companies. Titles and reporting lines vary a great deal. It may sit under the sales leader, operations or marketing, and in a small company it is one person. So ask, and draw the map.

The difference from training matters to you for a practical reason. An enablement lead is measured on a sales figure and has a calendar driven by launches and quarters. If you talk about learning objectives and course hours, you are answering a question she did not ask. If you talk about what sellers will be able to say and do by a date, and how you will both know, you are speaking her language.

why.title: Sales enablement: conceptualizing and developing a dynamic capability
why.found: The abstract reports an ethnographic study built mainly on 41 in-depth interviews with people who design or run sales enablement. It notes that empirical research on enablement is lacking and proposes a process model of how firms build it as a capability.
why.means: Treat what you read about enablement, including this page, as practice. Nobody has yet tested which enablement set-up produces better sales results.

try.text: Record yourself for two minutes explaining to a friend outside the industry what enablement is and how it differs from training. Use four of the terms below. Play it back, note where you hesitated, and record it again.

try.title: Terms you will hear in the first meeting

head: Term
Plain meaning
rows: The ongoing supply of content, training, coaching and tools to people who sell or serve customers.
Enablement for the sales team. Some clients say revenue enablement when it also covers customer success and partners.
The sellers and technical specialists who talk to customers, as opposed to head office.
Other companies that sell or fit the client's product: resellers, distributors, retailers.
The team that decides how a product is described and to whom. Usually the source of launch content.
The team that runs the sales system, targets and reports. Sometimes called revenue operations.
The sales target a seller must reach in a period.
The deals in progress, by stage.
How long a new seller takes to reach an agreed level, such as a first deal or full quota.
The share of deals pursued that are won.
A written guide to selling one product or to one kind of customer.
One page on how to answer a named competitor.
Sell-in is what the retailer buys from the client. Sell-out is what shoppers buy from the retailer.

items: Promising a commercial result that training alone cannot deliver. Say which part of the result your work can move and what else has to be true.
Assuming the learning team is your client. The budget often sits with sales or marketing.
Using the client's terms loosely. Ramp time has a different definition in every company. Ask for theirs and write it down.
Treating enablement as a new name for product training. The client will ask about content, coaching and tools as well.

topics.title: Plan a sales enablement cycle

situation.text: It is October. The client's enablement lead has next year's budget to defend and a list of forty requests from product teams. She asks you to help turn it into a plan the sales leader will accept.

items: Start from the client's fixed dates, not from the content. Mark the financial year, quarter ends, the sales kick-off, known product launches and the busiest selling weeks.
Protect selling time. Agree with the sales leader how many hours a seller may spend in training each quarter and where. A common rule is nothing live in the last two weeks of a quarter.

Sort every request into four layers. The annual plan holds the few themes for the year. Launches are tied to a product date. In-quarter campaigns push one skill or message for four to six weeks. Always-on resources are what a seller can look up at any time.
Give each quarter one campaign. If the list has three, ask the sales leader to choose. Everything else goes to always-on or to next quarter.
For each launch and campaign, write one line: what sellers will do differently, by when, and which figure should move.
Name an owner and a review date for every always-on resource. A playbook with no owner is out of date within two releases.
Leave one month in four with no new live training. Use it for manager coaching and for fixing what the last campaign showed.
Review the plan with the sales leader each quarter. Apply 2.3 when you shape each campaign.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. No study opened for this page tested one way of planning an enablement year against another.

The reasoning is about attention and timing. Sellers are paid on a quarterly target, so anything that takes them off the phone near quarter end will be skipped or resented. A plan built round their calendar gets attended.

The four layers stop two common failures. Without a campaign layer, each product team sends its own training and sellers receive a dozen unrelated asks a month. Without an always-on layer, every question becomes a request for a session. Sorting also gives the enablement lead a fair way to say no, which 9.14 covers.
The research on sales training is thin, as the review below shows. That is a reason to build a measure into each line of the plan.

why.title: Sales training: a state of the art and contemporary review
why.found: A review of 56 articles on sales training published from 1985 to 2014. Most were surveys and only two were experiments. Findings on effectiveness were generally positive but mixed, and several studies reported sellers returning to old habits once back in the field.
why.means: Do not tell a client that sales training is proven to raise sales. Plan the follow-up, and agree a figure to watch for each campaign.

try.text: Take the calendar below to a colleague and present it aloud in five minutes as if they were the sales leader. Ask them to interrupt with "why not in March?" and "can we add one more?". Hold to one campaign a quarter.

try.title: A worked example: one enablement year for an invented software company (financial year from January, 120 sellers, three regions)

head: Month
Fixed dates
Launch or campaign
Always-on work
rows: Kick-off sets the year's theme: selling to finance buyers
Campaign 1 starts: discovery questions for finance buyers, five weeks
Quarter end, no live sessions from the 15th
Managers review two live deals per seller
Launch readiness for the spring release, weeks 1 to 6
Launch week, then field questions collected
No new training. Fix launch content from field questions
Launch guide moved into the playbook
Managers coach on pricing in deal reviews
Launch readiness, smaller release, three weeks
Campaign 3: renewals and expansion, four weeks

items: The plan fills every week. Leave gaps, because a product date will move and something has to give.
Kick-off carries the whole year. Treat it as the start of the first campaign, with follow-up already booked.
Always-on becomes a dumping ground. If a resource has no owner and no review date, do not publish it.
Nobody agrees the figure to watch until the campaign is over. Agree it in the planning meeting, as 9.6 sets out.

quiz.q: Three product teams each want a live session for all sellers in the last fortnight of the quarter. What do you do?
quiz.a: Move all three out of that fortnight and ask the sales leader to pick one as next quarter's campaign. Sellers will not give attention at quarter end, and three unrelated asks compete with each other.

quiz.a: Find or appoint an owner, then update or retire it this week. Give every always-on resource a named owner and a review date so this does not recur.

topics.title: Get a team ready for a product launch

situation.text: The launch date is public and will not move. The product team changed the pricing yesterday, half of what you have been told is under embargo, and 400 sellers, 60 partner firms and a retail chain all need to be ready on the same morning.

items: Agree what ready means, per audience, in one sentence each. For a field seller: can explain who the product is for, run the three-minute demo and answer the five likeliest questions.
Get the embargo rules in writing from the launch owner. List who may know what, from which date, and what must never appear in a file sent outside the company.

Split content into stable and volatile. Customer problems and the audience rarely change late. Price, names, dates and screenshots do. Build the stable part first and keep volatile facts on one sheet that everything else points to.
Set a content freeze date and a change rule. After the freeze only the launch owner can approve a change, and each change is logged with a version number and date.
Plan the cascade in waves. The core team first, then regional leads and managers, then field sellers, then partners and retail as the embargo allows.
Build in practice, not only briefings. Every seller should say the pitch aloud and be heard by a manager or peer before launch day.
Run a readiness check a week before. Use a short spoken or recorded pitch, not only a quiz. Report the result by region to the launch owner.
Staff the first two weeks after launch. Collect field questions daily and answer them in one place.

why.text: Launch readiness is professional practice. No study opened for this page compared launch plans.

One piece of research does bear on what the training should do. A study that tracked industrial salespeople through two product launches found that sellers who felt positive about selling the new product and confident that they could sell it formed stronger intentions and grew sales faster. Pressure from others to sell it worked less well, and it weakened the other two effects. That fits the craft view that a launch needs practice until sellers feel able. It is one study in one setting.
Separating stable from volatile content is what makes a moving product manageable. A price on forty slides means forty edits. A price on one sheet is changed once.

why.title: Motivating salespeople to sell new products
why.found: A longitudinal study of industrial salespeople across two launches, using surveys and daily sales records. Positive attitudes to selling the new product and self-efficacy built selling intentions and faster sales growth. Perceived pressure from others was less effective and weakened those effects.
why.means: Spend launch training time on practice that builds confidence with the product. Do not rely on telling sellers how important the launch is.

try.text: Write the one-sentence definition of ready for a launch you know. Then, standing up, give a colleague the two-minute briefing you would give regional leads in week 4: what is fixed, what may change, what they must not share. Ask them to repeat back the embargo rule.

head: Week
Content

Sign-off
rows: Ready defined per audience. Embargo list agreed. Facts sheet started
Stable content drafted: customer problems, who it is for, questions to ask
Demo script and conversation guide drafted. Translation starts on stable content

Managers rehearse the pitch with each other
Partner and retail versions cut, embargoed facts removed

topics.title: Turn product knowledge into customer conversations

situation.text: The product manager has sent a 60-slide deck listing every feature. Sellers sat through it last quarter, passed the quiz, and still open customer calls by reading out the feature list.

items: Pick the three or four features that matter most to the customers these sellers meet. Leave the full list as a reference document.
For each one, ask the product manager and two good sellers the same question: which customer has this problem, and how do they describe it in their own words.

Write the feature up as a conversation guide, not a description. Use the six headings in the artefact: who cares, the problem, a question to ask, how to say it in one sentence, proof, and the likely objection.
Get the proof from the client. Use only customer stories and figures the client has approved for use. If there is none, write "no approved proof yet" and tell the launch owner.
Show the conversation done well and done badly. A two-minute recording of each is enough. Say what the rule is behind the good one.
Have every seller practise aloud in threes: seller, customer, observer. Give the customer a card with a role and one objection. Four minutes, then two minutes of feedback, then rotate.
Ask sellers to write one real account where they will use the guide this week, and tell their manager which.

why.text: Two bodies of research support the direction of this topic. Neither tested a conversation guide as such.

A meta-analysis of what predicts sales performance, covering studies from 1982 to 2008, found that selling-related knowledge had the strongest link with performance of the drivers it examined, followed closely by how well sellers adapt to the customer. Selling-related knowledge there means more than knowing the product. It includes knowing customers and how to present a solution to them. These are associations, not experiments.

The practice method in steps 5 and 6 is behaviour modelling: show the skill, state the rule, practise, get feedback. A meta-analysis of this method, read here through two published summaries, covered 117 studies. Those summaries report clear gains in knowledge and skill and smaller gains in behaviour back at work. They also report that transfer was better when learners saw poor examples as well as good ones, worked on scenarios they wrote themselves and set goals for use on the job.
The six headings are craft.

why.title: Drivers of sales performance: a contemporary meta-analysis
why.found: Synthesising studies from 1982 to 2008, five drivers were significantly related to sales performance. Selling-related knowledge was the strongest (standardised beta .28), then adaptiveness (.27), role ambiguity (negative, .25), cognitive aptitude (.23) and work engagement (.23).
why.means: Teach product knowledge in the form sellers use it: tied to customers and adapted to the person in front of them.

try.text: Take one feature of a product you know and write its guide. Then run the three-person practice with two colleagues and record it on a phone. Listen for the moment the seller stops asking and starts listing. That is the point to coach.

try.title: A worked example: one feature rewritten as a conversation guide (invented helpdesk software)
lines: Feature as the product team wrote it: Rules engine routes inbound email to queues by keyword, sender and language.
Who cares: the support team leader with more than ten agents and one shared inbox.
The problem in their words: "Messages sit unread because everyone assumes someone else has picked them up."
Ask: "When an email arrives in the shared inbox today, how does it get to the right person?"
Listen for: forwarding by hand, a morning triage rota, complaints about slow first replies.
Say it in one sentence: "Each message goes straight to the team that can answer it, so nobody has to sort the inbox."
Show: the 90-second demo. One email in French about a refund lands in the right queue. Stop there.
Proof: the approved customer story in the reference library. Do not quote figures that are not in it.
Likely objection: "We tried rules in our old system and they broke."
Reply: "What broke them? ... Here you can test a rule on last week's messages before you switch it on."
Next step: offer to set up two rules on their own inbox in a 30-minute session.
Do not say: anything about features not yet released.

items: The guide becomes a script and sellers read it out. Practise with different customer cards so they have to adapt.
Proof gets invented in the room. Only approved stories and figures may be used, and the guide should say where they are.
The quiz tests the feature list. Assess the conversation, as 2.25 sets out.
The product team wants all sixty features covered. Offer the reference document for the rest and hold the session to a few.
Role-play customers go easy. Give them a written objection.

quiz.a: Selling-related knowledge, with adaptiveness close behind.

quiz.a: Agree the few features that matter most to these sellers' customers and build conversation guides for those. Put the full list in a reference document, because sellers need to be able to hold a conversation, not recite a catalogue.

quiz.a: Play back or describe the moment they stopped asking, and have them redo the opening with the question from the guide. One specific correction followed by a second attempt does more than a general comment.

topics.title: Train retail and frontline staff
topics.theory: Training at the point of sale

situation.text: A phone maker wants store staff to explain its new handset well. The staff work for a retail chain, sell forty other products, get no time off the floor, and a third of them will have left by spring.

items: Find out what the retailer allows before you design. Ask who may enter the store, when, for how long, and whether staff may use their own phones for training.
Design for minutes. Plan one session of ten minutes before opening or at a quiet time, and follow-ups of two or three minutes. Assume nobody will do an hour.
Choose one customer conversation to improve. For a handset it might be the first thirty seconds when a shopper picks it up. Apply 2.10 and spend an hour on a shop floor first.
Put the knowledge on a job aid at the point of sale: a pocket card or a card behind the display. Three customer questions, three things to show, one line on who the product suits.
Practise on the floor with the real product. Show it once, have each person do it once with a colleague as the shopper, and give one piece of feedback.
Give the store manager or team leader a two-minute refresher to run at the weekly briefing. They are there every week and you are not.
Plan for turnover. Every new starter should be able to get the same ten minutes from the team leader and the card, without you.

Agree how it will be checked. Combine the retailer's sell-out figures, a short observation by the visiting field trainer and, if the client uses it, mystery shopping against a checklist you helped write.

why.text: Most of this is practitioner know-how from field trainers. No study opened for this page tested ten-minute floor sessions or pocket cards in retail.

The constraints do the designing. Store staff are employed and managed by the retailer, so the brand cannot instruct them to attend anything. Time on the floor is the retailer's money. High turnover means a one-off visit trains people who will soon be gone, which is why the job aid and the team leader matter more than the visit.

Be careful with mystery shopping as proof. A study using large data sets from three retail chains found that mystery shoppers' scores had no substantial relationship with what real customers said or with sales. A mystery shop can still tell you whether staff did a specific, visible thing, such as offering the handset to hold. Do not report it as a measure of customer satisfaction.

why.title: Do mystery shoppers really predict customer satisfaction and sales performance?
why.found: Using large-scale data from three service retail chains, mystery shopper assessments showed no substantial correlation with customer evaluations or with sales performance. Customer satisfaction measures were related to sales.
why.means: Use mystery shopping to check whether a trained behaviour happened. Use customer feedback and sell-out figures for the result.

try.text: Run the ten-minute session below with two friends and any object as the product, standing up, timed on a phone. If you run over, cut content, not practice.

topics.title: Train partners and resellers

situation.text: Your client sells through 200 reseller firms. Their sellers carry six competing brands, do not report to anyone at the client, and opened last quarter's training email at a rate nobody wants to say aloud.

items: Ask the client's partner manager how partners make money from this product. Training that helps a reseller win or keep a deal gets attention. Training that helps the vendor does not.
Segment the learners. A partner's sellers, technical staff and owner need different things. Write one line for each on what they must be able to do.

Make certification mean something. Tie each level to a benefit the partner values, such as deal registration, a better discount tier, leads or a listing in the partner directory. Agree this with the partner manager, who owns those benefits.
Assess the job, not attendance. A seller records a five-minute pitch. A technical person completes a set-up in a test environment. Apply 2.25.
Keep it short and findable. Put a 20-minute core path on the first screen of the portal, with search, no more than three clicks to any item, and a date on every page.
Give partner managers a part. They mention the next certification step in each quarterly review and run a short session at the partner's own team meeting.
Set an expiry. Certification lasts a year or until a major release. Send a short update module when the product changes, not the whole course again.
Report to the client by partner firm: who is certified, at what level, and whether certified partners register more deals. Say plainly that the last figure is a comparison, not proof of cause.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. A search for research on partner or reseller training and certification found vendor articles and analyst marketing and no study that could be opened and checked, so none is cited.

The reasoning starts from authority. With employees, a manager can require attendance. With partners nobody can, so the programme has to be worth a busy seller's time on its own terms. That is why benefits and the partner's commercial interest come before content.

Certification works here as a signal as much as a course. It tells the client which partners can be trusted with leads, and it tells customers who is competent. A certificate earned by clicking through slides signals nothing.
Keeping it current is the harder half. Partner portals fill with material from past releases, and a seller who finds one wrong price stops trusting the rest. 3.14 covers how completion is tracked.

Incentives need care. Rewards paid to another company's staff can conflict with that company's policies and, in some sectors, with rules on inducements. This page does not give legal guidance on that. Ask the client's legal team.

try.text: Phone someone who has worked for a reseller, or a colleague who will play one, and spend ten minutes asking what vendor training they completed last year and why. Say back to them in one minute what would make them finish yours. Then adjust the outline below.

try.title: A worked example: partner certification outline for an invented software vendor

head: Level
Who
What they do
How assessed
Benefit and renewal
rows: 20-minute core path: who the product is for, three questions to ask
Named sellers, at least two per firm
Core path plus conversation guide and demo practice, about two hours
Recorded five-minute pitch, marked by a partner manager against a rubric
Hands-on labs, about one day in total
Complete a set-up in a test environment
Listed as an installer. Renew at each major release
Holds two sales and one technical certification
Checked from portal records each quarter
Higher discount tier and lead sharing. Lost if certifications lapse
15 minutes on what changed in the release

items: Certification is free to get and worth nothing. Tie it to a benefit or do not call it certification.
The portal is organised by the vendor's product lines. Organise it by what the partner is trying to do: win a deal, install, renew.
Smaller partners are forgotten. Offer the core path in a form one person can do alone in 20 minutes.
Partner managers are not briefed. They are your only route into each firm, so give them a one-page guide.
Old content stays up. Remove anything past its review date.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: Why can you not design partner training the way you design employee training?
quiz.a: Partner staff do not work for the client and cannot be told to attend, so the training must be worth their time commercially.

quiz.q: A client wants every partner seller to complete a four-hour course by the end of the month. Completion so far is very low. What do you suggest?
quiz.a: Cut the required part to a 20-minute core path and tie the longer certification to a benefit such as deal registration. Partners give time to what helps them win business.

quiz.q: A partner seller tells you the portal still shows last year's pricing. What do you do?
quiz.a: Have it removed or corrected that day and check every page for a date and an owner. One wrong fact makes partners distrust the rest of the portal.

topics.tierReason: Practitioner judgement. No checkable research on partner or reseller training was found.
topics.bodyStatus: Practitioner craft. No research source.

topics.title: Coach through sales managers

situation.text: The workshop on discovery questions went well. Four weeks later deal reviews sound exactly as they did before: the manager asks for the close date and the amount, and nobody mentions the customer's problem.

items: Decide where reinforcement will happen before you design the workshop. In sales the two places that already exist are the deal review and the joint customer call.
Brief managers first. Run a 60-minute session for them a week before their teams are trained, so they see the skill, try it and know what to listen for.
Give each manager one page. Three questions to ask in every deal review for the next six weeks, and three things to listen for on a joint call. No more.
Have managers practise the coaching conversation with each other, aloud. Ten minutes in pairs using a real deal. 5.5 covers how to ask and wait.
Ask for a small, countable commitment: two deal reviews per seller and one joint call per seller in six weeks, using the page.
Teach managers to keep coaching apart from inspection. In a coaching review the manager asks about the customer first and the forecast last, or holds the two on different days.
Check in with managers at week 3. Fifteen minutes as a group: what they heard and what sellers found hard.
Report to the sales leader how many reviews and joint calls happened. If managers are not doing it, that is the finding. 2.4 covers the manager's wider role.

why.text: There is some direct research here, and it carries a warning.

A study in one pharmaceuticals company followed 1,246 sales representatives in 136 teams for a year. Managers whose coaching skill had been rated higher in a training exercise had teams that got closer to their annual sales goals, partly because those teams were clearer about their role. Coaching more often did not help by itself. Where the manager's skill was low, more frequent coaching went with lower goal attainment.

That is one company and an observed link, not an experiment. It still changes the brief. Telling managers to coach more may do harm. They need the skill first, which is why the manager session comes before the sellers' workshop and includes practice. The wider evidence on workplace coaching, and its gap on line managers, is in 5.5.
The rest is craft. Deal reviews and joint calls already happen every week, so reinforcement costs no extra meetings. Managers have their own targets and will not read more than a page.

why.title: Does coaching matter? Managerial coaching skill, frequency and sales goal attainment
why.found: Among 1,246 sales representatives in 136 teams at a pharmaceuticals organisation, tracked for a year, managers' coaching skill was related to their representatives' annual sales goal attainment, partly through team role clarity. When coaching skill was low, more frequent coaching was associated with lower attainment.
why.means: Build managers' coaching skill before asking for more coaching. Count coaching conversations, and also listen to how they are done.

try.text: Ask a colleague to play a seller with a real or invented deal. Run a five-minute coaching deal review using the page below and record it. Count how many of your turns were questions. Then swap.

try.title: A worked example: the manager's page for six weeks after a discovery workshop
lines: In every deal review, before the forecast, ask:
1. "What problem is this customer trying to fix, in their words?"
2. "Who else there has that problem, and have we spoken to them?"
3. "What question will you ask on the next call that you have not asked yet?"
Then wait. If the seller does not know, the next step is a call to find out, not a guess.
On a joint call, stay quiet and listen for:
1. Did the seller ask before presenting?
2. Did the customer do at least half the talking in the first ten minutes?
3. Did the seller say the problem back and get a yes?
Afterwards, within the hour: "What went well? What would you do differently? One thing from me."
Your commitment: two deal reviews and one joint call per seller by the end of week 6.
Week 3: fifteen minutes with the other managers to compare notes.

items: The manager takes over the joint call. Agree beforehand that the seller leads and the manager only steps in to save a deal.
Coaching turns into forecast inspection. Separate the two in time or in order.
You have no access after the workshop. Ask for the week 3 call in the proposal, and if you cannot have it, give the enablement lead the agenda to run.

items.label: Dahling, Taylor, Chau and Dwight (2016), Does coaching matter? A multilevel model linking managerial coaching skill and frequency to sales goal attainment. Personnel Psychology.

quiz.q: In the pharmaceuticals study, what happened when low-skill managers coached more often?
quiz.a: More frequent coaching was associated with lower sales goal attainment.

quiz.q: A sales leader says, "Just tell my managers to do a coaching session with everyone each week." What do you say?
quiz.a: Propose a manager session with practice first, then a small commitment of two deal reviews and one joint call per seller. The one study on this found that frequent coaching by unskilled managers went with worse results.

quiz.q: On a joint call you are observing, the manager answers the customer's questions and the seller goes quiet. What do you do afterwards?
quiz.a: Ask the manager what they wanted the seller to learn from the call and agree a rule for the next one: seller leads, manager listens. Reinforcement only happens if the seller does the skill.

topics.tierReason: One large study in a single company links managers' coaching skill, not frequency, with sales goal attainment. The one-page method is craft.
