topics.title: Run a large event or kick-off

situation.text: The sales kick-off has 150 people in a hotel ballroom, a chief executive who wants forty minutes, six breakout rooms and you as lead facilitator. Twelve people is what you are used to.

items: Agree one aim for the half day with the sponsor, in a sentence that names what people will do afterwards. Cut anything that does not serve it.
Use the main stage for what only it can do: direction from leaders, a customer voice, shared energy. Keep each main-stage item to 20 minutes or less and put a two-minute pair conversation after each.
Put the practice in breakouts of 20 to 25, each with a room host. Print the room on the badge. Allow ten minutes to move 150 people and seat them, with signs at every turn and a host at each door.
Write a run sheet to the minute and a one-page host guide. The guide gives the aim, the timings, the exact instructions to read out, and what to do if the room finishes early or late.
Brief the hosts twice. Forty-five minutes by video a week before, to walk the guide and try the activity. Fifteen minutes in the room on the morning, to check equipment and agree signals.
Run a producer's desk. One person, not you, watches the clock, cues speakers with countdown cards at five, two and zero minutes, and messages hosts on one group chat.
Rehearse the opening, every handover and the close in the room the evening before, with microphones and slides.
Close on the main stage with one action each, said to a neighbour, and tell people what happens next and when.

why.text: This is craft learned by running events. No research was found that tests how to structure a kick-off, and none is cited.

Scale changes what goes wrong. With twelve people you can see confusion and repair an instruction. With 150 a vague instruction produces 150 versions, so wording has to be written down and tested. A five-minute overrun on stage is five minutes lost in six rooms at once.

The main stage is a poor place to practise a skill, because most people are watching. It is a good place to give direction and to let people feel part of something. Breakouts do the opposite job. The room host is the person who makes the practice happen. 9.20 covers briefing people who deliver under your name.

Energy in a big room follows the timetable more than the facilitator. Long runs of speakers flatten it. Short items, pair conversation and a change of room lift it. 2.14 covers where to put the demanding work.

try.text: Read the first three minutes of your opening aloud in the largest room you can get into, standing, with a microphone if there is one. Then read the breakout instruction to two colleagues without explaining it, and watch whether they do what you meant.

try.title: A worked example: half-day sales kick-off run sheet (150 people, six breakout rooms of 25, invented software company)

head: Time
Where
What happens
Who
rows: Host briefing: equipment check, signals, questions
Arrival, coffee, badges show breakout room
Welcome. The one aim for the morning. How the day works
Where we are going this year, 20 minutes, three slides
Pairs: "What does that change for your accounts?" Two minutes. Three answers taken by roving microphone
A customer interviewed on stage, 15 minutes
Move to breakouts. Hosts at doors
Discovery practice in threes from the host guide. Three rounds of ten minutes
Each room agrees its best question and writes it on a card
Break. Hosts bring cards to the producer's desk
Six cards read out, one per room. Sales leader responds
One action each, told to a neighbour. What managers will ask next week
Hosts' debrief, ten minutes: what to change next time

items: A senior speaker overruns. Agree the countdown cards with them beforehand and tell them the break is what gets cut.
Hosts improvise the instruction and rooms do different things. Give them the words and ask them to read them.
Questions from the floor are inaudible. Use roving microphones or collect questions on cards.
The breakout is a discussion about the skill. Make it practice of the skill, in threes, with a customer card.
Nothing follows the event. Book the first manager deal reviews before the kick-off, as the topic on coaching through sales managers sets out.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: How long should you allow to move 150 people from a ballroom to breakout rooms and seat them?
quiz.a: About ten minutes, with signs and a host at each door.

quiz.q: The chief executive is at 28 minutes of a 20-minute slot and still talking. What happens?
quiz.a: The producer shows the zero card as agreed, and you step to the side of the stage ready to thank them. You then shorten the pair conversation or the break, because breakout practice is the part that serves the aim.

quiz.q: At 10:15 a host messages that her room has finished the first round early and people are on their phones. What do you tell her?
quiz.a: Start round two now and use the early-finish line in the host guide, a harder customer card. Keeping rooms on the same activity matters more than keeping them on the same minute.

stages.name: Make the materials
stages.question: How do we build slides, media and e-learning that teach?
stages.wordingStatus: Draft: part names and topic titles for this stage were written for the build pack and have not been seen by Mica

parts.title: Slides, visuals and story
parts.summary: What the research on words and pictures says about slides and charts.

topics.title: Judge every slide by what it asks of the learner

situation.text: The slide looks professional and the room is still lost. Looking good and teaching well are different things.

items: For each slide, ask what the learner has to do with it.
Help them pick out what matters.
Help them organise it.
Help them connect it to what they know.
Remove whatever does none of these.

why.text: The leading theory of learning from words and pictures rests on three ideas. People take in pictures and words through separate channels. Each channel holds little. Learning needs active work by the learner.
Design either supports that work or gets in its way. The principles shift with expertise, as with cognitive load.

items.title: Two channels
items.text: Words and pictures are handled separately.

items.title: Select, organise, connect
items.text: The work a slide should support.

try.text: Take a dense slide. Say what helps the learner select, organise and connect, and what obstructs.

try.title: One slide, before and after
try.text: Before: a slide with a process diagram, a paragraph and a stock photo. After: the diagram alone, with the one step being discussed highlighted. The learner now knows where to look and what to link it to.

items: A house template can fight these principles. Change what you can.
What helps a newcomer may be redundant for an expert.
Impressive is not the same as effective.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Mayer (2020), Multimedia Learning, 3rd edition. Cambridge University Press.
Kalyuga, Ayres, Chandler and Sweller (2003), The expertise reversal effect. Educational Psychologist, 38(1).

topics.bodyStatus: 2 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: What are the two channels?
quiz.a: One for pictures and one for words.

quiz.q: What three things should a slide help the learner do?
quiz.a: Select what matters, organise it, and connect it to what they know.

quiz.q: Is a professional-looking slide an effective one?
quiz.a: Not necessarily.

openPoints: The publisher's page for Mayer (2020) does not spell out the three assumptions (two channels, limited capacity, active processing). They are the standard account of his theory but were not seen on the page read.
Paivio on dual coding (candidate: Clark and Paivio 1991) and Baddeley and Hitch (1974) were not opened. No searches left.
The Cambridge address that opened carries an older ISBN in its path but shows the 3rd edition (2020). Worth a click to confirm it still resolves.
checkFindings: Mayer (2020) confirmed as the 3rd edition from Cambridge University Press. The publisher describes 15 design principles drawn from more than 200 experiments and a cognitive theory of learning from words and graphics. No text needed changing.
'The principles shift with expertise' is now sourced to Kalyuga and colleagues (2003), whose abstract says techniques that help novices can lose their value or do harm with more experienced learners.
Paivio and Baddeley and Hitch were removed from the list because neither could be opened. The 'see topic 1.1' label is gone with them.
topics.tierReason: The multimedia design principles rest on a large body of experiments, but their benefit depends on the learner's prior knowledge and most studies use short lessons.

topics.title: Cut what does not serve the point

situation.text: Every slide carries a paragraph, a photo and a logo, and you read the paragraph aloud.

items: Cut anything that does not serve the point.
Mark what is essential.
Do not narrate full sentences that are also on the screen, above all beside a diagram. Short labels and key terms on screen while you talk are fine.
Put words next to the picture they describe, and show them at the same time.
Cut the interesting aside that is off the point.

why.text: The main principles are coherence, signalling, redundancy and contiguity. The instinct to add more text, more decoration, more "engaging" extras often gets in the way of learning.

Interesting but irrelevant material tends to lower what people learn. A 2020 meta-analysis of 58 studies found this on average, with more harm on paper than on screen. That is the evidence behind cutting the fun but pointless bits. For material that passes quickly, narration with graphics can beat on-screen text with graphics.

The redundancy principle is narrower than "never read out what is on the screen". A meta-analysis of 57 studies found that narration with matching on-screen text beat narration alone, and did no worse than text alone. The benefit came when learners had little prior knowledge, when the material set the pace, when no pictures were present, and when the screen showed key terms and not the whole script. The harm is thought to come when a full script competes with a diagram for the eyes.

why.title: Keep it coherent: a meta-analysis of the seductive details effect
why.found: Across 58 studies with more than 7,500 students, people who learned with interesting but irrelevant extras scored lower than people who learned without them. The harm was greater on paper than on screen, and greater when the extra stayed in view beside a useful diagram.
why.means: Cut the joke, photo or music that does not serve the point, above all on handouts and beside diagrams.

items.title: Cut
items.text: What does not serve the point goes.

items.title: Together
items.text: Words and pictures side by side, at the same time.

try.text: Redesign a crowded slide using coherence, signalling and redundancy. Name the principle behind each change.

try.title: A crowded slide, cut
try.text: Before: a slide with a paragraph, a photo of a handshake and a logo, read aloud word for word. After: one labelled diagram on screen. You explain it in speech and the paragraph moves to the handout.

items: Stakeholders will ask for content to be added back. Offer a handout.
Captions and transcripts are not the redundancy problem. They are an access need.
These are tendencies with conditions, not fixed laws.
Most studies of irrelevant extras used lessons of 6 to 12 minutes. Less is known about a full day in a training room.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Mayer (2020), Multimedia Learning, 3rd edition. Cambridge University Press.
Sundararajan and Adesope (2020), Keep it coherent: a meta-analysis of the seductive details effect. Educational Psychology Review, 32(3). Washington State University's summary of the paper.

topics.bodyStatus: 2 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: What does the coherence principle say?
quiz.a: Cut what does not serve the point.

quiz.q: What should you not do with on-screen text?
quiz.a: Narrate it word for word when it is full sentences beside a picture. Short key terms on screen while you speak are fine.

quiz.q: What do interesting but irrelevant details do?
quiz.a: They tend to lower what people learn.

openPoints: Harp and Mayer (1998), How seductive details do their damage: not opened.
No overall effect size is given for seductive details because none was seen in the summary read.
Meta-analyses for modality (Ginns 2005), signalling (Schneider and colleagues 2018) and redundancy (Adesope and Nesbit 2012) were not opened. Those points rest on Mayer's book chapters only.
checkFindings: Mayer (2020): the contents list confirms chapters on coherence, signalling, redundancy, spatial contiguity, temporal contiguity and modality. This supports the four named principles and the narration point.
The seductive details claim was unconditional. It now cites the 2020 meta-analysis and its limits (short lessons, larger effect on paper).

Important: the journal abstract for Sundararajan and Adesope could not be opened (the repository record held citation details only and the other index refused). The findings were read in Washington State University's own news summary of the paper, written with the authors. The link and label say so. Replace with the journal abstract when it can be opened.
Harp and Mayer removed from the list. It had no year or title and was not opened.
topics.tierReason: Cutting irrelevant material, cueing and avoiding read-aloud text are backed by many experiments and a meta-analysis, but the effects vary with format, subject and learner, and most studies use lessons of a few minutes.

topics.title: Make charts honest and quick to read

situation.text: A chart in your deck has a cut-off axis, six colours and a 3D effect.

items: Use size, contrast and position to show what to read first.
Choose the chart that fits the comparison.
Start axes where they should start, and label them.
Remove decoration that competes with the data.
Do not rely on colour alone.

why.text: A visual should make the point faster and more truthfully than words. If it does not, it is decoration.
The same data can mislead or clarify. A trainer has a duty to clarify.

items.title: Hierarchy
items.text: Show people where to look first.

items.title: Honest axes
items.text: Start bars at zero. Label any other scale clearly.

try.text: Take a misleading chart. Redraw it to show the same data honestly and clearly.

try.title: A chart, redrawn
try.text: Before: a 3D bar chart in six colours with the axis starting at 80. After: flat bars from zero, in grey, with the one bar that matters in a dark shade and labelled directly.

items: A simple chart can still mislead through what it leaves out.
Check contrast, and add labels where colour carries meaning.
Design for the back row and for a phone.

topics.bodyStatus: 1 source checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: What should a visual do better than words?
quiz.a: Make the point faster and more truthfully.

quiz.q: Name one way a chart misleads.
quiz.a: A truncated axis, a misleading scale or decoration that distorts.

quiz.q: Why not rely on colour alone?
quiz.a: Some people cannot tell the colours apart.

topics.title: Put the claim in the headline and the evidence below

situation.text: Each slide has a topic label and five bullets. The audience has to work out the point.

items: Write the headline as a full sentence that states the claim.
Put the evidence for it underneath, as a picture where you can.
Give the sequence a shape: situation, complication, resolution.
Keep the story in service of the content.

why.text: A topic label over bullets asks the audience to assemble the meaning. A sentence headline does that work for them and leaves room for evidence.
People tend to follow and remember a narrative more easily than a list of points. Experts often structure explanations badly because they have forgotten what it was like not to know.

The best-known test compared two versions of one technical talk with 110 engineering students. The claim-and-evidence slides led to better understanding, fewer misconceptions and better recall later. The comparison slides broke several design principles at once, so the study supports the whole approach. It does not show how much the headline alone adds.

why.title: How slide design affects audience comprehension
why.found: 110 engineering students saw the same technical talk with one of two slide sets. Those who saw claim-and-evidence slides understood more, held fewer misconceptions, reported less mental effort and recalled more at a later test than those who saw default topic-and-bullet slides.
why.means: Rewrite topic labels as short claim sentences and replace bullets with the evidence, shown as a picture where you can.

try.text: Convert a run of topic-and-bullet slides into claim-and-evidence slides with one thread through them.

try.title: A headline that states the claim
try.text: Before: a slide headed "Customer complaints" with five bullets. After: the headline reads "Most complaints come from late deliveries" and a single bar chart below shows it.

items: Reference material does not want a story. Make it easy to scan.
A vivid story can outweigh the evidence. Check it is true to the point.
Sentence headlines need editing to stay short.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Garner and Alley (2013), How the design of presentation slides affects audience comprehension: a case for the assertion-evidence approach. International Journal of Engineering Education, 29(6).

topics.bodyStatus: 1 source checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: What should a slide headline be?
quiz.a: A full sentence that states the claim.

quiz.q: What goes underneath?
quiz.a: The evidence, as a picture where possible.

quiz.q: When is story the wrong tool?
quiz.a: For reference material people need to scan.

openPoints: Heath and Heath (2007), Made to Stick: not opened.
'People follow and remember narrative' has no checked source (candidate: Mar and colleagues 2021 meta-analysis).
The claim about experts has no checked source on this page (candidates: Camerer, Loewenstein and Weber 1989. Hinds 1999).
Situation, complication, resolution is usually credited to Minto, The Pyramid Principle. Not checked.
checkFindings: The vague reference 'Alley, the assertion-evidence approach' is replaced by the named study, Garner and Alley (2013), whose abstract supports the headline-and-evidence practice.
Added a paragraph saying what that study does and does not show. It tested a package of six design principles against default slides, with students, and one author developed the approach.
Softened the two unsourced sentences on narrative and on experts.
Heath and Heath removed from the list because the publisher page was not opened.
topics.tierReason: The sentence-headline approach has a small number of supporting experiments, mostly with engineering students and run by its originator's group, and the storytelling advice has no checked source.

parts.title: Choose the medium
parts.summary: Picking and combining media from the objective, not from fashion.

topics.title: Pick the medium after the objective

situation.text: The brief arrives as "we want a video" or "can you build an app".

items: Start from the objective and the constraints.
Ask what the objective needs: practice and feedback, discussion, or reference at the moment of use.
Weigh live against self-paced.
Check cost, audience size, how fast the content changes, and who can access it.
Then choose the medium.

why.text: Each medium has real strengths. The objective should decide between them. Choosing the medium first is a common and costly habit.
A new medium often shows inflated results that fade once the novelty wears off. That misleads buying decisions.

try.text: Take three objectives. Choose a medium for each and say why you rejected the alternatives.

try.title: "We want a video"
try.text: The objective is handling an angry caller. That needs practice and feedback, so you propose paired role-play with a short checklist, and a brief video only to model one good call.

items: Bandwidth, devices and accessibility are real limits.
The cheapest medium to make can be the dearest to maintain.
Do not let the supplier choose.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Howard, Gutworth and Jacobs (2021), A meta-analysis of virtual reality training programs. Computers in Human Behavior, 121.

topics.bodyStatus: 1 source checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: What decides the medium?
quiz.a: The objective and the constraints.

quiz.q: What is the basic trade-off between live and self-paced?
quiz.a: Richness of interaction against flexibility.

quiz.q: Why distrust early results for a new medium?
quiz.a: Novelty inflates them and then fades.

topics.tierReason: Choosing the medium from the objective is standard design practice backed by argument and by media comparison research, not a method tested directly.
openPoints: Clark and Mayer, e-Learning and the Science of Instruction (Wiley): publisher page not opened. The draft gives no year or edition. A fifth edition is believed to exist. Confirm before citing.

'A new medium often shows inflated results that fade once the novelty wears off' is unsourced. Candidate: Clark (1983), Reconsidering research on learning from media, Review of Educational Research, whose summary is believed to name novelty as a rival explanation. Not opened.
The web search allowance ran out before this topic was reached.
checkFindings: Softened an unsupported superlative.

Added Howard and colleagues (2021). Its summary reports that the fit between task and technology mattered for virtual reality training, while the display and input hardware did not. That supports letting the objective choose the medium. It is about virtual reality training only.

topics.title: Blend on purpose, and keep microlearning for what it suits

situation.text: Live time is spent presenting content people could have read. Meanwhile someone proposes turning the whole course into five-minute clips.

items: Move content delivery to pre-work.
Spend live time on practice, discussion and feedback.
Use short units for reminders and for help at the point of use.
Keep complex, joined-up skills in longer formats.

why.text: Blending means each mode does what it does best. Flipping moves content before the session so the scarce live time is used for interaction.

Short units suit reinforcement and performance support. They are a doubtful fit for complex skills, because the parts of a complex skill have to be practised together. That limit is a design judgement more than a research finding.

Expect a modest gain from flipping. A 2019 meta-analysis found flipped classes beat lecture-based teaching by a small margin, and by less in the larger studies. Checking the pre-work, for example with a short quiz, may add a little.

For microlearning, a 2025 review of 40 studies reports mostly positive results for knowledge, engagement and satisfaction. Its summary does not say how strong those studies were, so treat the support as early.

why.title: Does the flipped classroom improve learning and satisfaction?
why.found: Pooling 272 comparisons of flipped and lecture-based teaching, learning was a little better in flipped classes (Hedges' g = 0.35). In the 90 adequately powered studies the gain was smaller (g = 0.24). Satisfaction rose only slightly, and the authors suspect publication bias.
why.means: Flip to free live time for practice, check the pre-work was done, and promise a modest gain.

items.title: Blend on purpose
items.text: Say what each mode is for.

items.title: Micro has limits
items.text: Good for reminders. Poor for complex skills.

try.text: Take a single-mode course. Redesign it as a blend. State what each mode does and why.

try.title: A blend with a job for each part
try.text: A one-day product course becomes a short reading and quiz beforehand, a half-day of practice on customer cases, and three brief reminders over the following month. Each part has one stated job.

items: The flip fails if people skip the pre-work. Use it in the room.
Fragments without connection confuse.
More modes mean more handoffs to design.

quiz.a: Content delivery.

quiz.q: What is microlearning good for?
quiz.a: Reminders, spaced reinforcement and help at the point of use.

quiz.q: What is it poor for?
quiz.a: Complex, joined-up skills.

Flipping had no source. Added Låg and Sæle (2019) and a paragraph giving the size of the effect. The intended source (van Alten and colleagues 2019) did not come up with an openable page, so this meta-analysis of the same question was used.

topics.tierReason: Flipping shows a small average gain that shrinks in the better-powered studies, and the microlearning research is recent and of uncertain quality.

topics.title: Buy a medium for the method it makes possible

situation.text: A supplier promises that virtual reality, or an app, or video, will improve learning.

items: Do not expect a medium to teach by itself.
Ask which methods the objective needs.
Ask what this medium makes possible that others do not.
Buy it for those methods, then design them well.

why.text: One side of a long debate holds that media are vehicles: they deliver instruction and do not cause learning. The method teaches. The other side replies that a medium's capabilities can make methods possible that would otherwise be impractical.
Many studies comparing media find no difference. That usually means the method mattered, not the medium.

items.title: Affordances
items.text: What does this medium make possible?

try.text: Take a proposal to use a particular medium. Ask whether what it makes possible serves the method the objective needs.

try.title: Asking what the medium adds
try.text: A supplier offers an app for fire-safety training. You ask what it lets people do that a workshop cannot. The answer is spaced quiz reminders on a phone. You buy it for that, and keep the extinguisher practice live.

items: The same test applies to AI and virtual reality.
A good method in a poor medium still suffers.
Sunk cost keeps bad media in use.

quiz.a: The method, not the medium.

quiz.q: What is Kozma's reply?
quiz.a: A medium's capabilities can make some methods possible.

quiz.q: What does "no significant difference" usually mean?
quiz.a: The method mattered more than the medium.

topics.tierReason: This is a reasoned position taken from a long-running academic debate. It guides buying decisions but has not been tested as a practice.

'Many studies comparing media find no difference' is unsourced. It needs a review or meta-analysis of media comparison studies. Clark's reply, Clark (1994), Media will never influence learning, would also round out the debate.

The web search allowance ran out before this topic was reached.

topics.title: Offer print or self-pacing for dense reading
topics.theory: Screen versus paper, reading versus listening, handwriting versus typing

situation.text: A client wants everything on screen, or bans laptops because "handwriting is better for memory".

items: For dense reading, offer print or let people set their own pace.
Give transcripts with audio and video.
Do not ban screens outright.
Do not teach the handwriting claim as fact.

why.text: Reading comprehension can be slightly worse on screen than on paper. One meta-analysis of 54 studies found a small advantage for paper (g = -0.21 for screens against paper). The gap was larger when reading time was limited than when people set their own pace. It showed for informational text, and not for stories alone. It also grew over the years studied, so do not assume that familiarity with screens removes it.

The well-known claim that handwriting beats typing for memory has not held up. Two direct repeats of the original study found no consistent difference in test scores between people who wrote by hand and people who typed. The original explanation, that typing leads to word-for-word copying which harms learning, was not reliable in the repeat either. The fair summary is that neither tool has been shown to be better.

Adding audio to text helps less than you might expect. A review of 30 studies found only a very small overall benefit from listening while reading (g = 0.18 against reading alone), and no reliable benefit when people read at their own pace. Offer the transcript as a choice, not as something to follow alongside the audio.

why.title: Paper against screens: a meta-analysis of 54 studies
why.found: Across 54 studies, people understood text slightly better on paper than on screen (g = -0.21 for screens against paper). The gap was larger under time limits than with self-paced reading, and it showed for informational text but not for stories alone.
why.means: For dense reading, offer print or let people read in their own time, and do not treat the difference as large.

items.title: Small and conditional
items.text: The screen effect is real but slight.

items.title: Pen or keyboard
items.text: Neither is shown to be better. Let people choose.

try.text: Take three "medium X is better" claims, including the handwriting one. State the size of each effect and when it holds.

try.title: Dense reading, without a ban
try.text: A client wants a forty-page policy read on screen in a timed session. You offer a printed copy or a PDF to read beforehand at each person's own pace, and use the session to apply it.

items: People often feel they learn better one way and perform better another.
Print has an access cost for some learners.
Quote the conditions with the finding.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

Morehead, Dunlosky and Rawson (2019), How much mightier is the pen than the keyboard for note-taking? A replication and extension of Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014). Educational Psychology Review, 31.
Urry and colleagues (2021), Don't ditch the laptop just yet: a direct replication of Mueller and Oppenheimer's (2014) Study 1. Psychological Science, 32(3).

topics.bodyStatus: 4 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: How big is the screen reading effect?
quiz.a: Small, and mainly for explanatory text under time pressure.

quiz.q: What happened to the handwriting claim?
quiz.a: It did not hold up when the study was repeated.

quiz.q: What should you do about pen against keyboard?
quiz.a: Let people choose. Neither has been shown to be better.

topics.tierReason: A meta-analysis of 54 studies found a small advantage for paper that depends on time pressure and the kind of text, and the handwriting claim has not held up in direct repeats.
openPoints: Clinton (2019), Reading from paper compared to screens, Journal of Research in Reading: the publisher's abstract page could not be opened (the Wiley address was not reachable). A third-party copy of the abstract and a blog post by the author agree on the direction: a small negative effect of screens across 33 studies, limited to expository text, no difference in reading time, and better calibration on paper. Neither showed the effect size. The figure in the build note is therefore still unchecked, and the reference is left out of the list. The page states no Clinton figure.

Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014), The pen is mightier than the keyboard, Psychological Science: the PubMed page (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24760141/) returned no content and a PDF copy was blocked. Left out of the list. The two replications describe its claim.

The meta-analysis of reading against listening (Clinton-Lisell 2022, Listening ears or reading eyes, Review of Educational Research) could not be opened. The appended paragraph uses her 2023 review of reading while listening instead, which is a different question.
Watch item 'People often feel they learn better one way and perform better another' matches the calibration finding in Clinton (2019), which is not confirmed at source.
Whether summarising in your own words helps learning is a separate question with its own literature (generative learning). It was not checked and is no longer claimed on this page.
checkFindings: Build note followed. Delgado and colleagues (2018) report g = -0.21, confirmed on the abstract page hosted by the University of Haifa research portal (one author's institution, DOI 10.1016/j.edurev.2018.09.003). The draft page gave no figure, so the correct one was added.
The draft said the screen effect 'largely disappears' with self-paced reading. The summary says only that the paper advantage was larger under time limits. Corrected.
Added the finding that the paper advantage grew over the years studied, which a practitioner would expect to see.

Build note followed on handwriting. Morehead and colleagues (2019), read on the Springer publisher copy, found no consistent differences between longhand, laptop and eWriter groups and say a verdict either way is premature. A second direct replication, Urry and colleagues (2021), was added.

The draft kept 'putting ideas in your own words helps' as the lesson. Neither replication supports it. Urry and colleagues found the link between verbatim notes and worse scores was not robust. The paragraph, card and quiz item were changed.
The topic's theory line covers reading against listening, but the body had nothing on it. Added one paragraph from Clinton-Lisell (2023), read on the author's university repository and on ERIC.

topics.title: Design the handoffs between media

situation.text: The programme has a video, a workshop and a quiz. Each is fine. Nobody designed how one leads to the next.

items: Choose a pattern: content then live, live wrapped by self-paced, or short units spread over time.
Write the handoff between each pair: what to do next, and why now.
Keep terms, story and difficulty consistent across media.
Check nothing is left with no link to the rest.

why.text: A blend is only as good as its transitions. Learners should experience one programme, not a pile of separate assets.
In practice the handoff is a common place for a blend to break: instructions are missing, or the next piece does not use the last.

Research on blended design is thin on this point. A 2017 review of 20 studies names four design challenges: building in flexibility, getting people to interact, supporting how they learn, and creating a good climate for learning. It does not test handoffs as such, so treat this page as practitioner advice.

items.title: Design the joins
items.text: The transitions matter as much as the pieces.

try.text: Take a blended programme. Write the handoff between each pair of media.

try.title: A handoff, written down
try.text: The video ends with: "In the workshop you will use these four steps on your own case, so bring one." The workshop opens by asking for those cases. The quiz a week later uses the same four step names.

items: A great video followed by an unconnected quiz teaches little.
Different authors drift in terms. Keep a glossary.
Measuring across media is harder. Plan it early.

quiz.q: What is a blend only as good as?
quiz.a: Its transitions.

quiz.q: What should each handoff say?
quiz.a: What to do next, and why now.

quiz.q: What keeps a blend feeling like one programme?
quiz.a: Consistent terms, story and difficulty.

The Boelens abstract was read on a library index record that leaves the author field blank. Authors are taken from the search result title and the first-pass lead. The journal's own page was not opened.

Added Boelens and colleagues (2017) as the nearest review of blended design, with a plain statement that it does not test handoffs.
Softened 'usually break' to an experience claim.
topics.tierReason: Writing handoffs between media is sound professional practice, but no study read tests it directly.

topics.title: Use immersive technology for what it does best

situation.text: A client has bought headsets and wants "something in VR".

items: Ask what must be practised that is dangerous, rare, costly or impossible to stage.
Use immersive tools for that.
Keep sessions short and brief people before and after.
Offer an alternative for people who cannot use a headset.
Compare the cost with a simpler method.

why.text: Immersive technology earns its place where real practice is unsafe or impractical: emergencies, heights, costly equipment, difficult conversations. It lets people rehearse in a setting close to the real one.

The measured gains are modest. A meta-analysis of 48 studies in schools and universities found a small overall advantage for immersive virtual reality over computer-based or traditional resources (g = 0.38). The size of the gain depended on what it was compared with. A meta-analysis of workplace training found that virtual reality did better than the alternatives it was tested against, and that the fit between the task and the technology mattered while the type of headset or controller did not.

why.title: More presence, less learning
why.found: Fifty-two students learned from the same science simulation on a desktop or in a headset. Those in the headset reported much more presence but learned less (d = 0.80 in favour of the desktop), and brain-activity measures suggested higher cognitive load.
why.means: Do not assume that a more immersive version teaches better, and test learning as well as enjoyment.

try.text: List three skills in your field that cannot be practised safely for real. Say whether immersion would add anything a role-play could not.

try.title: A case for a headset
try.text: A warehouse team must learn what to do when a racking unit starts to fail. It cannot be staged safely. A ten-minute headset scenario lets each person rehearse the response, followed by a debrief. A seated tablet version is offered too.

items: Some people feel sick in headsets.
Novelty inflates early results.
Content dates and is costly to update.
More immersion can mean less learning. In one experiment, students felt more present in a headset and learned less than on a desktop.

parts.summary: Storyboards, production, interactivity and tracking.

topics.title: Storyboard before you produce anything

situation.text: You jump into recording and find the structure does not work once it is filmed.

items: Plan pictures, narration, on-screen text and interaction on paper first.
Write narration to be spoken, in plain conversational language.
Match words to pictures frame by frame.
Build a rough version and test it.

why.text: Changes are cheap on paper and expensive in the edit. The storyboard is where the decisions about load and layout are made.
An expert's raw material is not a script. It has to be reorganised for someone who does not know the subject.

try.text: Storyboard a two-minute teaching segment: picture, narration and on-screen text for each frame.

try.title: A storyboard catches the problem
try.text: A three-column page: sketch of the picture, the words to be spoken, and any on-screen text. Reading it aloud to a colleague shows that frame four explains a term before frame two has introduced it. You swap them on paper.

items: A storyboard nobody reviews saves nothing.
Plan decision points as well as the straight path.
Read the script aloud before recording.

quiz.q: Why storyboard first?
quiz.a: Changes are cheap on paper and expensive in the edit.

quiz.q: How should narration be written?
quiz.a: To be spoken, in plain conversational language.

quiz.q: What do you do before polishing?
quiz.a: Build a rough version and test it.

Ginns, Martin and Marsh (2013) meta-analysis on conversational style: not opened. The page gives no effect size for it.

topics.title: Get the sound right and keep videos short

situation.text: The video is forty minutes long, filmed beautifully, with echoing sound.

items: Get the audio clean first.
Keep each video short and on one point.
Let people pause, replay and skip.
Show a presenter only where a person adds something.
Cut what does not serve the objective.

why.text: Poor sound makes a video hard to follow, however good the pictures. Long, single-piece video goes against what is known about load and segmenting.
A face on screen can add social presence. It can also pull attention from the content.

The usual figure on length comes from a 2014 study of 6.9 million viewing sessions in four online university courses. People watched nearly all of a video under six minutes and far less of longer ones. That study measured how long people watched, not what they learned, so use it as a guide to attention.

why.title: How video production affects student engagement
why.found: Using 6.9 million viewing sessions from four online courses, the authors found that shorter videos held viewers much better and that informal talking-head videos held them better than polished studio ones. Engagement meant time watched and whether people tried the questions afterwards. Learning was not measured.
why.means: Keep each video to a few minutes and one point, and do not spend on studio polish.

try.text: Record and edit a short teaching video. Review it against segmenting and coherence.

try.title: One long video, remade
try.text: Before: one forty-minute recording of a whole session, made with a laptop microphone in an echoing room. After: six short videos, each on one question, recorded with a clip-on microphone, with captions and a transcript.

items: Add captions and a transcript.
Generated voices and video raise questions of quality and disclosure.
Polish is not the goal.
Sound first is production experience. The research reviews read for this page do not test audio quality.

topics.bodyStatus: 3 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: What matters more, sound or picture?
quiz.a: Sound. If people cannot hear the words clearly, good pictures will not rescue the video.

quiz.q: How long should a teaching video be?
quiz.a: Short, and on one point.

quiz.q: What control should learners have?
quiz.a: To pause, replay and skip.

Rey and colleagues (2019) meta-analysis of segmenting and Alemdag (2022) on instructor presence: not opened.
The Guo record read is a university repository entry that does not list the authors. Authors are taken from the search result and from Brame's citation of the study.
The watch item on generated voices and disclosure has no source.
checkFindings: Brame (2016) confirmed. It supports short segmented videos, cutting extras, cueing, conversational delivery and learner control (it cites a study in which learners who could move around a video did better).
Brame does not discuss audio quality at all. 'Get the audio clean first' and the 'Sound first' card are kept as production advice, with a new watch item saying so. The quiz answer was reworded.
Guo, Kim and Rubin (2014) added, with a paragraph making clear it measured watching in online university courses, not learning. The under-six-minutes figure was read in Brame's account of that study.

The presenter point is partly supported. Brame notes a talking head adds nothing to the visual channel when explaining a process. Guo and colleagues found informal talking-head videos were watched for longer. Text left as it is.

'Mayer, segmenting (see topic 2.14)' replaced by Clark and Mayer, whose contents list has a chapter on segmenting and one on instructional video. Clark and Mayer: Wiley's own page was not returned by a search, so the description and contents were read on the O'Reilly library page for the 5th edition (Wiley, listed as published December 2023). The link points to that page. Swap in the Wiley page if you prefer the publisher's own site.
topics.tierReason: Short, segmented video with learner control has supporting studies, but the length guidance comes from watching data, not learning, and the audio-first advice is production experience.

topics.title: Build interactions that make people think

situation.text: The e-learning is forty screens of "click next", with a drag-and-drop to break it up.

items: Make each interaction ask the learner to recall, decide or apply.
Give feedback that explains.
Use scenarios with choices to build judgement.
Remove interactions that only move the page on.

why.text: Interaction for its own sake adds load without learning. The useful kind makes people think: retrieve something, make a decision, see the result.
Choosing an authoring tool comes after deciding what interaction the objective needs.

try.text: Design one interaction that forces recall or a decision. Say why it is more than a click-through.

try.title: From click to decision
try.text: Before: click to reveal five facts about data handling. After: a customer email asks for a colleague's phone number. The learner chooses a reply, sees what happens next, and reads why the safer choice was right.

items: "Engaging" interactions can crowd out learning.
Branching multiplies the work. Keep the tree small.
Check it works with a keyboard and a screen reader.

quiz.q: What does interaction for its own sake add?
quiz.a: Load without learning.

quiz.q: What builds judgement in e-learning?
quiz.a: Scenarios with choices and consequences.

topics.title: Choose tracking that fits what you need to measure
topics.theory: Standards and platforms: SCORM, xAPI, cmi5

situation.text: IT asks whether your course is "SCORM compliant". You are not sure what you need to track.

items: Decide what you need to know about the learning.
Pick the standard that can record it.
Record a few things that will change a decision.
Keep content portable between platforms.

why.text: SCORM is the long-standing reference model for packaging e-learning and reporting progress to a learning management system. Its most recent release, SCORM 2004 4th Edition, dates from 2009. xAPI records learning activity in many more settings, such as mobile learning, simulations and offline work, and keeps it in a learning record store. Version 2.0 became an IEEE standard in 2023. cmi5 is a set of rules for using xAPI with a learning management system. It covers how content is launched and how results are reported.

Suppliers tend to describe a learning management system as built around administration and a learning experience platform as built around the learner. These are market labels, not standards, so check what each product records. The wrong choice quietly limits what you can measure later.
SCORM is still widely used. The body that created it says newer specifications are overtaking it, and US defence guidance now recommends xAPI and cmi5 for new e-learning.

items.title: Measure first
items.text: Decide what you need to know.

items.title: SCORM, xAPI, cmi5
items.text: Inside the platform, anywhere, or both.

try.text: For a given delivery scenario, choose the standard and list the few things you would track.

try.title: Tracking that fits the need
try.text: A client only needs to know who finished the fire-safety module and whether they passed. A basic completion and score record is enough. Detailed tracking of every click would add work and change no decision.

items: Tracking everything teaches you nothing.
Avoid lock-in to one supplier.
Standards change. Check the current specifications.
Ask which SCORM version is meant. SCORM 1.2 and SCORM 2004 are separate versions, and you need to know which one the platform accepts.

parts.title: Accessibility, experts and upkeep
parts.summary: Building to a professional standard that lasts.

topics.title: Build to WCAG 2.2 AA from the start

situation.text: Accessibility is on the list for "after launch". It is rarely reached.

items: Make content perceivable, operable, understandable and robust.
Aim for level AA of WCAG 2.2.
Fix the common failures first: text alternatives, contrast, keyboard use, colour as the only signal.
Caption video and provide transcripts.
Build it in from the start.

why.text: WCAG 2.2 is the version of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines that UK government guidance now points to. Its success criteria are graded by level. Government services are asked to meet all the A and AA criteria, so AA is the usual target. Building access in from the start is usually cheaper and easier than adding it later.
Access is wider than sight and hearing. It includes attention, memory and processing.

In the UK, what the law asks depends on who you work for. The accessibility regulations for public sector bodies require their websites, intranets and public-facing apps to meet WCAG 2.2 AA and to publish an accessibility statement. Some bodies and some content are exempt, for example live audio and video. The GOV.UK guidance lists the exemptions.

Those regulations do not cover private companies. Employers still have a duty to make reasonable adjustments for disabled workers, under the Equality Act 2010 in Great Britain and the Disability Discrimination Act 1995 in Northern Ireland. GOV.UK lists training opportunities among its examples. This is not legal advice. Ask the client which duties apply to them.

try.text: Audit a real asset against a WCAG 2.2 AA checklist. Fix the top failures.

try.title: Three common failures, fixed
try.text: Before: a module with a silent video, pale grey text and a drag-and-drop that needs a mouse. After: captions and a transcript, darker text, and the same question answerable with the keyboard alone.

items: Automated checkers catch only part of the problem.
Legal duties vary. Check which apply to you.
Test with a keyboard and a screen reader.

quiz.a: Perceivable, operable, understandable and robust.

quiz.q: Which level is the usual target?
quiz.a: AA.

quiz.q: Name two common failures.
quiz.a: Any two of: missing text alternatives, poor contrast, no keyboard access, colour as the only signal.

openPoints: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2: w3.org could not be opened, so the standard itself is not in the reference list. This is the main gap on this page. Add https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/ once it has been opened, and confirm the publication date (believed to be 5 October 2023) and the three levels A, AA and AAA.
The full title of the public sector regulations and the text of the Equality Act duty were not read on legislation.gov.uk.

Not checked: the European Accessibility Act, which may matter for e-learning sold into the European Union.
The GOV.UK requirements page shows 'last updated 30 September 2024'. Recheck before publishing in case the requirement has moved on.
'Access is wider than sight and hearing. It includes attention, memory and processing' has no direct source on the pages opened.
The page title and several steps name WCAG 2.2 AA as the target for everyone. For a private client this is good practice, not a stated legal requirement, on the pages read.

GOV.UK confirms that public sector bodies must meet WCAG 2.2 AA and publish an accessibility statement, that the four principles are perceivable, operable, understandable and robust, that intranets and extranets are covered, and that apps for specific groups such as employees are not.

GOV.UK confirms who monitors and enforces: the Government Digital Service monitors, the Equality and Human Rights Commission enforces in England, Scotland and Wales, and the Equality Commission for Northern Ireland enforces in Northern Ireland. This was not added to the page to keep it short.
The draft gave no account of what applies to whom. Added two short paragraphs and a not-legal-advice note.

topics.title: Write so it can be translated later

situation.text: The course is to be translated. The text is baked into the images and every example is about cricket.

items: Keep text out of images.
Leave room for text to grow.
Avoid idioms and examples that only work in one culture.
Plan a glossary and a review by a native speaker.

why.text: Design content so it can be adapted before you try to translate it. Localising is more than translating: examples, images and references have to work in the new setting.
Content not prepared for this is costly and error-prone to adapt later.

Text usually gets longer when translated from English, and short labels grow the most. W3C guidance quotes IBM figures of two to three times the length for strings of up to ten characters, and about 1.3 times for passages over 70 characters. Some scripts also need taller lines.

try.text: Take a piece of content. Find everything that would obstruct translation and redesign it.

try.title: Ready to translate
try.text: Before: a diagram with English labels drawn into the picture, and a cricket example. After: labels as editable text beside numbered points on the image, with spare room, and an example about queuing at a shop.

items: Machine translation needs human review.
Humour rarely survives.
Norms about directness and hierarchy change what works.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

W3C Internationalization, Text size in translation.

topics.bodyStatus: 2 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: What do you do before translating?
quiz.a: Design the content so it can be adapted.

quiz.q: Why is localising more than translating?
quiz.a: Examples, images and references must work in the new setting.

quiz.q: Where should text not be?
quiz.a: Baked into images.

openPoints: 'Keep text out of images': the W3C pages read warn about fitting text tightly into graphics but do not give this rule in those words. It is standard practice. A direct source was not opened.
'Machine translation needs human review' has no checked source (candidate: ISO 18587 on post-editing).
'Norms about directness and hierarchy change what works' has no checked source. W3C notes only that localisation may mean rethinking design where learning approaches differ.
checkFindings: The placeholder for 'localisation-industry guidance' is replaced by two W3C pages.

W3C's definitions match the draft: internationalisation is designing so that content can be adapted easily, and localisation is the adaptation itself, which goes beyond translation to formats, images, symbols and cultural fit. W3C also says adapting after the fact is much harder than designing for it, which supports 'costly and error-prone to adapt later'.
'Leave room for text to grow' is supported by the W3C article on text size. Added a paragraph with its figures, attributed to IBM as W3C does.
No text needed correcting.
topics.tierReason: Preparing content for translation is established professional practice set out in W3C guidance, not something tested in learning experiments.

topics.title: Draw out the steps experts no longer notice
topics.theory: Working with subject experts and the expert blind spot

situation.text: The expert hands you two hundred slides and says "it is all in there".

items: Ask the expert to do the task while talking through it.
Ask what they would check, and what could go wrong.
Write down the steps they did not mention.
Reorganise the material for someone new.
Agree scope: what a beginner needs first.

why.text: Experts have automated much of what they know and lose sight of what newcomers do not know. Their explanations skip steps. This is often called the expert blind spot, or the curse of knowledge.
Your job is not to transcribe the expert. It is to surface what they no longer notice and put it in learnable order.

In one study, trainee teachers with more advanced maths were more likely to assume pupils must master equations before word problems. Pupils' real results point the other way. Knowing a subject well can mislead you about how a beginner learns it.

why.title: Cognitive task analysis-based training: a meta-analysis
why.found: Training built on a structured analysis of how experts think and decide beat training built on other ways of gathering content, with a large average effect (Hedges' g = 0.871). The number of studies was small and results varied a good deal by method and setting.
why.means: Do not build from the expert's slides alone. Watch them work and question them about the decisions they make.

items.title: Reorganise
items.text: Expert order is not learning order.

try.text: Interview someone on a skill they know well. Find at least three steps they left out at first.

try.title: The steps nobody mentioned
try.text: A senior engineer explains a safety check in four steps. When you watch her do it, she also glances at a gauge and wipes a seal first. Neither was mentioned. Both go into the learner's version.

items: Experts disagree. Reconcile them before you build.
Protect learners from the information dump.
Respect the expert's time and credit them.
There are more than a hundred named methods for drawing out expert knowledge, and little evidence on which works best. Keep yours simple: watch, ask, write down, check back.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

Yates and Feldon (2011), Advancing the practice of cognitive task analysis: a call for taxonomic research. Theoretical Issues in Ergonomics Science, 12(6).

quiz.q: Why do experts skip steps?
quiz.a: They have automated them and no longer notice.

quiz.q: How do you surface hidden steps?
quiz.a: Watch the expert do the task while talking it through.

quiz.q: What is your job with expert material?
quiz.a: To reorganise it for someone new.

The Nathan and Petrosino abstract was read on a repository record that shows the abstract without the authors, year or journal. Those details come from the search result and the first-pass lead. The volume and issue were not seen and are left out of the label.

The meta-analysis tested formal cognitive task analysis. The simple watch-and-talk-through routine on this page is a light version of it and was not tested as such.

Nathan and Petrosino (2003): 48 trainee secondary teachers. Those with more advanced maths held views about the order of learning that pupils' actual performance contradicts. Added as a short paragraph.

Tofel-Grehl and Feldon (2013): confirmed as a journal article with Hedges' g = 0.871 for training based on cognitive task analysis against other ways of identifying content. The abstract warns that the number of studies is small. Added as the study block.
Yates and Feldon (2011) added as a caveat: over 100 methods exist and there is no firm basis for choosing between them. Added as a watch item.
Heath and Heath removed from the list because it was not opened. The text now leads with 'expert blind spot'.

topics.title: Keep one current version of everything
topics.theory: Asset management, versioning and the toolchain

situation.text: There are four versions of the deck in three folders, and nobody knows which is current.

items: Keep one approved version in one place.
Name and date versions the same way every time.
Build templates that already meet your design and access standards.
Decide who owns, reviews and retires each asset.
Tag assets so they can be found.

why.text: Content that cannot be found, updated or trusted decays and misleads. Production is a system to maintain, not a run of one-off files.
Templates make work faster and more consistent, and carry good practice with them.

try.text: Design a simple versioning scheme for a real content library. Say how a stale asset is found and retired.

try.title: One current deck
try.text: Before: "Induction deck FINAL v3 (new).pptx" in three folders. After: one file in one shared folder, named by course, version and date, with an owner and a review date on the first slide. Older copies go to an archive folder.

items: Rules nobody follows are worse than none. Keep them light.
Old versions linger in inboxes. Link, do not attach.
Review dates need someone to act on them.

parts.title: Materials for the room
parts.summary: The printed and physical things a face-to-face session runs on: the workbook, the facilitator guide, wall materials and slides people can read.

topics.title: Write a workbook people will use

situation.text: You hand out a printed copy of the slides. By lunch most copies are closed on the table, and at the end of the day half are left in the room.

items: Give the workbook two jobs and design for both. During the session it is where people work. Afterwards it is where they look things up. A copy of the slides does neither.
Build it from the activities, in session order. Give each activity its own page with the same layout: the task in one or two lines, the model or example, space to write, and a short notes box.
Number every page in large type and call the numbers out: "Turn to page 6." Put the page number on the matching slide.
Leave real room to write. Handwriting needs more space than you expect. Give at least a third of each working page to boxes or ruled lines, with lines about 8 to 10 mm apart.
Move the detail to a reference section at the back: the full model, definitions, the long table you cut from a slide. Topics 1.1 and 3.2 explain why it should come off the screen.
End with an action page: what I will do, with whom, by when. This is the page topic 5.2 asks for.
Design for cheap printing. A4, black and white, body text at 11 or 12 point, bold headings, no grey fills. Staple or wire-bind it so it lies flat on a table.
Print one copy and fill it in by hand, start to finish, with a pen. Fix every box that was too small and every instruction you had to read twice.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. There is no direct research here on workbook layout. The reasoning borrows from topics already on this site: people remember what they produce more than what they are handed, and working memory is small, so detail belongs on paper they can return to.

A workbook built from activities also protects the session. If the task and the space to do it are on the page, people can start without waiting for you to repeat the instruction, and a group that falls behind can catch up. When the projector fails, the day still runs.

Afterwards, the pages people filled in are the ones they keep, because their own words are in them. The printed model on page 14 matters less than the three lines they wrote beside it about their own team.

try.text: Take one activity from a session you know. Make its workbook page. Print it, give it to someone who was not there, and ask them to do the task with no help from you. Watch where their pen stops.

try.title: A worked example: contents page for a one-day workshop for new managers, "Giving feedback that helps"
lines: Page 1. Today at a glance: times, outcomes, who is in the room
Page 2. What I want from today (fill in before 09:45)
Page 3. Activity 1: the best and worst feedback I have received
Page 4. The four-part feedback model, with one worked example
Page 5. Activity 2: spot the four parts in two written examples
Page 6. Activity 3: prepare my real conversation
Page 7. Activity 4: practice in threes, with the observer's checklist
Page 8. Activity 5: when it goes badly. Three replies to plan for
Page 9. My plan: who, what, by when
Pages 10 to 12. Reference: the model in full, useful phrases, further reading
Back cover. Trainer's contact details and the date of the follow-up call

try.title: A worked example: page 6, filled in by a participant (their handwriting shown in quotation marks)
lines: ACTIVITY 3: PREPARE MY REAL CONVERSATION. 10 minutes, on your own.
Think of one person in your team you need to give feedback to in the next two weeks.
Who (initials only): "R.T."
1. What I saw or heard. Facts, no opinion: "Two client reports sent late in October, on the 3rd and the 17th. No warning either time."
2. The effect it had: "I found out from the client. We looked disorganised and I could not cover for it."
3. The question I will ask: "What got in the way on those two?"
4. What I will ask for: "Tell me the day before if a report will be late."
When and where I will have it: "Thursday one-to-one, 2pm, meeting room, not at desks."
What I am most worried they will say: "That I gave them too much work."
NOTES FROM PRACTICE (fill in after Activity 4): "Start with the question earlier. I talked for too long before asking."

items: The workbook is the slide deck with lines beside it. People read ahead and stop listening. Build pages round tasks.
Writing boxes are two lines deep. Nobody can fit a real answer. Test with a pen.
It runs to forty pages. People feel they have failed if they do not finish. Cut it to the pages you will use, plus reference.
Confidential details go into a book that gets left on a train. Ask for initials only, and say why.
Page numbers on slides and workbook drift apart after an edit. Check them last, after every change.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What two jobs does a workbook have?
quiz.a: A place to work during the session, and a reference afterwards.

quiz.q: A sponsor asks you to print the slides as the handout to save time. What do you do?
quiz.a: Offer a short workbook built from the activities, with the detail from the slides in a reference section at the back. People use pages they have written on, and it takes little longer to make.

quiz.q: In the test print, your colleague cannot fit their answer in the box on page 6 and asks you what question 3 means. What do you do?
quiz.a: Enlarge the box and rewrite the question until it needs no explanation. If one tester stumbles, a room of twelve will.

topics.tierReason: Rests on practitioner judgement. No research on workbook design was opened.
topics.bodyStatus: Practitioner craft. No research source.

topics.title: Write a facilitator guide someone else can deliver from

situation.text: You are ill on the morning of a workshop. A colleague steps in with your slides and a page of your notes that says "Do the angry caller exercise, about 40 minutes."

items: Write for a capable trainer who has never seen the session and cannot ring you. That reader knows how to run a room. They do not know what you meant.
Start with one page that sets up the day: purpose, outcomes, who it is for, group size range, room layout, kit list, and the timetable with clock times.
Give every activity the same block, with the same fields in the same order: time, method, purpose, what to say, what to watch for, materials, and what to do if short of time.
Write the instructions for each activity word for word, because small changes in set-up change what groups do. Write the rest of what you say as points, so the facilitator uses their own voice.
Write the debrief questions out in full, in order. Add the answers you are listening for and the common wrong turns.
Mark each block "keep" or "can cut", and say which outcome it serves. A facilitator running 20 minutes late needs to know what to drop without asking.
Put the slide number and the workbook page beside each block. Add the version number and date to the footer of every page. Topic 3.18 covers versions.
Test it cold. Ask someone to deliver one block from the guide while you watch in silence. Each time they stop, guess or ask, the guide needs another line.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. No research on facilitator guides was opened for this topic.

A guide is how a session outlives the person who designed it. Without one, each new facilitator rebuilds the session from the slides. They keep the parts that are easy to see, which is the content, and lose the parts that are not, which is the timing, the set-up and the debrief.

The split between exact wording and points is deliberate. Instructions fail when they are improvised: people start the wrong task, or the right task in the wrong groups. Stories and explanations fail when they are read out. So the guide scripts the first and leaves the second open. Writing down what to watch for passes on the thing that otherwise takes years to learn, which is what the activity looks like when it is going wrong.
It is also the document a client's learning team will ask to see if they plan to deliver the session with their own people. The topic "Design for scale" in Stage 2 starts from it.

try.text: Take a 20-minute activity you have run. Write its block in the format below. Give it to a colleague, leave the room for ten minutes while they read it, then have them deliver it to you. Say nothing until the end.

try.title: A worked example: one page of a guide. Customer service workshop, block 4 of 7: "The angry caller". Keep. Slides 14 to 16, workbook page 7. Version 1.3, 17 November 2026

head: Time
Method
What to say
What to watch for
rows: Points: most angry callers want two things, to be heard and to know what happens next. Show the three-step reply on slide 14: name it, own it, next step. Give one example from your own experience.
Keep it to five minutes. If people start telling their own stories, say you want those in a moment.
Say exactly: "I need one volunteer to be an angry caller. Read the card and give me a hard time for one minute. Everyone else, tick each of the three steps on page 7 when you hear it."
Pick someone who will not overplay it. If nobody offers, play the caller yourself and ask a confident participant to reply.

Say exactly: "In threes. One of you is the caller, one the agent, one the observer with page 7. Two minutes of call, two minutes of feedback, observer first. Then swap. Three rounds. Caller cards are on your table. Who is the first agent in each group? Hands up."
Do not start until a hand is up in every trio. A group of four runs four shorter rounds.
Call the swaps at four and eight minutes. Otherwise stay quiet. Stand where you can hear two groups.
Agents who jump to the fix and skip "name it". Callers who make it impossible. Step in only for the second.
Ask in this order: "Agents, which step was hardest to say?" "Callers, what did the agent do that calmed you?" "What will you say differently on your next real call?"
Listening for: naming the feeling felt awkward, and it worked. If people say it sounds false, ask the callers how it felt to hear.
Cut the demonstration and run two rounds, not three. Do not cut the debrief.

items: The guide is a script from start to finish. Facilitators read it out and the room hears it. Script the instructions only.
It describes the content and not the timing. Put a clock time on every block.
"Debrief the activity" with no questions. Write the questions and what a good answer sounds like.
Written after the first delivery and never updated. Note changes on your copy during each session and revise the master that week.
It only works for the group size you had. State the range, and what to change at each end.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: Which part of a facilitator guide should be written word for word?
quiz.a: The instructions for each activity. The rest is written as points.

quiz.q: A colleague delivering from your guide is running 20 minutes late before lunch and cannot reach you. What should the guide already tell them?
quiz.a: Which blocks are marked "can cut" and what each "keep" block is for. Then they can drop the right thing and protect the practice.

quiz.q: In a cold test, your colleague sets up the trios correctly and then asks the group, "So, how was that?" The debrief goes flat. What do you change?
quiz.a: Write the debrief questions into the guide in full and in order, with the answers to listen for. A general prompt was all they had.

topics.tierReason: Rests on practitioner judgement. No research on facilitator guides was opened.

topics.title: Prepare flipcharts, cards and wall materials

situation.text: The key model was on slide 9. By the afternoon nobody can remember the third step, and you have clicked back to it four times.

items: Decide what must stay visible all day: the timetable, the outcomes, the main model, the question list. Those go on the wall. A slide disappears when you move on.
Prepare flipchart sheets the day before. Write the headings and any diagram. Leave the parts the group will fill in blank. Pencil light notes for yourself in the corner, which nobody else will see.

Write large and dark. As a working rule, make letters at least 3 cm tall, and larger in a deep room. Use black or dark blue for text and keep red and green for marks and underlines. Six or seven lines to a sheet is plenty.
Check your own sheets from the furthest chair before people arrive. If you have to squint, rewrite.
Make cards for anything people sort, rank or act out. One idea per card, in marker, readable at arm's length. Number each set on the back and bring a spare.
Write role cards in four lines: who you are, what you want, what you will say first, and what you will only say if asked. The example below shows one.
Ask the venue in advance what may go on the walls and what the walls are made of. Bring your own low-tack tape and tack, and a second flipchart stand if you can.
Photograph every sheet before you take it down. Send the photographs to the group within two days, in session order.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement, and the sizes are working rules. Test them in the room you are given.

Wall materials do something slides cannot. They stay. A model on a flipchart is there when someone needs it at three o'clock, and you can point to it without stopping the session. Sheets the group has filled in also show progress, which matters on a long day.

Cards and printed cases change who is doing the work. When a group has to sort twelve cards into an order, every person can reach in and move one. The same task on a slide becomes a conversation between you and the two most confident people.

There is a practical reason too. A session that runs from walls, cards and a workbook does not stop when the projector fails or the room has no screen. Topic 4.13 asks you to carry a version that needs no technology, and this is that version. On a retreat or in an unusual venue it may be the only version.

try.text: Write one flipchart sheet for a model you teach. Stand it up, walk eight paces back and read it. Then present it aloud to an empty room for two minutes, pointing to each part without turning your back for more than a moment.

try.title: A worked example: materials list for a one-day workshop, twelve people at three tables

How many
What it is for

Timetable, outcomes, the model, "questions for later", ground rules
Test each one the night before
Check with the venue what is allowed
Colour shows which table an idea came from
4 sets of 12, numbered on the back
Three tables and a spare set
Caller, agent and observer for each trio
One each and one spare, stapled, pages numbered
First names, written large, both sides
Photograph every sheet before it comes down

try.title: A worked example: a role card for the caller in a customer service practice
lines: CALLER CARD 2
Who you are: a small business owner. Your card reader stopped working on Saturday, your busiest day.
What you want: a replacement tomorrow, and someone to say sorry.
Say first: "This is the third time I have rung about this."
Only if asked: you were promised a call back on Monday and did not get one.
Calm down a little if the agent names how annoying this is. Stay cross if they go straight to the fix.

items: You write with your back to the room for minutes at a time. Prepare the sheet, or write a few words and turn round.
Pale pens and small writing. Yellow, orange and light green cannot be read from the back. Keep them for highlighting.
Tape takes the paint off the wall. Ask first, test in a corner, or use stands and windows.
A card set has one missing. Number them and count them back in.
Sheets are binned at the end and the group's work goes with them. Photograph first.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What belongs on the wall and not on a slide?
quiz.a: Anything people need to see all day, such as the timetable, the outcomes and the main model.

quiz.q: You arrive to find the projector does not work and the technician is an hour away. What do you do?
quiz.a: Start on time from the prepared flipcharts, cards and workbook. Draw any model you need on a fresh sheet, and move slide-only detail to the reference pages.

quiz.q: The venue says nothing may be stuck to the walls. What do you do?
quiz.a: Bring or borrow extra flipchart stands, and use windows or tables for group work if the venue agrees. Decide this before the day, because the layout of the room changes.

topics.tierReason: Rests on practitioner judgement. The sizes are working rules to test in the room.
