topics.title: Make slides readable from the back of the room
topics.theory: Type size and contrast for projected slides

situation.text: You say "You probably cannot read this at the back" and carry on. The slide looked fine on your laptop.

items: Find out the room before you set the type: how far the back row sits from the screen, how large the screen is, and whether the lights stay on. If you cannot find out, design for a long room and a small screen.
Set minimum sizes and hold to them. As working practice on a standard widescreen slide: body text at 24 point or more, headings at 32 or more, and nothing under 18, labels and sources included.
Use the size limit to edit. If the text will not fit at 24 point, the slide has too much on it. Cut it, split it, or move it to the workbook. Topic 3.2 covers cutting.
Choose strong contrast between text and background: very dark on very light, or the reverse. Check the pair with a contrast checker. Avoid text on photographs unless you put a solid panel behind it.
Pick a plain typeface in a regular or medium weight. Thin weights and narrow faces break up when projected.
Label charts directly and at the same minimum size. A legend in 10 point defeats the chart. Topic 3.3 covers charts.
Do not rely on colour alone to carry meaning. Add a label, a shape or a position.

Test it. On your laptop, view the slide in the slide sorter at about a quarter of full size. If you cannot read it there, the back row will struggle. Then check in the real room, lights on, from the last chair.

why.text: The sizes are practitioner judgement. No standard for projected type was opened for this topic, and the right size depends on the screen and the distance. A fixed minimum is still useful, because it turns "design for the back row" in topic 3.3 into something you can check.

On contrast there is a published reference point. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, which topic 3.15 introduces, ask at level AA for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 between text and its background. Large text, meaning 18 point or 14 point bold, may drop to 3 to 1. The purpose is that people with moderately low vision can read the text without extra tools. The guideline is written for web content and its explanatory page does not discuss projection. Treat 4.5 to 1 as a floor for slides and aim well above it. A projector in a bright room shows less contrast than your laptop does.

Readable slides are partly an access matter and partly a matter of respect. Someone who cannot read the screen stops trying. And a client judging a trainer who used to be a designer will look at the slides first.

try.text: Open a deck you have used. Find the smallest text on each slide and write the size beside it. Fix the three worst. Then project the deck, or put it on a television, and read every slide aloud from the far wall with the lights on.

try.title: A worked example: minimum sizes for a widescreen slide, as working practice and not a standard

head: Element
Minimum
Note
rows: One line if you can, two at most
If it will not fit, cut or split the slide
Label lines and bars directly, no legend
Or move the source to the workbook
20 point, about five rows by four columns
Larger tables go in the workbook
At least 4.5 to 1, the WCAG level AA figure for normal text
Aim higher for projection. Check with a contrast checker
About eight to ten words a line
Shorter lines are easier to find from a distance

items: The client's template sets body text at 14 point. Keep the template's colours and logo, and raise the sizes. Say why.
Grey text on white looks elegant on a laptop and vanishes on a projector. Use near-black.
A screenshot of software carries tiny text. Crop to the part you are discussing and enlarge it.
You shrink the type to fit one more line. Move the line to the next slide.
You test in a dark office and deliver in a room with windows. Test with the lights on.

quiz.q: What contrast ratio does WCAG ask for at level AA for normal-sized text?
quiz.a: At least 4.5 to 1. Large text may be 3 to 1.

quiz.q: A comparison table will only fit on the slide at 14 point. What do you do?
quiz.a: Put the full table in the workbook and show only the two or three cells you are talking about, at 20 point or more. People cannot read and listen to a dense table at once in any case.

quiz.q: The client's brand template uses pale grey text on white. What do you do?
quiz.a: Keep the brand colours for panels and accents and set the text in near-black, then show the client both versions projected. Most agree once they see it from the back of the room.

stages.name: Run the room
stages.question: How do we facilitate, in person and online?
stages.wordingStatus: Draft: part names and topic titles for this stage were written for the build pack and have not been seen by Mica

parts.title: Hold the room
parts.summary: Presence, questions, group dynamics and story.

topics.title: Slow down and use the pause

situation.text: You talk fast when nervous, fill every silence, and have been told communication is "93 per cent non-verbal".

items: Slow down.
Pause after a key point and after a question.
Vary pace and volume on purpose.
Read nerves as readiness.
Prepare and rehearse. Presence is built.

why.text: Presence is the composure and attention that let you hold a room. It comes from preparation and practice more than personality. A pause gives people time to think and signals confidence.

The "93 per cent" figure adds 38 per cent for tone of voice to 55 per cent for the face, leaving 7 per cent for words. Those weights come from 1960s experiments on how people judge liking and disliking. Their author says they apply only when someone is talking about their own feelings or attitudes. When you teach, your words carry the content.

Nerves and excitement feel alike in the body. In one set of experiments, people who told themselves they were excited before singing, speaking in public or doing maths performed better than people who tried to calm down.

items.title: Content matters
items.text: The 93 per cent claim is a myth.

try.text: Deliver a short segment on camera. Get structured feedback on pace, pause and presence.

try.title: The same opening, twice
try.text: First run: a trainer reads the three aims in one breath and moves straight on. Second run: she says the first aim, stops for two slow breaths, looks round the room, then gives the next. Same words. The second version gives people time to take each aim in.

items: Claims about reading body language are overconfident.
Presence changes on camera. Practise both.
Do not perform a personality that is not yours.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Mehrabian (1981), Silent Messages: Implicit Communication of Emotions and Attitudes.
Brooks (2014), Get excited: Reappraising pre-performance anxiety as excitement.

topics.bodyStatus: 2 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: What does a pause do?
quiz.a: Gives people time to think and signals confidence.

quiz.q: Where does presence come from?
quiz.a: Preparation and practice.

quiz.q: What is wrong with "93 per cent non-verbal"?
quiz.a: It stretches findings about how people judge liking and disliking to all communication.

topics.tierReason: Slowing down, pausing and rehearsing are standard presentation practice with little direct testing in training rooms. Only the step on reading nerves as readiness has an experiment behind it.
openPoints: Mehrabian and Wiener (1967), Decoding of inconsistent communications: the PubMed page would not load. Not confirmed.

No source was found or opened for the claims that a pause signals confidence, that presence comes from practice more than personality, or that body-language reading is overconfident. They are left as practitioner statements.
No account of how the Mehrabian figures are misapplied was opened other than the author's own page.
Whether the Brooks (2014) result has been replicated was not checked.
checkFindings: The draft cited Mehrabian (1971). The author's own page for Silent Messages gives the 1981 Wadsworth edition and does not mention 1971, so the link is labelled 1981.

The draft said the 93 per cent figure comes from a narrow study. The author's page points to two original sources and describes experiments on like and dislike. Text and quiz answer changed to say experiments on liking and disliking.
The author's page states the weights apply only when a person is talking about their own feelings or attitudes. This supports calling the general claim a myth. The remember card was left as it is.
The draft sentence that what you say still matters most is not something the source says. It was replaced with a narrower sentence.

The step on reading nerves as readiness had no source. Brooks (2014) supports it: reappraising anxiety as excitement beat trying to calm down on singing, public speaking and maths tasks. A short paragraph was added and the paper linked.
The PubMed record for Mehrabian and Ferris (1967), Journal of Consulting Psychology, was opened and confirms the paper and date but shows no abstract, so it is not in the links.

topics.title: Ask, then wait

situation.text: You ask "any questions?", wait one second, and move on.

items: Decide whether this moment needs telling or drawing out.
Ask open questions.
After asking, wait several seconds.
Receive a wrong answer in a way that keeps the person contributing.
Use pairs first so everyone thinks.
Wait again after an answer before you respond.

why.text: Presenting sends content to an audience. Facilitating draws learning out of a group. A skilled trainer knows which the moment needs.

In studies of school lessons, teachers usually waited about one second after a question. When they waited three to five seconds, answers got longer, more pupils answered and pupils asked more questions. Most people wait far too little.

This research comes from school classrooms, not workplace training. Treat three seconds as a starting point, not a rule. A long silence after an unclear question only adds confusion, so make the question clear first.

why.title: Wait-time and rewards as instructional variables
why.found: From five years of recorded primary science lessons, teachers waited about one second for an answer and replied within about a second of getting one. When both waits were stretched to three to five seconds, pupils gave longer answers, offered more answers unprompted, asked more questions and sounded more confident.
why.means: Count to three in your head after you ask and again after someone answers, and expect to adapt this for adults.

try.text: Facilitate a short discussion with open questions and deliberate waiting. Note what the silence produced.

try.title: Any questions?
try.text: Before: "Any questions? No? Good." One second, then the next slide. After: "What would make this hard to use on Monday? Take a moment." The trainer counts slowly to five in her head. Someone speaks on four. She waits again before replying.

items: Silence feels longer to you than to the room.
Know when to hold your own expertise back.
Do not let the confident few answer everything.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Rowe (1972), Wait-Time and Rewards as Instructional Variables: Their Influence on Language, Logic, and Fate Control.
Rowe (1987), Wait Time: Slowing Down May Be a Way of Speeding Up. American Educator.
Tobin (1987), The Role of Wait Time in Higher Cognitive Level Learning.
Stahl (1994), Using "Think-Time" and "Wait-Time" Skillfully in the Classroom.

topics.bodyStatus: 4 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: What is the difference between presenting and facilitating?
quiz.a: Presenting sends content. Facilitating draws learning out of the group.

quiz.q: How long should you wait after a question?
quiz.a: Several seconds.

quiz.q: What does waiting produce?
quiz.a: More answers, and better ones.

topics.tierReason: School classroom studies, pulled together in a published review, link waits of three seconds or more to longer and more frequent answers. None of the summaries read covers adults in workplace training.
openPoints: Rowe (1986), Wait time: slowing down may be a way of speeding up, Journal of Teacher Education 37(1): journals.sagepub.com refused the request. Not confirmed directly.

Schwarz, The Skilled Facilitator (third edition, Wiley): the Wiley pages refused the request. Search results show the title, edition and publisher, but the description was not read, so it is not linked.
Bens, Facilitating with Ease! (fourth edition, Wiley): same position as Schwarz.

Duell (1994), Extended Wait Time and University Student Achievement, American Educational Research Journal, appeared in search results and may be the nearest study with adult learners. It could not be opened. Worth reading before the page says anything about adults.
No source was opened for the steps on receiving wrong answers or using pairs first.
checkFindings: The draft cited Rowe (1972, 1986). The 1972 paper was opened on ERIC and supports the claim. The 1986 Journal of Teacher Education article could not be opened (the publisher's site refused the request). The 1987 American Educator article with the same title was opened on ERIC and is linked in its place.
Rowe studied two waits: after the question and after the answer. The draft covered only the first. A step was added for the second.
The evidence read is all from schools. A caveat was added so the page does not imply it was tested with adults at work.
Stahl (1994) notes that three seconds is a convention, not a strict cut-off, and that silence after an unclear question adds confusion. Both points were added.

Tobin (1987) is a review across subjects and school grades and concludes that wait time appears to help higher-level learning by giving more time to think. It was added because the task asked for it to be checked.

topics.title: Manage the group, not only the content

situation.text: One person dominates, two have gone quiet, and a disagreement is brewing.

items: Watch the group as well as the content.
Give dominant voices a job and quieter ones a turn.
Build individual accountability into group tasks.
Deal with conflict early and in private where you can.
Protect safety while you do it.

why.text: Group dynamics do not sort themselves out. The well-known model of forming, storming, norming and performing is a useful lens. It was built from a review of about 50 earlier studies, many of them of therapy groups, and not from new data on work teams. Real groups do not move through the stages so neatly.
People tend to contribute less in a group than alone. Giving each person a visible part counters that.

try.text: Plan how you would handle three difficult-group situations while protecting safety. Role-play one.

try.title: A job for the loudest voice
try.text: One person answers every question. At the next task the trainer asks him to keep time and write up the group's points. She gives everyone two minutes to note an answer alone, then asks two quieter people to read theirs out first.

items: Norms about speaking up and silence differ between cultures.
Publicly correcting someone costs the whole room.
Large groups need structure, not volume.

Name people only after they have had time to prepare an answer, by writing alone or talking in a pair. Say in advance that you will ask people by name, and let anyone pass. That is what keeps the example on this page safe, and it squares 1.17 with the warning about public failure in 1.13.

Giving the loudest person the pen has a cost. The scribe decides what gets recorded, and the job can feel like a punishment. The part "Difficult moments" gives a fuller ladder for this and the other hard cases.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Tuckman (1984), This Week's Citation Classic: Developmental sequence in small groups. The author's own account of the 1965 paper.

topics.bodyStatus: 1 source checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: Do group dynamics resolve themselves?
quiz.a: No. They need managing.

quiz.q: How should you use the forming-storming model?
quiz.a: As a lens, not a script.

quiz.q: What counters people coasting in groups?
quiz.a: Individual accountability.

topics.tierReason: The stage model is a synthesis of older studies used as a lens, and the steps for handling a group are professional practice. The social loafing research behind individual accountability could not be opened in this run.
openPoints: Tuckman (1965), Developmental sequence in small groups, Psychological Bulletin 63: not opened.
Critics of the Tuckman model, for example Bonebright (2010), 40 years of storming, Human Resource Development International: the publisher page was not reachable. Not confirmed.

Latané, Williams and Harkins (1979), Many hands make light the work, and Karau and Williams (1993), Social loafing: a meta-analytic review: neither could be opened. The page's claim that people contribute less in a group than alone, and that individual accountability counters it, is therefore unreferenced for now.
A 2021 PubMed record on effort gains and losses in teams (PMID 34292010) appeared in search results and may be a newer meta-analysis. The page would not load.
checkFindings: The draft's caution about the stage model is supported by the author's own account: a literature synthesis, mostly therapy and training groups, uneven study quality. One sentence was added to say where the model came from.

The same account says a 1977 follow-up by Tuckman and Jensen reviewed 22 later studies, mostly supported the stages and added a fifth, adjourning. The page does not mention this and it was not added, as the follow-up paper itself was not opened.
The original 1965 paper could not be opened (PubMed and the APA site refused the request), so the link is to the author's commentary and is labelled as such.

topics.title: Use a story to make the point concrete
topics.theory: Storytelling and the curse of knowledge

situation.text: You explain an abstract idea three times and it does not land.

items: Find a short, true story that shows the idea.
Make it concrete: a person, a place, what happened.
Say the point it makes.
Use an analogy from something the group already knows.
Check the story serves the point.

why.text: A well-chosen story makes an abstract point concrete and easier to remember. A meta-analysis found that people understood and recalled stories better than essays. People who know a subject well find it hard to set that knowledge aside and judge what a newcomer will follow. This is called the curse of knowledge. Naming it helps you guard against it.
Practitioner writing on communication suggests that ideas which last tend to be concrete, unexpected and to carry some feeling. Treat that as a rule of thumb.

why.title: Stories against essays: a meta-analysis
why.found: Across more than 75 samples and over 33,000 participants, stories were understood and recalled better than essays. Results varied a great deal between studies and there were signs of publication bias.
why.means: Use a short story to carry an abstract point, and do not expect every story to help.

items.title: Concrete
items.text: A person and an event beat an abstraction.

try.text: Tell a short story that makes one abstract idea concrete. Check it against the risk of distraction.

try.title: From rule to story
try.text: Abstract: "Handover errors come from assumed knowledge." Story: "On a night shift a nurse wrote 'usual dose' on a chart. The agency nurse who took over had never met the patient." Then say the point: write what a stranger would need.

items: A vivid story can outweigh the evidence.
Keep a bank of stories and retire the stale ones.
Other people's stories need permission.
The authors of the story meta-analysis warn against forcing all content into story form. Use a story where it fits the point.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Mar and colleagues (2021), Memory and comprehension of narrative versus expository texts: a meta-analysis. Psychonomic Bulletin and Review.
Camerer, Loewenstein and Weber (1989), The curse of knowledge in economic settings: an experimental analysis. Journal of Political Economy.

topics.bodyStatus: 2 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: What does a story do for an abstract idea?
quiz.a: Makes it concrete and memorable.

quiz.q: Why do experts explain badly?
quiz.a: They find it hard to set aside what they know and see the subject as a newcomer does.

quiz.q: What must a story do?
quiz.a: Serve the point.

openPoints: Heath and Heath, Made to Stick: no publisher page was returned by the search, so it is not in the reference list. Add it once the Penguin Random House page has been read.
Hinds (1999), The curse of expertise, would be a closer source for experts misjudging novices. Not opened.
The seductive details research (Sundararajan and Adesope 2020) on the risk of distraction was not opened.
The watch item that a vivid story can outweigh the evidence has no source.
checkFindings: The draft said experts explain badly because they cannot remember not knowing. Camerer, Loewenstein and Weber (1989) say better-informed people struggle to ignore their extra information. The text and one quiz answer were reworded to match. The paper's experiments were on economic judgements, so its use here is an extension.
The claim that stories are memorable is now tied to Mar and colleagues (2021). No effect size is given on the page because I could not be sure the figure sits in the abstract itself.
The sentence on which ideas survive was unsourced and is now worded as practitioner advice.
Added a watch item with the meta-analysis authors' own caution about forcing content into narrative.
topics.tierReason: One meta-analysis found stories are understood and recalled better than essays, but the studies varied widely, showed signs of publication bias, and tested texts, not a trainer's spoken stories.

topics.title: Set up the room before you plan the session
topics.theory: The learning environment: physical, virtual and hybrid

situation.text: You arrive to find a boardroom table, no wall space and a projector at the far end.

items: Ask about the room before you design: layout, light, sound, wall space, access.
Arrange seating for the activity: small tables for group work, a horseshoe for discussion.
Check everyone can see, hear and get in.
Arrive early and move the furniture.
Online, the platform is the room. Set it up the same way.

why.text: The same content lands differently in a well or badly arranged space. Layout signals what kind of session this is: rows say "listen", small tables say "work together".
Research on learning spaces is mostly from schools and universities. For workplace training, treat this as informed practice.

One university study compared the same course, with the same lecturer, in a room with round tables and a room with rows. In the round-table room the lecturer talked less and led more discussion, although he meant to teach both groups the same way. It was one course with about forty students, so take it as an illustration.

items.title: Layout signals
items.text: Rows or tables send a message.

try.text: Draw the room for your next session. Mark where groups work, where you stand and what people can see.

try.title: The boardroom table
try.text: The room has one long table and the plan has four group tasks. The trainer arrives forty minutes early, pushes the table to the wall and sets four clusters of chairs round flipchart sheets taped to the windows. She checks the screen from the back seat.

try.title: A room access checklist
lines: Before the day: ask everyone, in the joining instructions, what would help them take part. Include food and prayer needs.
Microphone: if the room has one, use it, even if you think your voice carries. Ask about a hearing loop and whether it works.
Questions from the floor: repeat each one before you answer, so the whole room and anyone lip-reading has heard it.
Writing: large, dark letters on flipcharts. Do not use red against green to carry meaning.
Routes: walk the step-free route from the entrance to the room, the toilets, lunch and the fire exit yourself.
Seating: let people choose where to sit. Leave space at a table for a wheelchair and keep some chairs near the door.
Standing activities: give a seated version as part of the instruction.
Quiet space: find a room or corner where someone can step out, and say where it is in your opening.
Lighting: avoid glare on the screen and do not stand in front of a bright window. Keep the lights up enough to read and to see your face.
Printed copies: have paper copies of the slides and of any text on screen, including two in large print.
Breaks: fewer and longer, with a clear statement that anyone can step out at any time.

items: A fixed room may need a changed activity.
Check step-free access, hearing loops and quiet space.
Temperature and noise can distract. Check both.

items.label: Whiteside, Brooks and Walker (2010), Making the case for space: three years of empirical research on learning environments. EDUCAUSE Quarterly.

quiz.a: Before you design.

quiz.q: What does layout signal?
quiz.a: What kind of session it is.

quiz.q: What is the room when you teach online?
quiz.a: The platform.

Step-free access, hearing loops and quiet space: no official UK page was checked. The page does not say what the law requires and should not until the Equality and Human Rights Commission guidance on reasonable adjustments has been read.
The claim that rows say listen and small tables say work together is practitioner reasoning. The study above is consistent with it but did not test it directly.
checkFindings: The placeholder reference was replaced with Whiteside, Brooks and Walker (2010), an article by the researchers on the University of Minnesota classroom studies. It supports the claim that layout changes what happens in the room. The difference in final grades between the two rooms was not statistically significant, so the page makes no claim about results.
The buildNote gives no instruction or warning. Nothing was changed because of it.
The watch item on temperature and noise was softened because no source was found.
topics.tierReason: Room set-up is professional practice. The one study read is a small comparison in a single university course, with nothing on workplace training.

topics.title: Train the team together when the work is done together

situation.text: Five people from five teams attend a teamwork course. They return to teams who were not there.

items: Where the work is done as a team, train the team together.
Practise the team's real tasks.
Practise communication, handovers and speaking up.
Debrief as a team after practice and after real work.
Give each person a turn at another role.

why.text: Team skills are different from individual skills. A team has to coordinate, share a picture of the task and back each other up. Those are learned by practising together.

A meta-analysis of 93 results from 2,650 teams found that team training had a moderate, positive effect on how teams think, feel, work together and perform. A later meta-analysis of 129 healthcare studies found the same direction. A third found that teams and individuals who debriefed did about 20 to 25 per cent better than those who did not.

These studies compare team training with none. They show that what is trained, how stable the team is and how big it is all change the result. They do not test whether training the whole team beats training a few members, so treat that step as sound reasoning.

why.title: Does team training improve team performance?
why.found: Pooling 93 results from 2,650 teams, team training had a moderate, positive effect on team thinking, attitudes, teamwork and performance. Training content, team stability and team size changed the size of the effect.
why.means: Train teams on their real work, and expect better results from stable teams with focused content.

items.title: Debrief
items.text: After practice and after the real thing.

try.text: For one team you train, list the three moments where coordination fails. Design practice for one.

try.title: Same course, two ways
try.text: Before: five people from five teams spend a day on generic teamwork. After: one ward team spends a morning practising its own shift handover, swaps roles for the second run, and ends with fifteen minutes on what to keep and what to change.

items: Team-building days are not team training.
Rank silences people. Make it safe to speak up.
Releasing a whole team is costly. Plan cover.

items.label: Salas and colleagues (2008), Does team training improve team performance? A meta-analysis. Human Factors.
Hughes and colleagues (2016), Saving lives: a meta-analysis of team training in healthcare. Journal of Applied Psychology.
Tannenbaum and Cerasoli (2013), Do team and individual debriefs enhance performance? A meta-analysis. Human Factors.

quiz.q: When should you train a team together?
quiz.a: When the work is done as a team.

quiz.q: What do teams need to practise?
quiz.a: Communication, handovers and speaking up, on real tasks.

quiz.q: What helps teams learn from practice?
quiz.a: A structured debrief.

The step on giving each person a turn at another role (cross-training) was not confirmed in any summary read.

The watch item that team-building days are not team training is a distinction, not a finding. A separate meta-analysis on team building exists (Klein and colleagues 2009, seen in search results only) and reports that team building has effects of its own, so do not read the item as saying team building does nothing.
The Tannenbaum and Cerasoli abstract was read on the Epistemonikos record because PubMed and the journal page refused.

Hughes (2016): team training improved satisfaction and skills across settings, with positive effects on length of stay and mortality that rest on few studies. The page only says the direction was the same.
Tannenbaum and Cerasoli (2013): 46 samples, 2,136 people, debrief against no debrief, d = 0.67, about 20 to 25 per cent. The percentage is used on the page.
Added a caveat that the meta-analyses do not test intact-team attendance against mixed attendance.
topics.tierReason: Meta-analyses show team training and debriefs improve team results, but they compare training with no training, and do not test whether the whole team must attend together.

topics.title: Adjust for the cultures in the room

situation.text: A discussion method that works at home falls silent with a group from several countries.

items: Find out who will be in the room.
Vary how people contribute: writing first, pairs, then the group.
Be explicit about what you are asking for.
Speak plainly and avoid idiom.
Ask a local colleague what to watch for.

why.text: Groups differ in how directly people speak, how they treat rank, and what silence means. A method that assumes everyone will challenge the trainer does not travel.

Models that score countries on cultural dimensions are widely used and criticised for treating a country as one culture. A meta-analysis of 558 studies that used the best-known model found that about 80 per cent of the variation in cultural values lies within countries, not between them.

why.title: Does country equate with culture?
why.found: A meta-analysis of 558 studies using Hofstede's framework found that about 80 per cent of the variation in cultural values sits within countries. The authors conclude that country is often a weak stand-in for culture.
why.means: Find out about the people in the room. Do not predict a person from a passport.

try.text: Take one discussion activity. Add a written step and a pair step before the group step.

try.title: Three ways in
try.text: Before: "Who disagrees with this?" Silence. After: everyone writes one concern on a card. Pairs compare cards. Each pair reads out one concern, not their own. The trainer says plainly that she wants to hear the problems.

items: Guessing someone's culture from their name is a mistake.
Working in a second language is tiring. Slow down.
Humour and examples may not travel.
Books that place countries on scales are practitioner guides. Use them for questions to ask, not for predictions about a person.

quiz.a: Any two of: directness, treatment of rank, the meaning of silence.

quiz.q: How can you give everyone a way in?
quiz.a: Writing first, then pairs, then the group.

quiz.q: What is the risk of country models?
quiz.a: Stereotyping. People vary within a country.

parts.title: Teach online
parts.summary: Remote and hybrid sessions on their own terms.

topics.title: Design against video-call fatigue

situation.text: Your in-person day has been moved online unchanged. By mid-afternoon people are drained.

items: Use a wider view, and do not hold constant close-up eye contact.
Suggest people hide their own image.
Build in movement and audio-only stretches.
Reduce what people must watch at once: faces, chat and slides.
Give people a choice about cameras.

why.text: One researcher proposes four likely causes of video-call fatigue: too much close-up eye contact, seeing yourself constantly, sitting still, and the extra effort of sending and reading non-verbal cues. He says the four have not yet been tested directly, so treat them as likely, not proven. Each has a design answer.
Fatigue is a feature of the setting, not a failing of the learner.

why.title: A scale for video-call fatigue
why.found: The authors built a 15-item questionnaire covering general, social, emotional, visual and motivational fatigue, and tested it with 2,724 people. People with more frequent, longer and more closely packed video meetings reported more fatigue. This is survey data, so it shows a link, not a cause.
why.means: Shorten live blocks and put gaps between them.

try.text: Take a tiring online session. Redesign it against the four causes.

try.title: The afternoon block
try.text: Before: three hours of slides with all cameras on in gallery view. After: forty-minute blocks. One block is a phone call in pairs while walking. Cameras are optional during input, and the trainer shows people how to hide their own image.

items: Cameras on may help connection and may cost energy. Let people choose.
Splitting attention between chat and slides is a load problem.
In survey data, more frequent, longer and closely packed video meetings go with more fatigue. Keep live blocks short and leave gaps.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Bailenson (2021), Nonverbal overload: a theoretical argument for the causes of Zoom fatigue. Technology, Mind, and Behavior.
Fauville and colleagues (2021), Zoom Exhaustion and Fatigue Scale. Computers in Human Behavior Reports.

topics.bodyStatus: 2 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: Name the four proposed causes of video-call fatigue.
quiz.a: Close-up eye contact, seeing yourself, sitting still, and the effort of sending and reading cues.

quiz.q: Whose failing is the fatigue?
quiz.a: Nobody's. It comes from the setting.

quiz.q: What is the trade-off with cameras on?
quiz.a: Connection against energy.

openPoints: Fauville and colleagues' second paper, on non-verbal mechanisms and why fatigue is higher for women, is the survey test of the four causes. It appeared in search results but was not opened.
Shockley and colleagues (2021) on camera use and fatigue: not opened.
No source for cameras helping connection.
checkFindings: Bailenson (2021): the paper's four headings are eye gaze at a close distance, cognitive load, an all-day mirror and reduced mobility. The draft described the cognitive load argument as reading cues only. It covers sending them too. The why text and quiz answer were corrected.
The summary says the arguments rest on theory and earlier research and have not been tested directly in video calls. The first-pass softening was right and is now stated in the author's terms.
Bailenson's own remedies (hide self-view, smaller faces, audio-only calls, a set-up that lets you move) match the page's steps.
The watch item that shorter is better was replaced with the survey finding from Fauville and colleagues (2021). The camera item was softened.
topics.tierReason: The four causes are a theoretical argument that its author says has not been tested directly, and the supporting evidence read is survey data.

topics.title: Build connection, thinking and direction online

situation.text: The online course is a set of videos and a forum nobody posts in.

items: Help people feel present as real people.
Set tasks that make people think and discuss, and bring discussion to a conclusion.
Be visibly there: design, guide and steer.
Find the weakest of the three and add one move to strengthen it.

why.text: A widely used framework says good online learning needs three kinds of presence working together: social, cognitive and teaching. It was built to describe written, discussion-based courses in universities.
A common weak pattern is content with a thin teaching presence and little of the other two.

why.title: Learning in communities of inquiry: a review
why.found: The authors reviewed the studies that used the framework up to 2008. Few measured learning, and those that did mostly used a single survey question on how much students felt they had learned. They concluded the evidence did not show deep learning arising from the model.
why.means: Use the three presences as a design checklist, and measure learning yourself.

try.text: Audit an online course for the three presences. Add one move to strengthen the weakest.

try.title: The silent forum
try.text: Before: "Post your thoughts on week two." Nobody does. After: "Post one case from your own work where this failed. Reply to one other person with a question." On Friday the tutor posts a short summary of what the group concluded.

items: The framework is widely used and has its critics. A 2009 review found that few studies had measured learning at all, and most relied on students rating their own learning.
A forum needs a reason to post.
Presence takes facilitator time. Budget for it.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Garrison, Anderson and Archer, Critical thinking and computer conferencing: a model and tool to assess cognitive presence. A paper by the framework's authors that sets out the three presences.
Rourke and Kanuka (2009), Learning in communities of inquiry: a review of the literature. Journal of Distance Education.

quiz.q: What are the three presences?
quiz.a: Social, cognitive and teaching.

quiz.q: What does weak online learning often lack?
quiz.a: Social and cognitive presence.

quiz.q: What is teaching presence?
quiz.a: The design, guidance and steering that hold the rest together.

The sentence about most weak online learning, and its quiz question, were softened.

topics.title: Keep live time for interaction

situation.text: A two-hour webinar has ninety minutes of slides and ten minutes for questions.

items: Move anything one-way to pre-work.
Use polls, chat, breakout rooms and shared documents to get people thinking.
Give each breakout a clear task, a named reporter and a time.
Use pairs before whole-group discussion.
Have a second person run the technology.

why.text: Live time is scarce. Spend it on what needs real-time interaction. If a live session has no interaction, it should not be live.
The tools are instruments for taking part and recalling, not novelties.

The research is on formats, not on this advice. One meta-analysis found live online learning did slightly better than self-paced online learning on what people learned, and no clear difference from the classroom. Another found blended courses beat classroom teaching, but those courses also gave people more time and more interaction, so the mix alone may not be the cause.

try.text: Redesign an online session so every live minute is interactive. Move the rest to pre-work.

try.title: Ninety minutes of slides
try.text: Before: ninety minutes of slides, ten for questions. After: the slides go out as a twenty-minute recording. The live hour opens with a poll on the recording, then breakouts with one case each, a named reporter and eight minutes on the clock.

try.title: A breakout checklist
lines: Give the whole instruction before you open the rooms: the task, what to bring back, the time, who speaks.
Show the task on a slide and paste the same words into the chat, so people can still read it inside their room.
Groups of three or four. Pairs stall if one person drops out, and five is too many for everyone to speak.
One shared document per room, with the link in the chat and the room number at the top of the page.
Each room names a spokesperson before it starts on the task. Suggest a rule, such as the person whose first name comes first in the alphabet.
Give a time call into every room at the halfway point and at one minute to go.
Producer before the session: build the rooms, check the links to the shared documents, agree how you will reach each other privately.
Producer during: open the rooms on your word, send the time calls, move anyone left alone into another group, let latecomers in.
Producer throughout: watch the chat and the waiting room, and tell you if a room asks for help.
You: visit two or three rooms with your camera on, listen for a minute, and leave unless you are asked something.
On return: one point from each spokesperson, in room order, with no repeats.

items: An empty breakout room is a design failure.
Fewer cues online. Ask people what they are thinking.
Have a plan for when the platform fails.

quiz.a: What needs real-time interaction.

quiz.q: What does a breakout need?
quiz.a: A clear task, a named reporter and a time.

quiz.q: Why have a producer?
quiz.a: So the facilitator can attend to the learners.

topics.title: In hybrid, design for the remote person first

situation.text: Half the group is in the room and half is on a screen at the end of the table.

items: Design the remote experience first.
Give remote people a voice early and often.
Pair people so that the sound works. Pair room with room and remote with remote, or mix them only where each in-room partner has a headset and a separate corner or room.
Check sound and sightlines from the remote end.
For self-paced parts, build in recall, spacing and a steady rhythm.

why.text: Hybrid is hard to do well, because remote people easily become spectators. A review of 47 studies found that remote students often feel left out, take part less and struggle to signal that they want to speak. Designing for them first is a practical answer. It has not been tested head to head.
Self-paced study can lose people. Spacing, recall and a facilitator's regular presence are sensible ways to keep them going. No source on completion has been checked for this page.

why.title: Synchronous hybrid learning: a review
why.found: Reviewing 47 studies, the authors found that hybrid sessions widen access but are hard to teach. Remote students often feel excluded and are more passive, and sound quality is decisive. Most studies were case studies and only one was an experiment.
why.means: Plan the remote experience and the sound first, and check both from the remote end.

items.title: Equal experience
items.text: Design it. It will not happen by default.

try.text: Plan a hybrid session that gives remote and in-room people an equivalent experience. List the moves.

try.title: Who speaks first
try.text: Before: the room talks for ten minutes, then someone asks if the people online have anything to add. After: each question goes to a remote person first. For pair work, in-room people pair with each other and remote people pair in breakout rooms. Each remote pair has a named person in the room who reads out their point. For the one exercise where the trainer wants mixed pairs, each in-room partner takes a laptop and a headset to a separate corner or a side room and joins from there, with the main room's microphone and speakers muted. A colleague at the remote end checks the sound.

items: If you cannot make it fair, run it all online.
Room microphones decide whether remote people can take part.
Side conversations in the room exclude the screen.
The research on hybrid sessions is young. Most of it is case studies from universities, with very few comparisons.

Two devices on the same call in one room cause echo and a feedback howl. Keep one microphone and one set of speakers live in the room. Anyone else who joins from the room wears a headset or goes somewhere else. Test it with two laptops before the day.

quiz.a: The remote person's.

quiz.q: What happens otherwise?
quiz.a: They become spectators.

quiz.q: What helps people finish self-paced study?

parts.title: Judgement and recovery
parts.summary: What experienced trainers do when the plan stops working.

topics.title: Know why a tip works before you use it

situation.text: A colleague swears by a trick: always start with an icebreaker, always end on a quiz.

items: For each tip, ask what principle makes it work.
Keep the tips that rest on one.
Hold the ones that are only habit loosely. Try them, and watch what they do.
Write the principle next to the tip.
Adapt the tip when conditions change.

why.text: A tip you understand you can adapt. A tip you copy breaks when conditions change.

Most of what keeps a room running has never been tested in a study. That does not make it worthless. Some craft lore is sound and some is superstition, and the test is the one you apply to any learning claim (1.11). Call it the tip plus principle test. Say the tip, then name the principle that would make it work and the conditions it needs. If you can do that, keep the tip and adapt it. If you cannot, treat it as habit until you have seen what it does.

This topic is the way in to the craft on this site. Two parts of this stage, "Run a session" and "Difficult moments", are practitioner judgement and are labelled as craft. Each topic there gives an order of moves and the words to say, and names the principle it leans on. Use them as this page describes. Try the move, keep the reason, and change the wording until it sounds like you.

try.text: Ask an experienced trainer for the five tips they rely on most. For each one, say aloud to them the principle you think lies behind it, and ask when it has let them down. Write the tip, the principle and its limit in one line each.

try.title: Always start with an icebreaker
try.text: Tip: always start with an icebreaker. Principle: people speak up more once they have spoken once. Adapted for a team that already knows each other: skip the game and open with a paired question about the topic.

try.title: The test applied to eight common tips

head: Tip
Principle behind it
Verdict
rows: People speak more easily once they have spoken once.
Keep the principle. Open with a paired question on the topic.
Never turn your back on the room.
Your voice goes into the flipchart and you stop seeing people.
Keep. Write, turn round, then talk.
Tell them what you will tell them, tell them, then tell them what you told them.
Signposts help people follow the structure.
Half sound. Keep the signpost at the start. At the end, ask them to recall it (2.24).
Nobody can concentrate for more than twenty minutes.
Treat the number as habit, not a finding. Change what people are doing often and watch the room (4.14).
Put the hard content in the morning.
People have more energy for difficult material at some times than others.
Often sound. 2.14 says where it holds.
Never answer a question you can hand back to the group.
People remember what they work out for themselves.
Adapt. Hand back questions of judgement. Answer questions of fact quickly.
Give the restart as a clock time.
"Ten minutes" starts at a different moment for each person.
Keep. It is craft, and it costs nothing.
Recalling something strengthens the memory of it.
Keep the recall, but not as the last thing. End on the first-use plan (5.2).

items: Experienced people defend habits. Ask what it is for.
Breaking a rule is earned by knowing its purpose.
Your own favourites need the same test.

quiz.a: So you can adapt it when conditions change.

quiz.q: How do you tell sound lore from folklore?
quiz.a: Ask what principle makes it work.

quiz.q: When may you break a rule?
quiz.a: When you know what it is for.

topics.title: Rehearse what could go wrong

situation.text: The projector fails, a participant turns hostile, and the main activity falls flat.

items: Before the session, imagine it has gone badly and ask why.
List the three most likely failures.
Rehearse a response to each.
Carry a version that needs no technology.
When it happens, protect people's dignity first.

why.text: These are predictable situations, not rare accidents. A plan for recovery matters as much as the plan for the session.
Good improvising rests on preparation.

The pre-mortem comes from Gary Klein, who describes it as a team exercise at the start of a project. Everyone assumes the project has failed and writes down why. He cites earlier research suggesting that imagining an event has already happened helps people find reasons for it. Using it alone before a session is an adaptation.

try.text: Run a pre-mortem on a real session. List three likely failures and rehearse a recovery for each.

try.title: Ten minutes the night before
try.text: The trainer imagines the session went badly and writes why: the projector failed, the case study ran long, one person argued with everything. She prints the key slide as a handout, marks which exercise to cut, and plans a line for taking the argument to the break.

items: Over-planning for disaster can make you rigid.
Timing goes wrong more often than technology.
Know what you would cut.

quiz.a: People's dignity.

Keith and Frese (2008), the meta-analysis behind the linked error management mechanic: not opened.
No research on expert and novice trainers or teachers handling disruption was opened.
The watch item that timing goes wrong more often than technology has no source.

Klein reports a 1989 study by Mitchell, Russo and Pennington and gives a 30 per cent figure for it. The figure is second-hand, so it is not on the page.
The unsourced sentence comparing novices and experts was replaced, with its quiz question and answer.
The link is to a copy of the article held on another organisation's wiki, because that is the page that opened. Replace it with the hbr.org page once that has been read.

topics.title: Change the plan when the room tells you to

situation.text: You are twenty minutes into the plan and the room has gone quiet in the wrong way.

items: Watch for energy, confusion and withdrawal.
Ask the room what is happening.
Change the plan: slow down, switch activity, take a break.
Online, ask more often.

why.text: The plan is a guess to be revised against what the room tells you. Delivering the plan while the room switches off is a failure.
Be modest about reading people. Cues are easy to misread and may differ between people and cultures. Asking is a safer check than guessing.

The idea that experienced people read a situation quickly comes from studies of firefighters, paramedics, pilots and chess players. Research on teachers noticing what a class is doing comes mostly from schools and has not been checked for this page. Treat reading the room as a skill to practise, not a proven method.

try.text: Practise responding to a room that shifts from engaged to disengaged. Debrief what you noticed and did.

try.title: Quiet in the wrong way
try.text: Twenty minutes in, nobody is writing. The trainer stops. "I may have lost you. Hold up one to five fingers for how clear this is." Mostly twos. She drops the next two slides and works one example on the flipchart.

items: Silence can mean thinking.
Online there are fewer cues.
Do not abandon the plan at the first yawn.
The room tells you about attention and confusion. It does not tell you what people will remember next week (1.4). Use a recall check for that.

The room can tell you about attention and confusion. It cannot tell you what will last. A lively, fluent room is not proof that people will remember or use any of it (1.4), so read the room to steer the session and check the learning another way.

topics.title: Review your own sessions

situation.text: You have run the same workshop for five years and it has not improved.

items: After each session, write what worked, what did not, and why.
Pick one weakness to work on next time.
Ask a peer to watch and comment.
Swap cases with other trainers.
Sit in someone else's session as a learner.

why.text: Experience alone does not reliably turn into expertise. Reflection helps. There are two kinds: adjusting while it happens, and learning afterwards. The second kind has been tested. A meta-analysis found that people and teams who held a structured debrief did about 20 to 25 per cent better than those who did not.
Experts decide fast by drawing on experience. Reviewing cases is a deliberate way to add to that store.

The idea of reflecting while you work comes from Donald Schön, who studied five professions, none of them teaching or training. It is a way of describing practice, not a tested method. The debrief studies cover teams and individuals in many fields. A trainer's own written review is a reasonable extension.

why.title: Do debriefs improve performance?
why.found: Pooling 46 samples and 2,136 people, debriefs improved performance by about 20 to 25 per cent compared with no debrief (d = 0.67). The effect held for teams and individuals, and in real and simulated settings.
why.means: Review each session in a set format with a clear focus, and act on one point.

items.title: Other eyes
items.text: A peer sees what you cannot.

try.text: Design a routine for reviewing your own sessions. Say how you will target one weakness.

try.title: Three lines after each session
try.text: Worked: the paired case study. Did not: the closing summary ran out of time, again. Why: the plan has no slack after lunch. Next time: cut one afternoon exercise and ask a colleague to watch the last half hour.

items: As you improve, you forget what newcomers find hard.
Reflection without change is a diary.
Feedback forms are a weak source.

topics.title: Look after yourself, and know your professional limits

situation.text: You deliver four days a week, travel on the fifth, and a participant asks you for advice well outside your field.

items: Plan recovery after delivery days.
Limit consecutive delivery days.
Know what you are qualified to advise on, and say when something is outside it.
Keep what participants tell you in confidence, within stated limits.
Declare any interest you have in what you recommend.
Have a peer you can talk cases through with.

why.text: Facilitating is tiring work. A tired trainer is likely to notice less and have less patience.

Professional bodies publish codes of conduct. The CIPD Code of Conduct and Ethics, in force since 1 January 2023, asks members to refer on work outside their expertise, protect confidential information, act honestly and disclose conflicts of interest. It applies to CIPD members. This page gives general principles.

items.title: Your limits
items.text: Say when it is outside your field.

try.text: Write three lines: what you advise on, what you refer on, and who you refer to.

try.title: Outside your field
try.text: At the break a participant describes a dispute with her manager and asks if she has a legal case. The trainer says: "That is outside what I can advise on. Acas or your union rep would be the place to start." She does not offer a view.

items: A participant in distress needs referral, not coaching.
Selling a follow-on product from the front of the room is a conflict of interest.
Safeguarding duties may apply. Check them.

parts.summary: Working with a partner, the walls, your kit and your voice.

topics.title: Co-facilitate without tripping over each other

situation.text: You and a colleague are running a two-day programme together. In the first hour you both answer the same question, she adds "just one thing" to each of your segments, and neither of you is watching the clock.

items: Meet for thirty minutes before the day and walk through the plan. Put one name against every segment as lead. The other person is support for that segment.
Say what support does. The usual jobs are watching the room, keeping time, writing on the flipchart, handing out materials, and dealing with latecomers or the technology.
Agree three signals. One for time, such as five fingers held low for five minutes left. One for "I would like to add something", such as a raised pen. One for "move on".

Set the rule for adding. Support speaks when the lead invites it: "Anything to add, Tom?" One point, half a minute. If the lead says something wrong, pass a note, unless the error would send an exercise the wrong way.
Decide who goes to a participant in difficulty. It is the support person, so the lead can keep the room going.
Hand over out loud and swap places: "That is the model. Tom will take you into the practice." The outgoing lead moves to the side and sits down.
At each break, take two minutes together: time, energy, anyone you are worried about, any change to the next segment.
The same day, spend fifteen minutes on a debrief. Each says one thing to keep and one to change, first about the session and then about how you worked together. Write the changes into the plan.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. Two trainers can give a group more attention, a change of voice and cover when something goes wrong. Without an agreement they give the group two people competing for the floor, and clients notice.

The main idea is that the floor has one owner at a time. Participants need to know who to look at and whose instruction to follow. The spoken handover and the change of position tell them. A support trainer who stays standing at the front, nodding, is still half leading.

The rule on adding is strict on purpose. "Just one thing" is nearly always meant kindly and nearly always reads as a correction. Being invited in sounds like teamwork. Saving a point for the break costs nothing.

The debrief is where a pair improves. 4.15 covers reviewing your own sessions, and the same discipline applies here with one addition, which is that you talk about the partnership as well as the content.

try.text: With the colleague you will work with, run a ten-minute stretch of your session aloud, to an empty room if need be. Include one handover in each direction and one invited addition. Use the signals for real. Then hold the fifteen-minute debrief, standing, with a timer. If you finish with no "one thing to change" about how you worked together, you were being polite. Go round once more.

try.title: A pre-session agreement, filled in for a two-day new manager programme

head: Item
What we agreed
rows: Named on the run sheet. Jo leads mornings on day one, Tom leads afternoons. Swap on day two.
Watch the room, keep time, scribe when asked, hand out materials, meet latecomers at the door.
Five fingers held low means five minutes left. A flat hand means stop now.
Raise a pen. Speak only when the lead says "Anything to add?" One point, thirty seconds.
If the lead gets something wrong
Note on a sticky, passed at the next pause. Speak up only if an exercise would go wrong.
Never in front of the group. "Let's check that at the break."
Support goes. Lead keeps the room working.
Spoken link, then swap places. Outgoing lead sits at the side.
Two-minute check: time, energy, anyone we are worried about, changes.
Jo is the contact for the client. Both of us hear any feedback.
Fifteen minutes at 16:45 each day. One keep, one change, on the session and on us.

items: Do not split the day so that one person takes all the input and the other all the activities. The group will rank you.
Looking at your phone or laptop while in support tells the room the segment does not matter.
Two trainers both walking round small groups can crowd them. Agree which tables each of you takes.
If you are the junior of the pair, ask for the agreement anyway. It protects you most.
Skipping the debrief because the day went well is how small irritations become next month's problem.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: In a co-facilitated session, when does the support trainer add a point?
quiz.a: When the lead invites it. One point, kept to about half a minute.

quiz.q: Your co-trainer gives the group a wrong time for the exercise, twenty minutes when the plan says ten. You are in support. What do you do?
quiz.a: Use the signal to add and correct it when invited, or say "Can I check one thing on timing?", because this error would send the exercise wrong. Smaller slips go on a note.

quiz.q: A participant leaves the room upset while your colleague is leading. What do you do?
quiz.a: As support, you follow the participant and your colleague keeps the room working. You agreed that beforehand, so neither of you has to decide in the moment.

topics.title: Use flipcharts and walls

situation.text: By 11:00 you have filled six flipchart sheets. Nobody past the second row can read them, three are in pale green, and they are in a pile on the floor because the venue will not allow anything on the walls.

items: Ask the venue what may go on the walls and how. Many forbid tape or tack on painted surfaces. Bring your own fixings, and use windows, doors or spare flipchart stands if walls are off limits.
Write big. Letters about as tall as your thumb is long, in lower case print. Six to eight lines on a sheet. Then walk to the back seat and read it (4.5).
Use black or dark blue for words. Keep colour for headings, underlines and boxes. Do not use pale colours for text, and do not rely on red against green to carry meaning.
Draw in advance every chart you know you will need: the agenda, exercise instructions, the model, and a parking sheet. Pencil your own prompts faintly in a corner. Only you can see them.
Put the parking sheet by the door with sticky notes beside it. Go through it before the close. The part "Run a session" covers parking an off-topic issue.
When you record what people say, use their words and check: "Have I got that right?" Write, turn round, then talk. Do not speak to the paper.
Number and title each sheet and hang them in order round the room, so the day builds up on the walls.
At the end, photograph every sheet in order and check each photo is readable. Ask the group before you share any sheet that has names or sensitive comments on it. Send the photos within two days.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. No study was opened for this topic. The reasoning draws on one idea from 1.1: people can hold very little in mind at once. A slide disappears when you click on. A chart stays on the wall, so the group can look back at the agenda, the model and its own earlier answers without having to remember them.
Charts also show whose session it is. A sheet in the participants' own words, written in front of them, tells them their thinking is the material. That is why you check your wording with the speaker.
Drawing charts in advance saves time in the room and gives you neat, readable sheets for the things that matter most, such as exercise instructions.
The size and colour rules are about access as much as neatness. Someone at the back, someone with poor sight or someone who is colour-blind should get the same information as the person at the front.

try.text: Do this on your feet with real paper. Draw the instruction chart for one of your exercises, hang it, and read it from six metres away. Then ask a colleague to talk for three minutes about a problem at work while you record their points on a second sheet, checking your wording with them twice. Photograph both sheets on your phone and see whether you can read them on the small screen.

try.title: A worked example: the wall plan for a one-day new manager workshop

head: Sheet
Where it hangs
When it is made
rows: Title before, content with the group at 09:45
By the door, with sticky notes
5. Exercise one instructions: task, output, time, groups
On the stand, turned over until needed
6 to 9. Group charts: our hardest conversations
Side wall, next to the model

items: Venue pens are often dry. Carry your own and test them the night before.
Standing in front of the chart while you write hides it. Stand to one side and write with your arm out.
A wall exercise shuts out anyone who cannot stand for long. Put one chart on a table and say so in the instruction.
Take every sheet with you or destroy it. Client material left on a hotel wall is a confidentiality problem (4.16).

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: Which colours do you use for words on a flipchart?
quiz.a: Black or dark blue. Other colours are for headings, underlines and boxes.

quiz.q: A participant makes a long point and you write up a neat four-word version of it. They frown. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask "Have I got that right?" and rewrite it in their words. The chart should record the group's thinking, not your version of it.

quiz.q: You arrive and the venue tells you nothing may be fixed to the walls. Your plan has eight wall charts. What do you do?
quiz.a: Use windows, doors and spare flipchart stands, and lay group charts on tables. Ask about walls before the day next time, as part of the room questions in 4.5.

topics.title: Pack a trainer's kit

situation.text: The venue promised pens, a clicker and a cable. There are two dry markers, no clicker, and the screen takes a connector your laptop does not have. You start in twenty-five minutes.

items: Keep one bag packed all the time. Restock it the evening after a session, when you know what ran out, and not the night before the next one.
Pack in four groups so you can check quickly: the room, the technology, the paper, and you.
Carry your session in three forms. The deck on your laptop, a copy on a memory stick as a PDF, and the key slides printed. 4.13 asks for a version that needs no technology, and this is it.
Bring your own markers, tape and sticky notes even when the venue says it supplies them. Test every marker.
Count activity materials against the plan the night before: one set for each group, plus one spare.
Ask the venue in writing what it will provide, including the connector on the screen. Bring adaptors anyway.
On arrival, unpack in the same order every time: screen and sound first, then walls, then tables. Find out where the first-aid kit and the nearest first-aider are.
Put your name and number on the bag and on the clicker.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement, and the list below is one working trainer's version. Yours will change with your sessions.

The principle is that small failures in the first twenty minutes cost more than they should. A missing cable does not only delay the slides. It uses up the time you had set aside to move the furniture, check sightlines and greet people as they come in, which 4.5 treats as part of the session. A packed bag buys that time back.
Restocking straight after a session is the habit that makes it work. The evening before a job is when you find that the sticky notes ran out last week and the shops are closed.

Carrying three forms of the deck sounds like too much until the first time a client laptop refuses your memory stick or a hotel screen will not wake up. With printed key slides and a flipchart you can still run the day. Knowing that also does a good deal for your nerves (4.1).

try.text: Run a timed set-up drill. Take the packed bag to a meeting room or your kitchen, start a timer, and go from closed bag to ready to start: screen connected, first chart hung, pens tested, handouts laid out. Aim for fifteen minutes. Then shut the laptop and deliver the first five minutes of your session aloud using only what is in the bag. Note what you reached for and did not have.

try.title: A trainer's kit list

head: Group
What is in the bag
rows: Eight flipchart markers in black and dark blue, four in colours for headings, all tested
Masking tape, reusable tack, a pad of self-stick flipchart sheets
Sticky notes in two sizes, sticky dots for voting, scissors, a small bell or chime
Name badges or folded cards, twenty spare biros, a sign for the door
Laptop and charger, adaptors for the common screen connectors, a four-way extension lead
Clicker with spare batteries, small speaker, memory stick with the deck as a PDF
Phone charger, the venue's wifi details, the organiser's mobile number on paper
Run sheet with clock times, participant list, printed key slides
Handouts and activity materials, one set for each group plus a spare
Attendance sheet, feedback forms if they are on paper, parking sheet drawn in advance
A watch or small clock you can see without picking up your phone
Water bottle, throat sweets, something to eat that is not the venue's biscuits
Spare top, tissues, plasters, any medication you need

items: A kit that lives in three bags and a car boot is not a kit. If it does not fit in one bag, cut it.
Do not count on venue wifi for anything the session depends on. Download videos and files beforehand.
Check what you may plug in. Some sites require electrical items to be tested before they are used.
Participant lists and feedback forms carry personal data. Keep them in the bag and do not leave them in the room.
A new activity needs its own materials list. Add it to the bag check for that day only.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: When do you restock the kit bag?
quiz.a: The evening after a session, when you know what ran out.

quiz.q: The screen in the room will not connect to your laptop and you start in ten minutes. What do you do?
quiz.a: Stop trying at five minutes to go, hand out or hang the printed key slides and run from the flipchart. The first minutes with the group matter more than the slides.

quiz.q: The venue has emailed to say pens, flipcharts and a clicker are all provided. What do you pack?
quiz.a: The same bag as always, including your own tested markers, tape and clicker. Venue supplies are often worn out, and discovering that at 9:10 costs you your set-up time.

topics.title: Look after your voice and energy on a multi-day run

situation.text: It is the third morning of a five-day programme. Your voice is rough, you slept badly in the hotel, and you snapped at a fair question yesterday afternoon.

items: Travel the evening before day one, and get there in time to eat and sleep. 1.12 protects the learners' sleep. Protect your own in the same way.
Warm up your voice for five minutes before the room fills. Hum, slide gently from low notes to high, then say your opening lines aloud at full volume.
Keep water within reach and sip through the day. Take a drink each time the group starts a task.

Design the day so the group does most of the talking. As a working rule, do not speak for more than ten to fifteen minutes at a stretch, and plan the hour after lunch so that they talk and you listen.
Never shout over a working room. Use a signal to get attention, such as a raised hand or a chime, and wait. Ask for a microphone for large groups or noisy rooms.
Take your own break at every break. Five minutes outside or somewhere quiet, away from participants, before you answer anyone's questions. Eat a proper lunch, sitting down.
Sit down while groups work. Wear shoes you can stand in for seven hours.
Cap evening preparation at thirty minutes: lay out tomorrow's charts, write three lines on today (4.15), then stop. Keep one evening completely free on a five-day run.

why.text: This is a routine that working trainers use. It is practitioner judgement and it is not medical advice. If your voice stays hoarse, or you are unwell, see a pharmacist or your GP.

4.16 makes the case for planning recovery and limiting consecutive delivery days. This topic covers the days themselves. Delivery is physical work: hours of standing, projecting your voice and paying close attention to a dozen people. On day one you have reserves. By day three, what the group gets depends on how you spent days one and two.

The most effective single change is in the design. A trainer who talks for five hours a day will lose their voice whatever they drink. One who talks for ninety minutes, spread across the day, usually will not. The sessions tend to be better for it as well, since the earlier stages argue for practice over input throughout.

Patience runs out before the voice does. The sharp reply on day three is often the first sign. The quiet five minutes at each break are there to prevent it, even though it feels unfriendly to step away from a group that wants to chat.

try.text: Before your next delivery day, do the five-minute warm-up, then record the first two minutes of your opening, standing, at the volume the room needs. On the day, ask a colleague or use a phone timer to log how many minutes you speak in each hour. Afterwards, read the log aloud to yourself and name one block where the group could have done the talking.

try.title: A worked example: one delivery day in the middle of a five-day run

head: Time
What the trainer does
Why
rows: In the room. Charts up. Five minutes of humming and opening lines aloud.
Voice warm before the first hello.
Opens. Ten minutes of input, then the group works.
Break. Five minutes outside alone, then back for questions.
Lunch, sitting, away from the training room for twenty minutes.
Group activity on their feet. Trainer listens and sits where possible.
Rest the voice in the dip.
Break. Water, and a walk to the end of the corridor.
Nothing carried into the evening unspoken.
Thirty minutes: tomorrow's charts, three lines on today.
Dinner. No slides afterwards. In bed at a normal hour.

items: Coffee and alcohol in the evening both cost sleep. On a residential, decide your rule on alcohol before you arrive.
Clearing your throat hard and talking over noise both strain a tired voice. Sip water and wait for quiet.
Rewriting tomorrow's session at eleven at night rarely improves it. Make one change and go to bed.
Spending every break and meal with participants is generous on day one and a mistake by day three.
If your voice is going, change the plan for the next day so that groups carry more of it, and tell your co-trainer.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: As a working rule, how long do you speak at a stretch?
quiz.a: No more than ten to fifteen minutes, with the group doing most of the talking across the day.

quiz.q: It is the break on day three and a participant wants to talk through a problem at length. You are tired and your voice is rough. What do you do?
quiz.a: Say you will be with them in five minutes, take your quiet break first, and then give them your attention. A short recovery protects the rest of the day for everyone.

quiz.q: Your voice is hoarse at the end of day two of five. What do you change for day three?
quiz.a: Redesign day three so that groups do more of the talking and your input is shorter, use a signal and not volume to get attention, and warm up before the start. If it does not improve, see a pharmacist or GP.
