parts.title: Run a session
parts.summary: The moves that make up a face-to-face session, from the first ten minutes to the last fifteen, each with wording or a timetable you can use.

topics.title: Open a session

situation.text: It is 09:30. Twelve new managers are sitting with their coats on and two are still on their phones. Your first slide lists six objectives. What you do in the next ten minutes shows them whether today is something done to them or something they do.

items: Be ready fifteen minutes before the start: room set, first slide up, notes closed. Greet people at the door and learn four or five names before you begin.
Start on the advertised minute, even if two people are missing. Say "It's half past nine, so let's start." Latecomers get a nod and a chair. Do not recap for them.
Say who you are in two sentences and why the day exists in one. Name the problem in the group's own terms. Keep your biography short and off the screen.

Get every person speaking inside the first five minutes. Give pairs a question about the topic, allow two minutes, then take three answers. Topic 1.17 explains why speaking early matters, and 1.24 covers opening with a question.
Give the shape of the day as clock times: breaks, lunch and finish. Write them on a flipchart that stays up all day.
Cover housekeeping in under a minute: the fire exit and assembly point, whether an alarm test is planned, and the toilets. Ask the venue for these before the day.
Agree how the group will work (see the topic "Agree how the group will work"), then start the first real task. Aim to be in it by minute fifteen.
With 30 people, keep the same order. Pairs still work. Take four answers, and leave names to the table groups.

why.text: This is craft. Nobody has tested this opening against another one in a training room, and the timings are practitioner judgement.

The reasoning is about precedent. A group works out how much it is expected to do from what it is asked to do first. If the first fifteen minutes are you talking, people settle into listening and you spend the morning pulling them out of it. A two-minute paired question costs little and sets the pattern for the day.

Starting on the minute rewards the people who came on time, and it makes your break times believable later. Giving clock times for lunch and the finish removes a small, constant worry. People with a train to catch or a child to collect stop wondering and start listening.
Objectives on a slide are your language. Open with the problem in theirs, and show the objectives later if the client wants them shown.

try.text: Stand up, start a timer and deliver your opening aloud, three times. Record the third on your phone. Good looks like this: it finishes inside ten minutes, you talk for no more than six of them, the paired question comes by minute three, and you do not look at notes. When you listen back, mark every filler phrase and any apology.

try.title: A worked example: the first ten minutes for 12 new managers, on a day about giving feedback

head: Time
What happens
Words you say
rows: Start on the minute, standing, title slide only
"It's half past nine, so let's start. Good morning. I'm Sam. I've trained managers for ten years, and before that I was one, not very well at first."

"You've all taken on a team in the last year. Today is about one part of that job: telling someone, clearly and kindly, what you need them to do differently. You'll practise it twice, once on a real case of your own."
"Before anything else, turn to the person next to you. Tell them about one piece of feedback you were given that helped you. What made it useful? Two minutes, both of you. Go."
Walk the room, listen, give a time call
"Thirty seconds. Swap over if you haven't yet."
Take three answers. Write key words on the flipchart
"Let's hear three. What made it useful? Thank you. Keep those in mind. We'll build on that list in a few minutes."
Shape of the day, pointing at the flipchart
"Here's the day. Break at quarter to eleven. Lunch at half twelve for 45 minutes. Another break at half two. We finish at half past four, and I will keep to that."
"No alarm test is planned, so if it sounds, it's real. Out of that door, down the stairs, meet in the car park. Toilets are along the corridor on the left."
"One more thing before we start work, which is how we'll work together today."

items: You wait for latecomers. The people who were punctual learn that the times are loose. Start, and let the late ones catch up from their partner.
The opening runs to 25 minutes. The cause is nearly always round-the-room introductions or your own story. Time it in rehearsal and cut your biography first.
A senior person wants to say a few words. Agree it beforehand: two minutes on why this matters to the business, then they hand over to you by name.
You ask each person what they want from the day when the plan cannot change. Only ask if you can act on the answers.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: By when should every person in a group of 12 have spoken?
quiz.a: Inside the first five minutes, usually through a paired question.

quiz.q: It is 09:30 and three of twelve people have not arrived. The client contact suggests waiting ten minutes. What do you do?
quiz.a: Start on time with the paired question, which latecomers can join without a recap. Waiting teaches the group that your times are loose, and it costs you the break times later.

quiz.q: A director asks to open the day with a welcome. What do you agree beforehand?
quiz.a: Two minutes on why the training matters to the business, then a handover to you by name. An unplanned welcome can take fifteen minutes and set a listening mood before you have begun.

topics.tierReason: Craft. This rests on practitioner judgement. No study of this practice was opened for this page.
topics.bodyStatus: Practitioner craft. No research source.

topics.title: Run introductions that fit the group size

situation.text: Twenty people, and you ask for "name, role and one thing you want from today". The first person takes forty seconds. The eighth takes two minutes. At 10:05 nothing has been taught and the back row has stopped listening.

items: Do the sum first. Round-the-room introductions take about a minute a head once you count the handover between speakers. Twelve people is twelve minutes. Thirty people is half an hour.
Decide what the introductions are for: names, who does what, or what people need. Pick one or two. That choice sets the format.

Up to 8 people: go round the room with a strict form. Name, role, and one sentence answering a question about the topic. Model it yourself in fifteen seconds first, because people copy the length of the first answer.
From 9 to 16: pairs or threes talk for three minutes on the question. Then each person says only their name and role to the room, ten seconds each.

From 17 to 40: people introduce themselves at their tables. The room hears one line per table. Add a wall chart: on arrival each person writes their name, team and one question on a sticky note and puts it on a flipchart. Read it at the first break and refer to it.
For 100: no spoken introductions to the room. Map the room with hands ("Hands up if you manage people. Keep it up if it's more than ten."), then give two minutes with a neighbour.
Put first names on tent cards in thick marker, written on both sides. With 30 or more, use badges as well, since people move between tables.
If the group already knows each other, skip names and roles and keep the topic question.

why.text: This is craft, and the main point is arithmetic. New trainers plan five minutes for introductions and spend twenty, then lose the time from the practice at the end of the day.

A long round also gives little back. Trainers commonly notice that people waiting for their turn are rehearsing their own line and hear little of anyone else's. So the round costs a minute a head and most of the names are gone by the break.

Pairs and threes change that. Speaking to one person is easier than speaking to a room, so everyone talks early with little exposure, which is the condition topic 1.17 asks for. The wall chart gives you what you wanted from "one thing you want from today" without spending room time on it, and it is still on the wall at three o'clock when you need an example.

try.text: Stand and say your own model introduction aloud against a timer, five times, until it lands between 12 and 18 seconds every time. Then run the 12-person version with two or three colleagues or friends: give the paired question, call time, and take names and roles. Good looks like this: you gave the instruction once, your model answer set the length, and the whole thing took under five minutes.

try.title: A worked example: the same introduction for four group sizes

head: Group
Format
Time
What the room hears
rows: Round the room: name, role, one sentence on the topic question. Trainer models first
Pairs for 3 minutes on the question. Then name and role only, round the room
Twelve names and roles, 10 seconds each
At tables of five: names, roles and the question. One person per table gives one line. Sticky-note wall chart on arrival
Six lines, one per table. Names stay at the tables
Three shows of hands to map the room. Two minutes with a neighbour. Badges
Nobody individually. The room sees who is in it

items: Someone turns their introduction into a career history. Step in kindly at the first breath: "Thank you. I'll stop you there so we hear everyone."
The "fun fact about yourself" puts people on the spot and has nothing to do with the work. Ask about the topic.
The most senior person goes first and sets a formal tone. Start with pairs, or start the round on the other side of the room.
You skip introductions with strangers to save time, then ask them to practise in threes at eleven. People need each other's names before they practise together.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: Roughly how long do round-the-room introductions take per person?
quiz.a: About a minute each, once handovers are counted.

quiz.q: You have 30 people, a 09:30 start and the first exercise planned for 09:45. The client wants everyone to introduce themselves. What do you do?
quiz.a: Run introductions inside table groups and hear one line per table, with a sticky-note wall chart for names and questions. A full round would take about half an hour and push the exercise past ten o'clock.

quiz.q: In a group of 8, the first person speaks for two minutes. What should you have done, and what do you do now?
quiz.a: You should have modelled a fifteen-second answer first, because people copy the first length they hear. Now thank them, restate the form in one line, and ask the next person to keep to it.

topics.title: Agree how the group will work

situation.text: Mid-morning, a participant starts describing a problem with a colleague and then stops. "Is any of this going back to our manager?" The room looks at you. You have not agreed an answer with the client, and you have not said anything to the group.

items: Before the day, ask the client what they expect to hear afterwards. Offer themes with no names attached, and get the answer in an email. If the client wants individuals assessed, that is a different event and the invitation must say so.

In the room, do it straight after the opening and keep it to four minutes. For a one-day course, propose the agreement on a flipchart you wrote beforehand. Asking a room of strangers to invent ground rules takes fifteen minutes and produces the word "respect".

Cover five things: confidentiality, what gets reported to the client, phones and laptops, questions, and breaks. Add the right to watch a practice round before joining in, which 2.21 recommends promising in advance.
State the limit on confidentiality plainly. You can speak for yourself. You cannot guarantee what other participants do, and you would have to act if you heard about serious harm.
Ask for changes, then ask for agreement: "What would you add or change? Can everyone work with that?" Look round the whole room and wait, as in 4.2.
Leave the sheet on the wall. When you need it later, point at it: "We said phones away during practice."
Keep your own side. Restart and finish at the times you gave, and report only what you said you would.

do.title: Words you can use: a four-minute working agreement
lines: "Before we start, here's how I suggest we work today. It's on the flipchart, and you can change it."
"First, what's said here. You'll be talking about real people in your teams. Use the situation and leave out the name. What you hear from each other stays in this room."
"I'll keep to that myself. I can't promise it for everyone here, so share what you're comfortable sharing. And if someone told me about serious harm, I couldn't keep that to myself."
"Second, what your company hears from me. I'll tell them who attended and the general themes that came up. No names against comments, and nothing about how any one of you did in practice."
"Third, phones. Away during practice, please, because your partner deserves your attention. If you're waiting for a call you must take, tell me now and step out when it comes."
"Fourth, questions. Ask as we go if something is unclear. If it's a bigger issue I'll write it on the parked sheet and we'll come back to it before we finish."
"Fifth, time. I'll start and finish when I said I would. In return, please be back from breaks at the time on the clock."
"Last, the practice. Nobody performs in front of the room. You can watch the first round before you have a go."
"What would you add or change? ... Can everyone work with that? Good. It stays on the wall."

why.text: This is craft. Trainers call it contracting, and nothing here has been tested as a method. The fuller version for residentials, with levels of depth and a free pass, is in 8.3.

People decide how honest to be in practice from where they think their words will go. Most will not ask about reporting aloud, so you answer the question before it is asked. A vague answer is worse than a limited one. "Themes, no names" is a promise you can keep, and "everything here is confidential" is one you cannot.

An agreement made at 09:40 also gives you something to point at in the afternoon. When you remind someone about a phone, you are referring to the sheet the group accepted, and it lands as a reminder of that and less as a telling-off.
Proposing is right for a single day with strangers. An intact team, or a group together for several days, has more at stake and the time to write its own.

try.text: Record yourself saying the agreement aloud, standing, without notes. Then deliver it to one colleague and ask them to interrupt as a wary participant: "So will my manager hear how I did?" Answer aloud, on the spot. Good looks like this: under four minutes, and a reporting sentence nobody could mishear.

items: You promise total confidentiality. You cannot deliver it. Say what you will do and where the limit is.
The list grows to ten rules. Nobody remembers ten. Keep five or six and drop the ones you would never enforce.
After the course the client asks how one person did. Go back to the email: you agreed themes. Offer the themes, and suggest the manager asks the person directly.
A phone rule with no reason and no exit gets ignored by the busiest people. Give the reason and the way out together.
Latecomers miss it. Point them to the sheet at the first break and check they can work with it.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: Name the five things a working agreement for a one-day course should cover.
quiz.a: Confidentiality, what is reported to the client, phones and laptops, questions, and breaks or timekeeping.

quiz.q: A week after a course for a software company's team leads, their director emails: "How did Alex get on?" You agreed themes only. What do you reply?
quiz.a: Say that you agreed with the group, and with the client beforehand, to report attendance and themes without names, and send the themes. Breaking that once would undo the trust the next group gives you.

quiz.q: You have a one-day course with 14 strangers and a colleague suggests the group writes its own ground rules. What do you do?
quiz.a: Propose five lines on a prepared flipchart and invite changes, which takes about four minutes. Group-written rules suit an intact team or a multi-day event, where there is time and more at stake.

topics.title: Give instructions people can follow first time

situation.text: You say, "OK, so in your groups, have a chat about the case and think about what you'd do, and we'll come back in a bit." Chairs turn. At every table the first thing anyone says is, "What are we meant to be doing?"

items: Write every instruction word for word before the day. Put the task, the time, the grouping and the output on a slide or flipchart that stays visible while people work.
Get attention before you speak. Stand still in the same spot each time, say "Eyes up here for a minute, please", and wait for quiet. Never talk over the room.
Say why, in one sentence. People put more into a task when they can see what it is for.
Give the task as one action with a verb: "Write the first two sentences of your reply." If the task is new to them, show a thirty-second example.
Give the time twice, as a length and as a clock time: "Eight minutes, so until ten past."
Give the grouping and the output: who with, where, and what you will ask for at the end.
Check by asking one person to say it back: "Jo, so I can check I explained that properly, what are you about to do?" Pick someone at ease in the group. "Is that clear?" only ever gets a nod.
Hand out materials and move people last. Say "Off you go", start the timer, and walk past every group in the first two minutes.

why.text: This is craft, in an order many trainers arrive at by getting it wrong. Topic 5.10 names instructions as the first thing to coach in a new trainer, and unclear ones are a common reason an activity fails.

The order does most of the work. Paper in someone's hand wins against a voice from the front, so anything said after the handout is lost. People who are standing up and finding a group are not listening either. That is why materials and movement come after the last word.

Spoken instructions pass once and are gone, and Stage 1 explains how little people can hold in mind at a time. The flipchart holds the instruction for them. One task with one output is easier to hold than "discuss and think about".

The say-back is the only real check. Nobody wants to be the person who admits they did not follow, so a room will nod at "Is that clear?" and then ask each other. Frame the say-back as a test of your explaining, which it is.

try.text: Pick a real activity. Stand, record yourself giving the instruction on your phone, and keep it under ninety seconds. Play it back against the eight steps and tick each one you hear. Then give the instruction live to a colleague who has not seen the activity and ask them to say back what they would do. If they miss anything, rewrite and record again.

try.title: A worked example: one instruction, before and after (a customer support team of 12)
lines: Before: "Right, I'm going to give out this case study, here you go, pass those along. Have a read and get into groups, threes or fours, and discuss what went wrong and what you'd do. Take ten minutes or so. Oh, and someone make notes."
What goes wrong: the paper arrives first, so people read and stop listening. The group size is loose. There are two tasks and no output. Nobody knows when it ends.
After: "Eyes up here for a minute, please." (Wait for quiet.)
"You've seen the four steps for answering a complaint. Now you'll use them on a real email, because spotting the steps is easier than writing them."
"Your task: read the customer's email, then write the first two sentences of your reply. Only the first two."
"You have eight minutes. That takes us to ten past eleven."
"You'll work in threes, with the people at your table."
"At ten past, I'll ask each three to read their two sentences aloud."
"It's all on the flipchart: first two sentences, eight minutes, threes, read aloud."
"Jo, so I can check I explained that properly, what are you about to do?" (Jo says it back. Fill in anything missing.)
"Here are the emails, one each. Off you go." (Hand out the paper now. Start the timer. Walk to the furthest table first.)

items: You remember something after "Off you go" and call it across the noise. Half the room misses it. Stop everyone with your attention signal, say it once, and restart.
The task has three stages and you give them all at once. Give stage one, let them do it, then stop the room for stage two.
The instruction slide disappears when you click on. Put the instruction on a flipchart, or leave the slide alone until the task ends.
The say-back embarrasses a nervous person. Choose someone who has already spoken easily, and say that you are checking yourself.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: In the instruction sequence, when do you hand out the materials?
quiz.a: Last, after the say-back check and just before you say "Off you go".

quiz.q: You have set a case exercise. Two minutes in, you walk round and find two of four groups doing the wrong task. What do you do?
quiz.a: Stop the whole room with your attention signal and give the task and output again, pointing at the flipchart. Two groups wrong means the instruction failed, so fixing it table by table would waste more time.

quiz.q: You ask "Is that clear?" and everyone nods, but the groups start slowly and look at each other. What do you change next time?
quiz.a: Ask one person to say the task back before anyone moves, framed as a check on your explanation. A nod tells you nothing, because nobody wants to admit they did not follow.

topics.title: Form groups and move people

situation.text: You say "get into groups of four". Twelve people look at each other. Friends pair up fast, two people are left standing in the middle, and three minutes have gone before anyone starts.

items: Choose the size for the task. Pairs for thinking aloud and first attempts. Threes for practice with an observer. Fours for a case that needs several views. Avoid five or more unless the group is making something physical.

Decide groups before the day when it matters who is with whom: role-play threes, people from different teams, or keeping a manager apart from someone who reports to them. Write the groups on a flipchart.
For quick mixing, count off. Count up to the number of groups you want, not the size of each group. For four groups from twelve people, count one to four round the room.
Point to where each group will meet before anyone stands: "Ones by the window, twos at the door."
Other ways to mix: line up by years in the job and cut the line into threes, put coloured dots on name cards before people arrive, or say "find two people you haven't worked with yet today".
Let people choose their own partners for the first task of the day, when neighbours are enough, and whenever the material is personal, such as a real case from their own team.
Mix after the first break and again after lunch, so nobody spends the day with one partner.

Budget the time. Turning to a neighbour takes ten seconds. New threes in the same room take one to two minutes. Going to a breakout room takes three or four minutes each way, so keep tasks under fifteen minutes in the main room.

why.text: This is craft. The group sizes and timings are rules of thumb from practice.

Size decides how much each person talks. In a pair working for ten minutes, each person speaks for about five. In a group of six, it is under two, and one person usually says very little. Topic 4.3 notes that people tend to put in less as a group grows.

Left to choose, people sit and work with those they arrived with. That is comfortable, and it means the experienced people never meet the new ones. It also leaves someone standing alone while the room watches, which is a small humiliation you can prevent by assigning.

Movement has a cost and a benefit. It lifts energy, which helps in the dips that 2.14 describes, and it uses minutes that new trainers rarely plan for. Layout matters too. Small tables with chairs on three sides, often called cabaret style, let people work in fours and still see the front. Topic 4.5 covers setting the room.

try.text: Stand in an empty room, or your kitchen, and give the count-off instruction aloud for 12 imaginary people making four groups. Point to each corner as you name it. Do it until it takes under twenty seconds with no correction. Then try it for real at your next team meeting or family gathering of six or more: move people into threes with one instruction, and time how long it takes them to settle.

try.title: A worked example: which grouping for which task, in a room of 12

head: Grouping
Use it for
Time to form
Watch for
rows: Thinking aloud, a first attempt, checking understanding
An odd number. Make one three. Do not partner someone yourself
A manager and their own team member in one three
A case or problem that needs several views
Counting to four when you wanted three groups
Building something, or a short table discussion
Two people who say nothing. Split into threes for the hard part
Long practice that needs quiet, over 15 minutes
Losing sight of groups. Walk between rooms

items: You count to the group size by mistake and get the wrong number of groups. Say the sum to yourself first: twelve people, four groups, so count to four.
Thirteen people for work in threes. Make three threes and one four with two observers. Decide this before you speak.
Someone cannot move easily. Bring their group to them and say nothing about it.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: When you count off to form groups, what number do you count up to?
quiz.a: The number of groups you want, not the size of each group.

quiz.q: A retailer's store managers and their area managers are in one session, and the next task is practice in threes on a real staffing problem. How do you form the threes?
quiz.a: Assign them beforehand so that no store manager practises with their own area manager, and post the threes on a flipchart. People hold back when the person who appraises them is in the conversation.

quiz.q: You have a seven-minute discussion task and two breakout rooms down the corridor. Where do the groups work?
quiz.a: In the main room. Walking to a breakout room and back takes about as long as the task, and you cannot see or hear groups that have left.

topics.bodyStatus: Practitioner craft. No research source.

topics.title: Watch and support groups while they work

situation.text: The groups are working, so you sit down and look through your notes for the next section. One table finished after three minutes and is talking about the weekend. Another has spent six minutes on the wrong question. You find out both when you ask for reports.

items: For the first thirty seconds, stand still and look. Check that every group has started. Say nothing.
In the first two minutes, walk past every group once, starting with the one furthest from you. You are checking one thing: are they on the right task.
Then stand where you can see every face, usually a corner or the side wall. Do not stand over a group. People start performing for you when you do.
Listen for material. Write down exact phrases you can use in the debrief, with the table they came from. Note any misunderstanding that more than one group shares, and who has not spoken.
Step in for four reasons only: the wrong task, a group going round in circles for more than a couple of minutes, one person shut out, or something unkind. Otherwise stay out.
When you do step in, get down to their eye level and ask "Where have you got to?" before you offer anything. Leave as soon as they are moving again.
Call time at halfway and near the end, and say where they should be: "Four minutes left. You should be on the second question by now."
Have an extension ready for a group that finishes early, and tell a group that is behind which part to drop. To end, say "Finish the sentence you're on", then use your attention signal.

why.text: This is craft. It rests on what experienced trainers do and has not been tested as a method.

Group time is working time for you. It is when you learn what people have understood, and it is your only source for the specific moments a good debrief is built on. A trainer who spent the task reading notes has to open the debrief with "So, how did that go?"

Staying out is deliberate. The moment you answer a group's question, the thinking stops and the conversation turns to face you. Asking where they have got to keeps the work with them, and it often shows they were closer than they thought.

Time calls with a marker let groups pace themselves. "Four minutes left" alone tells them the time. Adding where they should be tells them whether to speed up. Topic 4.14 asks you to change the plan when the room tells you to, and the walk round is where the room tells you.

try.text: Ask two or three friends or colleagues to discuss any question for six minutes while you practise. Stand where you can see them all. Do not speak for the first two minutes. Write down three phrases word for word. Give a halfway call and a one-minute call aloud, each with a progress marker. Afterwards, read the three phrases back and ask whether you caught them accurately.

try.title: A worked example: what you see at a table, and what to do

head: What you see or hear
What it may mean
What you do
rows: Silence, phones out, three minutes in
Walk over. "Where have you got to?" Give the extension, or restate the task
One person talking, two looking at the table
"Let's hear how each of you would open it. Start with you."
Lively talk about last quarter's targets
"Sounds like a real issue. Park it on the sheet. Which question are you on?"
"What do you think the customer would make of it?" Then step away
Two groups making the same error
Your input or instruction was unclear
Stop the room. Correct it once for everyone
Stay away. Note one phrase for the debrief

items: You join a group and end up running it. Give yourself a limit of one minute at any table.
You visit the friendly table three times and the difficult one never. Walk the same circuit each time.
Time calls every minute break concentration. Two calls are enough for a task under fifteen minutes.
The groups are enjoying it, so you let it run on. The extra minutes come out of the debrief, which 1.25 tells you to protect. Add two minutes at most, and announce it.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: Name the four reasons to step into a working group.
quiz.a: They are on the wrong task, they are stuck in circles, one person is shut out, or something unkind is happening.

quiz.q: A group waves you over and asks, "Is this the right answer?" What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask what they think, or what the customer in the case would make of it, and then step away. If you supply the answer, their thinking stops and the group starts working for your approval.

quiz.q: Four minutes into an eight-minute task, one group has finished and the others are halfway. What do you do?
quiz.a: Give the finished group the extension you prepared, such as taking the hardest objection and writing a reply. Then make your halfway call to the room so the others know where they should be.

topics.tierReason: Craft. This rests on practitioner judgement. No study of this practice was opened for this page.
topics.bodyStatus: Practitioner craft. No research source.

topics.title: Take reports from groups without losing the room

situation.text: Four groups have worked on the same case. You ask each to present. The first takes seven minutes and covers nearly everything. The other three repeat it with apologies. Twenty-five minutes later most of the room is looking at a phone.

items: Choose the report format before the activity and say it in the instruction. It changes what groups produce.
Do the sum. "Five minutes each" for four groups is twenty-five minutes with handovers. For six groups it is over half an hour, and if all had the same task, most of it is repetition.

Default to one point per group: "One point from each group, the one you most want the others to hear. Nothing we've already had." Go round once, then ask for anything still missing. Start with a different group each time.

Harvest on a flipchart. Ask a narrow question, such as "What did you decide to say first?" Write the group's own words, key words only, large enough to read from the back. Ask "Who had something different?"

Use a gallery walk when groups have made something on paper. Put the sheets on the walls. Everyone walks round for six minutes with a pen and marks one idea to borrow and one question. Take the questions standing at the sheets.

When each group had a different case, reports are needed, because the others have not seen it. Give a form and a limit: ninety seconds, covering the case in one sentence, what we decided and why. Run a visible timer.
For speed with larger numbers, send one person from each group to the next table to report for two minutes. Every report happens at once.
Close it yourself. Name two patterns you heard, link them to the next section and move on. Do not teach each point again.

why.text: This is craft. The timings are from practice.

A report-back is for the room. The useful test is what the other groups need to hear, which is rarely everything a group discussed. Presenting in turn fails on that test. One person talks while eleven listen, the later groups have nothing new, and reporters tend to narrate their discussion when the room only needs the conclusion.

One point per group forces a choice, and choosing the most useful point is itself a small act of thinking about the content. The gallery walk gets people on their feet and reading each other's work at their own speed, which suits the afternoon dips described in 2.14.

Who holds the pen matters. If you turn each contribution into your own phrase, the list becomes yours and people stop offering. Writing their words, and checking "Have I got that right?", keeps the list theirs.

try.text: Tape a sheet of paper to a wall and practise harvesting. Ask one or two people to give you points on any easy question, such as what makes a good team meeting. Write each in their words while you stay half turned to them, and ask "Who had something different?" after each. Then walk four metres back and check you can read it. Record it and listen for how often you rephrased what they said.

try.title: A worked example: four ways to take reports from four groups of three

Use it when

"One point from each group. Nothing we've already had."

"What did you decide to say first? Who had something different?"

"Walk round with a pen. Mark one idea you'd borrow and one question."
Each group had a different case
"The case in a sentence, what you decided, and why. Ninety seconds."
Six or more groups, or little time
"One person from each table move one table clockwise and report. Two minutes."

items: A spokesperson starts a speech. Step in early: "Give me the headline in one sentence."
Time is short, so you skip the reports. The groups feel their work vanished. Take one point from each in three minutes.
The flipchart fills with your wording. Ask the speaker for the three words to write.
Sheets from a gallery walk go in the bin. Photograph them and send the photos with your follow-up.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: Why does "each group presents for five minutes" fail when all groups had the same task?
quiz.a: It takes about twenty-five minutes for four groups, and the later groups mostly repeat the first.

quiz.q: Six groups at a sales kick-off have each drawn an account plan on flipchart paper. You have twelve minutes. How do you take reports?
quiz.a: Run a gallery walk: sheets on the walls, six minutes walking with a pen to mark one idea to borrow and one question, then take questions at the sheets. Six presentations would take over half an hour.

quiz.q: During a harvest, a participant gives a long answer and you write a neat summary in your own words. They look unconvinced. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask "Have I got that right? Which words would you use?" and rewrite it. A list in your wording becomes your list, and people offer less.

topics.title: Debrief an activity

situation.text: The role-play ends and the room is buzzing. You ask, "So, how was that?" One person says "Good, yeah." Another says "A bit awkward." You say "Great" and click to the next slide.

items: Plan the debrief when you plan the activity and write the questions into your session plan. As a starting rule from practice, give it at least a third of the time the activity took.
Begin with one minute of silent writing: one thing that worked, and one moment that was harder than expected. Then everyone has something to say.

Ask first about what happened, and ask for specifics: "What exactly did you say in the first thirty seconds?" The people who did the task speak first, then the people they did it with, then observers.
Move to what it means: "Why do you think that worked?" Bring in the model you taught here, and correct anything that is wrong.
Move to work: "Where does this come up in your week?" Then to action. Each person writes one sentence they will say or one thing they will do.
Feed in what you heard while walking round: "At this table I heard, 'Help me understand what's behind that.' What happened next?" Raise mistakes without naming anyone.
Record on a flipchart in two columns, what worked and what to try next, in their words.
Speak last. Add at most two points the group missed.

why.text: Topic 1.25 gives the three questions and the meta-analysis that supports debriefing. That paper also says what counted as a debrief, which is the useful part when you run one.

The authors only counted a debrief if it had four features. Participants worked things out for themselves instead of being told. The purpose was improvement, with no judging or appraisal. The talk was about particular events. And the information came from more than one source, such as several team members or an observer. The steps above are built to meet those four: writing first, exact words, observers, and the trainer last.
The order of questions, the one-third rule and the two-column flipchart are craft. They have not been tested.

why.title: Do team and individual debriefs enhance performance?
why.found: Pooling 46 samples and 2,136 people, debriefs improved performance by about 25 per cent on average, or about 21 per cent with three outlying studies removed. Facilitated debriefs showed larger effects than unfacilitated ones, on little data. Video and similar aids added no meaningful benefit.
why.means: Ask before you tell, keep it about specific moments, bring in observers, and keep judgement out of it.

try.text: Run a five-minute debrief with two friends or colleagues, and record the sound. First give them a three-minute task, such as one persuading the other to change a weekend plan. Then debrief aloud: what was said, why it worked or did not, what each would do next time. Listen back and count your own talking time. Aim for under a third. Check that you asked for exact words and that each person finished with one thing to do.

try.title: A worked example: a ten-minute debrief after a sales role-play (12 people in threes, handling "it's too expensive")

head: Minute
What you say or do
What you are listening for
rows: "Stay in your threes. One minute on your own. Write one thing you said that moved the conversation on, and one moment you got stuck."
"Sellers first. When the customer said it was too expensive, what exactly did you say? Give me the words." Take four. Write them in the left column
"Customers, how did that land on your side? Which reply made you want to keep talking?"
The effect on the other person
"Observers, what happened in the ten seconds after the objection?"
Who paused, who asked a question, who cut the price
"Look at the left column. What do the replies that worked have in common?" Add the model only if they miss it

"Where did it come unstuck, and what would you try next time?" Write in the right column

"Write the first sentence you'll say when they raise price. One sentence, on your card." Hear two

"Keep that card. You'll use it in the second round after the break."

items: The activity overran and the debrief has four minutes left. Next time cut a round of the activity. Today, do the silent minute, one question on what happened and one on what they will do.
"How did that feel?" as the opener gets one-word answers. Ask what was said.
The debrief turns into a critique of one person's round. Move it to the situation: "That customer brief was the hardest one. What would any of us do with it?"

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Tannenbaum and Cerasoli (2013), Do team and individual debriefs enhance performance? A meta-analysis. Human Factors, 55(1).

quiz.q: In the 2013 meta-analysis, which four features did a discussion need in order to count as a debrief?
quiz.a: Participants working things out themselves, a developmental and non-judging purpose, a focus on specific events, and more than one source of information.

quiz.q: A practice exercise for a customer team overran by ten minutes. You have five minutes for a debrief you planned at fifteen. What do you do?
quiz.a: Keep a short version: one silent minute to write, one question on what was actually said, and one sentence each on what they will do. Dropping it altogether loses the part that the evidence supports.

quiz.q: In a debrief, an observer starts listing everything one colleague did wrong. What do you do?
quiz.a: Thank them, ask for one thing to keep and one to try, and widen it to what anyone would do with that case. A debrief is for improvement, and one person being judged in public shuts the rest of the room down.

topics.tierReason: A meta-analysis of 46 samples supports holding a facilitated debrief built on self-discovery and specific events. The order of questions and the timings on this page are practitioner judgement.

topics.title: Run a role-play that people do not dread

situation.text: You say "now for some role-play" and watch shoulders drop. Someone jokes about leaving early. Their last one was in front of the whole room, with a colleague playing an impossible customer for laughs.

items: Call it practice. Say in the invitation that the day includes it, as 2.21 advises, and say at the start that nobody performs in front of the room.
Work in threes: one person practises, one plays the other party, one observes. Run all the threes at once. The noise gives each group privacy.

Give each role a written brief of half a page. The practiser's brief gives the situation and the goal. The other party's brief says how to behave: "Push back twice. If you are asked a good question, answer it honestly. Do not make it impossible."
Demonstrate first for two minutes, with a volunteer or co-trainer, and leave in one clear flaw. The room gives you feedback from the observer sheet.
Keep rounds short: four minutes of conversation and three of feedback. Three rounds, rotating clockwise, so everyone practises once.
Give the observer a sheet with three things to watch for, tied to the steps you taught. They write exact words and stay out of the conversation.
Fix the order of feedback: the practiser first, then the other party on how it felt, then the observer. Each gives one thing to keep and one to try. Topic 2.27 covers what makes feedback usable.
Call the changes for the whole room: "Stop there, wherever you are. Three minutes of feedback, practiser first." Then debrief with everyone. Run a second set later on participants' own real cases.

why.text: The format here is craft. No study read for this page tests threes against other arrangements.

People rarely dread the practice. They dread the audience, and a partner who improvises. Threes working at once remove the audience. Written briefs remove the improvising: without one, the other party either gives in at once or turns into a caricature, and neither teaches anything.
The observer role earns its place twice. The observer supplies the second source of information that a good debrief needs, and watching a skill from outside is often when the steps make sense.

There is research on the wider method. Behaviour modelling training means showing a skill, having people practise it, and giving feedback. A research summary of a 2005 meta-analysis reports large effects on knowledge and skills, smaller ones on behaviour at work, and better transfer when people saw poor examples as well as good ones, when experienced learners wrote their own practice scenarios, and when key points were taught as rules to apply, not scripts to copy. That supports the flawed demonstration and the second set on real cases. Only the summary was read, not the paper.

try.text: Run one full round with two colleagues or friends, with you as timekeeper. Read the set-up aloud, hand out two short briefs, call "Stop there" at four minutes and run the feedback in order. Good looks like this: nobody asks what to do, the observer reads from the sheet, and the round is done in eight minutes.

try.title: A worked example: 30 minutes of practice in threes (a retailer's store managers, a conversation with a team member about lateness)

head: Minute
What happens
Who is talking
rows: Set-up: why, the threes on the flipchart, the timings. Briefs are not handed out yet
Demonstration with a volunteer. The trainer skips the question step on purpose
The room gives feedback on the demonstration from the observer sheet
Briefs handed out. Read in silence. Questions go to the trainer
"Stop there." Feedback: practiser, then team member, then observer
Rotate clockwise. New brief for the new team member
End of practice. The ten-minute debrief with the whole room follows

try.title: A worked example: the observer sheet
lines: Observer sheet. Round: ___ Practiser: ___
Your job is to watch and write. Do not join in. Do not rescue anyone.
1. The opening. Write the manager's first sentence, word for word.
2. Did the manager say what they had seen, with a day and a time? Yes or no. Their words:
3. Did the manager ask a question and then wait for the answer? Make a mark each time.
4. How did it end? Was a next step agreed, with a date? Write it down.
One thing to keep. Quote their words.
One thing to try next time. Say what to do, not what was wrong.
You speak last in the feedback. Two sentences, read from this sheet.

items: Someone plays the other party as a monster. Stop that three quietly and point at the brief: push back twice, then respond.
The observer joins in or coaches during the round. Remind them their turn comes at the end.
A participant does not want to take part. Offer the observer role for the first round, then ask again privately.
Real cases name a colleague someone in the room knows. Ask for changed names, and refer back to the working agreement.

items.label: Paul (2021), Umbrella summary: Behavior modeling training. Quality Improvement Center for Workforce Development. A plain-language summary of Taylor, Russ-Eft and Chan (2005), A meta-analytic review of behavior modeling training.

quiz.q: In a three, what is the order of feedback after a round?
quiz.a: The practiser first, then the other party, then the observer, each with one thing to keep and one to try.

quiz.q: A sales manager tells you her team hates role-play and asks you to drop it from a negotiation course. What do you offer?
quiz.a: Practice in threes with written briefs and an observer, all groups at once, and nobody in front of the room. What the team dislikes is the audience and the improvising, and a negotiation course with no practice will not change what they do.

quiz.q: During round two you see an observer leaning in and telling the practiser what to say. What do you do?
quiz.a: Go over, say quietly that their turn is in the feedback, and point at the sheet. The practiser needs an uninterrupted attempt, and the observer's notes are what make the feedback specific.

topics.title: Handle questions

situation.text: A hand goes up in the middle of your explanation and you do not know the answer. Ten minutes later someone folds their arms and says, "With respect, this would never work in our team." The room goes quiet to see what you do.

items: Say at the start how questions work: ask when something is unclear, and bigger issues go on the parked sheet. Put question points in your plan after each input as well as at the end.
To take a question: listen to the end, pause, and repeat it in one sentence for the room. Answer briefly, to everyone. Then check with the asker: "Does that cover it?"
Ask for questions in a way that gets some. "What questions do you have about the second step?" works better than "Any questions?" Topic 4.2 covers the wait.
When you do not know, say so, and say when you will. Write the question on the flipchart and send the answer when you promised. You can also ask the room whether anyone has dealt with it.

With a hostile question, do not defend. Agree with the part that is true, ask for the specific case, answer that briefly and move on. Allow one exchange and one follow-up in front of the room, then offer the break.
When a question is really a speech, wait for a breath. Use their name, sum up the point in a sentence, check it and thank them. Then take one other view and move on.
For an off-topic issue, park it. Keep a flipchart sheet headed "Parked", which many trainers call the car park. Write the question in the person's words and say when you will return to it.
Clear the parked sheet before the close. Answer each item, pass it to the client, or say it is outside today's scope.

do.title: Words you can use
lines: Asking for questions: "What questions do you have about the second step? Take a moment."
Repeating for the room: "The question is whether this works on a first call as well as a renewal."
The one you cannot answer: "I don't know. I'd be guessing, and I'd rather not. I'll find out and email all of you by Friday." (Write it up.)
Using the room: "Has anyone here dealt with that? What did you do?"
The hostile one: "You may well be right that it wouldn't work as it stands. Which part wouldn't fit your team?"
After their answer: "That's a real constraint. Here's how I'd adapt the first step for it. Let's see whether it holds up in the practice."
If it carries on: "I want to do that justice, and I want to keep us to time. Can you and I pick it up at the break?"
The speech: "Dev, let me check I've got your point. You're saying the targets make this impossible. Is that it? Thank you. Let's hear one other view, then I'll move us on."
Parking: "That matters, and it's bigger than today. I'll write it on the parked sheet in your words, and we'll come back to it at four."
Coming later: "That's coming at two o'clock. Hold me to it."

why.text: This is craft. The wording is one trainer's and you should change it until it sounds like you.

A group judges you more by how you handle not knowing than by how much you know. A confident guess that someone later finds to be wrong costs you the rest of the day. "I don't know, and I'll find out by Friday" costs nothing, provided the email arrives.

A hostile question is watched by everyone else as a test of whether it is safe to disagree here, the climate that 1.17 describes. If you flatten the person, the room learns to keep quiet. There is also usually something true inside it. "This wouldn't work in our team" is often accurate information about workload, targets or a manager, and those conditions decide whether training gets used, as 5.1 sets out.
Parking only works if you come back. A parked sheet nobody returns to shows the group it was a way of shutting people up.

try.text: Write three hostile questions about your own subject on cards. Ask a colleague to fire them at you with attitude, in random order, while you stand. Answer each aloud in under thirty seconds and record it. Good looks like this: your first words agree with something, there is no "but" in the first sentence, and you finish with a question back or a clear move on. Do the same with one question you cannot answer.

items: You give a five-minute answer to something one person cares about. Give the one-line answer and offer the rest at the break.
You argue to win. Even if you do, the rest of the room has stopped asking.
You promise an answer by Friday and forget. Photograph the flipchart before you leave the room.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What must happen to every item on the parked sheet before the session closes?
quiz.a: It is answered, passed to the client, or named as outside the day's scope.

quiz.q: During a product session for a software company's sales team, someone asks about a pricing rule you have not been briefed on. What do you say?
quiz.a: Say you do not know and will not guess, write the question up, and give a time by which you will send the answer to everyone. A wrong answer about pricing would travel to customers, and a kept promise builds more trust than a bluff.

quiz.q: A participant says, arms folded, "We tried this two years ago and it failed." What is your first move?
quiz.a: Agree that it may well have, and ask what happened. The answer usually tells you about real conditions at work, and the room is watching to see whether disagreement is safe.

topics.title: Keep time and cut content live

situation.text: It is 14:50 on a full day. Your plan says the final practice should be starting. You are one section behind, with an hour and forty minutes left and about two and a half hours of material.

items: Before the day, tag every segment. Must: the day fails without it. Should: it makes the day better. Could: good if there is time. As a rule of thumb, the musts should fill no more than two thirds of the working time.
Practice, debriefs and the close are musts. Most of your own input is a should or a could.
Next to each should and could, write the short version: drop it, halve it and how, or move it to a handout.
Write clock times down the left of the plan and mark three or four checkpoints: "By 11:00 I am starting the card sort." At each one, compare. If you are more than ten minutes behind, cut now.
Keep a clock where you can see it without looking at your wrist. A small travel clock on your table works. Use a visible timer for activities.

Cut in this order: your own stories, second examples and slides. Then full report-backs, which become one point per group. Then a could. Then a round of practice. Do not cut the debrief, the breaks or the close.
Cut silently. Never say "we've run out of time, so I'll skip this". Say nothing, or say "The sheet on that is in your pack."
Give break restarts as clock times and begin on that minute. A starting pattern from practice: 15 minutes mid-morning and mid-afternoon, and 45 to 60 minutes for lunch.

why.text: This is craft. The two-thirds rule and the break lengths are judgement, and you should adjust them as you learn your own pace.

Running over is the failure a client sees most easily. It also falls on the wrong part of the day. The close holds the first-use plan that 5.2 depends on, so a trainer who runs out of time loses the most useful fifteen minutes and keeps the slides.

Plans are nearly always too full, because they are written as if instructions, moving chairs and questions took no time. Tagging makes you say what the day is for while you are calm. A cut chosen the night before is better than one chosen at 14:50 with twelve people watching. Topic 4.13 makes the same case for rehearsing failures.
Talking faster does not recover time. People take in less, and the next activity starts with a confused room. Breaks stay because 2.14 treats them as part of the learning.

try.text: Tag your next plan and write the short versions. Then rehearse one cut aloud: deliver the last minute of the segment before it and the first minute of the segment after, as though the cut piece had never existed. Record it. Good looks like this: no apology, no mention of time, and a join a participant would not notice. Practise the break call aloud as well: "Back at five to eleven by that clock."

items: Everything is tagged must. Ask of each segment whether the day would fail without it. If the client insists on content, agree the tags with them before the day.
A guest speaker overruns. Agree their slot and a hand signal beforehand, and stand up when the time is reached.
You shorten the practice and keep every slide. Cut your talking first.
You lose ten minutes to a late start and push everything back. Cut a could in the first hour instead.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What do the tags must, should and could mean?
quiz.a: Must: the day fails without it. Should: it improves the day. Could: worth doing only if there is time.

quiz.q: At your 11:00 checkpoint you are twelve minutes behind, and the next segment is tagged could. What do you do?
quiz.a: Cut it now and say only that the handout is in the pack. Waiting in the hope of catching up moves the problem to the afternoon, where the cuts would fall on practice and the close.

quiz.q: It is 16:10 on a day that ends at 16:30, and your last practice round has one group still to go. What do you do?
quiz.a: Let that group finish its conversation, skip your recap, and start the close by 16:15. The close carries the first-use plan, and finishing late breaks the finish time you promised that morning.

topics.title: Close a session

situation.text: At 16:27 you reach the last slide. "We're nearly out of time, so, any questions? No? The forms are by the door. Thanks, everyone." People are zipping bags before you finish the sentence.

items: Give the close fifteen minutes in the plan, tag it must, and start it at the planned minute whatever is unfinished.
Take questions and clear the parked sheet first, for about three minutes. Questions belong before the end, not at it.
Do the feedback form next, in the room, in silence, for three minutes. A form filled in while leaving gets a row of ticks.
Then recall. Workbooks closed, each person writes from memory the three things they most want to keep, and compares with a neighbour. Topic 2.24 explains why recalling beats being told again.
Then first use. Each person writes one sentence on when and where they will use it, in the form 5.2 describes, and says it to a partner. The partner asks what might get in the way.
Say what happens next in under a minute: what you will send and when, any follow-up date, and what their managers have been told.
Finish with a round. Each person says the first thing they will do, in five words or fewer. You go first to set the length. With 30 people, do this at tables.
Say thank you, name the time, and stop. Stay in the room for fifteen minutes afterwards for anyone who wants a word.

why.text: The order is craft. Two parts borrow from research covered elsewhere on this site: the when-and-where plan in 5.2, and the finding in 2.18 that endings shape how a session is rated and remembered.

The thinking behind the order is simple. Whatever happens last is what people walk out with. If the last act is a form or a question from one person about parking, the day ends on paperwork. Put the questions and the form first and the day ends on each person saying what they will do.

Your own summary is the weakest way to close. When you list the key points, you are the one doing the remembering. Three minutes of recall from memory makes them do it, and the comparison in pairs fills gaps without you.

Ending on time is part of the agreement you made in the first ten minutes. People have trains and children to collect. Five minutes over, with half the room watching the clock, is worth less than nothing.

try.text: Deliver the whole close aloud, standing, against a timer, to a colleague or an empty room. Speak your lines and wait in silence where the group would be working. Record it. Good looks like this: your own words add up to under five of the fifteen minutes, you know your final sentence by heart, and you stop after it.

try.title: A worked example: a 15-minute close for 12 new managers, finishing at 16:30

head: Time
What happens
Words you say
rows: "Before we close, the parked sheet. Two items. The one about the appraisal form I can answer now. The one about pay bands is for your HR team, and I'll pass it on today. What else do you need to ask?"
"Three minutes for the form. Be blunt. It's how this course gets better. Turn it face down when you're done."
Recall, alone and then in pairs
"Workbooks closed. From memory, write the three things from today you most want to keep. Now compare with your neighbour. What did they have that you didn't?"
First use, written and then said to a partner
"Think of one person in your team who needs to hear something from you. Write: when I see them on which day, I will say what. Tell your partner. Partner, ask what might get in the way."

"Tomorrow I'll send the four steps on one page. In three weeks you'll get a short email asking how that conversation went. Your managers know you've each planned one conversation. They don't know who with."
"To finish: the first thing you'll do, in five words or fewer. I'll start. Book ten minutes with Priya. Round we go. Thank you, all of you. It's half past four."

items: You introduce a new idea in the last ten minutes because it was left over. It will not be remembered and it pushes out the plan for first use. Send it afterwards.
The round turns into speeches. Go first, in five words, and keep the pace with a nod to the next person.
A senior person wants to close the day. Give them one minute before the final round, so the last voices are the participants'.
At 16:15 you are mid-activity and tempted to finish it. Stop the activity. The close is the must.
You pack up while people fill in forms. Sit still. They take the form as seriously as you appear to.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: In the 15-minute close, what comes last?
quiz.a: A short round in which each person says the first thing they will do.

quiz.q: It is 16:15, your close is due to start and the group is halfway through a discussion they are enjoying. What do you do?
quiz.a: Stop the discussion with one closing remark and start the close. The recall and the first-use sentence are worth more than the end of the discussion, and finishing late breaks your agreement with the group.

quiz.q: The client asks you to end with their feedback form so that everyone completes it. How do you fit it in?
quiz.a: Put the form three minutes into the close, done in silence in the room, and finish with first use and the round. Everyone still completes it, and the day ends on what people will do.

topics.title: Write a session plan you can run from

situation.text: Your plan is the slide deck and a list of headings in a notebook. At 11:20 you cannot tell whether you are ahead or behind. The role cards for the next exercise are still in your bag.

items: Use one page, turned sideways, as a table with five columns: clock time, activity, method and grouping, materials, purpose. If you cannot write a segment's purpose in a few words, cut the segment.
Place the fixed points first: start, finish, lunch and two breaks. Then the opening and the fifteen-minute close. A day from 09:30 to 16:30 leaves about five hours of working time.
Put the hardest practice mid-morning, and something active and undemanding straight after lunch, following 2.14. Write the dips on the plan.
Add two recall points, one after lunch and one in the last hour. Both are done from memory, with notes closed.
Add up your own talking. As a starting rule from practice, keep it under a third of the working time, with no input longer than twenty minutes before the group does something.
Tag each row must, should or could, and mark your checkpoints, as in the topic "Keep time and cut content live".
Add two or three minutes to every activity for the instruction and the moving about. Leave ten minutes in the day unallocated.
Write the instruction for each activity on a card. Pack materials in plan order. Then walk the plan aloud once against a clock, and keep a printed copy on your table.

why.text: This is craft. The format is one that works for many trainers, and the proportions are judgement.

A plan you run from has a different job from a design document. You need to find your place in three seconds, standing, mid-sentence. That means one page, large type and clock times. Durations make you do sums while you are meant to be listening.

Each column answers a question you will otherwise face live. Method and grouping tells you who is talking and whether people need to move. Materials stops the hunt through a bag while twelve people wait. Purpose is what you consult when you have to cut, and it lets a co-trainer or the client see why each piece is there.
Writing it this way shows up an over-full day before the group does. If the times do not add up on paper, they will not add up in the room.

try.text: Write a one-page plan for a 90-minute session you could give. Then stand up and walk it through against a clock. Say the first sentence of each segment and every instruction in full, and move to where you would stand. Mark each place you ran over or hunted for something. Good looks like this: you can find your place from standing in three seconds, and every row has a purpose you can say aloud.

try.title: A worked example: a one-day plan for 12 new managers on giving feedback, 09:30 to 16:30

head: Time
Activity
Method and grouping
Materials
Purpose
rows: Open: paired question, shape of the day, working agreement
Timings flipchart. Agreement sheet. Name cards
Everyone speaks by 09:35. Reporting agreed. Must
Two feedback conversations compared, one vague and one specific
Trainer reads both. Pairs list differences. Harvest
The group builds its own list of what makes feedback usable. Must
The four steps: what I saw, the effect, a question, the next step
Ten minutes of input. Demonstration with one flaw. Room observes
Show the standard, and that a miss is normal. Must
Practice 1: written case, a team member who misses deadlines
Assigned threes. Three rounds of 4 plus 3 minutes
Hardest new skill while energy is highest. Must
One minute alone, then whole group
Two-column flipchart. Notes from walking round
From what was said, to why, to their own teams. Must
Prepare a real case: feedback you need to give this month
Alone for 15 minutes. Pairs test the opening sentence for 20
Real material for the afternoon. Quiet work before lunch. Should
Recall point 1: the four steps and one example, from memory
Pairs write on a blank card, then check against the step card
Recall. An easy, active start for the dip after lunch. Should
New threes, chosen by participants. Three rounds of 8 plus 5. Short debrief
Second attempt, on real work. Must
When it goes badly: denial, anger, tears
Fours take one reaction each. One point per group. Ten minutes of input
Prepare for the reply people fear. Should: two reactions if late
Recall point 2, then rehearse the first minute of the real conversation
Fours draw the day from memory. Gallery walk. Then pairs for 20 minutes
Recall on their feet in the afternoon dip. First minute ready. Must
Close: parked sheet, form, three things to keep, first use, final round
End on each person's first step. Finish at 16:30. Must

items: The plan becomes a script of four pages. You will not read it in the room. Keep one page and put the wording on instruction cards.
The plan follows the slides. Write the activities first and add slides only where a row needs one.
No slack anywhere. One long question and the day is late. Keep the ten spare minutes and the could rows.
Times were never tested aloud. Activities with real people run longer than they do in your head, so walk it through.
The plan stays in your bag. Put it beside the clock, where a glance takes in both.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What are the five columns of the one-page session plan?
quiz.a: Clock time, activity, method and grouping, materials, and purpose.

quiz.q: You are planning a day for a customer team and the client asks for the new policy briefing at 13:15, straight after lunch. What do you propose?
quiz.a: Open the afternoon with a short recall task in pairs and place the briefing mid-afternoon in a short slot. Straight after lunch is a dip, so it suits something active and undemanding, not twenty minutes of listening.

quiz.q: You add up your draft plan and find you are talking for three of the five working hours. What do you change?
quiz.a: Turn inputs into tasks, such as comparing two examples before you give the rule, and move reference content to a handout, until your talking is under about a third. Skills are built in the practice rows, and those are what the long inputs are squeezing.

parts.title: Difficult moments
parts.summary: Ladders of response, from light to firm, for the hard moments with people, with the words to say and whether to act in the room or at the break.

topics.title: The person who talks too much

situation.text: Twenty minutes in, one sales manager has answered every question. The others have stopped trying, and two of them are looking at you to see what you will do about it.

items: Change the structure before you say anything to the person. Give everyone two minutes to write an answer alone, then put them in pairs, then take one point from each pair in turn. Most over-talking stops here.
Move. Stand nearer to the talker, and turn your body and your eyes to the other side of the room when you ask the next question.
Thank and redirect, in the room: "Thanks, Dev. Let's hear from someone we have not heard from yet." Say it warmly, then wait (4.2).
Interrupt a long turn at a breath, with their name and a summary: "Dev, let me stop you there so I can hold on to that. Your point is that discounting starts too early. Who sees it differently?"

If it carries on, have a quiet word at the break. Start with what they bring, then ask for help: "You know this area well and I want the room to get the benefit. I also need to hear from the quieter people. Would you hold your answer until two others have spoken?"
Offer them a job that uses the energy, such as keeping time or summing up at the end of a discussion. Offer it. Do not impose it.
As the last rung, set a rule for everyone: "For this round, each person speaks once before anyone speaks twice."

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. No study tests this ladder. The order follows one idea: use the least public move that works. A change of structure costs the talker nothing. A remark in front of colleagues costs them something, and 4.3 notes that publicly correcting one person costs the whole room.

Most people who talk too much are keen, nervous, or used to being the one who knows. Very few are trying to spoil the session. If you treat it as enthusiasm you usually keep them on your side, and the quiet word works because it gives them a part to play with nobody watching.

Act in the room when other people are being shut out right now. Keep anything about the person's behaviour for the break. If the next break is an hour away and the structure change has not worked, make a break: "Let's take five minutes."

try.text: Rehearse this aloud. Ask a colleague to play someone who answers every question and to keep going until you stop them. Run three minutes of discussion and use rungs two to four. Record it on your phone. Listen for whether your interruption used their name, summed up their point and passed the question on within ten seconds. Then say the break-time line to them face to face and ask how it felt to hear.

try.title: The ladder at a glance: the person who talks too much

head: Rung
What you do
Where
rows: Write alone, then pairs, then one point from each pair
Stand near them and look elsewhere when you ask
Thank them and ask for a new voice
Interrupt with their name and a one-line summary
Quiet word: what they bring, then what you need
Offer a job: timekeeper, or summing up
A rule for all: once each before anyone goes twice

items: Handing them the pen has a risk that 4.3 does not mention. Whoever writes decides what gets recorded, and being made scribe can feel like a punishment. If you use it, check the sheet shows the group's points and not only theirs.
A joke at their expense gets a laugh and loses you a participant. Keep your tone level and friendly.
Do not start with the rule for everyone. It makes the whole group pay for one person.
Sometimes the talker is the only one who did the pre-work. Then the problem is the rest of the room. See the topic on the silent group.
Count your own talking time first. If you speak more than they do, start there.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What is the first rung of the ladder for someone who talks too much?
quiz.a: A change of structure: everyone writes alone, then pairs, then one point from each pair.

quiz.q: A participant has answered six questions in a row. You have tried pairs and you have asked for new voices. The break is in ten minutes. What do you do?
quiz.a: Hold on until the break and have the quiet word there: name what they bring, then ask them to wait until two others have spoken. Anything about a person's behaviour is better said in private.

quiz.q: You ask the loudest person to scribe. Ten minutes later the flipchart shows only their own three points. What do you do?
quiz.a: Go back to the group and ask what is missing from the sheet, then add it in their words. Next time take the pen yourself or rotate it, because the scribe controls the record.

topics.title: The silent group

situation.text: You ask a good question. Twelve retail team leaders look at the table. You count to five, and then to five again, and nobody says a word.

items: Check the question first. If it was long, vague or had two parts, ask it again in one short sentence and put it on the screen or the flipchart.
Wait properly (4.2). Then lower the cost of answering: "Take one minute and write down your answer. Nobody will see it."
Go to pairs: "Compare what you wrote with the person next to you. Two minutes." Walk round and listen. You will hear whether they have answers.
Collect from pairs, not from individuals: "Give me one thing your partner said." Reporting someone else's point is easier than owning your own.
If the room is still flat, ask a question that needs no words. A show of hands, one to five fingers (4.14), or a sticky dot on a scale on the wall.
Say what you see and ask about it: "It has gone quiet, and I can't tell if that is thinking, tiredness or me losing you. Talk to your neighbour for one minute about which it is, then tell me."
At the break, ask one or two people on their own: "Is there something about today or this group that I should know?" Then ask the organiser the same thing.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. The wait itself has classroom research behind it, covered in 4.2. The rest is craft that trainers pass on.

Silence has several causes and the ladder tests them in order of how easy they are to fix. The cheapest cause is your question. Next comes the risk of being wrong in front of colleagues, which writing and pairs reduce (1.17). After that come causes you cannot see from the front: the group heard bad news this morning, their manager is in the room, they were told to attend, or the content is aimed at the wrong level. You find those out by asking, and people will tell you at the break what they would never say in the room.
Stay in the room for the first six rungs. They are all changes to the task and single nobody out. Go to the break when you suspect the reason is about people or about the organisation.
One caution. A group that is silent in plenary may be working hard in pairs. If the pair talk is lively, the session is fine. Stop asking the whole room and run more of the day in small groups.

try.text: Run this with three or four colleagues or friends. Brief them to stay silent whatever you ask in the first minute. Ask your question, wait five full seconds, and then go down the ladder aloud: the written minute, the pairs, one thing your partner said. Have one person time your waits with a phone. Afterwards ask them at which rung they would have started talking in a real session.

try.title: Words you can use
lines: Let me ask that more simply. What is the hardest part of giving feedback to someone older than you?
Take one minute and write down your answer. Nobody will see it.
Now compare with the person next to you. Two minutes.
Give me one thing your partner said.
Hands up if you have had this conversation in the last month. Keep them up if it went well.
It has gone quiet, and I can't tell if that is thinking, tiredness or me losing you. One minute with your neighbour: which is it?
At the break: Is there something about today or this group that I should know?

items: Answering your own question teaches the group that waiting works. Hold the silence, then change the task.
Do not pick on someone by name to break the silence. Name people only after they have had time to prepare (4.3).
Jokes about the quiet ("Don't all speak at once") put the blame on the group.
Silence can mean thinking. If people are writing or looking up and away, give them longer.
Norms about speaking up differ between groups and cultures (4.7). Written and paired steps work across most of them.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: When a group is silent, what do you check before anything else?
quiz.a: The question. Ask it again in one short sentence and put it where people can see it.

quiz.q: Nobody answers in plenary, but when you set a pair task the room is loud and busy. What do you do?
quiz.a: Run more of the session in pairs and small groups and collect from pairs. The group can do the thinking. It is the whole-room setting that is stopping them.

quiz.q: You have tried writing, pairs and a show of hands and the room is still closed. The organiser is in the corridor at the break. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask the organiser, and one or two participants privately, whether something about today or the group explains it. The cause is probably outside the session, and you need to know it before you change the plan.
