topics.title: The cynic, and the person who was sent

situation.text: Arms folded, chair pushed back. "We did this two years ago with the last lot and nothing changed." Next to him sits someone whose manager booked her on the course without asking.

items: Deal with it before it appears. In your opening say: "Some of you chose to be here and some of you were told to come. Both are fine. All I ask is that you look for one thing that is worth your afternoon."
Ask for the doubts early and write them up: "What have you seen in training like this that did not work?" Keep the sheet on the wall and come back to it.
When the cynical remark comes, take it as information. Find the true part and ask for detail: "You have seen three sales methods come and go. What happened to the last one?"
Widen it to the group so it does not become a duel: "Who has had a different experience? Who has had the same?"
Set a test in place of an argument: "Don't take my word for it. Try it in the next exercise and tell me where it breaks."
At the break, speak to the person alone: "I get the sense this is not where you would choose to be today. What would make the rest of it useful to you?" Offer a real choice about how they take part.
If the remarks are stopping others, be plain and private: "It is fine to disagree with this. I need you not to make it harder for other people to try it. Can we agree on that?"

why.text: This is practitioner judgement, with one link to research covered elsewhere on the site. Adults engage more when they know why something matters to them and have some choice (1.5, 1.16). A person who was sent has had neither, so the opening line gives back a little of both.

The cynic is often right about the past. Programmes do get launched and dropped. If you defend the training you are arguing with their experience, and you will lose. If you ask what happened last time, you learn what the follow-up needs to avoid, and the room sees you can take a challenge.

A cynic may also be saying what others think. Sometimes the complaint is that training is the wrong answer to this problem, which 1.20 treats as a real possibility. Note it and take it to the client afterwards, without naming the person.
Rungs one to five belong in the room because they are about the content. The last two are about a person's behaviour and belong in the break.

try.text: Ask a colleague to play the cynic and give them three lines to throw at you, such as "This is common sense", "Head office has no idea what we do" and "I was told to come". Stand up and answer each aloud, using the pattern of true part, question, then test. Record it. Listen for any sentence where you defended the course, and say that reply again without the defence.

try.title: Words you can use
lines: Opening: Some of you chose to be here and some of you were told to come. Both are fine.
Opening: What have you seen in training like this that did not work? I'll write them up.
In the room: That is a fair point. What happened to the last one?
In the room: Who has had a different experience?
In the room: Don't take my word for it. Try it in the next exercise and tell me where it breaks.
At the break: What would make the rest of today useful to you?
At the break: It is fine to disagree. I need you not to make it harder for others to try it.
To the client afterwards: Several people doubted the follow-up, because of what happened last time.

items: Do not try to win them over in front of the group. The more attention the doubt gets, the more of the session it takes.
Avoid "I hear you, but". People hear only what comes after the "but".
Check what the client has agreed before you tell anyone they are free to leave. Attendance may be a condition of their job or of a certificate.
Do not report a named individual's attitude to their manager unless you said at the start that you would. It breaks the confidence that 4.16 asks you to keep.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What do you say in the opening to people who were sent?
quiz.a: That some chose to come and some were told to, that both are fine, and that you ask them to look for one thing worth their time.

quiz.q: A participant says: "We did this two years ago and nothing changed." What do you do?
quiz.a: Agree with the true part and ask what happened last time, then ask who has had a different experience. You gain information for the follow-up and avoid defending the course against their own history.

quiz.q: After two private conversations one person is still making remarks that put others off practising. What do you say, and where?
quiz.a: At the break, in private: it is fine to disagree, and you need them not to make it harder for others to try it. Ask for their agreement to that and nothing more.

topics.title: The expert in the room
topics.theory: Participants who know more than you

situation.text: You are training a software company's support team on a new escalation process. One engineer has run the platform for six years and corrects your second slide.

items: Find out before the day. Ask the organiser: "Who in the group knows this area deeply?" At the start, ask the room for a show of hands on years of experience.
Acknowledge the expert early, in public, without handing over the session: "Priya has run this platform for six years. I'll be asking her to keep me honest on the detail."
Ask them for cases, not for theory: "Priya, where have you seen this go wrong on a live account?" A case adds to your session. A lecture replaces it.
When they correct you and they are right, say so in one breath: "You're right, thank you. Let me fix that." Change it on the flipchart and carry on.
When you are not sure, do not bluff: "I have not come across that. I'll check at the break and come back to it." Then come back to it, out loud.
When it is a difference of view, name both and test them: "There are two schools on this. Here is why the course uses this one. Let's try both on the next case."

At the break, ask for their help and set a limit: "I want your experience in the room. I also need the group to work things out before they hear the answer. Could you hold back for the first few minutes of each exercise, then add what we have missed?"

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. The thinking behind it is that your authority in the room comes from running the process well. It does not come from knowing more than everyone present. A trainer who competes with an expert on content usually loses, and loses the group's trust on the way.

An expert who is named and used tends to relax. One who is ignored will keep proving what they know. Asking for cases gives them a way to contribute that helps the others, because real examples from their own workplace are what the group will remember.
Admitting a mistake quickly also shows the group the behaviour you want from them. 1.17 makes the point that people take risks when they see errors handled without fuss.
The correction and the admission happen in the room, at once, because the group heard the error. The request to hold back happens at the break, because it is about how one person takes part.

try.text: Ask a colleague who knows a subject better than you to sit in while you explain it for five minutes, standing up. Their brief is to correct you twice, once fairly and once on a matter of opinion. Practise the two replies aloud: the fast admission, and "two schools, let's test both". Record it and check that neither reply ran longer than fifteen seconds.

try.title: The ladder at a glance: the expert in the room

head: Moment
Words
Where
rows: Who in the group knows this area deeply?
Priya has run this platform for six years. I'll ask her to keep me honest.
Where have you seen this go wrong on a live account?
You're right, thank you. Let me fix that.
I have not come across that. I'll check at the break and come back to it.
In the room, then the break
Here is why the course uses this one. Let's try both on the next case.
Could you hold back for the first few minutes of each exercise?

items: Never bluff. One invented answer costs more than ten honest gaps.
Do not let the expert become a second trainer. If the group starts looking to them after every question, take the questions to pairs first.
Expert detail can bury beginners. If the answer is beyond what the group needs, say: "That is the advanced version. Let's take it at the break for those who want it."
Someone who only believes they are the expert gets the same ladder. Ask for a case and let the case do the work.
If the correction shows the material is wrong, tell whoever owns the design the same day.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: Where does a trainer's authority come from when someone in the room knows more?
quiz.a: From running the process well, not from knowing the most.

quiz.q: An experienced participant corrects a figure on your slide and you can see they are right. What do you do?
quiz.a: Say "You're right, thank you", correct it where everyone can see, and move on. A quick admission keeps trust and shows the group how to handle being wrong.

quiz.q: The expert answers every exercise question before the group has thought about it. What do you do?
quiz.a: At the break, ask them to hold back for the first few minutes of each exercise and then add what was missed. In the room, send questions to pairs first so there is thinking time.

topics.title: The senior person who takes over

situation.text: The sales director has joined your workshop for her regional managers. Each time you ask the group a question she answers it, and each time she finishes, the room agrees with her.

items: Brief them before the day. Ask for ten minutes by phone and make three requests: speak last, ask before you tell, and say at the start that you want to hear disagreement.
In the same call, agree what you will do if it goes wrong: "If I think the room is waiting for your view, I'll ask you to hold it. Is that all right with you?"
Decide together how much they attend. Opening the day and returning for the conclusions is often better than sitting in all of it.
Use structure in the room. Everyone writes first, then you take a round and say in advance: "Sam, I'll come to you last." Seat them at the side, not at the head of the table.
For group work, do not put one senior person in a group of juniors. Put them with the people closest to their own level, or ask them to visit groups as someone to consult.
When they take over, hold them gently and in public: "Sam, hold that thought. I'd like two more views before yours."
At the break, remind them of the agreement: "The room is waiting to hear what you think before they speak. In the next session, could you ask two questions before you give a view?"
If nothing changes, propose that they step out: "People will be more candid in the practice without you. Would you come back at three for their conclusions?"

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. 2.9 warns that the most senior person can close a room down by speaking first, and 1.13 says to have senior people go second. Neither works reliably on the day unless the person has agreed to it beforehand. The briefing is the move that makes the others possible.

Senior people rarely mean to take over. They are used to being asked for a decision, and silence feels to them like a gap they should fill. Most are glad to be told what would help. The briefing gives them a job, which is to draw their people out. It also lets you step in later without that looking like a challenge to their rank, which is far easier for a new trainer when the person has already said yes.
The first three rungs happen before the day. Structure and the single holding line belong in the room. Everything else is for the break, and never in front of their team.

try.text: Ask a colleague to play a director. First, make the briefing call for real, on the phone, using the three requests and the "if I think the room is waiting" line. Then run a five-minute discussion with two more people, in which the director answers first every time. Say the holding line aloud at least twice. Afterwards ask the director how each one landed.

try.title: Words for the briefing call
lines: Thanks for making time. I want your team to get the most from having you there.
People tend to wait for the most senior person and then agree. So I have three requests.
One. In discussions, would you speak last? I'll come to you at the end of each round.
Two. When you do come in, start with a question before you give your view.
Three. In the first five minutes, would you say that you want to hear where people disagree, with each other and with you?
If I think the room is waiting for your view, I'll ask you to hold it. Is that all right with you?
For the practice after lunch, I'd suggest you step out and come back at three to hear what they concluded.
Is there anything you want me to know about the group before we start?

items: If you cannot get the call, use the sixty-second version at the door before the start. Speak last, ask first.
Do not seat them in a small group of their own staff and expect an honest practice round.
A senior person who stays silent all day can worry the room as much as one who talks. Ask them to say something encouraging at the start and at the end.
If they are also the client, the topic on an observer at the back applies too.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What three things do you ask a senior person to do when you brief them?
quiz.a: Speak last, ask before telling, and say at the start that they want to hear disagreement.

quiz.q: A director will attend your workshop for her own team. You have a week. What do you do first?
quiz.a: Ask for a ten-minute call and brief her: the three requests, and agreement that you may ask her to hold her view. Moves made in the room work far better when she has agreed to them beforehand.

quiz.q: During a discussion the most senior person answers before anyone else for the third time. You briefed them yesterday. What do you say?
quiz.a: "Sam, hold that thought. I'd like two more views before yours." Then at the break, remind them of the agreement in private and ask for two questions before each view.

topics.bodyStatus: Practitioner craft. No research source.

topics.title: Side conversations and phones

situation.text: Two people at the back table are whispering through your explanation. A third has her phone under the desk, and a fourth has opened his laptop to his inbox.

items: Set it up in the opening. State break times as clock times so people know when they can check messages, and say: "If you need to take a call, step out. You don't need to ask."
Leave a short side conversation alone. People are often helping each other, translating, or reacting to what you just said.
If it goes on, stop talking. Pause mid-sentence, look at the slide or your notes, and wait. The quiet usually ends it without a word from you.
Move. Carry on teaching from beside their table.
Bring it into the room, lightly and without sarcasm: "Let's have one conversation. Is there something from that side worth sharing?"
If several conversations have started, the room is telling you something (4.14). Turn it into the task: "Take two minutes with your neighbour on what you make of this so far."

At the break, ask and do not accuse: "You two were talking a fair bit. Have I missed a question?" For a phone: "It looks like something is going on at work. Do you need ten minutes to sort it out? I'd sooner you did that and came back properly."
If devices are pulling the whole room away, make a request of everyone with an end time: "For the next forty minutes, lids down and phones face down. Then a ten-minute break for messages."

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. The ladder starts with the room and your own behaviour, because those cost nobody anything. It ends with a request to everyone, because a rule aimed at one person in public is a correction, and 4.3 notes what that costs.

Side talk is information before it is misbehaviour. Two people whispering may be confused, bored, or ahead of you. A room full of it means the input has gone on too long. So the early rungs give the talk somewhere to go.

Phones are different. Participants have jobs that carry on while they are with you. Clear break times and permission to step out remove most of the checking under the table. What is left is usually one person with a real problem at work, and ten minutes outside serves them better than two hours half present.
In hybrid sessions this matters more, because talk in the room that the remote people cannot hear shuts them out (4.11).

try.text: Practise the pause. Ask two colleagues to start whispering one minute into a three-minute explanation that you deliver standing. Stop mid-sentence and wait, looking at your notes, until they stop. Then do it again and use the line "Let's have one conversation". Record both and time the silence. Most people find they waited under three seconds the first time.

try.title: Words you can use
lines: Opening: Breaks are at 10:45, 12:30 and 15:00. Messages can wait until then.
Opening: If you need to take a call, step out. You don't need to ask.
In the room: Let's have one conversation. Is there something from that side worth sharing?
In the room: Take two minutes with your neighbour on what you make of this so far.
At the break: You two were talking a fair bit. Have I missed a question?
At the break: Do you need ten minutes to sort that out? I'd sooner you did that and came back properly.
To everyone: For the next forty minutes, lids down and phones face down. Then ten minutes for messages.

items: A phone or laptop may be how someone takes notes, reads the slides at a larger size or translates. Do not ban devices outright (2.23).
Someone may be on call for work or for a person they care for. Ask about this at the start: "Is anyone on call today?"
Staring at the talkers until they notice turns the room against you. Look at your notes.
Do not ask a whisperer a content question to catch them out. It is a public correction in disguise.
If the same pair talks all day, split the groups for everyone at the next activity by numbering off.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What do you say about calls in your opening?
quiz.a: That anyone who needs to take a call can step out without asking, and when the breaks are, as clock times.

quiz.q: Two people have been whispering for a minute while you explain a model. What is your first move?
quiz.a: Stop talking, look at your notes and wait. The silence usually ends it, and nobody has been corrected in public.

quiz.q: Halfway through the afternoon, four separate side conversations have started. What do you do?
quiz.a: Treat it as a message from the room and turn it into a two-minute pair task on what they make of the content so far. Then shorten or change the input that caused it.

topics.title: Late arrivals and people who leave early
topics.theory: Protecting the start and the close

situation.text: It is 9:30 and eight of fourteen people are in the room. At 9:50 the door opens twice. At lunch, three people tell you they have a train at four.

items: Fix what you can beforehand. Joining instructions give two times: "Coffee from 9:15, we start at 9:30." They also give the finish time and ask people to say now if they must leave before it.
Start on time, with a soft start. The first five minutes are a paired question on the screen, which a latecomer can miss. Introductions and the key content begin once it is done.
When someone walks in late, nod, point to a seat near the door with a handout on it, and keep going. No recap, no joke, no comment.
Catch them up at the next pair task: "Ana, would you bring Tom up to date in two minutes?" Or do it yourself while the groups work.
After breaks, give the restart as a clock time, write it up, and begin at that time with something worth being there for.
If the same person is late three times, ask at the break: "You have missed the start of the last two sessions. Is something getting in the way? The next part builds on the piece before lunch."
In the opening, ask: "Does anyone need to leave before 4:30?" If several do, move the close. Run the first-use plan (5.2) before they go, and use the last stretch for optional extra practice.
For one early leaver, close with them on their own at the last break: "Before you go, tell me the first thing you will try, and when."

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. Two things are being protected. One is the people who arrived on time, who learn from a late start that the stated time is not the real one. The other is the close, which Stage 5 depends on and which is the first thing to be lost when people drift away.

The soft start solves a real conflict. If you wait, you punish the punctual. If you launch into the main content, a third of the room misses it. A short opening task that matters a little, but not too much, lets you begin on time and still have everyone present for the important part.
Saying nothing to a latecomer is deliberate. They already know. A remark costs them standing in front of colleagues, and a recap makes everyone else sit through the material again.
Nearly all of this is done by design and in the room. Only the repeated case goes to the break.

try.text: Stand up and deliver your opening five minutes to an empty room or a colleague, as a soft start: greet, put the paired question up, give the instruction, then begin properly. Have the colleague walk in ninety seconds late and practise carrying on without a break in your sentence. Then say the three-times-late line aloud until it sounds like concern and not a telling-off.

try.title: A worked example: a soft start and a moved close for a one-day workshop

head: Time
What happens
Why
rows: Coffee. Paired question already on the screen.
Early arrivals have something to do.
Start. Pairs discuss the question for four minutes.
On time for those present. Latecomers miss little.
Welcome, the aims, how the day runs, introductions.
By now most people are in.
Break. "Back at 11:00" written on the flipchart.
Restart with a two-minute recall question in pairs.
Worth being back for, and quick to join.
First-use plan and close, moved from 16:15.
Three people leave at 15:50 for a train.
Optional practice round for those staying.
Useful, and no one misses the close.
As stated in the joining instructions.

items: A latecomer placed straight into a group that is mid-task slows the group. Give them two minutes with you first.
Where attendance counts towards a certificate or a compliance record, note what was missed and tell the organiser. That rule is the client's to apply, not yours.
If half the group is late, the cause is the venue, the travel or the invitation. Ask, and tell the client.
Finishing late to make up for a late start breaks your promise to the people with trains. Cut content instead.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What is a soft start?
quiz.a: Beginning on time with a short paired task that latecomers can miss, and starting the introductions and main content once it is done.

quiz.q: A participant comes in twenty minutes late while you are explaining the first model. What do you do?
quiz.a: Nod, point to the seat by the door and carry on. Catch them up during the next pair task, so they are not embarrassed and nobody else hears the content twice.

quiz.q: At 9:40 three people tell you they must leave at 15:50, and your close is planned for 16:15. What do you do?
quiz.a: Move the first-use plan and close to 15:30 and use the time after 15:50 for optional practice. The close matters more than the last exercise.

topics.title: Conflict between two participants

situation.text: Two store managers disagree about a rota policy. The second exchange is sharper than the first. On the third, one says: "That is typical of your branch." The rest of the table goes still.

items: Decide which kind it is. A disagreement about ideas is useful and you should keep it going. A remark about a person is where you step in.

For an argument about ideas, slow it down. Write both positions on the flipchart as "View A" and "View B", with no names on them. Ask each person to state the other view to that person's satisfaction.
Bring in the group: "Who has a case that supports A? And B?" The two are no longer facing each other.

If it heats up, stand where you break their line of sight and say: "Let me pause you both. Both views are on the chart. I'm going to move us on, and we can come back to it after the break if it still matters."
Change the structure. Give a short task done alone, then form new groups by numbering off round the whole room, so the two are apart and nobody has been moved by name.
At the break, speak to each one separately and briefly: "That got sharp. Are you all right? Is there anything I need to know to make this afternoon workable?"
If a personal remark is repeated, name it once, plainly: "Paul, that was about Ana, not about her point. Challenge the idea, not the person."

If a remark is abusive or discriminatory, stop it at once: "That is not acceptable in this room." Call a break. Speak to the person it was aimed at and then to the person who said it. Write down what was said, and tell the client contact the same day.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. 4.3 says to deal with conflict early and in private where you can. This topic adds which parts cannot wait for privacy.

A room with no disagreement is usually a room being polite, so the early rungs keep the argument and take the heat out of it. Writing the views on a chart moves them off the two people and on to the wall.
A personal remark is different. Everyone heard it, so everyone needs to see it dealt with, in a few words. One flat sentence and a change of activity is enough.

You are not a mediator. A dispute that started before your session belongs to their managers. Your job is to make the room workable for the hours you have. For abusive or discriminatory remarks the client will have its own conduct policy, and your part is to stop it, look after the person, record what happened and pass it on.

try.text: Rehearse with two colleagues. Brief them to argue about something trivial and to make it personal on the third exchange. Practise standing between them and saying the pause line aloud, then the "challenge the idea" line. Do it three times, with them escalating faster each time. Ask them afterwards whether your voice stayed level. That is the thing to work on.

try.title: Words you can use
lines: Ideas: Let me get both of these on the chart. View A is... View B is...
Ideas: Before you reply, tell me her point in a way she would agree with.
Ideas: Who has a case that supports A? And B?
Heating up: Let me pause you both. Both views are on the chart. We'll come back to it after the break if it still matters.
Personal: That was about Ana, not about her point. Challenge the idea, not the person.
Unacceptable: That is not acceptable in this room. We'll take ten minutes.
At the break, to each: That got sharp. Are you all right? Is there anything I need to know for this afternoon?

items: Do not take a side on the content while tempers are up, even if one of them is right. Come back to it later with a case.
If you have a working agreement from the opening, point to it. If you have none, this is the reason to make one next time (see the part "Run a session").
Tell the organiser about a serious incident yourself. Do not leave them to hear it from a participant.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: Which kind of disagreement do you keep going, and which do you stop?
quiz.a: Keep a disagreement about ideas going. Step in when a remark is about a person.

quiz.q: Two participants are arguing hard about a policy. Nothing personal has been said. What do you do?
quiz.a: Write both positions on the flipchart without names and ask each to state the other's view, then ask the group for cases. This keeps a useful argument and takes it off the two people.

quiz.q: One participant says of another: "That is typical of people like you." What do you do?
quiz.a: Stop it at once with one flat sentence and call a break. Speak to each privately, starting with the person it was aimed at, write down what was said, and tell the client contact that day.

topics.title: When someone is upset

situation.text: You are running a feedback exercise with new managers. In one of the trios a woman has stopped talking and is crying quietly. Her partners are looking at you.

items: Keep your voice and pace steady and do not draw the room's eyes to her. If you are speaking, carry on for a sentence and move so that people look away from her table.
Give the group something to do: "Take five minutes in your pairs on the next question." Or call the break early.
Go to her quietly, or ask your co-facilitator to. Get down to her level and speak low: "Would you like to step outside for a minute? I can come with you, or you can go on your own."
Outside, say little: "Take your time. You don't need to explain." Then offer choices: "What would help? A few minutes alone, some water, someone to sit with you, or to head home?"
Ask whether there is a colleague she would like with her. Fetch that person and no one else.

Listen if she wants to talk. Do not probe, advise or tell a story of your own. If it is about work or health, point to help she already has: her manager, HR, an employee assistance line if her employer has one, or her GP.
Leave the way back open: "Come back whenever you are ready, or not at all. Nobody will ask." To the group, say one line or nothing: "Sara is taking a few minutes. Let's carry on."
Check in at the next break, and agree what is passed on: "I won't mention this to anyone unless you want me to."

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. It is not counselling and it is not medical advice. 4.16 says a participant in distress needs referral, not coaching, and 1.13 says to give everyone a way to step out. This topic is the minute in between.

People cry in ordinary workshops, about feedback, change, redundancy, or something from home that the exercise touched. Usually what they want most is not to be watched. So the order is cover first, then privacy, then choice.

Your limits are the point of the topic. You are there to make the next ten minutes bearable and to leave the person in charge of what happens. You are not there to find out what is wrong or to fix it.

There is one exception to keeping it private. If you believe someone may be in danger, say so to them, stay with them or have someone else stay, and tell the client's named contact. If the danger is immediate, call 999. On a residential, the duty-of-care plan in 8.5 should already name who does this.

try.text: Practise the words, because they are hard to find in the moment. With a colleague playing the participant, say the cover instruction to an imagined room, walk over, crouch and say the step-outside line at low volume. Then say the three corridor lines. Swap roles so you hear them from the other chair.

try.title: Words you can use
lines: To the room: Take five minutes in your pairs on the next question.
To the person, quietly: Would you like to step outside for a minute? I can come with you, or you can go on your own.
Outside: Take your time. You don't need to explain.
Outside: What would help? A few minutes alone, some water, someone to sit with you, or to head home?
Outside: Is there someone here you'd like with you?
If it is beyond you: That sounds hard, and it is outside what I can help with. Who do you have that you could talk to?
The way back: Come back whenever you are ready, or not at all. Nobody will ask.
To the room: Sara is taking a few minutes. Let's carry on.
At the break: I won't mention this to anyone unless you want me to.

items: If you are the only trainer, set a task of ten minutes, not two, and stand in the doorway where you can see the room and the corridor.
Do not discuss it with the group, and do not let the group discuss it. Move on to the next activity.
If your exercise caused it, look at the design afterwards. 2.21 covers telling people in advance what an activity will ask of them and letting them observe first.
Tell the client contact only what the person has agreed to, unless you think someone is at risk.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What comes first when someone becomes upset: going to them, or setting the group a task?
quiz.a: Setting the group a task, or calling a break. It takes the room's attention away before you go over.

quiz.q: A participant leaves the room in tears during a feedback exercise. You have a co-facilitator. What do you do?
quiz.a: Keep the room working and ask your co-facilitator to follow, offer privacy and ask what would help. The person chooses whether to return, and the group is told one line at most.

quiz.q: In the corridor, a participant starts to tell you about a serious problem at home and asks what you think she should do. What do you say?
quiz.a: That it sounds hard and is outside what you can help with, and ask who she has that she could talk to, such as her GP or an employee assistance line. Listening is fine. Advising is beyond your role.

topics.tierReason: Practitioner judgement about the first few minutes. It is not counselling or medical advice, and no study was opened for it.
topics.bodyStatus: Practitioner craft. No research source.

topics.title: The slot after lunch

situation.text: It is 13:40. Lunch was sandwiches and pastries in a warm room. You are four slides into the afternoon's main model and two people have their chins on their hands.

items: Design the slot before the day. 1.14 and 2.14 cover planning around energy. Applied here: no input in the first twenty minutes after lunch. Put an activity there in which people talk, move and make something.
Change the room during lunch. Open a window, turn the lights up, turn the projector off if the first task does not need it.
Restart at the stated time with a task that begins on people's feet: "Find someone you have not worked with yet and go to a flipchart."
If energy drops during input, stop talking and get them talking: "Turn to your neighbour. Two minutes. Where would this fail in your team?"
Next rung: get people up. A vote by standing along a wall, or a walk round the charts to add a comment (1.15). Offer a seated way to take part.
Next: name it and take a short break. "We have hit the afternoon dip. Five minutes of fresh air, back at 14:25."
The firm rung is to cut. Drop the rest of the input and go straight to practice. Move the heavy piece to tomorrow morning, or to a handout with a recall question at the next session.
Afterwards, write in your plan what you would move next time (4.15).

why.text: 1.14 sets out what is known about energy across the day. The rest of this topic is practitioner judgement about one hour that goes wrong often.

The dip is predictable, so most of the answer is design. A trainer who puts the hardest slides at 13:30 and then tries to rescue the room with enthusiasm is solving the wrong problem. People who are standing, talking and writing on a chart stay awake without being asked to.

The ladder for the day itself moves from changing who is talking, to changing what bodies are doing, to stopping. Each rung costs more time than the one before. Cutting content feels like failure, but material delivered to a room that is half asleep has not been delivered.

All of this happens in the room, with one exception. If lunch itself is the problem, because it is heavy, late or too long, raise it with the organiser at the afternoon break for tomorrow, or before the next booking.

try.text: Take the first thirty minutes after lunch from a session you run and deliver the restart aloud, on your feet: the instruction that gets people up, the task and the time call. Then rehearse the rescue. Start explaining a slide, stop yourself at one minute and say the pair question. Record it and listen to how long you take to hand over to the room. Aim for under twenty seconds.

try.title: A worked example: the first hour after lunch, twelve new managers

head: Time
What happens
Why
rows: Lunch. Trainer opens the windows and puts four flipcharts round the room.
Cooler room, and the task is ready.
Restart, standing. New pairs go to a flipchart.
Pairs list the three hardest conversations they had this month.
Walk round. Each pair adds a tick to the two they share most.
Sit. Trainer gives ten minutes of input on the conversation model, using the top-voted case.
Input is short and tied to their case.
A planned pause before the dip returns.
Groups report one thing to keep and one to change.
Leads into the afternoon break at 14:45.

items: Do not show a long video in a darkened room at 13:30.
An energiser with no link to the content can feel like being made to play. 1.23 covers using play on purpose.
Do not tell the group they look tired. Say the session has hit the dip and change something.
Standing activities need a seated version, said as part of the instruction and not as an afterthought.
A very long lunch does not fix the dip. It shortens the afternoon.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What should not happen in the first twenty minutes after lunch?
quiz.a: Input from the trainer. Use an activity in which people talk, move and make something.

quiz.q: At 13:50 you are halfway through explaining a model and you can see people drifting. What do you do first?
quiz.a: Stop talking and set a two-minute pair question on the content. It changes who is doing the work at the lowest cost in time.

quiz.q: It is 14:20, you have tried pairs and a standing vote, and you still have twenty minutes of slides left. What do you do?
quiz.a: Take a five-minute break, then cut the slides and go straight to practice. Move the remaining input to the next morning or to a handout.

topics.tierReason: Practitioner judgement. The research on energy across the day sits in 1.14 and was not opened again for this topic.
topics.bodyStatus: Practitioner craft. No research source.

topics.title: The client or an observer sitting at the back

situation.text: The client's head of learning has come to see the pilot. She sits behind the group with a laptop. Twice she adds a comment from the back, and the participants keep glancing round at her.

items: Ask in advance who is coming and why. They may be there to assess you, to see the content, or to watch their own people. The answer changes what you agree.
Offer the better option first: "People behave differently when they are watched. Would you join a table and take part?"
If they will observe, agree the terms. They sit at the side, not behind the group. They stay out of small-group work. Comments come to you at breaks. They do not report on how individuals performed.
Introduce them at the start and say why they are there: "Jo is from the learning team. She is here to see how the course runs, not to assess anyone."
Then teach the room. Do not look to the back for approval or aim your examples at them.

If they comment from the back, thank them and bridge: "Thanks, Jo. Let me take that into the next exercise." If you want their view, ask for it at a moment you choose: "Jo, what does the business need from this?"
At the break, ask for the change: "It helps the group if comments come through me. Could you pass me a note and I'll bring it in?"
If the room has gone quiet because of them, ask them to step out: "The group has been careful since the practice started. Could you leave us for the role-plays and come back for the debrief?"

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. An observer changes a room in two ways. The participants become careful, most of all in practice, because nobody wants to get it wrong in front of the person who reports to their director. And the trainer starts performing for one person at the back and stops attending to the fourteen in front.
Both problems are mostly solved before the day. An observer who has been told where to sit, what they are watching for and when to speak is rarely a difficulty.
The introduction matters more than it seems. Left unexplained, a stranger taking notes will be assumed to be assessing the participants. One sentence removes that.

The bridging line is for the room, where a client has to be treated with respect in front of their own staff. The request to change, and the request to step out, are for the break. Afterwards, ask for fifteen minutes of feedback on two things you chose, so the observation is useful to you too.

try.text: Ask a colleague to sit behind you with a laptop while you run ten minutes of a real session for two or three others. Their brief is to type throughout and to interrupt once. Practise the introduction, then the bridging line, without turning your body to the back. Afterwards ask the others how often you looked at the observer. Then say the step-out request aloud to your colleague, face to face.

try.title: A message to send an observer before the day
lines: Thanks for coming on Thursday. A few things will help the group get the most from it.
If you can, join a table and take part. People are more open with a fellow participant than with an observer.
If you would prefer to watch, please sit at the side by the window, not behind the group.
I'll introduce you at the start and say you are there to see the course, not to assess anyone.
During the practice rounds, please stay at your seat. People find it hard to try things with someone listening in.
If you spot something, pass me a note or catch me at a break and I'll bring it in.
Please don't share how individuals did with their managers. I have told the group that practice is private.
Could we have fifteen minutes at the end? I'd value your view on the pace and on the afternoon exercise.

items: An observer who is also the most senior person present needs the briefing in the topic on the senior person who takes over.
If they correct a participant directly, step in with the bridge at once and raise it at the break.
Typing behind people is distracting whatever is being typed. Ask for handwritten notes, or a seat at the side.
If you promised the group that practice is private, check that the observer has agreed to that before you say it.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What do you say when you introduce an observer to the group?
quiz.a: Who they are and why they are there, including that they are not assessing the participants.

quiz.q: The client arrives unannounced five minutes before the start and sits behind the group with a laptop. What do you do?
quiz.a: Go over and ask, kindly, for a seat at the side and for comments to come to you at breaks, then introduce them to the group. A short word at the door prevents most of the trouble.

quiz.q: Since the observer arrived, the role-plays have gone flat and people are choosing safe examples. What do you do?
quiz.a: At the break, ask the observer to step out for the practice rounds and come back for the debrief. People will not risk getting it wrong in front of someone who may report on them.

stages.name: Make it stick
stages.question: How does it survive the return to work?
stages.wordingStatus: Draft: part names and topic titles for this stage were written for the build pack and have not been seen by Mica

parts.title: Get it used at work
parts.summary: Transfer, follow-up and coaching.

topics.title: Treat transfer as a design problem

situation.text: People leave the course keen, and a month later they work exactly as before.

items: Treat use at work as the goal of the design.
Check the three influences: the learner, the design, the workplace.
Find where it broke down.
Design for new situations as well as familiar ones.

why.text: Transfer is the point of training and it often fails. You will hear that only 10 per cent of training transfers to the job. That figure traces to a 1982 magazine article, which opened with a training director's guess and gave no data. A 2011 review found no behavioural evidence behind it. No single percentage fits all training, so do not quote one. The problem behind it is real.
Applying a skill to a similar situation is easier than applying it to a new one. The second has to be designed for.

A meta-analysis of 89 studies found transfer was linked to the learner's ability, conscientiousness and motivation, and to a supportive workplace. These links were stronger for open skills such as leadership than for closed skills such as using software. Results looked better than they were when the same person rated both the training and its use.

why.title: Transfer of training: a meta-analytic review
why.found: Across 89 studies, transfer was positively related to cognitive ability, conscientiousness, motivation and a supportive work environment. Most links were stronger for open skills such as leadership than for closed skills such as software. Links were inflated when one source supplied both measures in the same setting.
why.means: Check the learner, the design and the workplace, and get evidence of use from someone other than the learner.

items.title: Transfer is the point
items.text: A good event is not enough.

items.title: A guess
items.text: The 10 per cent figure has no data behind it.

try.text: Take a programme that did not transfer. Check it against the three influences and find where it failed.

try.title: Finding where it broke
try.text: Illustration. A team learns a new handover routine and says they like it. A month on, nobody uses it. The trainer checks the three influences. People can do it and the practice was realistic. The shift pattern leaves no time for it. The fix is in the workplace.

items: The workplace is easy to neglect. A supportive one is linked to more transfer.
Blaming the learner is the easy answer.
Do not quote the 10 per cent figure. Say what you saw change at work instead.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Baldwin and Ford (1988), Transfer of training: a review and directions for future research.
Blume and colleagues (2010), Transfer of training: a meta-analytic review.
Ford, Yelon and Billington (2011), How much is transferred from training to the job? The 10% delusion as a catalyst for thinking about transfer.
Georgenson (1982), The problem of transfer calls for partnership.

topics.bodyStatus: 4 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: What are the three influences on transfer?
quiz.a: The learner, the training design and the workplace.

quiz.q: How should you treat the "10 per cent of training transfers" figure?
quiz.a: As a guess with no data behind it. Do not quote it.

quiz.q: Which kind of transfer is harder?
quiz.a: Applying a skill to a new situation.

topics.tierReason: A meta-analysis of 89 studies links transfer to the learner, the training and the workplace, but the links vary with the kind of skill and with how transfer was measured.
openPoints: The near and far transfer paragraph ('Applying a skill to a similar situation is easier than applying it to a new one') has no opened source. Candidate to check: Barnett and Ceci (2002), Psychological Bulletin. Not opened.

Grossman and Salas (2011), The transfer of training: what really matters, was read only as a copy on a third-party site, not the publisher's page, so it is not in the links. It groups the best-supported factors under the same three headings and would be worth adding once the Wiley page can be opened.

Publisher pages for Baldwin and Ford (Wiley) and Blume (Sage) refused access. Abstracts were read on an index record and a library catalogue record. Swap the URLs for the DOI links: 10.1111/j.1744-6570.1988.tb00632.x and 10.1177/0149206309352880. Ford and colleagues is 10.1002/piq.20108.
checkFindings: BuildNote followed. Opened Georgenson (1982) on the publisher's site (the article itself, not a summary): the 10 per cent is an unnamed training director's estimate in the opening line, with no source. Opened the ERIC record for Ford, Yelon and Billington (2011): the belief lacks empirical, behavioural evidence. The draft's 'disputed estimate' was too kind, so the paragraph, card, watch item and quiz now say it is a guess and should not be quoted.
The draft said '10 to 20 per cent'. No opened source gives 20 per cent. Removed.
Baldwin and Ford (1988) confirmed as the source of the three influences: trainee characteristics, training design and work environment.
Blume and colleagues (2010) confirmed: 89 studies. Added its two main caveats (open against closed skills, same-source inflation) because a practitioner would expect them.
'The workplace is the most neglected of the three' could not be supported and was softened.
Added a study block (Blume 2010) and an example.

topics.title: Plan the first use at work before people leave

situation.text: The course ends with "any final questions?" and a feedback form.

items: Practise on tasks that look like the job.
Vary the examples and settings.
Before people leave, have each write when and where they will first use it.
Use the form "when X happens, I will do Y".
Tell their manager what they planned.

why.text: Practice across varied examples helps people apply a skill in new settings more than repeating one example. Transfer should be built into every part of a course, not added on the last afternoon.

A specific if-then plan makes follow-through more likely than a general intention. A meta-analysis of 94 tests found a medium to large benefit for people who added such a plan to a goal, compared with holding the goal alone.
The if-then evidence comes from health, study and laboratory goals, not from training courses. Treat the plan as a well-supported bet borrowed from another field.

why.title: Implementation intentions and goal achievement
why.found: Across 94 independent tests, people who formed an if-then plan reached their goals more often than people who only held the goal. The effect was medium to large (d = .65). The plans helped people get started and stay on course.
why.means: Have each person write one when-and-where plan for first use before they leave the room.

items.title: When X, I will do Y
Before they leave
items.text: Plan the first use in the room.

try.text: Take a course that ends at the event. Add varied practice, a first-use plan and an if-then statement.

try.title: Before and after
try.text: Illustration. Before: "I will give better feedback." After: "When I finish Friday's one-to-one with each person, I will name one thing they did well and one thing to change." The second names the moment and the action.

items: Action plans written in a rush are forgotten.
A plan with no follow-up is weak.
Prior knowledge changes what transfers.

topics.title: Use 70-20-10 as a reminder, not a formula

situation.text: A strategy document says learning should be "70 per cent experience, 20 per cent social, 10 per cent formal".

items: Use the model as a reminder that most learning happens outside courses.
Do not use the numbers to set budgets.
Design the on-the-job part: stretch tasks, reflection, feedback.
Design the social part: coaching, peers, communities.

why.text: The numbers come from Center for Creative Leadership research in the 1980s, in which successful executives looked back on the events that had shaped them. The ratio itself was set out later, in a 1996 planning guide by Lombardo and Eichinger. A 2018 review found the evidence for the 70 per cent claim weak and the studies behind it inconsistent. The model is a useful reminder and not a validated formula.
Experience alone does not build expertise. Without reflection and feedback it levels off.
The Center for Creative Leadership itself says well-designed courses strengthen the other two parts. The model's own home does not treat it as a case for cutting formal training.

items.title: A reminder
items.text: Most learning is outside the course.

try.text: Take a "70-20-10 strategy". Rewrite it so the intent survives and the false precision goes.

try.title: Rewriting the line
try.text: Illustration. Before: "70 per cent of learning will come from experience, so the course budget falls by 70 per cent." After: "Most development happens in the work. We will design stretch tasks, feedback and peer support, and keep courses where a skill needs teaching."

items: The model is used to justify cutting formal training. That does not follow.
"Learning on the job" with no design is hoping.
Say where the numbers came from when you use them.

topics.title: Schedule the follow-up at 30, 60 and 90 days
topics.theory: Spaced reinforcement after the event, relapse prevention and coaching cycles

situation.text: The course was a success in March. By June nobody mentions it.

items: Schedule recall and a task to apply at 30, 60 and 90 days.
Ask people what will pull them back to old habits, and plan for it.
Set up regular check-ins with a manager or coach.
Send short prompts at the point of use.

why.text: A well-run event with no follow-through is likely to fade. How fast depends on the kind of task and how well it was learned in the first place, which the topic "Plan refreshers before skills fade" covers. Follow-up is part of the design.
Relapse prevention means naming the obstacles in advance and planning what to do when they come. Regular check-ins keep the new behaviour in view while it becomes routine.

items.title: Check-ins
items.text: Someone asks how it is going.

try.text: Design a 30, 60 and 90-day plan for a real programme. Include a step for relapse.

try.title: A relapse step
try.text: Illustration. At 30 days each person recalls the three steps from memory and tries one on a live task. Their plan includes a line such as: "When the week is too busy for the full routine, I will do step one only."

items: Follow-up needs an owner.
Reminders that only repeat content are ignored.
Measure whether it is working.
Treat 30, 60 and 90 days as a convenient convention. Fit the dates to when people will next use the skill.

If you are external and lose access after the event, build the follow-up before you leave. Write the manager's step into the contract, hand the client a ready-made follow-up pack with the recall questions, the task and the dates, and include one 30-minute call at about 30 days.

quiz.a: At 30, 60 and 90 days.

topics.title: Coach with questions, not answers
topics.theory: Coaching and mentoring as a skill

situation.text: A manager says they "support the learning". In practice they tell people the answer.

items: Decide whether the moment needs coaching, mentoring or teaching.
Agree the goal.
Ask where things stand now.
Ask what the options are.
Ask what the person will do, and when.
Listen, and wait.

why.text: Coaching draws the answer out of the person. Mentoring shares experience. Teaching passes on knowledge. A common structure for a coaching conversation, set out in Whitmore's Coaching for Performance, runs through goal, reality, options and will. Will means what the person will do. Some versions call the last step way forward.

Two meta-analyses find that workplace coaching has positive effects on skills, performance, wellbeing and how people pursue their goals. The studies are few. One of the two looked only at coaching by trained internal or external coaches and left out managers coaching their own staff, so the evidence for manager coaching is thinner. Coaching is also a common way to follow up after a course.

why.title: Does workplace coaching work?
why.found: Pooling 17 studies of coaching by internal or external coaches, the authors found positive effects on skills, on attitudes and on results. Internal coaches did better than external ones. Face-to-face and online coaching did not differ, and nor did longer and shorter programmes. Coaching by line managers was left out.
why.means: Offer coaching as follow-up with some confidence, and do not assume a manager's coaching will work as well as a trained coach's.

try.text: Run a coaching conversation on a peer's real goal. Get feedback on your questions and your waiting.

try.title: Telling and asking
try.text: Illustration. Telling: "Send the client the revised plan today." Coaching: "What do you want from this client by Friday? Where are things now? What could you do? Which will you do, and when?" Then the manager waits.

items: A structure can become a script. Listen first.
Some people need telling. Know when.
Managers need time to coach.
The research is mostly on trained coaches. A manager also judges the person's work, which can make open answers harder to give.

topics.title: Make the new behaviour easy to start and easy to repeat

situation.text: People know what to do and agree with it. They do not do it.

items: Pick one behaviour and make it specific.
Attach it to something that already happens: after the Monday meeting, I will.
Make the first step small.
Remove an obstacle: a template, a shortcut, a reminder at the point of use.
Have someone notice when it happens.

why.text: Knowing is not doing. One widely used model says behaviour depends on capability, opportunity and motivation together. A course usually addresses the first.

Habits form when an action is repeated in the same setting until the setting prompts it. In one study, 96 volunteers repeated a chosen eating, drinking or activity behaviour daily for 12 weeks. The time to become close to automatic ranged from 18 to 254 days. Among the people whose progress could be tracked well, half took longer than about two months.

In the same study, missing a single day did not noticeably set people back. The behaviours were simple health actions that people chose for themselves, so treat the timings as a rough guide for workplace skills.

A meta-analysis of 94 tests found that people who wrote an if-then plan reached their goals more often than people who only held the goal. That is the reason for attaching the behaviour to something that already happens.

why.cite: Lally, van Jaarsveld, Potts and Wardle (2010)
why.title: How are habits formed
why.found: 96 volunteers repeated a self-chosen eating, drinking or activity behaviour daily for 12 weeks and rated how automatic it felt. Time to near-peak automaticity ranged from 18 to 254 days. Missing one opportunity did not materially affect the process.
why.means: Plan support for months, not weeks, and tell people one missed day does not undo the habit.

try.text: Take one behaviour from a course. Write the cue, the small first step and one obstacle to remove.

try.title: Cue, small step, obstacle removed
try.text: Illustration. Behaviour: log each client call. Cue: "When I put the phone down, I will open the log." Small first step: one line only. Obstacle removed: a pinned shortcut to the log. The team lead mentions it at the weekly meeting.

items: There is no fixed number of days for a habit. Popular figures of a few weeks have no support in the study above.
If the workplace punishes the new behaviour, it stops.
Too many new behaviours at once means none.

parts.title: Keep learning going
parts.summary: Job aids, communities, alumni and new trainers.

topics.title: Build a job aid when a course is the wrong tool
topics.theory: Learning in the flow of work

situation.text: People are in the middle of a task and stuck. They do not need a course. They need the answer.

items: Ask when people will need this: learning it, applying it, fixing a problem, or coping with a change.
For applying, fixing and changing, build a job aid.
Write it to be scanned.
Put it where the work happens.

why.text: One framework, from Gottfredson and Mosher, lists five moments of need: when something is new, when people want more, when they must apply it, when something goes wrong, and when things change. The last three happen during work. It is a practitioner model and has not been tested as a whole.
At those moments a checklist that can be found is often more use than a course that has to be remembered.
A standard book on job aids splits them into two kinds. Planners are used just before or after the task. Sidekicks are used during it. Decide which you are building before you write.

try.text: Take a task. Design a job aid for the moment of need.

try.title: A course or a card
try.text: Illustration. Staff run a month-end report once every four weeks and forget the steps each time. A half-day course would be forgotten too. A one-page checklist pinned inside the reporting tool answers the question at the moment it comes up.

items: A job aid nobody can find is useless.
Some skills must be in the head. Do not replace those.
Keep it current.

topics.title: Grow a community of practice, do not announce one

situation.text: Leadership announces a "community of practice" and sets up a channel. Three weeks later it is silent.

items: Start from a shared problem people care about.
Set a regular rhythm of contact.
Make it safe to share half-finished work.
Seed it, then step back.

why.text: A community of practice is a group who share a concern for something they do and get better at it by interacting regularly. Some organise themselves. Most need cultivating, and an announcement alone does not make one.
All three parts are needed: a shared domain, a real community and a developing practice.

try.text: Design the launch conditions for a community: its domain, its rhythm, and how safety will be built.

try.title: Announced and grown
try.text: Illustration. Announced: a new channel called "Facilitators' community" and a launch message. Grown: five facilitators who all struggle with quiet online groups meet for 30 minutes each fortnight, bring one half-finished plan each, and invite others once it is useful.

items: A community needs someone to tend it.
Newcomers learn at the edge first.
Measure usefulness, not posts.

topics.title: Keep graduates involved

situation.text: The programme ends with a certificate and you never hear from the group again.

items: Plan what happens after the last session.
Give graduates a reason to stay in touch.
Offer mentoring and peer groups.
Invite graduates to teach or support newer learners.

why.text: Graduation can be a move into a continuing relationship. A network of past learners can keep the learning in use and supply new teachers. This is practice wisdom and not a research finding.
Teaching newer learners can deepen the graduate's own learning.

why.title: Learning by teaching
why.found: A meta-analysis of 28 studies compared students who prepared to teach, or prepared and then taught, with students who studied without expecting to teach. Both groups learned more, and those who went on to teach learned most. Teaching with real interaction helped more than teaching without it.
why.means: When graduates help a newer cohort, have them explain and answer questions, not only sit in.

try.text: Design a plan that gives graduates a reason to stay connected and a way to contribute.

try.title: After the certificate
try.text: Illustration. Six weeks after the last session, graduates are invited to a one-hour meeting to bring one case each. Two volunteer to sit in on the next cohort's practice session and give feedback. The ask is one hour.

items: A mailing list is not a community.
Keep the ask small.
Get consent before using graduates as proof.

topics.title: Teach others to train

situation.text: Demand outgrows what you can deliver. Someone else has to run your sessions.

items: Let new trainers watch you first.
Have them deliver a part while you watch.
Give feedback on one thing at a time.
Pass on the reasons, not only the slides.
Observe before you sign someone off.

why.text: Trainers learn the craft by watching, guided practice and feedback. Teaching people to teach multiplies your reach.
It is also how standards spread or slip. Hand on the evidence and the caveats with the material.

The research here is thin and comes mostly from health and social care. One review found that train-the-trainer programmes usually improved knowledge or practice. Programmes that mixed interactive methods with written materials looked best, and the right mix is still unclear.

why.title: Does train-the-trainer work?
why.found: A systematic review found 18 studies in health and social care. Thirteen reported better knowledge, clinical behaviour or patient outcomes, three a possible effect and one none. The studies were too varied to pool and carried a moderate risk of bias.
why.means: Build your handover from interactive practice plus materials, and check the result by observing, since the evidence will not do that for you.

items.title: Observe
items.text: Sign off on what you have seen.

try.text: Design a short train-the-trainer plan for one skill. Say how you would observe, give feedback and judge readiness.

try.title: Handing over a session
try.text: Illustration. A new trainer watches the session once. Next time she runs the 20-minute practice activity while you observe. You give feedback on one thing: her instructions. She runs the whole session only after you have watched her do each part.

items: Quality drifts as more people deliver.
A script produces readers, not trainers.
Budget time to observe.

topics.title: Curate what exists before you create more

situation.text: You are asked for a new course on a subject where good material already exists, inside and outside the organisation.

items: Search what exists first.
Judge each source: accurate, current, right level.
Choose a few and put them in order.
Add what is missing: your context, a task, a check.
Credit sources and respect licences.
Set a review date.

why.text: Making new content is slow and costly. Selecting and arranging good existing material can meet the need faster, if someone exercises judgement over it.
A list of links is not curation. The value is in the selection, the order and the task that makes people use it.

UK copyright law has a narrow exception for copying to illustrate a point in teaching. Official guidance says the use must be non-commercial, fair and acknowledged. If your training is commercial, do not assume it covers you. Link to the material, or get permission or a licence. This is general information and not legal advice.

try.text: For one topic, pick three existing sources. Write one line on why each, and one task that uses them.

try.title: A list and a curated set
try.text: Illustration. A list: twelve links on giving feedback. Curated: three sources in order, one line on why each is there, and a task. "Read the second, then rewrite the feedback you gave last week." A review date sits at the top.

items: Links break. Check them.
Copyright applies to training materials.
Too many sources is the same as none.

topics.title: Build a culture where learning is expected
topics.theory: Learning culture and the learning organisation

situation.text: The organisation says it values learning. Nobody has time for it, and mistakes are hidden.

items: Look at what leaders do, not what the posters say.
Ask whether people have time, permission and a reason to learn.
Make one practice routine: a short review after each project.
Have leaders talk about what they are learning and what went wrong.
Notice and credit people who share what they know.

why.text: Culture is what people do repeatedly and what is rewarded. A trainer cannot install it. A trainer can help leaders change a few routines.

The "learning organisation" is an influential management idea. One well-known article breaks it into three parts: a supportive environment, concrete learning processes, and leaders who reinforce learning. The article comes with a survey for scoring each part. Treat a score as a prompt for discussion and the idea as a direction. It is a framework and not a tested method.
The review routine is the best-supported step here. Research on debriefs, also called after-action reviews, finds that teams and individuals who hold them perform better than those who do not.

why.title: Do debriefs improve performance?
why.found: A meta-analysis of 46 samples compared people and teams who held debriefs with control groups who did not. Debriefs improved performance by roughly a fifth to a quarter (d = 0.67). The effect was similar for teams and individuals and in real and simulated settings.
why.means: Start with a short, structured review after each project, with a clear focus and the right people in the room.

try.text: Ask three people in one team when they last learned something at work and what made it possible.

try.title: One routine
try.text: Illustration. After each project the team spends 20 minutes on three questions: what did we expect, what happened, what will we do differently. The director goes first and names one decision she got wrong. Notes go where the next project team will see them.

items: A learning platform is not a culture.
Reviews that hunt for blame teach people to hide.
Change takes years. Promise a start.

parts.title: Practice and consolidation
parts.summary: How to schedule practice so it lasts.

topics.title: Leave time for memory to settle

situation.text: The schedule is back-to-back from Monday to Friday, with revision the night before the test.

items: Leave gaps between practice sessions.
Protect sleep.
Come back to material by recalling it.
Avoid teaching similar things back to back.

why.text: Memories are stabilised over time, and sleep helps. How much it helps depends on what was learned and when the sleep comes. The gaps between practice give that time, which is one likely reason spreading practice works.

Recalling something makes it easier to recall later. One proposed reason is that a recalled memory is stored again. That idea, called reconsolidation, is less settled in people than it is often made to sound, so do not build a design on it. New learning can also disturb recent learning, and gaps may reduce that.
A large review of spaced practice found that the best gap grows with how long the memory has to last. For something people must keep for months, space the sessions by days or weeks and not by hours.

try.text: Take a crammed schedule. Redesign its rhythm so memory has time to settle.

try.title: A week with room in it
try.text: Illustration. Before: five full days, a new topic each hour, revision on Thursday night. After: new material in the mornings, practice in the afternoons, ten minutes of recall at the start of each day, and the two similar procedures on different days.

items: Keep claims about sleep stages modest.
Gaps without recall are just gaps.
Clients read white space as wasted time. Explain it.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

quiz.a: In the gaps between practice, and during sleep.

quiz.q: What does recalling a memory do?
quiz.a: Makes it easier to recall later. Why it does so is still debated.

quiz.q: What reduces interference between new and recent learning?
quiz.a: Gaps between sessions may help, and so does not teaching similar things back to back.

topics.title: Space and mix the practice, then stop drilling

situation.text: The group drills one procedure fifty times in a row and looks excellent by the end of the hour.

items: Mix related tasks.
Set recall at widening or regular intervals over days and weeks.
For facts and concepts, stop drilling once people can do it.
Use the time saved for a later session.
Drill to automatic only the basics that free up thinking.
For a rare, high-stakes procedure, such as an emergency response, keep practising past the first correct run and put refreshers in the calendar.

why.text: Blocked practice looks better during the session. Mixed practice often produces better learning later, though the benefit depends on the material. It is strongest when the things being learned are easy to confuse with each other. Practising past the point of first success helps a lot a week later, and the advantage shrinks over the following weeks.
The time is better spent on a later, spaced session than on more repetition now.

The advice to stop is for facts and concepts, which is what the study behind it tested. Procedures that are rarely used and costly to get wrong are a different case. A meta-analysis of overlearning (Driskell, Willis and Copper, 1992) found that practice past first mastery had a moderate overall effect on retention. The size depended on how much extra practice there was, the type of task and how long people had to retain it. Pair the extra practice with scheduled refreshers. See the topic "Plan refreshers before skills fade" and the aviation case study, where emergency drills are repeated on a fixed cycle.

why.title: What overlearning buys
why.found: In two experiments 218 students learned geography facts or word definitions, some to a low level and some well past the first perfect run. One week later the overlearners recalled far more. Tested up to nine weeks later, most of that advantage had gone.
why.means: For facts and definitions, stop once people have it right, and spend the saved time on a later session.

items.title: Mix
items.text: Looks worse now, often lasts longer.

try.text: Design a spaced, mixed practice plan for a real skill. Say when you stop drilling.

try.title: Fifty in a row, or fewer and mixed
try.text: Illustration. Before: one procedure drilled fifty times in an hour. After: three related procedures practised in mixed order until each person gets each right twice. Then stop. The same three come back for ten minutes two days later and again the next week.

items: Newcomers may need some blocked practice first.
Learners prefer blocked practice. Explain the choice.
Recall that always fails is dispiriting. Pitch it.
Mixing does not suit everything. In one meta-analysis it helped with pictures and maths problems and did worse than blocking for word lists.
The studies behind this are of facts, categories and maths problems. For a hands-on procedure, test the mixed version on a small group first.
Do not apply "stop drilling" to first aid, fire response or any emergency procedure. Stopping at the first success is the wrong advice there.

topics.title: Add a follow-up layer to any format

situation.text: You run a retreat, a webinar series and a self-paced course. None has anything after the end.

items: For each format, plan what follows: recall, a task to apply, a review.
Put dates on it.
Deliver it through the channel people already use.
Check whether it is being used.

why.text: Spacing and recall have helped across many ages, materials and settings, so they are a sound bet for any format. Few studies test them after a retreat or a webinar series. Without follow-up, expect much of the content to fade.
How the follow-up is delivered depends on the format: a cadence of calls after a retreat, spaced quizzes in a self-paced course.

why.title: Spaced questions by email
why.found: In a randomised trial 115 medical students were emailed short case questions with explanations on one of two topics, repeated over several months. They learned their emailed topic better than the other group did. About nine months later the gain had lasted for one topic and not the other. The authors could not separate spacing from simply seeing more content.
why.means: Send short spaced questions through a channel people already use, and check whether the gain lasts.

items.title: A layer
items.text: Follow-up is part of the product.

try.text: Take one format. Design its follow-up in full: what, when and how spaced.

try.title: A layer after a webinar series
try.text: Illustration. After the last webinar, three short messages go out in the team's usual chat at one, three and six weeks. Each asks one recall question and sets one small task. A 30-minute review call is in the diary at week eight.

items: Spaced-repetition tools suit facts better than judgement.
Too many messages get muted.
Sell it with the event, not after.

If you are a supplier with no access afterwards, you can still do three things. Agree in the contract who on the client side sends the follow-up, give them the messages already written and dated, and book one 30-minute review call before the event ends.

topics.title: Teach learners how to study

situation.text: Learners revise by re-reading and highlighting, and feel well prepared.

items: Teach self-testing, spacing, explaining in your own words, and teaching someone else.
Explain why effortful study works better than it feels.
Help people build a routine they will keep.
Have them plan, check and review their own study.

why.text: Re-reading and highlighting are what learners say they rely on, and a major review rates both as low value. It rates self-testing and spaced practice highest. Explaining in your own words comes in the middle, with less evidence behind it. Learners need to be told this, because easy study feels productive.
The most lasting thing a course can leave is a learner who knows how to make anything stick.

why.title: Which study techniques work
why.found: A review of ten study techniques rated practice testing and spaced practice as high utility, because they help across ages, materials and real classrooms. Self-explanation and mixed practice were rated moderate. Re-reading, highlighting and summarising were rated low.
why.means: Teach self-testing and spacing first, and tell learners plainly that re-reading and highlighting do little.

try.text: Write a personal plan for consolidating what you have learned. Choose techniques you will keep up.

try.title: Showing why feelings mislead
try.text: Illustration. Half the group re-reads a page twice. The other half reads it once, then writes down what they recall. Each person predicts their score. A short quiz two days later lets them compare the prediction with what happened.

items: People return to highlighting under pressure.
A plan too ambitious is dropped.
Model the techniques in your own sessions.
