parts.title: Fading and transfer
parts.summary: Why skills fade, why they do not travel far, and what to do about both.

topics.title: Plan refreshers before skills fade

situation.text: Store staff were trained in March on what to do when a customer collapses. Everyone passed. It is now November, nobody has needed it, and the manager assumes they still can.

items: List the skills from the course. Mark each one that is used rarely and is costly to get wrong.
For every skill, ask when it will next be used for real. If the answer is this month, the job is the practice and no refresher is needed.
For the marked skills, practise past the first correct run in the original session, then set a refresher date before people leave. Topic 5.14 covers the extra practice.
As a rule of thumb, refresh a rarely used procedure within about six months, and sooner when the stakes are high.
Run the refresher as doing, from memory, before any reminder.
Make the refresher look like the real moment: the real kit, the real place, the same people.
Score accuracy, not only speed. People stay quick longer than they stay correct.
Give the refresher an owner on the client side and put it in a shared calendar. Record what was missed and adjust the next gap.

why.text: Skills that are not used fade, and the loss is large. A meta-analysis of 53 articles found almost no loss straight after training and a loss of about 1.4 standard deviations after more than a year without practice or use.

Some things faded faster. Cognitive tasks decayed more than physical ones. Accuracy decayed more than speed. Loss was greater when people had to recall than when they only had to recognise, and it was much smaller when the retention test resembled the conditions of training, though that last comparison rested on very few results. Too few studies reported extra practice past first mastery for this analysis to judge it. A separate meta-analysis of overlearning found a moderate benefit for retention.

A 2025 meta-analysis of procedural skills, covering 457 reports, puts rough timings on this. Accuracy fell by about 0.08 standard deviations a month and speed by about 0.06. On average, half of what was gained in training had gone after about six and a half months for accuracy and about thirteen months for speed.

The size and pattern of decay are research. The six-month rule of thumb is this site's reading of that average. It is not a tested schedule, and decay varies with the task and with how well it was first learned.

why.title: Factors that influence skill decay and retention
why.found: A meta-analysis of 189 results from 53 articles. Skill loss grew with the length of non-use, from d of about -0.01 straight after training to about -1.4 after more than 365 days. Physical tasks decayed less than cognitive tasks and speed less than accuracy.
why.means: Find the skills that will sit unused, and schedule practice for them before the loss shows up in a real event.

try.text: Pick one procedure you were trained in more than six months ago and have not used since. Without looking anything up, perform it or talk it through aloud to a colleague while they check against the written steps. Count what you missed.

try.title: A worked example: refresher plan for a retailer's store staff

head: Skill
Next real use
If it goes wrong
Refresher
Owner
rows: None. Daily use is the practice.
Processing a refund without a receipt
Five-minute walk-through at a team huddle each quarter. Job aid at the till.
Full drill on the floor every six months, unannounced to staff, with a two-minute debrief.
15-minute hands-on practice at three months, then every six. Attempt first, then correct.
Closing the till with a discrepancy
Mixed case in the quarterly huddle. Recall the steps before opening the guide.

items: Refreshing by re-showing the slides. That tests recognition, which holds up longer than recall and flatters everyone. Have people do it first.
One interval for everything. Sort the skills before you schedule.
No owner. A refresher that depends on the external trainer remembering will not happen.
Where a regulator or a qualification sets a refresher interval, that interval comes first. Check the official requirement for the skill.

quiz.q: In the skill decay meta-analyses, which fades faster: speed or accuracy?
quiz.a: Accuracy.

quiz.q: A software company trains its on-call engineers once a year on a recovery procedure they use perhaps twice a year. The last incident went badly. What do you propose?
quiz.a: Add a short hands-on refresher at about the halfway point, done from memory on a test system before any reminder. A rare, costly procedure is exactly what fades, and attempting it shows what has gone.

quiz.q: A client asks for a six-monthly refresher on a task their staff do every day. What do you say?
quiz.a: Say it is not needed, because daily use keeps the skill up. Spend the time on the rare tasks from the same course.

topics.title: Know why far transfer is hard

situation.text: A sales team spends a happy afternoon on a negotiation game about trading spice routes. The debrief is lively. On Monday a customer asks for a discount and every one of them gives it away as before.

items: Write down the real moment you are training for in one sentence.

Compare your practice task with that moment on six points: the subject matter, the place, the time gap, the purpose, whether people are alone or with others, and the format (spoken, written, hands-on).
Count the points where practice and the real moment differ.
Close the gaps you can. Use their product, their price list, their customer's words. If the real thing is a phone call, practise by phone.
Plan for the gaps you cannot close. Time is the usual one: add a first-use plan (5.2) and a refresher.
If you keep a far-off exercise for energy or insight, follow it the same day with practice on the real task. Do not expect the exercise to carry over unaided.
Test with a case that differs from practice on the point that matters. If people only succeed on the case they rehearsed, you have near transfer and should say so.

why.text: Near transfer is using what you learned in a situation much like the one you practised in. Far transfer is using it somewhere that differs in important ways.

Barnett and Ceci reviewed a century of argument over whether far transfer happens. Their answer is that the argument stalled because researchers compared unlike things. "Far" can mean a different subject, a different place, a long delay, a different purpose, a different social setting or a different format, and studies rarely said which. They proposed a taxonomy of nine dimensions, three describing what is transferred and six describing the context. They argue that a single effect size for far transfer makes no sense.

Their reading of the evidence is balanced. Transfer under some conditions is well supported. For many of the conditions people care about most, the tests have not been done. For a designer, each dimension on which practice differs from the job is a risk to manage.

The taxonomy is a research framework for classifying studies. Using its six context dimensions as a design check is this site's application and has not been tested as a method. Topic 5.1 covers the workplace side of transfer.

why.title: A taxonomy for far transfer
why.found: A review arguing that a century of debate about far transfer made little progress because the dimensions of transfer were not specified. It offers a framework of nine dimensions for classifying studies, and concludes that evidence for transfer under some conditions is substantial while many key conditions remain untested.
why.means: Describe how far your practice is from the job, dimension by dimension, and close the gaps that matter.

try.text: Take one practice activity you run. Stand at a flipchart and talk a colleague through the six comparisons below, out loud, filling in the three columns as you go. Ask them to challenge any gap you wave away. Then redesign the activity to close two gaps.

try.title: A worked example: a discount role-play for a software company's sales team

head: Point of comparison
Practice in the room
The real moment
Gap and fix
rows: Their own product and price list
Far. Rewrite the case on a real renewal.
At their desk, on a call
Far. Run the practice as a phone call from separate rooms.
Next request may be weeks away
Cannot close. Each rep writes a when-and-then plan. Ten-minute practice at the next team meeting.
Keep the customer and the margin
Far. Score the practice on margin kept and next step agreed.
Far. Practise in pairs, one rep and one customer, with an observer.
Spoken, with the account record open
Far. Use the real account screen.

items: Selling general gains. "Builds critical thinking" or "improves resilience" from a single exercise is a far transfer claim on nearly every dimension. Promise the specific behaviour you practised.
Realism for its own sake. Match only the dimensions that change what people have to think and do.
Calling it transfer when the test repeats the practice case. Change one thing that matters.
Dropping every game. A far-off exercise can earn its place as a way in. It needs real-task practice straight after.

quiz.q: A client wants a raft-building afternoon at an offsite to improve how the team runs project handovers. What do you do?
quiz.a: Keep the raft only if real handover practice follows the same day, on their own projects and in their own format. The raft differs from a handover on almost every dimension, so little will carry over unaided.

quiz.q: After your course, reps handle the rehearsed objection well and fail on a new one. What does that tell you, and what next?
quiz.a: You have near transfer only. Add practice on varied objections and test with one they have not seen.

topics.title: Decide what you will measure before you design
topics.theory: Evaluation planning, baselines and success measures

situation.text: Evaluation is discussed for the first time after the course has run.

items: Before you design, agree what will change if the programme works.
Choose two or three measures of that.
Record where things stand now.
Decide who collects what, and when.
Write it into the proposal.

why.text: You cannot show a change without a starting point. Deciding measures first also sharpens the design, because it forces agreement on what the programme is for.
This is the same discipline as designing backwards from objectives, applied to the whole programme.

try.text: For one programme, write what will change, two measures and where each stands today.

try.title: Illustrative: a measure agreed up front
try.text: Before: "We will send a feedback form afterwards." After: "Managers should give feedback in every monthly one-to-one. We will count how many do so now, and count again eight weeks after the course."

items: Sponsors may not have data. Help them find a proxy.
Measures chosen late favour what is easy.
Agree who owns the data.

topics.title: Use Kirkpatrick as vocabulary, not proof

situation.text: The evaluation is a feedback form. Scores are high, so the course is declared a success.

items: Use the four levels as shared words: reaction, learning, behaviour, results.
Do not assume one level leads to the next.
Plan to reach behaviour and results.
Consider other approaches that ask different questions.

why.text: The four-level model is the dominant framework and a useful vocabulary. The levels are often wrongly treated as a causal chain. How much people liked a course relates only weakly to what they learned.
Evaluation often stops at reaction and learning, the levels furthest from what a sponsor is paying for. People can also mistake a session that felt easy for one they learned from.

Critics go further than the causal chain. Holton argued the four levels are a list of outcomes, not a model, because they leave out what sits between a course and a result, such as motivation and the workplace. Bates added that the levels tell you whether training worked but not how to make it work better. Kirkpatrick's reply was that the levels are meant to be practical.

The evidence on reaction forms is not all one way. One meta-analysis found that ratings of usefulness were a better guide to learning and to use at work than ratings of enjoyment. A later one found no difference between the two. Neither supports reading a happy room as a trained one.

Will Thalheimer's Learning-Transfer Evaluation Model, known as LTEM, offers a second vocabulary. It has eight tiers. His page on the model says the lower tiers are methods that are inadequate for validating learning success, and that the upper half can be used to validate efforts to create transfer. The current version is 13, released on 31 October 2024. The table under Try it gives the tiers as his 2018 report describes them.

why.title: How the levels of training evaluation relate to each other
why.found: This meta-analysis split reactions into enjoyment and usefulness, and split learning into immediate, retained and demonstrated skill. Ratings of usefulness were more strongly related to learning and to performance on the job than ratings of enjoyment were.
why.means: If you use a reaction form, ask whether the content is useful for the job, and still measure learning and behaviour separately.

items.title: Vocabulary, not proof
items.text: The levels are not a chain.

items.title: Liking is not learning
items.text: Reaction scores say little about learning.

try.text: Take a real feedback-form evaluation. Redesign the plan to reach behaviour and results.

try.title: Illustrative: two evaluation summaries
try.text: Before: "People loved the day, so it worked." After: "People rated the day highly. In a short scenario test most could handle the task. In six weeks we will ask managers what they see."

try.title: LTEM: the eight tiers, as described in Thalheimer's 2018 report

head: Tier
What is measured
What the report says about it
rows: Whether people sign up, start, attend or complete
Satisfaction questions are inadequate. Questions about learning effectiveness can hint at outcomes and should be paired with objective measures.
Recall of facts and terms, straight away or after several days
Whether people make the right decisions in realistic scenarios
Adequate when tested after several days or more. Testing straight away is not fully adequate.
Whether people decide and act correctly in realistic tasks
Adequate when tested after several days or more. Testing straight away is not fully adequate.
Whether people use what they learned at work, shown by objective measures

items: Return on investment figures need cautious assumptions.

quiz.q: What are the four levels?
quiz.a: Reaction, learning, behaviour and results.

quiz.q: Do high reaction scores show learning?
quiz.a: No. The link is weak.

quiz.q: Where does evaluation often stop?
quiz.a: At reaction and learning.

topics.tierReason: The warning not to read reaction scores as proof of learning is backed by meta-analyses in training and in university teaching, but the four levels themselves are a practitioner framework and the size of the link depends on what the form asks.
openPoints: Kirkpatrick and Kirkpatrick, third edition: the publisher's page shows a 2008 date for the listing. The third edition is generally cited as 2006, which the label uses. Check against the book's copyright page.

Phillips, Return on Investment in Training and Performance Improvement Programs: the publisher's page does not state the year. 2003 is the usual citation for the second edition. Check before publishing.
How often evaluation stops at each level: Alliger and Janak counted this in published studies, but the summary does not give the result. No current survey figure was found.
Thalheimer's LTEM is a natural "other approach" for step four but is cited on the survey and analytics pages, not here. Consider a cross-link.

Kirwan (2025), Measuring the effectiveness of L&D: time to move on from Kirkpatrick and Phillips, International Journal of Training and Development, looks relevant but the journal page would not open.
checkFindings: Alliger and Janak (1989): the summary confirms the paper questions three assumptions of the four levels, that they ascend, are causally linked and are positively correlated. This supports "do not assume one level leads to the next". The summary gives no figures, so none are used.

Alliger and colleagues (1997) added. Its summary says usefulness ratings relate more strongly to learning and transfer than enjoyment ratings. It gives no correlations in the summary, so no numbers are on the page.

Sitzmann and colleagues (2008) added, with a caution. Its summary does not state the size of the reaction to learning link. It says reactions mainly reflect course features and the trainer's style, predict changes in motivation and confidence, and that enjoyment and usefulness reactions did not differ in their relation to learning. This disagrees with Alliger and colleagues on usefulness, so the page now reports both.

Uttl and colleagues (2017) added for university teaching: no significant link between student ratings and learning in multi-section studies, and earlier positive results put down to small studies and publication bias. This is about students rating lecturers, not workplace training, and is used only as supporting evidence.
Holton (1996) and Bates (2004) added and summarised in a new paragraph, since the draft named critics only through Alliger and Janak.
Softened "Most evaluation stops at reaction and learning, the levels a sponsor cares about least" and the matching quiz question. Softened "People can even rate easy, fluent sessions highest".
Kirkpatrick book: the publisher's page confirms the four levels are reaction, learning, behaviour and results.

topics.title: Ask better questions on the feedback form

situation.text: The form asks "How would you rate the trainer?" and "Was the venue comfortable?"

items: Ask what people can now do, in specific terms.
Ask what they will use, and when.
Ask what would stop them.
Use answer choices that describe a level, not a number from one to five.
Keep it short, and leave one open question.

why.text: Satisfaction scores relate weakly to learning. They tell you more about the course and the trainer's style, and about people's confidence. A form can still be useful if it asks about understanding, intention to use and support at work.

Will Thalheimer argues for surveys that ask about learning effectiveness, such as understanding, realistic practice and motivation to apply, in place of satisfaction ratings. He proposes answer choices that describe a level in words. This is a practitioner's method. Even a well-written form is a hint, to be backed by a measure of what people can do.

The rewritten question in the example below is a confidence item. It records what people believe they can do. A 2010 meta-analysis by Sitzmann and colleagues, covering education and workplace training, found that self-assessed knowledge related most strongly to motivation and satisfaction and only moderately to tested learning. Nearly a third of the evaluation studies it reviewed had treated self-assessment as evidence of learning. Pair each confidence item with one performance item, a short scenario with a right answer.

Be frank with yourself about one more thing. Many training companies and clients decide whether to rebook a trainer from these forms. If you swap recaps for recall and make practice harder, as 1.3 advises, the day may feel harder and score lower. There are ways to handle that. Tell the group why the harder practice is there. Ask your usefulness questions as well as the client's standard ones. Agree with your manager or client beforehand what the scores will and will not be used for. Hand the form out before the final close, while people are still seated, and not as they leave.

why.title: What trainee reactions do and do not reflect
why.found: This meta-analysis found that reactions mainly reflect features of the course. The strongest predictors of reactions were the trainer's instructional style (rho = .66) and human interaction (rho = .56). Reactions predicted changes in motivation and confidence from before to after training.
why.means: Read reaction scores as feedback on delivery and on confidence, not as a measure of learning.

items.title: Barriers
items.text: What will get in the way?

try.text: Rewrite a feedback form to five questions. None may ask whether people enjoyed it.

try.title: Illustrative: one question rewritten
try.text: Before: "How would you rate the trainer? 1 to 5." After: "How able are you to give feedback using the model? I could not do it yet. I could do it with my notes. I could do it unaided. I could show a colleague how."

try.title: A worked example: a confidence item paired with a performance item
lines: Confidence item: How able are you to give corrective feedback using the model? I could not do it yet. I could do it with my notes. I could do it unaided. I could show a colleague how.
Performance item: A team member has missed two deadlines this month. Write the first two sentences you would say to them.
Marking the performance item: one mark if it names the behaviour, one if it states the effect. Mark it yourself after the session.
Report the two side by side. Where confidence is high and marks are low, that is the gap to close.

items: People answer politely. Make it anonymous.
A form cannot show behaviour change.
Read the open answers.
Confidence is not competence. A question that begins "How able are you to" is a confidence item. Label it as one and pair it with a performance item, a short scenario answered on the same form.

items: Decide which behaviour should change and how you would see it.
Use observation, manager reports and performance data.
Link the behaviour to the outcome named in the needs analysis.
Claim contribution, not sole cause.
Look for early signs before the result shows.

why.text: Training rarely acts alone. Other things change at the same time. An honest, modest claim is believed. A large one is not.
A comparison group strengthens the case where one is possible.

items: Self-report flatters. Where you can, use a source other than the learner.
Agree the measures before the course.

topics.title: Go back later to see what stuck

situation.text: You measured on the last afternoon. Everyone could do it.

items: Set a date to check again, some weeks later. Four to twelve weeks is a common rule of thumb, not a research finding.
Ask people to do the task, or recall it, without warning them to revise.
Ask managers what they have seen.
Compare with the end-of-course result.
Use the gap to improve the follow-up.

why.text: Performance at the end of a session is a poor guide to what lasts. A delayed check shows what people kept and what they use.
A drop is normal and useful. It tells you where follow-up is needed.

The gap can run either way. Some methods that make the last afternoon look good produce little lasting learning, and some that make it look worse produce more. Only a later check tells you which you had.

why.title: Learning versus performance
why.found: This review of motor and verbal learning research concludes that performance during training is often an unreliable guide to lasting learning. Learning can happen with no visible gain at the time, and gains at the time can fade. People tend to mistake how well practice went for how much they learned.
why.means: Do not treat an end-of-course result as the measure of the course. Check again after a delay.

try.text: For one course, design a ten-minute check to run six weeks later.

try.title: Illustrative: a six-week check
try.text: On the day, everyone completes the incident form correctly with the guide open. Six weeks later, each person completes one from a short scenario with no guide. The steps most often missed become the subject of a reminder and a job aid.

items: Response rates fall with time. Keep it short.
A check that feels like a test raises anxiety. Explain why.
Agree it with the sponsor in advance.

topics.title: Separate the effect of training from everything else

situation.text: Sales rose after the sales course. They also rose in the region that did not attend.

items: Where you can, compare a group that attended with one that has not yet.
Stagger the roll-out to create that comparison.
Measure before and after in both.
List what else changed at the same time.
Keep participants' and managers' own estimates of the share due to training as a last resort. If you use them, label them as opinion and discount them.
State your confidence plainly.
When you stagger the roll-out, measure the waiting groups on the same dates as the trained ones. The later groups then act as the comparison for the earlier ones.

Where no comparison group is possible, plot the measure month by month for several months before the course and several after. A change in the trend at the point of training is stronger evidence than a single before and after pair.

why.text: Without a comparison, any change after training may have happened anyway. A staggered roll-out is often the most practical way to get a comparison group.
Estimates from participants are weak evidence. Use them as a last resort and say what they are.

items.title: Compared with what?
items.text: The question for your own work too.

items.title: Stagger
items.text: A waiting group is a comparison.

try.text: For one programme, describe the comparison you could set up at no extra cost.

try.title: Illustrative: a comparison at no extra cost
try.text: Four depots need the same course. Two attend in March and two in May. Error rates are recorded at all four in February and April. In April the May depots are the comparison.

items: Groups differ before training. Check the starting point.
Small groups give noisy results.
Do not withhold training people need for safety.
People who volunteer first often differ from those who wait. Let the timetable decide who goes first, not enthusiasm.
Estimates of the share due to training are opinion, and finance colleagues rarely accept them. Never lead a report with one.

why.text: Return on investment compares the money value of results with the cost. It persuades where the link from training to result is clear, and misleads where it is not.

parts.title: Go further with evaluation
parts.summary: How much to evaluate, getting the data, business measures and the money.

topics.title: Match the evaluation to the stakes

situation.text: A client runs forty programmes a year and asks you to "evaluate properly" a single half-day workshop. The evaluation you first sketch would cost more than the workshop.

items: Ask three things before you propose anything: what the programme costs in fees and people's time, how many people it reaches, and what decision the evaluation will inform.

Sort it into one of three levels of effort. Light for a one-off session. Standard for a programme reaching a few hundred people. Full for a company-wide programme, or one a senior sponsor is watching.
For light, use a short form with a usefulness question and one scenario item (6.3). Four weeks later, send the sponsor one message asking what they have seen. Budget about an hour of your time.
For standard, add a baseline (6.1), a delayed check with a sample of people (6.5), a manager observation and one business measure tracked as a trend.
For full, add a comparison built into the roll-out (6.6), data from the client's own analyst, success cases, and a cost and benefit case agreed with finance.
Write the level and its price into the proposal as a separate line. The client can then see what it buys and choose a lower level knowingly.
When the client asks for operating measures, report them under their own heading: cost per learner, fill rate and no-shows. Say that they describe efficiency and do not show learning.
Move a programme up a level if it will be repeated many times, or if a decision to scale depends on it.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. No study read for this site tests how much evaluation a programme should get. The reasoning is about cost. Evaluation uses the client's money and people's time, so it should be in proportion to what is lost if the programme does not work.

The Phillips handbooks take the same line for their most demanding level. In the chapter opened for this topic, a return on investment study is reserved for programmes that are expensive, reach many people, drive business impact, have the attention of senior managers or are highly visible. The same chapter says that when you do go that far, you still report results at the lower levels.

A learning team inside a large company runs hundreds of programmes and cannot fund deep work on each. A supplier who proposes the right depth, and says why, is easier to buy from than one who proposes the full treatment every time. Light does not mean nothing. Even a one-off workshop can end with one question that shows what people can do.
Time to competence is sometimes listed with the operating measures. It is closer to a result than the others. If the client reports it, ask how they define competent.

try.text: Take three pieces of work you know: a single workshop, a mid-sized programme and a large one. Give each a level and write one sentence defending it. Then say that sentence aloud, as you would to a sponsor who has asked for more.

try.title: A worked example: three levels of evaluation effort

head: Level
Example
What you measure
Who does the work
Your time
rows: Half-day feedback workshop for 14 new managers at a software company
Usefulness question and one scenario item on the form. One message to the sponsor at four weeks.
Product launch training for 300 store staff at a retailer, run over six weeks
Baseline and scenario check. Delayed check with a sample of 30. Store manager observation. One sales measure as a monthly trend.
You, with store managers and one client analyst
New sales method for 2,000 people in eight markets
Everything in standard. Staggered roll-out as a comparison. Success cases. Cost and benefit case built with finance.
You, a named client analyst, finance and the internal learning team
Scoped and priced as its own piece of work

items: Clients ask for the full treatment and budget for light. Show the three levels with a price beside each and let them choose.
A light evaluation repeated across fifty workshops adds up. Pool the forms once a quarter and report on the set.
Operating measures look precise and get mistaken for results. Keep them under their own heading.
A small programme can carry high risk, such as a safety task or a regulated one. Let the risk set the level, whatever the headcount.

topics.title: Get the data you need from the client

situation.text: Your plan says "compare complaint rates before and after". The course has run. The client's analyst has never heard of you, and the sponsor says the figures are "with HR".

items: At proposal stage, ask the sponsor about each measure in the plan: who owns this figure, and who can pull it.
Ask to be introduced to that person. It is usually an analyst in sales operations, customer operations or HR. Explain the purpose in two lines and ask what is easy for them to produce.
Request the least you need. Team or store totals by month are usually enough. Ask for no names, no staff numbers and no free text.
Offer the client the option of running the comparison in its own systems and sending you a summary table. You then never hold individual records.
Ask what minimum group size the client applies before it shares a figure, and combine small teams to meet it.
Write it into the statement of work: the measures, the format, who supplies them, the dates for the baseline and the follow-up, and who may see the result.
Allow weeks. The request may need a data protection review, and the analyst has other work. Ask for the baseline before the first session.
If the answer is no, switch to measures you can collect yourself: an observation checklist, a scenario check, a short manager survey. Say in the report that business data was not available.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement about how client organisations work. A supplier has no access to a client's sales, quality or HR systems, and many evaluation plans fail here. The plan is sound and the data never arrives. Agreeing it before the work starts turns a favour into a commitment with a name and a date.

Asking for totals makes the request easier to grant. The ICO's guidance on anonymisation says information is anonymous when the risk of identifying a person is sufficiently remote, and that removing obvious identifiers is not enough if someone can still be singled out or records can be linked. It mentions an NHS standard of five as one example of a minimum group size. Small teams are where this bites. A store with three staff and one complaint points at a person.
Topic 9.24 covers what you may collect and keep about learners. The same care applies to anything the client sends you. This is general information, not legal advice.
When the client keeps the analysis in house, you give up some control over the method. Agree the comparison in writing first, so that the table you receive answers the question you asked.

try.text: Pick one programme and one business measure. Draft the request using the example below. Then make the ask aloud, as a two-minute request to a sponsor in a kick-off meeting, and time yourself.

try.title: A worked example: a data request to a client analyst
lines: Subject: Figures for the store launch training evaluation
Hello Sam. Priya suggested I contact you. I am evaluating the September launch training for store staff.
What I need: attach rate for the new accessory range, by store, by month.
Period: June to November, which is three months before the training and three after.
Level: store totals only. No names, staff numbers or till IDs.
Small stores: please combine any store with fewer than five staff into its area total.
Format: one spreadsheet, one row per store per month.
If it is easier, run the before and after comparison yourself and send me the summary table.
Dates: June to August figures by 5 September. September to November figures by 12 December.
Use: one summary chart in the report to the sponsor. I will delete the file when the report is signed off.
Who sees it: the sponsor, the learning team and me.
Is any of this hard to pull? If there is a simpler figure you already report, I would sooner use that.

You are sent individual records you did not ask for. Do not work from them. Tell the client, delete the file and ask again for totals.
The figures arrive in a different layout each month. Send a blank table with the columns you need.
The client cannot share anything in writing. Ask a client manager to talk you through the trend on a call and confirm the direction by email.
The measure is defined differently in each market. Ask for the definition with the first file.

topics.title: Use the Success Case Method

situation.text: A customer service programme has run for 120 advisers. There is no comparison group. The sponsor wants to know whether it worked and what to change.

items: Plan the study with the sponsor: the decision it will inform, who will be surveyed, and when. Six to eight weeks after the programme is a workable point, as a rule of thumb.
Write an impact model on one page. It says what success would look like: the behaviour people would use at work and the result it should lead to.
Send a short survey to everyone who took part. Its only job is to find the people who used the training with most success and those who used it least. Three or four questions are enough.
Pick a handful from each end. As a working number, interview five or six of the most successful and three or four of the least.
Interview each person for 20 to 30 minutes. Ask what they did, what happened as a result, what helped and what got in the way.
Confirm each success story with someone who would know, such as the person's manager, or against a record. Report only what you can confirm.
Report what the best cases achieved, what was different for those who got nothing from it, and what to change. Include how many survey replies fell at each end.

why.text: Robert Brinkerhoff set out the method in a 2003 book. The publisher describes it as quicker and cheaper than other approaches, built on accounts of how people used an initiative, and able to find success even when it is rare. An evaluation guidance page lists five steps: plan the study, create an impact model, survey to find the best and worst cases, interview and document the cases, then communicate findings and recommendations.

The logic is to study the two ends and leave the average alone. If a few people got a real result, their stories show what the programme can do and what made that possible. The people who got nothing show what blocked it. In practice the block is often a manager or a system, which is a judgement from experience and not a finding.

The method has limits. A success case is the best that happened. It does not tell you the typical result and it cannot stand in for a comparison (6.6). It rests on people's own accounts, which is why the confirming step matters. One review of the book reports Brinkerhoff's test that a story should be able to stand up in court. The guidance page adds practical conditions. You need to reach participants and someone who can confirm what they say, and the work has to be planned and budgeted from the start.
This is a practitioner method. No test of the method itself was read for this site.

try.text: Write the impact model for one programme you know. Then run a practice interview aloud with a colleague playing a participant, using the questions below, and record it. Listen back for the moments where you suggested the answer.

try.title: A worked example: outline of a two-page success case study for a customer service programme

head: Section
What goes in it
rows: Decide whether to run the call-handling programme for the next two intakes, and what to change first.
All 120 advisers who completed it, surveyed seven weeks after their last session.
Advisers confirm the customer's problem in their own words before offering a fix. Expected result: fewer repeat contacts about the same problem.
Four questions. Have you used the confirm step on live calls. How often. What happened as a result. May we talk to you.
Six advisers who report frequent use and a clear result. Four who report no use.
25 minutes each by video call. What did you do, what happened, what helped, what got in the way.
The team leader confirms each success story. Where possible, check the adviser's repeat contact figures for the same weeks.
What the best cases achieved, in two short confirmed stories. How many survey replies fell at each end.
What blocked the others. Three changes for the next intake. What the study cannot show: the average effect.
Survey in week seven. Interviews in weeks eight and nine. Report in week ten.

try.title: Words you can use: interview questions
lines: Tell me about one call where you used the confirm step. Talk me through it.
What did you do that you would not have done before?
What happened next, for the customer and for you?
How do you know that? Is there anything I could look at?
What made it possible? Who or what helped?
For someone who has not used it: what got in the way?
If we ran this again, what one thing should we change?

items: Only the keen reply to the survey. Send it through team leaders and keep it to two minutes.
The success stories get presented as the typical result. Put the number of replies at each end on the first page.
A story cannot be confirmed. Leave it out, however good it sounds.
The interviews with people who did not use it turn into blame. Ask what got in the way, and report barriers by type with no names.
You quote someone without asking. Get consent first (6.10).

topics.theory: Enablement measures for sales, product and retail training

situation.text: A technology client is launching a product in six markets. The contract says the training will be judged on "readiness". Nobody has said which figure that is.

items: Ask the client which business figure the training is meant to move, and write down its exact definition. Ramp time and win rate are defined differently from one company to the next.
Pick one result measure. Add one or two leading indicators you can observe yourself, such as a demo certification or a scored call.
Find where each figure lives and who owns it. Use the table below as a starting list, then make the request as the topic on getting data from the client sets out.
Record the baseline for the previous cohort or the previous quarter before the first session.
List what else will move the figure in the same period: price changes, promotions, the season, territory changes, the mix of new hires, stock.
Report by cohort or by market, as a trend. Add a comparison where the roll-out allows one (6.6).
State what you claim. Certification and observation scores show what people can do. Business figures show what happened, with training as one contributor (6.4).

why.text: This topic is practitioner judgement. No research on these measures was read for it. They are figures that sales, product and retail clients already use to run the business, which is why a sponsor accepts them more readily than a learning score.

Attribution is hard, and the reasons are worth saying to the client early. The figures respond to many things at once, and a launch usually arrives with a price, a campaign and new stock. They also lag. A win rate for a long sales cycle may not move for two quarters. Small groups swing widely too, so one large deal can change a whole market's figure.

That is the case for pairing a slow business measure with a fast one you control. A certification pass or a mystery shopping score will not prove revenue. It shows whether people can do what the training taught, soon enough to act on it.
Completion by market still has a place, because many clients contract on it. Report it as activity (6.7) and set it beside a measure of what people can do.

topics.title: Build the cost and benefit case
topics.theory: Cost and benefit analysis and the Phillips ROI formula

situation.text: The finance director has seen the proposal and asks for "the numbers". You have a fee and a hope.

items: List every cost line: needs analysis, design, delivery fees, venue and travel, platform and administration, evaluation. Then add learner time, which is days away from work multiplied by a daily cost.
Ask the client's finance team for the daily cost of a person's time and use their figure. Do the same for any unit value in the benefit. Finance should own the unit costs.

Choose one benefit you can defend, tied to the measure agreed at the start (6.1). Write the chain in one sentence: the training changes this behaviour, which changes this figure, which is worth this much.
Estimate the benefit three times: low, mid and high. Count the first year only. Reduce each estimate for the share that other causes could explain (6.6).
Work out the break-even point first. It is the size of improvement at which the benefit equals the cost. Ask the sponsor whether that improvement is plausible.

Then calculate the two Phillips figures. The benefit-cost ratio is programme benefits divided by programme costs. Return on investment, as a percentage, is net programme benefits divided by programme costs, multiplied by 100. Net benefits are benefits minus costs.
Show the assumptions on the same page as the result, and list the benefits you did not price.

why.text: The formulas come from Jack and Patricia Phillips. In the chapter opened for this topic they define the benefit-cost ratio on gross benefits and return on investment on net benefits. They add a payback period, which is costs divided by benefits. Their guiding principles ask for the most conservative option where there is a choice, fully loaded costs, first-year benefits only for short-term programmes, and at least one method of isolating the programme's effect from other influences.

That chapter names needs assessment, design, delivery and evaluation as costs. Learner time is added here as this site's judgement, in line with 6.8. It is often the largest line, and a finance reader will look for it.

A benefit estimate is only as honest as its weakest link. The value of a unit comes from finance. The size of the change comes from your evaluation and is uncertain. Three cases put that uncertainty on the page. Break-even reasoning often persuades more than a return figure, because it asks something the sponsor can judge from experience.
As 6.8 says, this is a practitioner framework with little independent testing.

items: Use AI for first drafts, question items, summaries and storyboards.
Brief it with the objective, the audience and the constraints.

Keep a named, qualified person accountable.
Do the diagnosis and design decisions yourself.

why.text: AI speeds work you already know how to do well. It does not replace diagnosis, alignment and judgement about evidence.
It drafts. A professional decides.

A 2026 OECD review of the research points the same way for classrooms. Tools built or used with a clear teaching purpose tend to help. Getting a task done with a general chatbot does not by itself lead to learning.

topics.title: Expect moderate gains from adaptive tools
topics.theory: Adaptive tutoring and the honest evidence

situation.text: A vendor claims its adaptive platform "doubles learning".

items: Ask for the size of the effect and what it was compared with.
Expect moderate gains from well-designed systems.
Treat very large figures as outliers.
Ask what in the design produces the gain.

why.text: Reviews of intelligent tutoring systems find real, moderate gains. One review of 50 controlled evaluations found a median gain of 0.66 standard deviations over conventional teaching, and the size depended heavily on the test used. Another found a gain of 0.42 over teacher-led classes and no significant difference from one-to-one human tutoring. The famous "two sigma" figure for human tutoring has not held up. A 2011 review put human tutoring at about 0.79 against no tutoring, with step-based tutoring systems close behind at 0.76.
The gain comes from the design, not from the label.

Generative AI tutors are newer and the evidence is thinner. In one field experiment with nearly a thousand secondary school maths pupils, a plain chatbot raised practice grades, but those pupils then scored lower on a test without it than pupils who never had it. A version with teaching guardrails largely avoided the harm. In one university physics course, a carefully designed AI tutor beat an active-learning class on a short test. A 2026 OECD review draws the same line between general chatbots and tools built for teaching.

why.title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning
why.found: In a field experiment with nearly a thousand secondary school maths pupils, a standard chatbot improved practice grades by 48% and a tutor version with guardrails by 127%. Once access was removed, pupils who had used the standard chatbot scored 17% lower than pupils who never had access. The guardrails largely prevented that drop.
why.means: Judge an AI learning tool by what people can do without it, and ask what in its design stops it handing over answers.

try.text: Take three vendor claims for AI or virtual reality learning. Restate each with its real effect and conditions.

try.title: Illustration: restating a claim
try.text: Vendor line: "Our adaptive platform doubles learning." Restated after questions: "In one study, people using the platform scored moderately higher on the vendor's own test than a group who read a manual. No comparison with a good trainer. No follow-up test."

items: Marketing quotes the best study.
Gains in schools may not carry to your workplace.
Adaptive pacing helps some content more than others.
Better scores while people use a tool are not proof of learning. Test them without the tool.
No adult workplace study was read for this topic. The evidence comes from schools and universities, so treat the size of any gain as untested for staff at work.

topics.title: Set the guardrails before you scale

situation.text: The team is already using AI tools. Nobody has written down what is allowed.

items: List the risks: wrong facts, bias, privacy, loss of trust.
Require human review of anything that reaches a learner.
Disclose where AI is used.
Set rules for learner data.
Say what AI may not decide.
Name who is accountable.

why.text: The failures harm learners and your credibility directly. Rules written in advance make responsible use repeatable.
Bias in the data a tool learned from shows up in what it produces.

In the UK, data protection law applies whenever an AI tool handles personal data about learners. The ICO's guidance on AI covers accountability, transparency, lawfulness, accuracy, fairness and bias, security and data minimisation. It is under review after the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, so read the current version. Significant decisions about a person made with no meaningful human involvement have their own rules and safeguards.

If you work with clients in the EU, the EU AI Act applies to organisations that provide or deploy AI systems. The European Commission's pages, read on 17 November 2026, say the following. Article 4 on AI literacy has applied since 2 February 2025, and national authorities have supervised it since 2 August 2026. An amending law, the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744), entered into force on 27 July 2026. Since then, providers and deployers must take measures to support AI literacy among their staff and others who use AI systems on their behalf. No set level is required and no certificate is needed, and internal records of training are enough. The Commission lists AI used in education, such as scoring exams, and AI used to manage workers, such as software that sorts CVs, among high-risk uses. The rules for those uses now apply from 2 December 2027, a date moved back by the same amendment. If a tool you build or recommend scores learners or informs decisions about staff, raise it with the client's legal team early. This is general information, not legal advice.

The law is changing. Check current rules.
Monitoring learners has a trust cost.

topics.title: Train people to check the AI's work
topics.theory: Training people for an AI world

situation.text: Staff paste AI answers into reports without reading them.

items: Teach what AI can and cannot do.
Practise spotting answers that sound right and are wrong.
Keep the person accountable for the result.
Build the skills that gain value: judgement, evaluation, working with others.

why.text: As AI takes over some tasks, employers still ask for human skills such as communication, collaboration and leadership alongside AI skills. Judgement and critical evaluation matter more when a tool can produce plausible work on demand.
Checking AI output uses the same test as any claim: what is the evidence, and compared with what?

Demand for AI skills shows up in job adverts. PwC's 2025 analysis of close to a billion adverts found that jobs asking for AI skills paid 56% more on average than similar jobs that did not, up from 25% a year earlier. It also reports the skills employers ask for changing 66% faster in the occupations most exposed to AI. An industry consortium found AI skills in 78% of the 50 technology roles it studied across the G7. In a survey commissioned by the UK government and published in January 2026, 97% of respondents named at least one AI skills gap.

Treat these as signals, not forecasts. They come from job adverts and employer surveys, they show links and not causes, and two of the three come from firms that sell AI services or training. In one school experiment, pupils who leaned on a plain chatbot did worse once it was taken away, which is the habit this training is meant to prevent.

try.text: For a real role, list which skills AI may automate and which gain value. Sketch training for the second list.

try.text: Give pairs of people three AI-written summaries of a policy they know well. One contains a confident error. Each pair marks what they would check before sending it on, and how. Then reveal the error and compare the checks people chose.

items: Predictions about jobs are uncertain. Say so.
Tools change faster than courses.
Fear gets in the way. Make it safe to ask basic questions.

situation.text: A client says half its roles will change in three years and asks for a reskilling plan.

items: List the skills the work will need, not the job titles.
Find out what skills people have now.
Find the adjacent moves: who is closest to what is needed.
Build routes with practice on real work.
Give time, and a job at the end.
Review yearly.

why.text: Planning around skills lets an organisation move people between roles as work changes. It depends on knowing what skills people have, which most organisations do not.
Forecasts of which jobs will change are uncertain. Plan for adaptability over a single prediction.

There are signs that skills needs are moving quickly. PwC's 2025 analysis of job adverts reports the skills employers ask for changing 66% faster in the occupations most exposed to AI. A 2026 UK survey for the government found that 88% of organisations rely on on-the-job training for AI skills in place of structured programmes.

quiz.a: A move to a role close to what someone can already do.

quiz.q: What must be at the end of a reskilling route?

parts.title: Use AI in your own practice
parts.summary: Briefing a tool, checking what it gives you, sorting feedback, AI in the room, and an honest account of how you used it.

topics.title: Brief an AI tool well

situation.text: You type "write a one-day course on feedback for managers" and get a tidy, generic agenda that could be for anyone.

items: State the task and your role in one sentence, and say that you will check and rewrite the output.
Give the context: who the learners are, how many, where, for how long, and what they do now.
Paste the source material, such as your needs analysis notes. Tell the tool to use only that for facts about the client. Remove names and anything confidential first (7.1).
State the objective as something people will do. Add the constraints: timings, share of practice, room and kit.
Show the format you want with one example row or paragraph.
Ask it to list what it was unsure about, and to criticise its own draft as a sceptical trainer would.
Read the draft against your notes. Send one correction at a time, saying what was wrong and why.
Keep the brief. Next time, change the context and reuse the rest.

why.text: A general tool knows nothing about your client. Whatever you leave out, it fills with the most common answer, which is why a thin request returns a generic agenda.

One vendor's guidance for its own model, opened for this topic, makes the same points. Be explicit about the output and the constraints. Give the reason behind an instruction. Say what to do in place of what to avoid. Include examples, separate source material from instructions, and ask the model to check its work against your criteria. It offers a test worth borrowing: if a colleague with little context would be confused by your brief, the tool probably will be too.
That guidance is product help from one company. Other tools differ in detail and all of them change. Treat the method as craft that carries across tools, and the specifics as temporary.
Asking for a critique does not make the output right. It gives you a list of places to look first. The design decisions stay with you, as 7.1 sets out.

try.text: Take a real needs analysis with names removed. Write a brief using the example below as a pattern, and run it in a tool your organisation allows. Mark every line of the output that you cannot trace to your notes.

try.title: A worked example: a brief for a session outline
lines: I am a trainer. Help me draft a session outline. I will check and rewrite what you produce.
Context: 12 team leaders in a software company's customer support team, all promoted in the last year. In person, one day, 09:30 to 16:30, one trainer.
The need, from interviews with their manager and four team leaders: they avoid corrective feedback, and when they give it, it is vague.
The manager wants every team leader to give specific feedback in each fortnightly one-to-one.
My notes are pasted below under the heading NEEDS ANALYSIS. Use only those for facts about the team. If something is missing, ask me. Do not fill the gap.
Objective: by the end, each person can give two minutes of corrective feedback on a real case from their own team, naming the behaviour, its effect and the change they want.
Constraints: at least half the day is practice in threes. No input block longer than 15 minutes. Lunch 12:30 to 13:15. Two breaks.
Format: a table with clock time, what happens, who is talking, and the reason for the block. Plain UK English.
One row in the style I want: 10:15. Threes practise case one, observer uses the checklist. Participants talking. Reason: a first attempt before any model answer.
Before you finish, list three weaknesses in the outline as a sceptical trainer would see them, and anything you were unsure about.

try.title: Illustration: common faults in a first draft, and the correction to send

head: What came back
Why it is wrong
The correction to send
rows: A 45-minute opening block on feedback theory
Breaks the 15-minute limit and delays practice
Cut the opening input to 10 minutes. Start the first practice round by 10:15.
A statement about the team that is not in the notes
Remove every statement about the team that is not in the needs analysis. List what you removed.
The objective asks for real cases from their own teams
Replace the case studies with a step where each person writes up one real case, with names removed.
Timings that run past the end of the day
Recalculate the clock times so the day ends at 16:30 with lunch and both breaks included.

items: The output reads well, so you stop checking. Fluent is how these tools write. Check it against your notes line by line.
You paste a client document with names in it. Strip personal and confidential details first, and use only an approved tool.
You rewrite the whole brief after each poor answer. Change one thing at a time so you learn what made the difference.
The tool agrees with every correction. Agreement is not evidence. Check the new draft as carefully as the first.

topics.title: Check AI output before it reaches a learner

situation.text: An AI tool has drafted a handout with six statistics and four references. It looks finished. The session is tomorrow.

items: Facts first. Underline every factual claim and check each against a source you open yourself. Delete what you cannot confirm.
Sources next. Search for every reference by title. Confirm that it exists, that the authors and year are right, and that it says what the draft claims.
Numbers. Trace each figure to its original page, with its unit, its date and what it was compared with. Redo any arithmetic.
Bias. Read the examples and the names. Look at who is shown as the manager, the customer, the expert and the problem. Rewrite anything that leans one way.
Tone. Read a paragraph aloud. Cut anything you would not say to this group, and anything that claims too much.
Fit. Hold each item against the objective and remove what does not serve it.
Sign off. The named person from 7.1 records what was checked and the date. For technical or legal content, a subject expert signs as well.

why.text: Language tools produce text that sounds right, including references that do not exist. In a 2023 test, 55% of the citations written by one model and 18% of those written by its successor were fabricated, and many of the real ones contained errors. A 2025 experiment with a newer model found that about one in five citations could not be traced to a real source. Fabrication was more common on less familiar topics.

These are tests of particular models on particular dates, in academic writing. Tools that search the web may do better or fail in other ways, and no study of that was read here. What carries over is the pattern. Errors gather where the subject is specialist and public material is thin, which describes most client-specific training content.

The UK government's AI Playbook, written for civil servants, gives the same instruction in general terms. These systems are not guaranteed to be accurate, outputs need a process for testing, and people should validate high-risk decisions that AI has influenced.
The order of the routine is craft. Facts and sources come first because an invented reference in a handout does most damage to your standing with a client.

why.title: Fabricated citations from a current model
why.found: The researchers asked a widely used model for six literature reviews on mental health topics and checked all 176 citations. Thirty-five (19.9%) could not be traced to a real source. Of the 141 real ones, 64 (45.4%) had at least one error, most often in the DOI. Fabrication ran at 6% for the most familiar topic and 28% to 29% for the two less familiar ones.
why.means: Look up every reference an AI tool gives you, and expect more errors the more specialist the topic.

try.text: Ask a tool for a one-page handout with five references, on a subject you know well. Run the routine and time it. Then tell a colleague aloud what you found, in one minute, without softening it.

try.title: A worked example: a check sheet for one AI-drafted handout

head: Check
How
Passes when
rows: Each claim matched to a source you opened
Every claim has a source or has been deleted
It exists, the details are right and it supports the claim
Each figure traced to its original page
Unit, date and comparison are stated
Examples and names read for who plays which role
No group is always the problem or always the boss
You would say it to this group
Each item held against the objective
Nothing is there only because the tool wrote it
Name, date and what was checked
A second name is added for technical or legal content

items: A reference has a working link, so you assume it is sound. Open it and read the summary. Real papers get cited for things they do not say.
You check the facts you doubt and skip the ones you like. Check all of them.
You ask the same tool to verify its own output. Use it to find sources, then read them yourself.
The deadline is tomorrow. Cut the parts you could not verify. A shorter handout is safer than a wrong one.

quiz.a: About one in five.

quiz.a: Read the paper's summary and check that it supports the claim made. A real paper cited for something it does not say is as damaging as an invented one.

quiz.a: Delete them and adjust the text. You sign for what reaches learners, and a shorter handout does less harm than a wrong figure.

topics.title: Use AI to sort and summarise feedback

situation.text: Three hundred people have answered "What would have made this more useful?" You have an afternoon.

items: Check that you may. Free-text comments can identify people. Confirm that the client agrees, that there is a lawful basis for this use, and that the tool is one the client has approved.
Remove names, job titles, team names and anything else that points to a person before the comments go anywhere.
Read fifty comments yourself first and note the themes you see. This is your check on the tool.
Ask the tool for themes. For each, ask for a one-line definition, a count, and three comments quoted exactly with their row numbers.
Ask separately for comments that fit no theme, and for the ten most critical.
Verify. Find every quoted comment in your file. Recount two themes by hand. Compare the tool's themes with your own list.
Write the summary yourself. Give counts as approximate, say that a tool sorted the comments, and say how you checked.

why.text: Sorting comments by hand is slow, and these tools are quick at grouping similar wording. The evidence on how well they do it is recent and thin.

In a 2025 study by researchers at a large technology company, AI models judged whether theme summaries of more than 13,000 staff survey comments matched the comments. Agreement with human raters was moderate. The models sometimes passed summaries in which people found gaps in coverage or quotes that did not fit. A small 2026 study compared a chatbot's themes with human coding of answers from 134 people. The themes overlapped well, but the tool counted far fewer answers under one theme because it caught only simple statements. Its author treats the tool as a supplement to human coders.
So the counts are the weak part, and the quotes need checking against the file. Reading a sample first protects you from accepting a tidy list that missed what mattered.

On privacy, ICO guidance says you need a lawful basis whenever you process personal data, and that includes using an AI system. Its anonymisation guidance says removing obvious identifiers is not enough if a person can still be singled out. A comment that begins "as the only night manager in my region" identifies its author. See 9.24. This is general information, not legal advice.

try.text: Take a set of comments you are allowed to use, or write thirty yourself. Run the steps. Then give a colleague a two-minute spoken summary, and have them ask how you know each count.

try.title: A worked example: a brief for sorting comments
lines: Below are 300 anonymous comments from a course feedback form, one per row, each with a row number.
The question was: What would have made this more useful?
Group them into no more than eight themes. Give each theme a name and a one-line definition.
For each theme, give the number of comments and three comments quoted exactly, with row numbers.
A comment may sit in more than one theme. Say how many do.
List separately any comments that fit no theme. Do not force them into one.
List the ten most critical comments, with row numbers.
Do not summarise, reword or correct the quotes. Do not guess who wrote anything.
Finish by telling me which themes you were least sure about, and why.

try.title: A worked example: checks before you report

head: Check
How
If it fails
rows: Search the file for each quoted comment
Drop the quote and look again at the theme
Report themes as common, some or few, with no numbers
Compare with the themes from your own fifty
Add the theme and run it again
Read the ten most critical in full
Make sure the summary carries their point
Reread every quote you plan to use

items: The tool produces a neat quote that nobody wrote. Search for every quote before it goes in a report.
Rare but serious comments vanish into a theme. Read the unthemed list and the most critical list yourself.
You paste raw comments into a personal account. Use the client's approved tool, or sort by hand.
The summary sounds more positive than the comments. Compare its tone with your sample of fifty.

quiz.a: Confirm the client's agreement, a lawful basis and an approved tool, and remove anything that identifies a person.

quiz.a: Drop that quote, recount the theme by hand and check the other quotes. An invented quote means the count cannot be trusted either.

quiz.a: Do not paste them in. Ask for the client's approved tool or for the comments with names removed, and if neither is possible, sort a sample by hand and say so.

topics.title: Set a rule for AI in the room

situation.text: Ten minutes into a workshop, one person is typing the exercise into a chatbot, another has a note-taking app recording, and the hands-on demo will not log in.

items: Before the day, ask the client which AI tools staff may use, and whether sessions may be recorded or transcribed. Put the answer in the joining note.
In the first ten minutes, state the rule as part of how the group will work. Say which exercises are done with tools closed and why, and which will use them.
Ask before anything records. Say what will be captured, who will see it and when it will be deleted. If anyone says no, nothing records. Offer a written summary in its place.
For exercises with tools closed, give the reason in a sentence: the point is to practise the thinking, and the tool would do it for you.
For exercises that use a tool, ask people to show what they asked and what they changed, so the group can compare.
For a hands-on AI session, prepare three fall-backs: a shared demo on your screen, pairs on one working account, and printed prompts with printed outputs to critique.
Test logins on the client's network the day before, with a participant's account and not your own.
At the close, say what was recorded, if anything, and where it will go.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. Stating the rule at the start is easier than correcting someone halfway through an exercise, and it treats tool use as a design choice. Some practice only works unaided. Topic 7.2 reports an experiment in which pupils who leaned on a plain chatbot during practice did worse once it was removed.

Recording changes what people are willing to say, and a transcript of a session is personal data about the people in it. Product help for one widely used meeting tool says that all participants are notified when a recording starts, and that depending on where you are you may need everyone's permission before you record them. A notice on a screen is not agreement. Ask first, aloud, and accept a no without fuss. Topic 9.24 covers the data protection duties.

Hands-on sessions often fail on access before they fail on content. That is a common report from trainers, not a finding. Licences have not been assigned, the network blocks the site, or a login needs a phone that is in a locker. A fall-back prepared in advance keeps the learning going while someone fixes it.

try.text: Say the room rule aloud, standing, in under a minute, and record it. Then rehearse the recording request with a colleague who refuses, and practise accepting the no in one sentence.

try.title: Words you can use: the room rule and the recording request
lines: A word about AI tools before we start.
For the first two exercises, please keep them closed. I want you to do the thinking, and the tool would do it for you.
After the break we will use them on purpose. I will ask you to show what you asked and what you changed.
Nothing in this room is being recorded or transcribed.
If you use a note-taking app that records, please switch it off for today. I will send a written summary.
If we lose the tool this afternoon, we carry on in pairs with printed examples. You will not miss the point.
Is everyone happy to work that way?
If you do want a recording: I would like to record the last half hour so I can write up your actions.
Only I will hear it, and I will delete it on Friday.
If anyone would prefer I did not, say so now or tell me at the break, and I will take notes instead.

head: If this fails
Do this
Prepared in advance

Pair each with someone who can. The person without access directs and the other types.
Seating in pairs from the start
Run the exercise as a shared demo on your screen. The group calls out the prompts.
Your own account, tested on the client's network
The tool or the network is down
Hand out printed prompts with printed outputs. Pairs mark what they would check.
The tool gives a wrong answer live
Use it. Ask the group how they would have caught it.

topics.title: Show how this site was made
topics.theory: Disclosing AI use in your own work

situation.text: Your manager asks how you built a whole learning site so quickly, and whether the content can be trusted.

items: Say plainly that an AI assistant was used, and for what: planning, design and build.
Say where the content came from: your own source documents first, then research to fill the gaps.
Say how it was checked. The source material was reviewed and fact-checked, and claims that did not hold up were corrected or removed, including claims in your own sources.
Say what a person signed off, step by step: the content review, the site plan, the design, then the build.
Say what is still weak. Papers were read in summary and not in full, some on a university or index copy. A few topics have had no sources opened, and say so.
Offer one page as a sample and invite the listener to check any claim on it against its source.
Keep the account to one minute spoken, or one short page.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. Topic 7.1 says to tell learners where AI was used. The same applies to a manager or a client looking at your work. An account that names the tool's part, the checks and the limits is more convincing than silence, and more convincing than a claim that everything was verified.

The limits are the part people remember. Saying that papers were read in summary tells the reader how far to trust a citation and where to look harder. It also protects you. If someone finds an error, you have already said how the content was checked and where the gaps are.

Describe only what was done. Do not add checks that did not happen, and do not give a tally you cannot stand behind. The About page is the public version of this account. The example below is the same content arranged for a conversation.

try.text: Say the account below aloud to a colleague in one minute. Ask them for the first thing a sceptical manager would ask, and answer it without adding anything you did not do.

try.title: A worked example: the account of this site, for a manager
lines: I planned, designed and built this site with an AI assistant. I signed off each step: the content review, the site plan, the design, then the build.
The content started from three sources: a curriculum outline for trainers, a toolkit of methods, mechanics and session recipes, and a report on AI skills and training.
Where those had gaps, they were filled by research.
The source material was reviewed and fact-checked on 17 November 2026.
Claims that did not hold up were corrected or removed. Some of those were in my own sources.
The figures that held up are listed on the numbers page, each with its source.
Every practice carries an evidence rating, so you can see what rests on studies and what is craft.
The limits: papers were read in summary, not in full. Some were read on a university or index copy because the publisher's page would not open.
Nearly every topic has had its sources opened. The few that have not say so on the page.
Pick any claim and I will show you the source it rests on.

items: You say "fact-checked" and are asked what that means. Have the answer ready: sources opened and read in summary.
You overstate your own part, or the tool's. Say who did what.
The account goes out of date as the site changes. Date it, and review it when the content changes.
You are asked how many claims were corrected. If you did not count, say so.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: How were the papers behind this site read?
quiz.a: In summary, not in full, and some on a university or index copy.

quiz.q: A manager asks, "So the AI wrote it and you checked it?" What do you say?
quiz.a: Give the actual split: an AI assistant was used to plan, design and build, the source material was fact-checked, and you signed off each step. Then name the limits before you are asked.

quiz.q: A colleague finds a claim on the site that the cited paper does not support. What do you do?
quiz.a: Thank them, correct or remove the claim, and note the change. The account already says papers were read in summary, so the error is the kind you warned of.
