parts.title: AI for learners at work
parts.summary: AI practice partners, assistants that answer the question during work, and the risk of people leaning on them too far.

topics.title: Use AI as a practice partner

situation.text: A sales director wants every seller to practise the new pricing conversation before launch. There are 200 sellers, six managers and two weeks.

items: Teach the model of a good conversation first, in ten minutes, with one worked example. Then send people to practise.
Write the scenario from the client's real work: the customer, the objection, the product. Give the AI partner a brief with a manner and a level of difficulty.
Give people a rubric of three or four behaviours before they start, so they know what good looks like.
Limit feedback after each attempt to two points: one thing to keep and one to change.
Ask for a second attempt on a different scenario. Getting better at the same scenario shows little.
Bring a person in. A peer or manager hears one conversation live, or reads one transcript, and debriefs for ten minutes.
Judge the result outside the simulator, with an observed call or a manager's report (6.4).

why.text: The controlled evidence is new and small. In a 2026 experiment, 145 managers in the United States practised a difficult conversation with a text-based AI partner. They were randomly given practice only, practice with structured feedback, or both together with a short primer on a conversation model. Confidence rose, and scores improved from the first session to the second. On a new scenario that nobody had practised, the group with the primer and the feedback did better than the group that only practised.

The paper is plain about its limits. The conversations were typed. The scores came from an AI judge inside the same system. Nobody checked whether anything changed at work, or lasted. Confidence is also the easiest thing to raise (6.3).

Two other sources help with design. In interviews, 17 managers who tried a role-play prototype wanted scenarios from their own workplace and control over how hard the partner was. Many saw it as an addition to a human coach. A set of field experiments with sales agents at two financial technology firms looked at AI feedback on their customer conversations, which is coaching on real work and not role-play. Middle-ranked agents gained most. The lowest-ranked were swamped by the amount of feedback and did better when it was cut back, and the highest-ranked resisted it. Feedback from the AI passed on by a human manager beat either alone.
No study read here shows an AI practice partner improving real sales results.

why.title: Practising difficult conversations with an AI partner
why.found: Managers were randomly assigned to practice only, practice with feedback, or a full version with a teaching primer. Confidence and scores rose after practice. On an unpractised scenario, the full version outperformed practice alone. Scoring was inside the text simulation, and lasting change at work was not tested.
why.means: Teach the model before the practice, add feedback, and test on a fresh scenario. Do not treat a simulator score as proof of skill at work.

try.text: Set up one scenario in an approved tool using the sheet below. Run it yourself twice, speaking your side aloud if the tool takes voice. Then have a colleague watch your second attempt and give you one thing to keep and one to change.

try.title: A worked example: design sheet for pricing conversation practice

head: Element
Decision
rows: 200 sellers at a software company, in the two weeks before a price change
Ten-minute video of one good conversation, with the four rubric behaviours named
A long-standing customer says the increase is unjustified and mentions a competitor
Finance lead, polite, well prepared, will not accept vague answers. Medium difficulty.
Acknowledges the concern. States the new price once, plainly. Links the price to one named benefit. Agrees a next step.
One behaviour to keep and one to change. No score out of ten.
A new customer asks for a discount in return for signing this quarter
Each seller does one live practice with a peer. Each manager sits in on five and debriefs for ten minutes.
Managers observe a sample of real pricing calls in the first month, using the same rubric
No real customer names in scenarios. Transcripts deleted after the debrief.

items: Scores inside the tool rise and get reported as skill. Report them as practice done, and measure outside the tool.
Feedback runs to a page and weaker performers stop reading. Cap it at two points.
The AI partner is too agreeable. Test the scenario yourself and raise the difficulty.
Strong performers dismiss it. Ask them to write or test the scenarios.
Sellers paste real customer details into the scenario. Give them the scenario ready-made.

quiz.q: In the 2026 experiment, which group did best on the scenario nobody had practised?
quiz.a: The group that had a short teaching primer and structured feedback as well as practice.

quiz.q: A vendor's dashboard shows your sellers' role-play scores up by a third in two weeks. The sales director asks if the training worked. What do you say?
quiz.a: That the scores show practice inside the tool, judged by the tool. You will know more when managers have observed real calls against the same rubric.

quiz.q: Your weakest sellers get a full page of AI feedback after each attempt and their scores are flat. What do you change?
quiz.a: Cut the feedback to one thing to keep and one to change. In the sales field experiments, the lowest-ranked agents were swamped by volume and did better with less.

topics.title: Design for AI in the flow of work
topics.theory: AI assistants and what is left to train

situation.text: A support team gets an AI assistant that suggests replies. The head of support asks whether the three-week product course for new starters is still needed.

items: Pick one real workflow, such as answering a billing query. Map its steps with someone who does the job.
Mark each step: the assistant does it, the assistant drafts and a person checks, or a person does it alone.
For every step the assistant now answers, move that content out of the course and into the tool or a job aid (5.7).
List what the person still has to do. It is usually judging whether the answer fits this case, checking it against a source, and deciding when to stop and ask someone.
Train those with real cases: good answers, wrong answers, and answers that are right in general and wrong for this customer.
Teach what good looks like. Show three strong replies and have people say what makes them strong, before they see any AI drafts.
Redesign the work round the tool, then train people on the redesigned work. Keep a short unaided check for new starters (6.5).

why.text: Two field studies show what an assistant changes. Among 5,179 customer support agents given an AI assistant in a staggered roll-out, issues resolved per hour rose by 14% on average and by 34% for novice and lower-skilled agents, with little change for the most experienced. The authors offer suggestive evidence that the tool spreads the habits of abler agents to newer ones. That supports cutting some product teaching for new starters, because the tool now carries it.

The second study is the warning. In an experiment with 758 consultants, those using an AI model did more work, and better work, on tasks within its ability. On one task chosen to lie outside it, they were 19 percentage points less likely to reach the right answer than consultants working without it. The tool does not announce which kind of task it is facing.

What remains to train, then, is the part the tool cannot do for you: recognising a good answer, checking, and knowing where the tool's ability ends in your own work. That is this site's reading of the two studies. Neither tested a training design.
Topic 5.7 treats a job aid as the answer when people need help in the middle of a task. An assistant is a job aid that talks, and it can be confidently wrong. Topic 7.4 covers the checking practice.

try.text: Map one workflow with someone who does the job, using the table below as a pattern. Then explain aloud, in two minutes, what you would stop teaching and what you would add. Record it.

Assistant

Where the source of truth is, and how to check a date

items: The course is cut and nothing replaces it. Put the freed time into judgement cases.
People are trained on the tool's buttons while the work stays as it was. Redesign the workflow first.
New starters never do the task unaided and cannot tell a good answer from a bad one. Keep some unaided practice.
The assistant changes after an update. Review the map when the tool changes.

quiz.a: Novice and lower-skilled agents, whose output rose by about a third.

quiz.q: An assistant now answers product questions for new support staff. The client wants to drop the product course entirely. What do you propose?
quiz.a: Cut the content the tool carries and use the time for judgement: real cases where the suggested answer is wrong or does not fit the customer. Keep a short unaided check so you know new starters can tell good from bad.

quiz.a: Name that task type, show cases from it, and make the check a visible step for it. In the consultants' experiment, people using AI did worse than those without it on exactly that kind of task.

topics.title: Guard against over-reliance

situation.text: Six months after an AI assistant arrived, a team leader notices that nobody questions its drafts any more. Two experienced people say they have forgotten how to do the task by hand.

items: Decide which tasks people must still be able to do without the tool. Keep the list short and write the reason beside each.
For those tasks, have people attempt first and use the assistant second while they are learning.
Run an unaided check at intervals, such as one task a quarter done without the tool. Judge skill by that.
Build checking into the workflow as a visible step: a field that says what was checked and against which source. Do not rely on a reminder to be careful.
Give people time to check. Checking is the first thing to go when several tasks compete.
Now and then, plant a known error in practice material. Review it as a group, without blame.
Ask people to rate their confidence in themselves on the task and in the tool. Low in the first with high in the second is the pairing to watch.

why.text: A 2010 review of studies of people working with automated systems describes two linked problems. Complacency is monitoring the system too little, and it is most likely when people are handling several tasks at once. Automation bias is leaning on a decision aid, so that people miss problems the aid did not flag or act on advice that is wrong. The review reports that both affect experts as well as novices, and that automation bias is not prevented by training or instructions. That finding is the reason the steps above change the workflow and do not stop at a warning.

Three recent studies point the same way for AI tools. In the school experiment described in 7.2, pupils who used a plain chatbot in practice scored lower once it was taken away. In a survey of 319 knowledge workers, higher confidence in the AI tool went with less critical thinking, and higher confidence in oneself went with more. In an observational study at four endoscopy centres in Poland, experienced clinicians' detection rate in procedures done without AI was lower after AI assistance had been introduced than before. The authors caution that other factors may explain it.
None of these is an experiment on adults in ordinary office work, and the survey rests on self-report. The steps are craft and were not tested. Topic 7.4 covers teaching people to check.

why.title: Complacency and bias in human use of automation
why.found: This review treats complacency and automation bias as overlapping effects with attention at the centre. Complacency appears when manual tasks compete with watching the automation. Automation bias produces errors of omission and commission when a decision aid is imperfect. Both are found in novices and experts. Complacency is not overcome by simple practice.
why.means: Do not expect a warning to stop people leaning on an AI tool. Make checking a required, visible step with time allowed.

try.text: Choose one task your learners now do with an assistant. Write the unaided check for it. Then brief it aloud to a colleague as you would to a team, explaining why it is there, in under a minute.

Early sign
Design response

They cannot explain why an answer is right

items: You answer the risk with a warning slide. The review found that instructions do not prevent automation bias. Change the workflow.
Unaided checks feel like punishment. Explain the reason, keep them short and keep the results out of performance ratings.
Planted errors turn into a trap. Tell people in advance that drills happen.
You keep every manual skill alive out of caution. Keep only those that matter when the tool is wrong or absent.

quiz.a: No. The review reports that it is not prevented by training or instructions, and that experts are affected as well as novices.

quiz.q: A manager wants to deal with over-reliance by adding a slide that says "Always check the AI's answer". What do you propose?
quiz.a: A change to the workflow: a required field recording what was checked, and time allowed for it. The review found instructions do not prevent the bias.

quiz.q: An experienced team says the unaided quarterly task is insulting. What do you do?
quiz.a: Explain that experts are affected too, keep the task short and keep results out of ratings. Then ask them which tasks matter most when the tool is wrong, and check those.

topics.title: Promise the conditions, never the transformation
topics.source: Skills building: Transformational Experiences, topic TX.1

situation.text: The proposal for a leadership offsite promises the client "a transformation" of its management team.

items: Separate ordinary learning from deep change in your aims.
Design the conditions in which deep change may happen.
Promise the conditions and the work.
Take guarantees out of your proposal and your marketing.

why.text: One account, Jack Mezirow's, describes transformative learning as a deep shift in how someone makes sense of their experience, worked through by reflection.
People do report change of this kind, but it is hard to measure and no method produces it on demand. Promising it is a promise you cannot keep.

The research behind the idea is mostly qualitative. A 2007 review of 40 published studies found that interviews and case studies still dominated, with work on reflection, relationships and context. That is useful description. It is not proof that a programme can cause the change.

why.title: A review of research on transformative learning
why.found: The review covered 40 peer-reviewed studies published after the previous review in 1998. Research had moved towards how to encourage transformative learning, and qualitative designs still dominated.
why.means: Describe transformation as something some people report, and do not present it as a measured result of your programme.

items.title: Not on demand
items.text: Do not expect it from everyone.

try.text: For a real programme, mark which outcomes are ordinary learning and which would need deep change. Adjust your claims.

try.title: Illustration: rewriting the brochure
try.text: Before: "Three days that will transform your leadership." After: "Three days away from the office with time to think, honest feedback from peers and a coach, and a plan you test in your first week back."

items: Clients like big promises. Offer honest ones.
Discomfort is not proof of depth.
Most valuable learning is incremental.
A business retreat is bought for a business result. Name that result and the conditions you will provide. Personal change may happen for some people and is not the product.

quiz.q: What is transformative learning, in Mezirow's account?
quiz.a: A deep shift in how someone makes sense of their experience, worked through by reflection.

quiz.q: Can it be produced on demand?
quiz.a: No.

quiz.q: What can you honestly promise?
quiz.a: The conditions, not the outcome.

openPoints: The 'disorienting dilemma' and 'critical reflection' wording of Mezirow's account: not confirmed in a page that could be opened.
Mezirow and associates (2000), Learning as Transformation, and a published critique such as Newman (2012): not searched for, the search cap was reached.
The statement that deep change is hard to measure and cannot be produced on demand has no direct source. Taylor's abstract supports only that the research is mostly qualitative.
checkFindings: The placeholder reference 'Mezirow, Transformative Learning' is replaced by Mezirow's 1991 book, confirmed on Wiley's own site (author, title, year, chapters on meaning perspectives, reflection and perspective transformation).

The detail that transformative learning is set off by a disorienting experience was not in either summary read. It was removed from the paragraph and the quiz. It is the usual account of Mezirow and can go back once a source stating it is opened.
Taylor (2007) added as the evidence review. Its abstract says 40 peer-reviewed studies, mostly qualitative. A short paragraph and a study block say so.
Rated D, strictly: the page's practice is an honest-marketing stance, and the underlying idea is a theory without experimental support in the sources read.
topics.tierReason: Transformative learning is a theory studied mostly through qualitative research, and no checked source tests a method that produces it, so promising only the conditions is sound professional practice, not a tested technique.

topics.title: Design for absorption, not intensity
topics.source: Skills building: Transformational Experiences, topic TX.2

situation.text: The sales kick-off is built around a dramatic high point: a stage show, a raft race, an awards night.

items: Set clear goals for each activity.
Give immediate feedback.
Match the challenge to people's skill.
Keep the high point tied to the objective.

why.text: Flow is the name given to an absorbed state that people report when challenge and skill are balanced. You can set up conditions that make it more likely. You cannot guarantee it.
Intense moments are remembered. That is not the same as lasting learning, so larger claims about "peak states" need caution.

A meta-analysis of 28 studies found a moderate link between the balance of challenge and skill and reported flow. Clear goals and a sense of control were linked to it as well. The link was weaker in work and education settings. Treat the balance as a helpful condition, not a switch.

why.title: Challenge-skill balance and flow: a meta-analysis
why.found: Across 28 studies, the balance of challenge and skill had a moderate relationship with flow. The relationship was weaker in work and education settings, and clear goals and a sense of control were also linked to flow.
why.means: Match the challenge to each person's skill and set clear goals, and do not promise that flow will follow.

items.title: Intensity is not learning
items.text: Memorable is not the same as useful.

try.text: Design a segment of a retreat for absorption. State the goal, the feedback and the balance of challenge and skill.

try.title: Illustration: the night hike, redesigned
try.text: Before: everyone does the same steep night hike. After: three routes of rising difficulty, a clear task at each checkpoint, a guide giving feedback as teams navigate, and a debrief that ties the task back to how the team makes decisions at work.

items: Chasing intensity can harm people.
A challenge too great for some excludes them. Offer levels.
Debrief, or the moment stays a story.
Ask what the high point is for. If nobody can link it to the business result, give the time to practice.

quiz.q: When does flow arise?
quiz.a: When challenge and skill are balanced.

quiz.q: What two things are proposed to support it?
quiz.a: Clear goals and immediate feedback.

quiz.q: Is an intense experience lasting learning?
quiz.a: Not by itself.

topics.title: Build trust before you ask for openness
topics.source: Skills building: Transformational Experiences, topic TX.3

situation.text: On the first evening of a leadership offsite you ask people to share something personal. Some do. Several shut down, and one asks afterwards whether HR will hear what was said.

items: Agree ground rules and confidentiality at the start.
Go first, at a modest level.
Let people choose how much to share, and to pass.
Stay calm and steady yourself.
Notice who needs support.
Before the event, agree in writing with the sponsor what you will report about individuals and what you will not. Tell participants the rule in the first ten minutes.

why.text: People take personal risks in a group more readily when they believe it is safe to do so. Researchers call that shared belief psychological safety, and studies of work teams link it to learning behaviour. Most of that research is on teams at work, not on retreats.
Calm breathing and a steady facilitator are sensible practices. Present them as practical ways to keep the room settled. Do not attach a scientific explanation you cannot source.

why.title: Psychological safety in 51 work teams
why.found: In a field study of 51 work teams in a manufacturing company, teams that shared a belief that it was safe to take interpersonal risks showed more learning behaviour. Learning behaviour in turn was linked to team performance.
why.means: Build safety first with ground rules, modest disclosure from you and a free choice to pass, and remember the evidence comes from work teams.

items.title: Keep the practice, drop the claim
items.text: Do not claim science you cannot source.

try.text: Design the opening that builds trust for an intensive session. Rewrite any scientific-sounding justification you cannot source in plain terms.

try.title: Illustration: a first evening
try.text: Before: "Share your biggest failure with the group." After: agree confidentiality and its limits, then the facilitator shares one small work mistake. People choose a question from three levels of depth, talk in pairs, and anyone may pass without giving a reason.

try.title: Words you can use: what goes back to the employer
lines: "Before we start, here is what your employer will and will not hear from me."
"I will send a short summary of what the group worked on and what you decided together."
"I will not report what any one of you said, or how any one of you got on in the practice."
"The exception is safety. If I think someone is at risk of harm, I will tell Jo, your host, and I will tell you first."
"What you say to each other stays in this room in the same way. Is everyone willing to work on that basis?"

items: Pressure to share is a breach of care.
Confidentiality has limits. Say what they are.
You are not a therapist.

The employer is paying, and sponsors do ask who struggled or who was negative. Report themes and group progress. Do not report what a named person said or how they performed unless that was agreed beforehand and participants were told at the start. If a sponsor asks later, hold the rule: "We agreed I would report on the group. I can tell you what the group found hard." Topic 9.24 covers the data protection side.

topics.title: Take people out of their routine, and plan the return
topics.source: Skills building: Transformational Experiences, topic TX.4

situation.text: The offsite is a success at the venue. On Monday the inbox wins.

items: Mark the start with a clear threshold.
Take people out of their usual setting and roles.
Mark the end.
Design the return: what people take back, who they tell, what they do in the first week.

why.text: Anthropologists use the idea of a threshold, or liminal, stage for the in-between period in a rite of passage, when people have left one role and not yet taken up the next. Retreat designers borrow the idea when they take people out of their normal setting. Treat it as a design idea, not a proven mechanism of change.
The return is the part most often neglected. Without it, what happened stays there.

Time outdoors has some support, from small studies. In one, 36 city adults had lower stress hormone levels after spending time in nature, with 20 to 30 minutes the most efficient dose. In another, hikers tested about four days into a wilderness trip scored around half as much again on a creative reasoning test as hikers tested before setting off. Neither study could separate nature from rest, time off screens or who chose to take part.

try.text: Sketch a retreat's beginning, middle and end. Design the return step.

try.title: Illustration: the first week back
try.text: Before leaving, each person writes one thing to try, who they will tell and when they will do it. Managers get a short note on Friday saying what to ask about on Monday. The group meets for twenty minutes a fortnight later to compare what happened.

items: Ritual can feel forced. Keep it simple and offer a way out.
The setting supports the work. It is not the work.
Tell managers what to expect on Monday.
Do not sell the setting as science. The nature studies are small and say nothing about what people do back at work.
The topic "Plan the return to work" in this stage gives the first week back in detail, with a manager note.

quiz.q: Why do retreats take people away?
quiz.a: To step out of usual settings and roles. It is a design idea, not a proven mechanism.

quiz.q: Which part is most often neglected?
quiz.a: The return to work.

quiz.q: What should the return include?
quiz.a: What people take back, who they tell and what they do in the first week.

openPoints: Antonelli and colleagues (2019): not searched for, cap reached.
van Gennep, The Rites of Passage: not opened. Turner's description names him as the origin of the liminal phase.
The definition of the liminal stage as leaving one role before taking up the next is the standard reading but is not spelled out in the publisher's description.
The claim that the return is the part most often neglected has no checked source. Research on transfer of training is the place to look.
checkFindings: Turner (1969) confirmed on the Routledge page. The description says Turner extends van Gennep's liminal phase of rites of passage and develops the idea of communitas. That supports the page's cautious sentence about anthropologists and thresholds.

Build note followed. The SPIRIT framework is not used. Of the three studies the note names, Hunter (2019) and Atchley (2012) were read on PubMed Central and are added with their limits. Antonelli (2019) was not reached.

Hunter and colleagues: 36 participants with usable data, mostly women, self-selected, no control group, chose their own time and place. The page gives the 20 to 30 minute finding without the per-hour percentages.

Atchley and colleagues: 56 hikers, 24 tested before the trip and 32 on the trip, different people in each group. The authors report about a 50% higher score and say they cannot tell nature from time away from technology. The paper says four days in the abstract and three in one later section, so the page says 'about four days'.
No study block: no single study carries this topic.
topics.tierReason: Liminality is an anthropological idea borrowed as a design principle, and the two nature studies read are small, uncontrolled and do not test retreats or the return to work.

topics.title: Write the duty-of-care plan first
topics.source: Skills building: Transformational Experiences, topic TX.5

situation.text: The plan for a three-day leadership residential is full of demanding exercises. Nobody has written down what happens if someone is distressed or hurt.

items: Write the duty-of-care plan before the programme.
Tell participants in advance what is involved, and get consent.
Let people opt out without penalty.
Know your limits and have a route to professional help.
Ask each person in advance, in private, whether anything about the programme would be difficult for them, and adjust it. Do not run health screening of a client's employees yourself.

Do a risk assessment: identify the hazards, assess the risks, control them, record what you found and review it. Plan for incidents and emergencies, and count participants in when you assess first aid needs.

why.text: Intense experiences can bring distress to the surface. The facilitator's first duty is participant wellbeing. A trainer is not a therapist.
Long days away from home, with colleagues and managers present, carry real risk.

In Great Britain, the Health and Safety at Work etc Act 1974 puts duties on employers towards their employees and towards members of the public. It also covers self-employed people whose work could put others at risk. HSE's guidance for events says the organiser has prime responsibility for the health and safety of workers, contractors and the people attending, and that planning should be in proportion to the scale and risk of the event. HSE guidance covers Great Britain. This page is general information, not legal advice.

On a business retreat the employer usually chooses who attends, so consent is not fully free. Agree with the client in writing that declining an exercise, or the overnight stay, carries no mark against anyone, and offer a non-residential alternative before invitations go out. The topics on incidents and on people who cannot stay overnight in this stage give the detail.

items.title: Informed consent
items.text: People know what they are joining.

Informed consent, opt-out and referral routes are professional good practice here and have no checked source.
checkFindings: The placeholder is replaced with HSE guidance, read on hse.gov.uk and treated as a legal topic.

HSE's page on the Health and Safety at Work etc Act 1974 says the Act sets duties for employers towards employees and members of the public, and for certain self-employed people towards themselves and others. HSE's self-employed guidance says the law applies if you employ anyone or your work poses a potential risk to the health and safety of others. A paragraph was added to why.

HSE risk assessment guidance (updated 24 March 2025) gives five steps: identify hazards, assess the risks, control the risks, record your findings, review the controls. Employers with five or more staff must write down significant findings. A step was added to do.

HSE event safety guidance says organisers have prime responsibility for the health and safety of workers, the public attending and contractors, that planning should be proportionate to scale and risk (page updated 11 October 2024), that organisers must have plans to respond to incidents and emergencies, and that HSE strongly recommends including the visiting public in the first aid assessment (page updated 20 January 2026).

HSE's mental health page (updated 22 April 2025) says work-related mental health risks should be assessed like other hazards. It concerns employees, which matters when participants are the client's staff and for the facilitators themselves.
A not-legal-advice note was added because the draft had none.

Debrief while it is fresh.

why.text: A residential setting gives time and distance from work, which makes play easier. Shared play may help people get to know each other faster.
It can also exclude. Physical challenges, alcohol and late nights leave some people out, and work against sleep.

parts.title: Design and run a business retreat
parts.summary: How to decide on, design, staff, cost and safely run a company offsite or residential course tied to a business result.

topics.title: Decide whether to take people away
topics.theory: The case for and against a residential

situation.text: A sales director at a software company asks for "three days away for the managers". The budget is approved. Nobody has asked what the three days are for, or whether four mornings in the office would do the same job.

items: Ask the sponsor for the business result first. Use these words: "Six months from now, what will these people be doing that they are not doing today?" Write the answer down and read it back.

Sort the work into two piles. One pile is skill that needs repeated practice over weeks. The other is work that needs the whole group together for long stretches: a hard decision, a plan, a relationship that has gone wrong.

Price both options before you recommend either. Cost the residential with the method in the costing topic in this part, including people's time. Cost a spaced on-site version next to it, for example four half days over six weeks.

Count who would be shut out by an overnight stay. Ask the sponsor's HR contact how many of the group have caring duties, a disability or health condition, part-time hours or a faith practice that the dates or the venue would cut across.
Run the decision test below with the sponsor in the room. Read out each row and mark it together.

Recommend the residential only when the together-for-long-stretches pile is the larger one and nobody is shut out without a real alternative. Otherwise recommend the spaced version, or a mix: one night away followed by three short sessions back at work.
Put the recommendation in writing with the result, the cost of each option and the follow-up dates.

why.text: A residential buys three things an office programme struggles to give: long unbroken time, the whole group in one place, and distance from the inbox. Those claims are practitioner judgement. No study opened for this topic compares a residential with the same content spread out on site.

Two findings from research pull the other way. A review of spacing found that people recalled more when study was spread out than when it was packed together, with the same total study time. A meta-analysis of leadership training listed spaced sessions and an on-site location among the features of programmes with stronger results. The next topic in this part gives both in detail, with their limits.

So the test is about fit. A decision that needs sixteen people to argue it through suits two days away. A skill such as coaching a sales call suits short sessions with practice at work in between. Many briefs contain both, which is why the mixed option is often the honest answer.

try.text: Rehearse the conversation aloud with a colleague playing the sponsor. Your task is to recommend the cheaper spaced option to someone who wants the hotel. Record it on your phone. Listen for the moment you name the business result and the moment you give the two costs.

try.title: Words you can use with the sponsor
lines: "Before we talk about venues, can I check what you want to be different by the spring?"
"From what you have said, most of this is a skill. Skills hold better when the practice is spread out."
"I have costed both, with everyone's time counted. Here are the two totals side by side."
"Three of the group cannot stay overnight. If we go away, they need a version that is as good, and I would want that agreed first."
"My recommendation is the spaced version. If the team also needs time together, add one day away at the start."

items: The sponsor has already promised the team a trip. Keep the trip and change its job: use it for the group work, and move the skill practice into sessions back at work.
The "cost" you compared leaves out people's time. Add it, because for senior groups it is often the largest line.
You assume nobody minds staying away. Ask through HR before dates are fixed, and treat the answers as private.
The spaced option quietly dies because no one protects the dates. Book all the sessions before the first one runs.

quiz.a: Practice spread over time, and for leadership training an on-site location.

quiz.q: A head of customer support wants a two-night retreat to teach 20 team leaders a new coaching routine. The leaders share one office. What do you recommend?
quiz.a: A spaced on-site programme, because the work is a skill that needs repeated practice and the group is already together. Offer one day away only if there is group work that needs it.

quiz.a: A short residential fits: the work is a group decision that needs long unbroken time and the group never meets. Check first that everyone can travel and stay.

topics.title: Know what the evidence says a retreat can and cannot do
topics.theory: Evidence for and against residential training

situation.text: You are pitching a three-day leadership residential. The client's head of learning asks: "What is the evidence that taking people away works better than training them here?"

items: Give the short answer first: "No study I have read compares a residential with the same programme run on site. There is evidence on three nearby questions, and some of it cuts against going away."
State the spacing problem plainly. A residential packs the practice into one block. Research on memory favours practice spread over time.
State the on-site finding. A large review of leadership training lists an on-site location among the features of stronger programmes.
State what the outdoor education evidence shows and who it studied: long adventure programmes, with gains in how people see themselves.
Say what you will do about each one. Add spaced follow-up sessions after the event, bring real work into the venue, and promise no change in character.
Keep claims about the setting out of the proposal. Sell the time, the practice and the follow-up.
Offer the sources. Send the three links the same day.

why.text: Spacing first. Cepeda and colleagues pooled 271 comparisons of massed and spaced study. All but 12 favoured spacing, and average recall was about 47 per cent for spaced items against about 37 per cent for massed ones. The best gap grew as the time to the final test grew. The studies were laboratory tests of verbal recall, mostly with young adults, and the authors say their findings do not settle the question for skill learning. A residential is not a memory experiment. Still, the direction is clear enough that one block with nothing after it is a poor bet.

Next, location. Lacerenza and colleagues pooled 335 samples of leadership training. The abstract reports that training worked on average and that several features went with stronger effects, among them spaced sessions, an on-site location and face-to-face delivery. The abstract does not say why on-site training did better or how large the difference was. It is a pattern across many different programmes, not a trial of one design against another.

Then the outdoors. Hattie and colleagues pooled 96 studies of adventure programmes. The average gain at the end was 0.34, with a further 0.17 at follow-up. Effects varied a great deal between programmes and outcomes. They were larger for longer programmes and for older participants. The outcomes named in the abstract are self-concept, locus of control and leadership. A news report at the time described the participants as students and the typical programme as 20 to 26 days. That is a long way from two nights in a hotel for managers.

why.title: Spaced against massed study
why.found: Of 271 comparisons, 259 favoured spaced study over massed study with equal study time. The studies tested verbal recall, mostly in laboratories.
why.means: Do not let the residential be the whole programme. Plan practice after it.

why.title: What goes with stronger leadership training
why.found: Across 335 samples, leadership training improved reactions, learning, transfer and results. Needs analysis, feedback, several delivery methods with practice, spaced sessions, an on-site location and face-to-face delivery went with stronger effects.
why.means: Going off site is not an advantage in this evidence. Bring the workplace into the design.

why.title: Adventure programmes
why.found: Across 96 studies the average effect was 0.34 at the end and a further 0.17 later. Effects varied by programme and outcome and grew with programme length and participant age.
why.means: Evidence from long adventure courses does not transfer to a short business retreat. Do not cite it as proof for one.

try.text: Say it aloud. Set a timer for ninety seconds and answer the head of learning's question to a colleague, without notes. Then ask them which of the three findings they could repeat back. Do it again until all three survive.

You can say

items: You quote 0.34 as if it applied to your event. It comes from programmes that mostly ran for weeks.
You hide the on-site finding because it is awkward. A client's sceptic will find it. Raise it first.
You treat spacing as a rule for every kind of learning. The review covers verbal recall, so apply it with care to group decisions and relationships.
You overcorrect and talk the client out of a retreat that suits the work. Use the decision test in the first topic of this part.
You have read only abstracts for two of the three. Say so if pressed.

quiz.q: In the Lacerenza meta-analysis, was an on-site or an off-site location linked with stronger leadership training?
quiz.a: On-site.

quiz.q: A venue's brochure says "research shows outdoor residentials build lasting leadership". Your client wants to quote it in the invitation. What do you do?
quiz.a: Advise against it. The main review covers long adventure programmes and measures such as self-concept, so it does not support a short business retreat.

quiz.q: A sponsor says the residential is the whole programme and there is no budget for anything after. What do you say?
quiz.a: That one packed block with no later practice goes against the spacing evidence. Shorten the residential by half a day and spend the saving on two short follow-up sessions.

topics.title: Choose the format

situation.text: A client says "we want an offsite". In the next ten minutes they describe a sales kick-off, a strategy session and a team social, all in the same two days.

items: Ask one question to find the format: "When people drive home, what must exist that did not exist when they arrived?" A decision, a plan, a skill and a relationship each point to a different format.
Match the answer to the table below. Read the "what it is for" column aloud and ask the sponsor to choose one.
Set the group size from the work. Decisions need a group small enough for everyone to speak. Skills practice needs groups of three with an observer or a facilitator close by.
Set the length from the work as well. Start with the shortest length in the table and add time only when you can name what the extra half day is for.
If the sponsor wants two formats, give each its own block with its own outcome and a break between them. A strategy morning and a skills afternoon can share a venue. They cannot share a session.
Write the format, the outcome, the group size and the length in one sentence and send it to the sponsor the same day.
Check the sentence against the decision test in the first topic of this part before anyone books a venue.

why.text: The formats below are practitioner judgement. No research opened for this build compares one format with another, and the lengths and group sizes are working ranges that trainers and event teams commonly use. Treat them as a starting point for a conversation.

The reason to name a format is that each one has a different product at the end. A sales kick-off produces a sales team that knows the plan for the year and has practised the new pitch. A strategy offsite produces decisions with owners. When the format is left vague, the timetable fills with a little of everything and people leave with nothing finished.

Size changes the craft. Twelve people can hold one conversation. Eighty people cannot, so a large kick-off needs short plenary sessions and most of the time in small groups with a facilitator or a briefed manager at each. That in turn changes staffing and cost, which the later topics in this part cover.

try.text: Ring a colleague and have them play a client who wants "a bit of everything". Ask the format question aloud and hold your ground until they pick one. Time it. If it takes more than five minutes, shorten your question.

try.title: Words you can use when the brief mixes formats
lines: "I can hear three events in what you have described. Which one would you keep if you could only have one?"
"If the main thing is decisions, I would keep the group to the twelve who will carry them out."
"We can add pitch practice on the second afternoon. It needs its own outcome and its own two hours."
"Here is the sentence I will design from: a two-day strategy offsite for twelve leaders that ends with three priorities, each with an owner."

items: The guest list grows after the format is chosen. Go back to the sponsor: a strategy offsite for thirty is a conference, and it needs a different design.
A kick-off is planned as two days of slides. Ask for half of every session to be practice in small groups, and offer to brief the managers who will lead them.
A skills intensive is sold with no follow-up. Apply topic 5.4 before you agree the dates.
A leadership offsite drifts into personal disclosure. Keep the work on how the team leads the business, and apply topic 8.3.
You design for the format you like running. Let the sponsor's answer to the first question choose.

quiz.q: What single question helps you find the right format?
quiz.a: What must exist when people leave that did not exist when they arrived.

quiz.q: A chief executive wants a strategy offsite and invites all 45 managers "so everyone feels included". What do you do?
quiz.a: Explain that 45 people cannot make decisions in one conversation. Offer a decision group of about twelve, with a short session afterwards that shares the decisions with the other managers.

quiz.q: A sales leader wants a three-day kick-off with product presentations from nine to five each day. What do you suggest?
quiz.a: Cut the presentations and give at least half of each session to pitch practice in small groups. The format exists to send people home able to do something.

topics.title: Build the timetable

situation.text: The draft agenda runs from 08:00 to 21:30 on both days, with a "fireside session" after dinner. The sponsor says people can sleep at the weekend.

items: Fix the outcome for each day before you fill a single slot. Write it at the top of the timetable.

Start late on arrival day. People have travelled and cleared their desks. On a two-night event begin after lunch and keep the first afternoon light: purpose, working agreement, one easy piece of real work.
Use the first evening for dinner and nothing else. No exercise, no speeches after 20:30, and say that leaving the table early is fine.
Build each full day from work blocks of about ninety minutes with a break between. Put the hardest work in the morning. Plan no more than four blocks a day.
Give real free time in daylight, at least ninety minutes on a full day, and put it in the printed timetable so it is not the first thing cut.
Open each morning with fifteen to thirty minutes recalling the day before, as topic 1.12 sets out.

Finish before lunch on the last day, or straight after it. People start leaving for trains from mid-afternoon whatever the agenda says. Put the plans for first use at work in the last full block, not in the final ten minutes.
Print the clock times and keep to them. Starting and ending on time is how the group learns that the free time is real.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. Topic 1.12 covers the research on sleep, and no study opened for this build tests one residential timetable against another.

The pattern comes from what trainers see on residentials. Energy is low on arrival and after lunch on the middle day. Attention falls quickly in a fifth or sixth work block. The last afternoon loses people to travel. A timetable that plans for these points gets more work done in fewer hours.

Free time is part of the design. It is when people talk over what happened, rest, ring home and deal with the email that would otherwise pull them out of a session. Evenings need the most care, and a later topic in this part sets the rules for them.

Both examples below are for the same group: 16 new managers at a software company, two facilitators, and one outcome. Each manager leaves able to open a difficult conversation and with a date to hold a real one.

try.text: Stand up and deliver the first fifteen minutes of the opening from the timetable, aloud, to a colleague or a recording: the purpose, the plan for the days, the finish times and what is optional. Check your timing against the slot.

quiz.q: On a two-night residential, when should the programme start on arrival day?
quiz.a: After lunch, with a light first afternoon.

quiz.q: At 16:00 on the middle day you are forty minutes behind. The next items are a fourth work block and ninety minutes of free time. What do you do?
quiz.a: Shorten or drop the fourth block and keep the free time. Tired people get little from a late block, and cutting the break teaches the group that the timetable cannot be trusted.

quiz.q: The sponsor wants action plans written in the last fifteen minutes before the coaches leave. What do you change?
quiz.a: Move the plans into the last full work block of the morning so each person writes one, says it aloud and gets a question on it. Plans written in a rush at the door are forgotten.

topics.title: Choose and brief the venue
topics.theory: Venue selection and the site visit

situation.text: The client's assistant has found a country house hotel with good photographs. On the day, the main room turns out to be the bar with the tables pushed back, and a wedding party arrives at four.

items: Write the brief before anyone searches: dates, numbers, the outcome, how many rooms you need for work, bedrooms, access needs already known, and the longest travel time you will accept. For most groups aim for under two hours door to door.
Shortlist two or three venues by phone. Ask each the same first question: "Will we have the building, or our part of it, to ourselves?"

Visit before you sign. Go at the time of day you will be working and take the checklist below. If you cannot visit, ask for a video call walked through the rooms by the person who will be your contact.

Stand in the main room and test it. Check daylight, a flat floor, wall space for flipcharts, enough room for 16 chairs in a horseshoe and for groups of three to spread out. Play a phone at speaking volume from the far end.
Walk the route a wheelchair user would take from the car park to the main room, a breakout room, a bedroom, the dining room and a toilet. Do it yourself. Do not accept "mostly accessible".
Test phone signal and wifi where you will work, and find the spot where a mobile call to 999 would connect.

Send the venue a written brief two weeks ahead: the timetable with break and meal times, room layouts, dietary and access needs, who the venue contact is on each shift, and who may authorise extra spending.
On arrival, walk the rooms again with the venue contact before participants arrive.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement, built from what goes wrong. No research on venue choice was opened. Topic 9.19 covers the risk assessment and insurance side, and topic 4.5 covers room layout.

The venue decides how much of your timetable survives. Shared public rooms mean interruptions and no privacy for hard conversations. One room with no breakouts means sixteen people practising in the same space and hearing each other. Poor access tells some participants they were an afterthought, and it may leave the employer short of its duties to disabled staff, which a later topic in this part covers.

A quiet room matters more on a residential than on a training day. People are in company from breakfast until bedtime. Somewhere to sit alone, pray, take medication or make a private call makes it possible for more people to stay the course.
The written brief exists because venue staff work shifts. The person who showed you round may not be there on the day.

try.text: Take the checklist to any hotel or conference venue near you and ask to see a meeting room. Walk the step-free route and ask the questions aloud to the duty manager. Twenty minutes of doing this once will teach you more than reading the list again.

items: You book from photographs. Visit, or have the venue walk you through on video.
"Exclusive use" covers only the meeting room. Ask about the bar, the lounge and the grounds.
The accessible bedroom is in an annexe across a gravel yard. Check the route in the dark as well.
Twin rooms are offered to save money. Adults at a work event should not be asked to share a bedroom.
The brief goes to the sales office and never reaches the duty manager. Hand a printed copy to your contact on arrival.

quiz.q: What is the first question to ask a venue on the phone?
quiz.a: Whether you will have the building, or your part of it, to yourselves.

quiz.q: On the site visit the manager says the house is "mostly accessible, just two steps into the dining room". One participant uses a wheelchair. What do you do?
quiz.a: Treat it as not accessible until there is a working ramp or another dining arrangement for the whole group. Ask for the solution in writing or choose another venue.

quiz.q: The venue you like has one large room and no breakouts. The programme is rehearsal in threes. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask for two more rooms or look elsewhere. Sixteen people rehearsing in one room cannot hear themselves, and private practice is the point of the event.

topics.title: Staff it
topics.theory: Roles and ratios on a residential

situation.text: You are quoted as the only facilitator for 16 people over two nights. At 22:40 on the first night a participant knocks on your door in tears, and you are due to open the morning session at 08:45.

items: Set a floor of two facilitators for any overnight event, whatever the group size. One person cannot run the room, look after someone who is unwell and stay fit to work the next day.

Size the team from the practice. For rehearsal in threes, plan one facilitator for every eight to twelve participants. A group of 16 needs two. Above 24, add a third or brief line managers to lead groups.
Name a lead facilitator. They hold the timetable, make the calls when the plan changes and are the one voice to the client.
Ask the client for a host who attends throughout: someone senior enough to make decisions about their own staff and to speak for the employer if a participant's conduct becomes a problem.
Get one named venue contact for each shift, with a mobile number, including overnight.
Decide who holds the emergency contacts and any health or access information, and who is on call each night. Write the names on one page. Share the nights between you.
Hold a facilitator debrief each day, fifteen minutes straight after the last session. Cover what happened, who you are concerned about and what changes tomorrow.
Put the roles table in the proposal so the client can see what the second fee pays for.

why.text: These ratios are practitioner judgement. No research opened for this build tests facilitator numbers on a residential, and other experienced trainers work to different figures.

The case for two is about care as much as teaching. If someone is distressed or hurt, one facilitator stays with them and the other keeps the group working. With one facilitator, either the person or the group is left alone. A second facilitator also means nobody is alone with a participant late at night, which protects both of them.

The client host matters because you have no authority over the client's employees. You can ask someone to step out of a session. You cannot deal with a complaint between two colleagues or send someone home. The employer can, and its own policies apply.

Facilitators on a residential are on duty for long hours. Sharing the on-call nights and ending the facilitator debrief on time is how you are still useful on the last morning. Topic 4.16 covers looking after yourself.

try.text: Run a fifteen minute facilitator debrief with a colleague after any session you deliver this month. Use three questions aloud: what happened, who are we concerned about, what changes tomorrow. Keep to time with a phone timer.

head: Role
Who
Holds

Half the practice groups, materials, the incident log
Client, senior manager or HR partner
Authority over the client's staff, the employer's policies, emergency contacts for employees

try.title: Words you can use when the client questions the second facilitator
lines: "With sixteen people practising in threes, one of me can hear two groups at a time. Two of us can give every group feedback."
"It is also a safety point. If someone is unwell at night, one of us stays with them and the programme still starts on time."
"If budget is fixed, I would sooner cut half a day than run this alone."

items: The client offers their own trainer as the second facilitator. Accept if you can rehearse together for half a day first, and agree who leads.
The client host is the participants' own boss. People will hold back. Ask for an HR partner or a manager from another team.
Both facilitators stay up until the last person leaves the bar. Agree who is on duty and let the other go to bed.
The emergency contact list lives on one person's phone. Keep a sealed paper copy with the second facilitator.
The debrief turns into an hour of stories. Three questions, fifteen minutes, then stop.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What is the minimum number of facilitators for an overnight event in this topic's advice?
quiz.a: Two.

quiz.q: A client wants you to run a two-night skills residential for 14 people alone, to save money. What do you say?
quiz.a: Decline to run it alone and explain why: practice groups need feedback, and one person cannot look after an unwell participant and run the room. Offer a shorter event with two facilitators.

quiz.q: During the second evening one participant tells you a colleague has been making comments she finds offensive. What is your first move?
quiz.a: Listen, note the time and what she said, and bring in the client host, because the employer's policy applies and you have no authority over its staff. Tell her that is what you are going to do before you do it.

topics.title: Cost it
topics.theory: The full cost of a residential

situation.text: The sponsor says the retreat will cost "about twelve thousand, that is what the hotel quoted". The hotel quote covers rooms and food. Nothing else has been counted.

items: List every cost line before you look at any quote: venue hire, bedrooms, food and drink, travel, facilitator fees, design time, materials, insurance and contingency.
Count heads for each line. Bedrooms and meals include the facilitators and the client host. Travel includes yours.
Get the venue's price as a day-delegate or 24-hour rate and ask exactly what it includes. Ask about minimum numbers and the cancellation scale.
Add contingency as its own visible line. Ten per cent of the cash subtotal is a common working figure. It covers a late dietary need, a taxi, an extra room.
Cost people's time as a separate line below the cash total. Ask the client's finance contact for an average daily cost for the group. Multiply by people and by days, including travel days.
Show two totals: cash, and cash plus time. Divide each by the number of participants.
Cost the alternative from the decision test in the same table shape, so the sponsor compares like with like.
State what is not included, in a single line under the table.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement about how to lay out a cost, with no research behind it. Topic 9.4 covers scoping and pricing your own fee.

The cash lines are the ones a sponsor expects. The line most often missing is time. Sixteen managers away for three days is 48 working days that the business pays for and gets no other work from. For senior groups it can be the largest single line. Leaving it out makes every residential look cheaper than a spaced programme, which uses hours instead of days.
A visible contingency line is honest. Without it, small extras either come out of your fee or arrive as a surprise invoice, and both damage trust.
The figures below are made up and round, chosen so the sums are easy to follow. Real prices vary widely by region, season and venue. Use the shape and get real quotes for every line.

try.text: Talk a colleague through the table in two minutes, as if they were the sponsor. Say both totals aloud and the cost per head. Record it. If you hear yourself apologising for the time line, practise that sentence again.

try.title: Illustration with made-up figures: 16 managers, two nights, two facilitators

head: Cost line
How it is worked out
Amount
rows: Main room and two breakouts, three days, exclusive use of one wing
Package quoted for 18 people: three lunches, two dinners, breaks
2 people for 3 days at £1,500 a day
16 managers for 3 days at £400 a day

try.title: Words you can use
lines: "The hotel's figure covers two lines of nine. Here is the whole picture."
"The cash total is the invoice side. Below it I have added the cost of everyone's time, because the business pays that too."
"Not included: staff cover back at work, and anything spent at the bar."
"The same table for four half days on site is on the next page."

items: The time line makes the sponsor uncomfortable and you delete it. Keep it, shown separately, so the comparison with other options is fair.
Made-up figures from a page like this one get quoted as real. Label illustrations clearly and replace every figure with a quote.
The venue's minimum numbers are higher than your group. You pay for empty rooms. Check before signing.
Bar spending is left undefined. Agree in advance what the client pays for and say it to participants.
Your own design days are hidden inside the delivery fee. Show them, or the client will expect the next design for nothing.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: Which cost line is most often left out of a retreat budget?
quiz.a: The cost of people's time away from work.

quiz.q: A sponsor compares your £33,000 residential with a £9,000 quote for on-site sessions and says the retreat is "only" £24,000 more. What do you add?
quiz.a: The time line for both options. Three days away for 16 people costs far more in time than four half days, so the real gap is wider.

quiz.q: Two days before the event a participant tells the venue about a severe allergy and the kitchen charges for separate preparation. Where does the cost go?
quiz.a: Against the contingency line, which exists for this. Tell the client host the same day so the spend is no surprise.

topics.title: Set the rules for evenings, alcohol and free time

situation.text: It is 22:15 on the first night. The work went well. The sponsor has put a card behind the bar, three people have gone to bed, and a participant asks you to stay for "one more".

items: Agree the rules with the client before invitations go out. Put them in writing: what the employer pays for at the bar and until when, which policy applies to conduct, and who participants go to with a concern.

Make everything after the last session optional, and say so twice: in the invitation and in the opening. Include dinner if you can. If dinner is expected, say that leaving after the main course is fine.
Make opting out easy. Print the end time of each evening. Offer a second space that is not the bar, with good soft drinks and hot drinks. Never ask anyone why they are leaving.
Set your own rule on alcohol and keep it. A workable rule is none, or one drink with dinner and none after. You are at work until you close your bedroom door.
Stay in public spaces. Do not go to a participant's bedroom or invite one to yours. If someone needs a private talk at night, use a lounge and tell your co-facilitator where you are.
Agree with your co-facilitator who is on duty each evening and what time that person leaves the bar. The other one goes to bed.
Do not connect with participants on personal social media during the event. Say you will connect on a work network afterwards.

why.text: Most of this is practitioner judgement. Trainers who run residentials report that incidents cluster late in the evening, when people are tired, away from home and drinking with colleagues and managers. No research on this was opened.

Two points come from official guidance. Acas says that from 30 October 2026 an employer is liable for harassment of its workers by third parties as well as by other workers, unless it has taken all reasonable steps to prevent it. Acas adds that being at work can include business travel, external training and office parties. A residential is an employer's event in that sense, which is why the conduct rules are the client's to set and yours to follow. You may be one of the third parties.

Acas also says that training needed for the job counts as working time, and that workers are entitled to 11 hours of rest between working days. A timetable that expects people in the bar until midnight and in the room at eight sits badly with that. This is general information, not legal advice.
Your own conduct carries more weight than the written rules. People copy the facilitator. If you leave at ten with a soft drink in your hand, leaving at ten becomes ordinary.

try.text: Say the opening statement below aloud, standing, three times. Record the third. It should take under a minute and sound like information, not a warning. Then practise one sentence for declining a drink without making it awkward.

try.title: A worked example: evening and free-time rules agreed with the client
lines: Everything after the last session of the day is optional, including the quiz on night two.
Dinner is at 19:00. People may leave any time after the main course.
The company pays for drinks with dinner. The bar tab closes at 21:30.
A lounge with soft drinks, tea and coffee is open all evening as a second space.
The company's code of conduct applies for the whole event, including evenings and travel.
Concerns go to the client host or to either facilitator. Mobile numbers are on the back of the name badge.
Facilitators do not drink after dinner and one is on duty each evening until 22:30.
Free time is free. No tasks are set for it and nobody is asked how they spent it.

try.title: Words you can use in the opening
lines: "A word about evenings. We finish at five fifteen and the rest of the day is yours."
"Dinner is at seven. Come if you would like to, and leave when you like. Nobody will ask."
"There is a lounge next to the dining room if the bar is not your thing."
"We are still at work while we are here, so your company's usual standards apply in the evening as well."
"If anything worries you, at any hour, my number and Sam's are on the back of your badge."
And to the offer of one more: "Not for me, thanks. I am on at quarter to nine. See you at breakfast."

items: The senior person stays late and everyone feels they must. Ask the client host beforehand to leave by ten and say goodnight.
"Optional" activities are noticed by who does not come. Never report attendance at social events to the employer, and say so.
The only evening space is the bar. Book the lounge when you book the venue.
A participant shares something personal with you late at night. Listen, do not advise, and raise it with your co-facilitator in the morning without detail the person would not want passed on.

Acas, Working time rules: understanding the Working Time Regulations.

quiz.q: According to Acas, can an employer's duty to prevent harassment cover external training and work social events?
quiz.a: Yes. Acas lists business travel, external training and office parties as examples of being in the course of employment.

quiz.q: The sponsor proposes a free bar until midnight "as a thank you". What do you suggest?
quiz.a: Drinks with dinner and a tab that closes at a stated time, with a second space that is not the bar. A long free bar raises the chance of an incident and makes it harder for people to opt out.

quiz.q: A participant you get on well with suggests carrying on a conversation in their room because the bar is closing. What do you do?
quiz.a: Decline and offer the lounge or breakfast. A facilitator stays in public spaces and is still at work.

topics.title: Plan for incidents

situation.text: At 23:30 a participant slips on the steps outside the hotel and cannot put weight on her ankle. Her manager is in bed, the night porter is new, and nobody knows who has her emergency contact.

items: Name one incident lead for the event and a deputy. On a small residential this is the lead facilitator with the second facilitator as deputy. Put both mobile numbers on the back of every name badge.
Write the risk assessment with the client and the venue, following topic 9.19. Add the residential risks: evenings, alcohol, paths in the dark, travel and distress.

Agree in writing who collects health, access and dietary information and who sees it. The simplest route is that the employer collects it and passes on only what the venue and the facilitators must act on.

Collect the minimum. Ask what the person needs, not what their diagnosis is: "Is there anything we should know to keep you safe and comfortable, such as an allergy, an access need or medication that must be kept cold?"
Prepare a one-page "who calls whom" sheet and an incident log, both shown below. Carry them on paper.
Find out the venue's first aid arrangements: who the first aider or appointed person is on each shift, where the kit is, and how far the nearest emergency department is.
Talk through three scenarios aloud with the client host and venue contact before participants arrive: an injury at night, a person in distress, a complaint about another participant.
After any incident, write the log entry the same day and tell the client host.

why.text: HSE sets out risk assessment as five steps, covered in topic 9.19, and says to consider visitors and members of the public as well as employees. Its first aid guidance says an employer must make arrangements that fit the workplace and its risks, with at least a stocked kit, an appointed person and information for employees. It adds that a first aider may give initial support to someone in acute mental distress if they know how to reach professional help.
HSE's event guidance says organisers need plans for incidents in proportion to the risk, with people appointed to carry them out. It suggests working through scenarios round a table beforehand.

Health details fall under the ICO's rules on special category data. You need a lawful basis and a separate condition, you must keep to the minimum needed, and the sensitivity of the data should shape how you secure it. The ICO says consent is usually not appropriate where power is unequal, and it names employers. Its example for the vital interests condition is sharing an unconscious employee's allergy details with an ambulance crew. Ask the client's data protection lead which basis fits your event.
The log and the named lead are practitioner judgement. This is general information, not legal advice.

try.text: Run the table-top with a colleague. One of you reads a scenario aloud: "It is 23:30, someone has fallen on the steps." The other says, out loud and in order, what they do and who they call, using the sheet. Swap, and mark every point where you had to guess.

try.title: A worked example: who calls whom
lines: Life at risk: anyone calls 999 first, then the incident lead.
Incident lead: Priya, lead facilitator. Deputy: Sam, second facilitator. Numbers on every badge.
Injury or illness: fetch the venue's first aider through reception. The incident lead stays with the person.
The deputy keeps the group working or closes the session calmly.
The incident lead tells the client host. The client host contacts the person's emergency contact and their manager.
Nobody goes to hospital alone. The client host or a facilitator goes with them, and the other facilitator runs the room.
Distress without injury: one facilitator sits with the person in the quiet room, door open, and asks what they need. We listen. We do not counsel.
If the person may be at risk of harm: 999, or NHS 111 for urgent advice, and tell the client host.
A complaint about another participant: listen, write down what was said, and take it to the client host. The employer's policy applies.
Health and contact details: one sealed paper copy with the client host, one with the incident lead. Shredded when the event ends.
Log every incident the same day.

Venue first aider attended. Taxi to emergency department with client host

items: You collect a full medical questionnaire "to be safe". Ask only what you need to act on, and agree with the client who holds it.
A distressed person is left alone to "have some space". Offer the quiet room and stay nearby unless they ask you to go.
The log records opinions. Write what you saw, what was said and what you did, with times.

quiz.a: A suitably stocked first aid kit, an appointed person and information for employees about the arrangements.

quiz.q: A client suggests you email all participants a form asking for medical conditions and medication, to be returned to you. What do you propose instead?

quiz.q: At 07:30 a participant tells you he has not slept and cannot face the day. Your co-facilitator is setting up. What do you do?

topics.title: Include people who cannot or will not stay overnight
topics.theory: Inclusion and reasonable adjustments on residentials

situation.text: The invitation says attendance at the two-night offsite is "expected". One manager cares for a parent every evening. Another uses a wheelchair. A third does not want to be anywhere built round a bar. None of them has said anything yet.

items: Raise it with the sponsor before the format is fixed. Ask: "Who in this group might find two nights away difficult, and what will we offer them?"
Have the invitation come from the employer with a named, private contact, usually in HR, and a plain sentence that says adjustments are normal.
Design a day-attendance version from the start. Put all the work that leads to the outcome between 09:00 and 17:15, so someone who goes home each night misses nothing that counts.
Offer options before people have to ask: daily travel paid for, a single night, a ground-floor bedroom, a fridge for medication, a quiet room for prayer, food that meets religious and medical needs.
Talk with each person who raises a need about what would help. Do not guess from a label and do not ask for a reason beyond what is needed to arrange it.
Keep evening events free of work content and decisions. If the team's plan is settled over drinks, the people who left are shut out of it.
If someone cannot attend at all, agree with the sponsor an equivalent: the same practice in two on-site sessions with a facilitator, and a place in the follow-up.

why.text: GOV.UK says employers must make reasonable adjustments so that workers with disabilities or health conditions are not substantially disadvantaged, and lists offering training opportunities among its examples. Acas says the duty applies when the employer knows, or could be expected to know, that someone is disabled, or when the person asks. The employer should talk with the person, avoid assumptions and pay for the adjustment.

Acas describes indirect discrimination as a rule that is the same for everyone and has a worse effect on some people because of a protected characteristic such as disability, religion or belief, or sex. Working hours are among the practices it lists. Such a rule can be lawful only if the employer shows a legitimate aim and a proportionate way of reaching it. On religion, Acas gives the example of a change to break times that disadvantaged staff who used them for prayer. It also warns against leaving someone out of an event because of an assumption about alcohol and their partner's faith.

A compulsory overnight stay applies to everyone and may fall harder on some groups. Whether it is lawful in a given case is for the employer and its advisers. Your part is to see that the question is asked early and that a real alternative exists. This is general information, not legal advice.
Cost, and simply not wanting to stay, are not covered by the pages opened for this topic. Making room for both is practitioner judgement.

try.text: Say the invitation wording below aloud to a colleague as if briefing the sponsor, then ask the colleague to push back with "everyone has to come, it is a team event". Practise your reply until it is short and calm.

Venue contact knows, without the diagnosis

Does not drink, or avoids bars
Lounge with soft drinks, evening activity that is not built round alcohol
Second space is open and staffed
Attend on working days, or time off in lieu agreed by the employer

lines: "We know two nights away does not suit everyone."
"You can attend by day and go home each evening. All the work happens between nine and quarter past five."
"If anything about the venue, the dates, the food or the overnight stay would be difficult, tell Jo in HR by the 14th. You do not need to give a reason."
"Evenings are optional and nothing is decided at them."

Day attendance exists on paper and the key session is after dinner. Move the session.
The alternative is a set of slides to read. Make it practice with a facilitator, or it is not equivalent.
Dates are fixed before anyone checks religious festivals and school holidays. Check first.

quiz.a: When the employer knows, or could reasonably be expected to know, that someone is disabled, or when a disabled person asks for adjustments.

quiz.q: A sponsor says: "Attendance is compulsory. If we let one person go home at night, half of them will." What do you say?
quiz.a: That a blanket rule can disadvantage carers, disabled staff and others, and the employer would need to justify it. Suggest designing the days so that going home costs nobody the outcome, and let HR handle individual requests.

quiz.q: A participant tells you on arrival that she fasts during the day this week and will eat after sunset. Dinner is at 19:00 and sunset is at 20:10. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask her what would help, then arrange with the venue for a meal to be kept or served later and a place to eat it. Do it quietly and do not single her out in the room.
