topics.title: Work out your day rate
topics.theory: Building a rate from income, costs and sellable days

situation.text: A client asks, "What is your day rate?" You take your last salary, divide it by the working days in a year and say the answer. Six months later you are busy and short of money.

items: Write down your target income for the year: what you need to take out of the business before tax, including pension contributions.
Add up a year of business costs: insurance, accountant, software, equipment, memberships, your own training, marketing and travel you cannot recharge.
Count the days. Start with 260 weekdays. Take off holiday and bank holidays, and an allowance for illness.
Take off the days you work and cannot sell: finding and proposing work, administration and finance, your own learning, and gaps left by cancellations.
Divide the money by the days that remain. That is your floor rate for each day you sell. Below it, you are paying to do the work.

Decide what a sold day is in your market. If design and preparation are charged as separate lines, the floor applies to each of those days. If clients pay only for delivery days, count the unpaid days behind each one and raise the rate to carry them.
Check the floor against value. Ask what the result is worth to the client (9.4).

Check it against the market. Ask three people who buy or sell similar work what range they see, and note which of your own quotes were accepted. Move up from the floor when the checks allow it. Do not go below it.

why.text: The method is arithmetic and practitioner judgement. No research sits behind it.

The salary sum fails for two reasons. An employee is paid on days they do not work. GOV.UK says almost all workers are entitled to 5.6 weeks of paid holiday a year, which is 28 days on a five-day week, and that self-employed people get no holiday or sick pay. You fund those days yourself. The second reason is larger. Much of a working week in a small business goes on selling, quoting, invoicing and learning, and nobody pays for that directly.
No market rates are given here because none was checked against a source. Your floor does not depend on them.

The same sum explains an agency's rate card. An employed trainer's salary and share of overheads are spread across the days the agency can bill for them. That is why your billable days matter to an employer. Tax and VAT sit outside this sum. Ask an accountant how they apply to you.

try.text: Run the sum with your own figures. Then say your rate aloud to a colleague and stop talking. Have them reply, "That is more than we expected." Practise answering by changing the scope and leaving the rate alone. Record it.

try.title: Illustration with made-up figures: a floor day rate

head: Line
Working
Result
rows: Target income before tax, with pension
Insurance, accountant, software, equipment, training, travel
If only delivery is paid, with one unpaid day behind each

try.title: Words you can use: when the rate is challenged
lines: "That is the rate. Let us look at what is in the work and see what we can change."
"If we use your existing case studies, I can take a day out of design."
"For six cohorts booked together I can offer a lower rate from the third onwards."
"I would not remove the follow-up session. It is the part that makes the two days stick."

items: You count 220 sellable days. Almost nobody sells that many. Log where your days go for three months and use the real figure.
You forget the unpaid days behind a delivery day. Topic 9.4 says design usually takes longer than delivery. Charge for it as a line, or carry it in the rate.
You set the rate once and never revisit it. Rerun the sum each year with your logged hours and actual costs.
You quote an associate rate to a direct client. An associate fee leaves out selling and administration because the company does them. Direct work has to pay for both.
You treat these figures as typical. They are invented to show the arithmetic.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: GOV.UK, Holiday entitlement.
GOV.UK, Employment status: self-employed and contractor.

quiz.q: What do you divide by what to get a floor day rate?
quiz.a: Target income plus business costs, divided by the days you can realistically sell.

quiz.q: Your floor is £500 per sold day. A client will pay only for two delivery days, and the job needs three days of design. What do you do?
quiz.a: Price all five days, either as separate design and delivery lines or as a higher delivery rate that carries the design. Quoting two days at the floor means three days unpaid.

quiz.q: A buyer says your quote is 15% over budget. What do you do?
quiz.a: Keep the rate and change the scope: remove a line, reuse their material or agree a volume price. Keep the follow-up in, because it is what makes the programme work.

topics.title: Reshape the brief when training is the wrong answer
topics.theory: Turning a training request into work that will help

situation.text: A retailer's operations manager asks for a half-day customer service course for 200 store staff. Two store managers tell you on a call that staff know what good service looks like. The queue builds because a refund takes eleven screens on the till.

items: Find the cause before you answer the request (9.14). If you are external, use the small version: a 30-minute call with two of the people who do the job and one of their managers.
Say the cause back to the client in their own words, with what you saw or heard as evidence. "Three people told me the refund takes eleven screens."
Match the cause to a piece of work, using the table below. Most causes that training cannot fix still have work in them that a learning person does well.

Offer the reshaped brief as options (9.5). One addresses the cause. One adds a short session if skill is part of the problem. One is the original request, with a plain statement of what it will and will not change.
Price the new work properly. Diagnosis, a job aid and a manager guide are design days (9.4).
Say what lies outside your skill and who should do it. System changes, staffing and pay are the client's. Recommend, and do not pretend.

If the client still wants the original course and you believe it will not help, choose. Deliver it with the limits written down (9.6), or decline and suggest someone else. If you are employed or an associate, take it to the account lead. The decision is theirs.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement, built on the performance analysis tradition that topic 9.14 names.

Topics 1.20 and 9.14 say to be ready to decline. That is right, and it is the last move. The client has a real problem and a deadline. Walking away leaves them with both, and often with a supplier who will run the course without asking anything.

Much of what fixes a non-training cause is work a trainer already knows how to do. A job aid is a design task. A manager coaching guide is a short piece of curriculum. A change message is clear writing for a defined audience. Offering these keeps you useful and keeps the client's money pointed at the cause.

There is a risk on the other side. If every cause turns into something you sell, you have stopped diagnosing. Some rows in the table end with a recommendation and a small fee, or none. Leave them that way.

try.text: Ask a colleague to play the operations manager who wants the course. Aloud, in five minutes, play back the cause, offer two options and say what you cannot fix. Record it. Check whether you blamed anyone and whether you gave a price for the reshaped work.

"A course would cost you 200 half-days and the queue would still be there."

items: You announce the diagnosis as a correction. The client asked in good faith. Present what you heard and let them reach the conclusion.
You offer work you cannot do well. Process redesign and communications each have specialists. Bring one in or hand it over.
You do the diagnosis free and the client takes it to someone cheaper. Keep free discovery short (9.3) and price anything beyond it.
You reshape a brief that belongs to your employer's account. Tell the account lead what you found and let them take it to the client.
You never say no. Some requests should still be declined. Reshaping is the first resort, and declining remains open.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: Name two kinds of paid work, other than a course, that can address a performance problem.
quiz.a: Any two of: a job aid, a process workshop with evidence, manager coaching, communications, a written standard.

quiz.q: A sales leader wants negotiation training. Two reps tell you they give discounts because approval for anything else takes a week. What do you propose?
quiz.a: Play back the cause with the evidence, and offer a session with whoever owns approvals plus a one-page guide to what reps can agree alone. Offer the course as a second option, with its limits stated.

quiz.q: You are an associate and discover on a briefing call that the course you have been booked to deliver will not fix the client's problem. What do you do?
quiz.a: Tell the account lead at the company what you heard and what you would suggest. The client and the decision are theirs, and you deliver what they agree.

topics.title: Work inside the client's tools
topics.theory: Guest access, the client's learning platform and their security rules

situation.text: You build the programme tracker in your own workspace and send a link. The client's laptops block it. Their learning partner then asks you to record attendance in the company's learning platform, which you cannot log in to.

items: In week one, ask which collaboration suite the client uses and how suppliers get in: guest access, a client account or a client laptop. Ask who requests it and how long it takes. Start the request that day.
Use one identity, the email address they invite. Open the shared space and a file before your first meeting.
Keep the current version of every working file in the client's space. Drafts can stay with you.
Ask the platform owner how content gets on to the learning platform: who loads it, which formats it accepts and the lead time.
Treat their platform as the record of attendance and completion. Do not keep a rival register. Send attendance in the format they ask for on the day of the session.
Ask about file rules: their slide template, size limits, and whether video and outside links play on their network.

Ask the security questions before you plan activities. Can participants reach outside polling or whiteboard sites from work devices? May sessions be recorded? May you use your own laptop, or outside tools, with their material?

Test inside their environment a week ahead. Ask one participant to open the deck, play the video and join the poll from a work device. At the end, move final files to the agreed place and ask for your access to be removed (9.26).

why.text: This is practitioner judgement, with one product page for the guest access details.

Topics 9.22 and 9.23 show how to run a programme in tools you choose. A large client has already chosen. Its staff work in one suite, and its learning platform holds the official record of who completed what. A second attendance list creates two versions of the truth and a data protection question (9.24).

Guest access takes time. Microsoft's documentation for Teams is one example. A guest is someone outside the organisation who is given access to teams, channel files, chats and meetings. The client's administrators switch guest access on or off for the whole organisation. A guest account is created in the client's directory, and access can take up to 12 hours to appear after you are added. Leaving a team does not delete the account. An administrator has to remove it. Other suites have their own rules, which were not checked for this page.
The security questions come first because they change the design. An activity built round an outside whiteboard fails in a company that blocks it.

try.text: Take a session you have already built. Assume the client blocks every outside site and accepts only its own slide template. Rework one activity so it runs with what is left, then run that activity aloud with a colleague as participant.

try.title: Week one questions about the client's tools
lines: Which suite do you use for chat, files and meetings?
How do suppliers get access, who requests it and how long does it take?
Where should programme files live, and who else can see that space?
Who owns the learning platform, and who loads content?
Which file formats does the platform accept, and what is the lead time?
How is attendance recorded, by whom, and by when do you need it?
Is there a slide template, and which software version do people use?
Do video and outside links play on your network?
Can participants use outside polling or whiteboard sites on work devices?
May sessions be recorded, and where are recordings kept?
May I use my own laptop? Which tools are not allowed with your material?
What happens to my access and the files when the programme ends?

Client's shared team space, then the platform
None. You send a list the same day.

items: You ask for access the week before delivery. Ask on day one.
You email files to a personal address or carry them on a memory stick to get round a block. Ask for the approved route.
You keep your own copy of the attendance list "just in case". It is personal data you no longer need. Send it, confirm it arrived and delete it.
You assume the room has the internet your activity needs. Test from a work device on the client's network.
You leave guest accounts open after the programme. Ask the client to remove them and note the date in your close-out.

topics.title: Deliver someone else's design
topics.theory: Delivering to a brief you did not write

situation.text: The agency sends you 140 slides and a facilitator guide on Thursday. On Tuesday you deliver it to a client's sales team. You did not design the day and you have never met the client.

items: Before you say yes, ask the questions in the list below.
Ask for the full pack five working days ahead: facilitator guide, slides, participant materials, the timed plan and the original brief. Ask for 30 minutes with the designer.
Read for intent first. Beside each block write one line: what people should be able to do after it. Where you cannot, you have a question for the designer.

Sort the day into fixed and flexible. Fixed, unless you are told otherwise: the objectives, any assessed activity, the client's product facts and policy wording, the branding, and timings shared with another room. Flexible: your own stories, how you form groups, your wording of instructions and the order of your debrief questions.
Rehearse aloud the three parts most likely to go wrong: the first ten minutes, the hardest activity to set up and the section you understand least.
If you see a problem in the design, raise it before the day, in writing, with whoever owns the design. State the problem, the risk and one fix that fits the same time. Then deliver what they decide.
If something fails on the day, make the smallest change that protects the objective. Note the time and what you did.
Within 24 hours send a one-page delivery report: what ran to time, what you changed and why, questions the materials could not answer, and anything the client said about future work.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. No study tests it. The design carries promises you were not there to hear. Somebody agreed the objectives with the client, and the assessed activities are often what the client paid for, so those parts are fixed. Your stories and your way with a group are yours.
Topic 9.20 tells the hirer to brief the reasons behind the design. From the other chair, you ask for them. A facilitator who knows what an activity is for can shorten it well when the room runs late.

Peter Block describes three roles a consultant can take: expert, pair of hands and collaborator. Delivering another person's design starts as pair of hands. Raising a problem early, with a fix, moves you towards collaborator. Raising it on the day does the opposite. Nobody can approve a change at 09:15, and the client sees a supplier arguing with itself.

try.text: Take a session plan someone else wrote. Mark each block fixed or flexible. Then deliver the opening and the first activity set-up aloud to a colleague, in your own words. Ask them what the objective was. If they cannot say, you changed more than the wording.

try.title: Questions to ask before you accept the booking
lines: Who is the end client, and who is my contact on the day?
What should people be able to do by the end, and how will anyone know?
Who is in the room: roles, how many, how long in the job, and what were they told about why they are coming?
Has this design run before? What happened, and what was changed afterwards?
When do I get the full pack, and can I speak to the designer?
What may I adapt, and what must stay exactly as written?
Who do I tell if I see a problem with the design, and by what date?
Is preparation time paid, and how much is expected?
Room or platform, equipment, co-facilitator or producer: who provides each and who sets up?
Will senior people or the client's learning team be in the room?
What gets reported afterwards about the session, and about individuals?
What do I say if someone asks me about further work?

try.title: Words you can use: raising a design problem before the day
lines: "I have been through the pack for Tuesday and I have one concern and a suggestion."
"The role-play at 11:15 gives each pair eight minutes. With 16 people and one of me, I can observe two pairs at most."
"The risk is that most people practise the call with nobody watching and repeat their old habits."
"Could we run it in threes with an observer using the checklist on page 12? It fits the same 40 minutes."
"If you would rather keep pairs, I will run it as written. Could you let me know by Friday noon?"

items: You rewrite the day because you would have designed it differently. If the objective is not at risk, deliver it as written and put your idea in the report.
The pack arrives the night before. Tell the agency that evening which sections you can deliver as designed and which you will simplify.
You distance yourself in the room with a line such as "I did not write this slide". Present the content as yours for the day.
You improve the client's product facts or policy wording. Deliver them exactly and report any that looked wrong.
You send no report. The designer's only view of the room is yours, and agencies rebook the people who make the next run better.

quiz.a: Protect the assessed practice and shorten something flexible, such as a discussion or an energy break. Note the time and the change, and put it in your report the same day.

topics.title: Work as an associate
topics.theory: Associate terms: bookings, day rates and whose client it is

situation.text: A training company emails: "Are you free on the 14th and 15th? Software firm, new managers, our design, usual day rate." You have never seen their associate agreement and you do not know what the usual rate covers.

items: Ask for the associate agreement before the first booking and read it while no date depends on it.

Know which of three states a booking is in. An enquiry asks if you are free. A provisional hold, often called a pencil, reserves the date with no commitment. A confirmed booking is in writing with dates, place and fee. Give every hold a release time.
Ask what the day rate includes, line by line. Use the table below. Anything nobody mentions is unpaid.
Agree expenses before you travel: what is repaid, any limits, and who books.
Read cancellation in both directions: what you are paid if the client cancels late, and what notice you must give to withdraw.

Read the clauses about the client. Expect to represent the company's brand, to pass on every enquiry about further work, and not to approach its clients for a period. Check how long, and which clients.
Check the materials clause. Their materials stay theirs. If you bring a handout of your own, say in writing beforehand that it stays yours.
Ask how you get paid: when to invoice, what reference to quote, and whether you are paid on fixed terms or only once the client has paid the company. Invoice the day after delivery.

why.text: Most of this is practitioner judgement. The tax and payment points come from GOV.UK.

Associate work is a trade. The company finds the client, wins the work and carries the risk. You accept a lower fee than you would charge direct, and the client stays theirs. Non-solicitation clauses protect what the company spent to win that client. Topic 9.20 covers the same arrangement from the hirer's side.
A day rate means little until you know how many unpaid days sit behind it. Divide the fee by every day the booking takes and compare the answer with your floor (see "Work out your day rate").

GOV.UK says self-employed people get no holiday or sick pay and have the rights their contract with the client gives them. So the agreement is your protection. If you work through your own limited company, the off-payroll working rules (IR35) may apply. GOV.UK says the client decides your employment status for tax where it is in the public sector or is a medium or large private business. Where the client is small and outside the public sector, your own company decides. Agencies in the chain have responsibilities whatever their size. If the rules apply, tax and National Insurance are deducted from the fee before it reaches your company. This is general information, not legal advice.

try.text: Ask a colleague to play the company's resourcing manager. Aloud, in three minutes, ask what the rate includes, when the hold is released and how you get paid. Record it and listen for apologies.

try.title: What the day rate covers: ask line by line

head: Item
Question to ask
Answers you will hear
rows: How much is expected, and is it paid?
Included in the rate. A half-day fee for a first delivery. Nothing.
How long, and is it paid?
Usually unpaid if under an hour.
Is attendance required, and at what fee?
A reduced rate, the full rate, or unpaid.
Is long travel or an overnight stay paid?
Expenses only. A travel fee over a set number of hours.
What time must I be on site, and who sets the room?
Included. Ask for the arrival time in writing.
Are marking, reports or follow-up calls expected?
A short report is included. Marking is charged by the hour.
What am I paid, and from how many days out?
A sliding share of the fee. Nothing unless the company is paid.
What is repaid, and what are the limits?
Standard class rail, a hotel cap, mileage at a set rate.

try.title: Words you can use
lines: On a hold: "Happy to pencil those in. I will hold them until Friday at five and release them if I have not heard."
On the rate: "Before I confirm, can you tell me what the rate covers? I am thinking of preparation, the briefing call and travel."
On payment: "When should I invoice, and what reference do you need on it?"
When a participant asks if you run courses yourself: "I am here with the team at the company today, so they are the right people to ask. I will pass your name on this afternoon."

items: A pencil with no release date. You turn down paid work for a hold that quietly lapses.
The client asks you to work for them direct. Name your contact at the company and pass it on the same day. Taking it may break your agreement.
Paid when paid. Ask for fixed terms. GOV.UK says that where no date is agreed, a business payment is late 30 days after the invoice or the service, whichever is later.
Blurring the brands. Showing your own logo, or connecting with participants from your business profile, may breach the agreement. Ask.

topics.title: Know your contract before you build your own thing
topics.theory: Employment terms on intellectual property, outside interests and restrictions after leaving

situation.text: You work for a training company. In the evenings you are building a website, a set of templates and a plan for a business of your own. Nobody at work knows yet.

items: Gather the documents: your employment contract, any letters that changed it, the staff handbook and the policies on intellectual property, conflicts of interest and company equipment.
Find the intellectual property clause. Note what it claims. Some cover only work done as part of your job. Others reach anything connected with the employer's business.
Find the clause on outside interests, which may be headed exclusivity or conflicts of interest. Note whether you need written consent before you start a business or take other paid work.
Find the confidentiality clause. Note what it covers and whether it continues after you leave.
Find the restrictions after leaving. For each one write down how long it lasts, which clients or colleagues it covers and any area it names.
Keep the two bodies of work apart from today. Use your own laptop, accounts and time. Keep dated records of what you made. Copy nothing from your employer or its clients, even as a starting point.
Tell your manager about the second business early and in writing. Ask for a written reply that says what is agreed, including who owns any named piece of work.
Take advice from an employment solicitor before you rely on your own reading or sign anything new.

why.text: This is general information, not legal advice.

The Intellectual Property Office says the person who creates a work is usually the first owner of the copyright. The exception is work an employee creates in the course of employment. There the employer is the first owner, unless an agreement says otherwise. The Act does not define "in the course of employment". The page says courts have asked whether the person worked under a contract of service, as an employee, or a contract for services, as a freelancer. It does not say where the line falls for something you make at home that is close to your day job. That depends on your contract and the facts, which is why you take advice.

Acas says an employer may include terms that limit what you do. An exclusivity clause stops you working for another employer, or requires consent first. Restrictive covenants apply after you leave. Acas lists four kinds: not competing, not disclosing confidential information, not encouraging colleagues to leave with you, and not trying to win the former employer's clients. It says an employer usually cannot enforce these unless they are clear, specific and limited in time, and it calls this area of law complex.
Telling your manager early is practitioner judgement. No rule on these pages requires it. A side business found out later costs more trust than one that was declared.

try.text: Read your own contract with the sheet below beside you. Fill one row per clause in your own words. The questions are what you take to the solicitor.

items: You assume evening work is automatically yours. The official page gives the default and does not settle your case. The contract may reach further. Read it and ask.
You draft your own materials on the work laptop or in work accounts. Move nothing across in either direction.
You reuse a client example or an activity you built at work. Rebuild from your own sources or leave it out.
You rely on a spoken "that is fine". Managers move on. Get it in an email.
You sign a new contract or a promotion letter without rereading these clauses. Terms often change at that moment.

topics.title: Know the client's learning function
topics.theory: Who sits in and around a large client's learning team

situation.text: The sales director who wants the programme says, "Just send me the proposal." Two weeks later an email arrives from a learning partner you have never heard of. She asks why she found out about the programme from procurement.

items: In the first conversation with any sponsor, ask two questions: "Who in your learning team should know about this?" and "How does a new supplier get set up here?"
Draw the stakeholder map in the first week. Use the table below. Put one name against each role, or write "not known yet" and find out.
Meet the learning team early and come with questions. What already exists on this subject? Which models and terms do people here already use? What else is on the calendar for this audience?
Ask how their year runs: when budgets are set, when the plan is fixed, and which weeks are closed to training. For a sales team that is often quarter end. For store staff it is peak trading.
Ask what the head of learning reports upward, and shape your own reporting to feed it.
Agree in writing who does what. Cover bookings, messages to participants, loading content to the platform, attendance records and contact with line managers.
Send the sponsor and the learning team the same one-page update on the same day (9.21). Neither should hear news from the other.

why.text: This is practitioner knowledge of how large organisations tend to be arranged. Titles and structures vary, so treat the table as questions to ask.

Topic 9.1 separates the buyer, the sponsor and the learner. In a large company the buyer is itself several people. A head of learning sets priorities and answers for the budget. Learning partners each look after one part of the business and are the usual way in. Specialists design and run programmes. Somebody owns the learning platform. Beside the team sit HR business partners, who know the managers and the people issues, and procurement, IT and security, who decide whether you can be paid and what you can connect to.

Each of them is judged on something different. The sponsor wants a result in their team. The head of learning has to defend spend and avoid duplication. Procurement wants a compliant supplier at a fair price. Security wants no new risk. A proposal that pleases the sponsor and ignores the rest stalls for reasons the sponsor cannot see.

Going round the learning team is the usual way suppliers lose their place. You duplicate what exists, you use different words for the same idea, and you ask for things only the learning team can give. Meeting them first costs an hour.

try.text: Fill in the map for a client or employer you know. Then say aloud, to a colleague, your one-minute introduction to a learning partner who feels bypassed. Record it and check that you asked more than you told.

items: The sponsor tells you not to bother the learning team. Say you will keep it light, and tell them anyway. They control the platform, the calendar and often the purchase order.
You bring your own model for something the client already has a model for. Ask first and use their words.
You ask the learning team for access to line managers as if they could grant it. Often they cannot. Ask who can, which is usually the sponsor or the HR partner.
You map the roles once and never update it. People move. Check the names at every service review.

quiz.q: Name four roles in or beside a large client's learning function, other than the sponsor.
quiz.a: Any four of: head of learning, learning partner, HR business partner, procurement, IT and security, platform owner.

quiz.q: A business sponsor says, "Do not involve the learning team, they slow everything down." What do you do?
quiz.a: Say you will keep their involvement short, and still tell the learning partner what is planned. They control the platform, the calendar and often the purchase order, and they will find out anyway.

quiz.q: In week one you learn the client already teaches a feedback model different from the one in your design. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask the learning team which model people use and rebuild your activity round theirs. Two models for one skill confuse learners and set you against the internal team.

topics.title: Understand how large organisations buy
topics.theory: Supplier onboarding, tenders, contracts and purchase orders

situation.text: A technology company's enablement lead says yes on a call in March. The first session runs in June. The weeks between went on forms, a security questionnaire, a contract and a purchase order.

items: At the first sign of interest ask: "Are we already set up as a supplier? If not, what does it involve and how long does it usually take?"
Prepare for supplier onboarding. Expect a form asking for company and bank details, insurance certificates and policies on data protection, security and equality. Keep current copies in one folder.

If the work goes to tender, read the scoring before the questions. Note the criteria, the weight on each, the word limits and the deadline for clarification questions. Answer under their headings, in their order.

Learn the two contract documents. A master agreement sets the general terms once: ownership of materials, confidentiality, liability, data and payment. A statement of work then describes each job: what is delivered, dates, named people and price.
Read the ownership clause against topic 9.9. Large clients often expect to own what they pay for. Ask to keep the material you brought with you and license it to them.
Answer the security and data questionnaire truthfully and briefly. "Not applicable, we hold none of your data" is a complete answer.
Get the purchase order number before any work starts. Put it on every invoice and send the invoice where the order says.
Read the payment terms and plan your cash for the gap. Put every buying step on the programme plan with a date (9.18).

why.text: The steps above describe common practice, and each organisation has its own version. A large organisation separates the person who wants something from the people who commit money and accept risk. For you that means time. The sponsor's yes begins a second process.

For UK public bodies the position is set by the Procurement Act 2023, whose rules took effect on 24 February 2025. The government's guide for suppliers says you register free on the central digital platform, Find a Tender, and store your business details once for reuse across bids. Official guidance says a public contract is awarded to the most advantageous tender, meaning the best tender when assessed against the published award criteria and assessment method. The authority must set out the criteria and their relative importance. Awarding on price alone is possible, and the guidance says it is unlikely to suit most contracts. Suppliers whose tenders were assessed receive an assessment summary. The supplier guide also says 30-day payment terms will reach more public sector contracts. This is general information, not legal advice.

Private companies set their own rules. GOV.UK publishes reports from large businesses showing the average time they take to pay suppliers and the share of payments made late. On security, some buyers ask suppliers to hold Cyber Essentials, which the National Cyber Security Centre describes as a government certification scheme against common cyber attacks.

try.text: Pick one large organisation you would like to work for. Look up its payment report on GOV.UK. Then build your onboarding folder: insurance certificates, policies and a one-page company summary.

quiz.a: The master agreement sets the general terms once. A statement of work describes one piece of work under it: what is delivered, dates, people and price.

quiz.q: A sponsor says, "Procurement will catch up, can you start design on Monday?" What do you do?

topics.title: Look after an account
topics.theory: Service reviews, changes of sponsor, budget freezes and renewals

situation.text: The programme is in month four of nine. Your sponsor emails to say she is moving to another division and her successor will be in touch. In the same week the client's finance team freezes discretionary spending.

items: Hold a service review on a fixed rhythm: monthly for the first three months, then quarterly. Keep it to 45 minutes and use the same agenda each time.
Bring evidence. Show what ran, who attended, what participants and managers reported, what is off track and what you propose to change (9.21).
When a sponsor leaves, ask them for two things before they go: a call with you and the successor, and a short written note of what was agreed and why.
Meet the new sponsor within two weeks. Start with their priorities. Then confirm the success measures in writing again (9.6), because they did not agree the first set.

When a freeze lands, do not argue with it. Read your contract's pause and cancellation terms first. Then offer options in writing: pause with dates held, cut to the part tied most closely to the business result, spread the remaining sessions over a longer period, or stop cleanly with a handover (9.26).

Where other suppliers or an internal team work with the same people, agree who owns what, share your calendar and use the terms the client already uses. If two programmes teach clashing models, take it to the learning team with a proposal.

Start the renewal conversation three months before the end. Ask what the sponsor would need to see to continue. Bring results against the agreed measures, and one recommendation that makes the work smaller somewhere.
Write a short account note after every meeting, so that a colleague could take over tomorrow.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. It rests on experience of client work and no research was found that tests it.

Programmes are seldom lost in the classroom. They end when the person who wanted them leaves, when money tightens, or when the supplier has become hard work. A regular review gives small problems somewhere to go before they grow. It also means a successor finds a record.

A new sponsor did not choose you. They inherit a cost they will be asked to defend, and they have plans of their own. Opening with your history asks them to honour someone else's decision. Opening with their priorities lets them make it theirs.

A freeze is rarely about you. Offering options keeps you in the conversation and shows you can tell which parts of the programme matter most. Recommending less work now and then has the same effect at renewal. The client learns that your advice is not always an invoice.

try.text: Ask a colleague to play a new sponsor who has inherited your programme and is unsure about it. Run the first ten minutes of that call aloud. Record it and count how many minutes passed before you asked about their priorities.

try.title: Words you can use
lines: To a new sponsor: "Before I tell you anything about the programme, what are you being asked to deliver this year?"
"Here is one page on what was agreed and what has happened so far. Tell me what no longer fits."
On a freeze: "Understood. I do not want to add to the pressure. Can I send you four options by Thursday, from a pause to a clean stop?"
"If only one part carries on, I would keep the manager sessions. They are the part tied to the result you named."
On another supplier's model: "Your leadership course uses a different feedback model. I suggest we adopt theirs so people hear one thing."

items: You have one relationship. When that person leaves, so does the account. Keep at least two, and make one of them the learning team.
A review that reports only good news. The first hidden problem that surfaces costs you the client's belief in every earlier report.
You treat a pause as a cancellation and send the invoice. Check the contract, then talk. A client who is helped through a freeze usually comes back.
You criticise another supplier to the client. It reads as selling. Raise a clash as a problem for learners and offer a fix.
You leave renewal to the last month. Budgets are set earlier than that (9.1).

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: How long before the end of a programme should the renewal conversation start?
quiz.a: About three months.

quiz.q: Your sponsor is leaving in two weeks. What do you ask her for?
quiz.a: A call with you and her successor, and a short written note of what was agreed and why. Then meet the successor within two weeks and confirm the success measures again.

quiz.q: Finance freezes spending halfway through a programme. The sponsor sounds embarrassed. What do you do?
quiz.a: Check your pause and cancellation terms, then send written options from a pause to a clean stop, and say which part you would keep. Options keep you part of the decision.
